In particular, she said the Trump administration must stop enforcing any notices to terminate immigration statuses issued between the date the most recent policy went into effect on Oct. 14, to Oct 27, the date of this decision.
… Defendants are prohibited from terminating those individuals’ refugee status based on failure to respond to any notice to respond issued during that time,” she wrote.
The resettlement groups and several impacted refugees sued to stop the Trump administration from using three policies to stop refugees from obtaining green cards, re-assessing their status with new court hearings and speeding up the process of ending their legal immigration status.
Two of the Massachusetts refugee organizations that GBH News spoke to on Monday represented at least 2,000 impacted individuals.
text:
A federal judge has issued a temporary pause on the Trump administration accelerating refugee status revocations. Federal immigration authorities tried to cut the amount of time that refugees have to contest decisions issued to remove their legal status from 30 days to 10.

District of Massachusetts Judge Julia Kobick enjoined the federal government on Tuesday. In particular, she said the Trump administration must stop enforcing any notices to terminate immigration statuses issued between the date the most recent policy went into effect on Oct. 14, to Oct 27, the date of this decision.

“The individuals to whom such notices to terminate were issued shall not be required to respond. … Defendants are prohibited from terminating those individuals’ refugee status based on failure to respond to any notice to respond issued during that time,” she wrote.

The lawsuit was filed on Monday in the Boston federal court. The resettlement groups and several impacted refugees sued to stop the Trump administration from using three policies to stop refugees from obtaining green cards, re-assessing their status with new court hearings and speeding up the process of ending their legal immigration status. The final one has been enjoined.

The 30-day response period has been the norm for more than four decades.

“This temporary ruling provides immediate relief to thousands of refugees across the country,” said Jeff Thielman, executive director of International Institute of New England, one of the plaintiffs.

“We are seeking to permanently invalidate the rule, alongside two other policies that indefinitely freeze green card applications and subject lawfully admitted refugees to mass re-vetting,” he said.

The impact of these policies has resulted in people being blocked on their path to citizenship after years in the U.S. despite extensive, years-long vetting. It has also caused termination of work authorization. People put into removal proceedings face indefinite detention and deportation.

“This lawsuit is yet another frivolous attempt to disrupt the Trump administration’s commitment to enforce our country’s immigration laws as intended by Congress,” said U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesman Zach Kahler. The agency is one of the defendants, along with its larger organization, the Department of Homeland Security.

“U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services found an alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures under the Biden Administration in order to rush processing and maximize the number of refugees admitted to the United States,” he said.

Two of the Massachusetts refugee organizations that GBH News spoke to on Monday represented at least 2,000 impacted individuals. According to the federal government’s own figures, about 113,000 refugees have pending applications for permanent residency, and the new termination rule could affect as many as 186,000 refugee cases.

text:
The Supreme Court, with no noted dissents, has allowed an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice ending a Biden-era immigration rule to go into effect.

The Biden administration adopted the rule in 2024, formally establishing procedures for immigration judges to temporarily pause certain deportation proceedings through a practice known as "administrative closure," including when migrants were pursuing immigration relief through other federal proceedings. The Supreme Court's move leaves in place a lower court ruling eliminating that rule, stripping away a procedure that allowed certain deportation cases to be put on hold.

Texas sued the federal government in June, arguing that the rule was adopted without proper legal authority.

The Department of Justice agreed with Texas, asking the judge overseeing the case to vacate the rule and prevent similar rules from being adopted in the future.

JUDGE WHO APOLOGIZED TO ACCUSED WOULD-BE TRUMP ASSASSIN LIGHTS UP DOJ IN HUNTER BIDEN FBI CASE

Opponents accused Texas and the Justice Department of colluding to eliminate the Biden-era rule, arguing that the two sides worked together despite being on opposite sides of the lawsuit.

On the same day the DOJ made its request, District Judge Reed O’Connor, an appointee of President George W. Bush, granted it.

TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE SLAMS DOOR ON DOJ AS COURT LOSSES PILE UP DAYS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS'

In August, however, three cities with large immigrant populations — Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio — joined with Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal advocacy group, in an effort to intervene in the case and defend the Biden-era rule on appeal.

The cities argued that eliminating the rule could lead to residents being deported, reducing their tax revenues and giving them legal standing to challenge the agreement. O’Connor rejected that argument.

On Oct. 9, the three cities and Centro Legal de la Raza asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block the lower court's judgment while their appeal proceeded, accusing Texas and the federal government of engaging in "egregious collusion" to eliminate the Biden-era rule.

Republican Rep. Andrew Garbarino and Democratic challenger Pat Halpin are offering voters sharply different visions as they compete for a South Shore congressional seat less than a week before Election Day.

Garbarino, of Bayport, currently serves as chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, a position that has placed him at the forefront of debates over immigration and national security. Despite the high-profile role, Garbarino says his focus remains on Long Island.

"When I go to Congress, I make sure I'm Long Island first," Garbarino said.

The Congressman points to several accomplishments he says have benefited residents.

"The SALT deduction increase, fully funding the 9/11 World Trade Center Health Program, returning over 2 billion dollars to New York state that was being held up by FEMA," Garbarino said.

His opponent, former Suffolk County Executive and former state Assemblyman Pat Halpin of Oak Beach, says concerns about the nation's direction prompted him to return to politics after years away from elected office.

"I'm running for Congress because I've got two adult daughters, a granddaughter, what kind of country are they going to have?" Halpin said.

Halpin said frustration with President Donald Trump's administration and congressional Republicans motivated his campaign.

"The Republican Party that I have always worked with as county executive, as a state assemblyman, that party is gone. It's now the MAGA party," Halpin said.

The Democrat also links affordability concerns to the ongoing war in Iran and argues Congress, and Garbarino, should have done more to stop it.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS — A former federal immigration judge says Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., who is under investigation, could face both criminal charges and denaturalization.

There are two federal probes ongoing into the congresswoman — the first into alleged immigration fraud and the second involving her financial disclosures and a sharp discrepancy reported just one year apart.

"If somebody who's a naturalized citizen — which I believe Ilhan Omar is — is convicted of a crime, that doesn't automatically mean that they face denaturalization or anything like that," Nathan Hansen, an attorney of 23 years, told Fox News Digital. "They would be handled by any type of other normal punishment that would come from the court."

Hansen was appointed by former Attorney General Pam Bondi to serve as an immigration judge earlier this year. He served in the role for four months.

GREGG JARRETT: ILHAN OMAR COULD FACE INDICTMENT, DENATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION

Denaturalization proceedings are separate from any criminal case that could arise from the federal investigation into Omar, whose "real name," according to sources familiar with the investigation, is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Omar is under investigation for alleged immigration fraud related to the way she or her late father filled out her citizenship paperwork.

"A denaturalization proceeding, or somebody to strip somebody of their naturalization, is another proceeding, which would be a civil proceeding brought by the Department of Justice, presumably maybe on behalf of the Department for Homeland Security, who handles most of these things," said Hansen.

HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN

"If there was some sort of nexus between the criminal conviction and somebody's citizenship, it might be more likely that the Department of Justice would bring a denaturalization proceeding," Hansen continued. "But I think it would be a discretionary matter within the people who are running the Justice Department."

Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the principal investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), in the early morning hours of Oct. 12.

During the raid, investigators reportedly seized the congresswoman's phone, passport and computer. Fox News later confirmed that authorities are in possession of her DNA.

Regarding the case, observers have speculated that if indeed Omar has broken the law, statutes of limitations could hinder a prosecution. Hansen has seen those claims but doesn't believe them to be valid.

"My view of that is generally that fraud stops any statute of limitations. In other words, if something isn't disclosed or something's hidden, then it would be unfair to the other party to toll a statute of limitations against them," said Hansen. "That's just sort of a general principle of law."

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

Asked about the prevalence of immigration fraud in general, Hansen pointed to the sheer number of pending immigration and removal cases across the country and in Minnesota.

"I think I would take it from a 30,000-foot view of just the amount of cases that the United States is facing right now of people coming here," he said. "It's got to be in the tens of millions of people coming here, I think, but certainly millions."

He said that in Minnesota alone, there are 20,000 to 30,000 removal cases pending that do not have a scheduled court date, due to a massive backlog of immigration-related cases.

"Whether you want to call it fraud or whatever, it's like an overwhelming of the system and the system is not being used in the way in which it was intended," he explained.

Bogus asylum claims are also contributing to the backlog, Hansen explained.

ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS

"Asylum relief has to do with protected grounds," he said. "The most common ones are that, 'I was persecuted at the acquiescence or directly at the behest at the government I am fleeing from based upon my race, my religion, my ethnicity [or] my political views.' These are common claims."

Hansen said that during the time when he was an immigration judge, he frequently saw claims that "just totally didn't add up," or documents provided by the applicant were "clearly fake."

"I mean, people would — I've seen cases where people would say, 'Well, people insulted me in my country.' text:
MEXICALI, Mexico — As the smell of manure from California’s Imperial Valley wafted across the border into this sprawling Mexican industrial city, Luis Arreguin glanced up at a burnt-orange cathedral in the downtown square.

It was the first time he’d seen it since he left Mexico as a child, decades ago.

Arreguin, 54, had called a small community near Fresno home since he was 5.

But on Oct. 1, federal immigration agents pulled him over on his way to work. He was among the first of about 130 people who advocates say were taken into custody during the opening days of the Trump administration’s latest immigration enforcement surge in the San Joaquin Valley.

“My whole life got destroyed,” said Arreguin, who is married and has four children.

The skilled laborer’s rapid removal to Mexico shows how fast Trump’s deportation machinery is moving, almost dizzying in its efficiency. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement removed more than 356,000 people in the first nine and a half months of the 2026 fiscal year, which began Oct. 1, 2025, according to agency data. That surpasses the roughly 320,000 removals it carried out in all of fiscal year 2025.

The expanded enforcement that caught Arreguin later spread to the rest of California, and became known as “Operation Safe California.”

Arreguin spent just 15 days in federal custody before agents put him on a jam-packed deportation flight to Tapachula in southern Chiapas, near Mexico’s southern border with Guatemala. From there, he took buses back up to the country’s northern border where his daughter rented him a motel room in Mexicali.

“I had a five-bedroom house (in Fresno.) I don’t have nothing now,” he said.

Once a launchpad for people headed north, Mexicali is now an island for outcasts, as close as the deported may ever be again to their families and car payments and mortgages in the United States.

Located just across the border from the solar farms and alfalfa fields in Imperial County, Mexicali is known for exquisite Chinese food and being the state capital of Baja California. But many residents here also struggle with poverty and crime.

People shower with hoses in the public park. One day last week, criminals left a narcomanta at a public kindergarten warning Baja California officials not to cooperate with “Los Rusos,” a faction of the Sinaloa cartel.

Arreguin doesn’t know what he’s going to do. Mexico is a country he doesn’t know. He understands Spanish, if it’s spoken slowly enough, but he doesn’t speak it.

“Poquito,” he says, apologizing to people passing him on the sidewalk in front of the church. “I don’t mean to disrespect the people.”

Last week, his wife visited from Fresno, a seven-and-a-half-hour drive away. In 31 years of marriage, he said, they had never spent a night apart until his arrest.

“She said, ‘I’m gonna cry the whole way down.’ I said, “Well, I’m gonna cry too,” you know. We try not to think about it. We’re just trying to make the best of the days we have with each other,” Arreguin said, his voice cracking.

‘I’ve been watching you’

Arreguin still doesn’t know why he was targeted. The ICE agent who stopped him on his way to work near Fresno told him, “I’ve been watching you.”

But Arreguin is not sure he believes he was under surveillance. That same morning, agents swept the small farmworker town where the family lived, emptying the streets.

“My whole community works in the fields. They did a sweep on my little town, and my wife called me and said, “It’s empty, babe. It’s empty,” he said.

He said he’s had no recent interactions with law enforcement. A public records search returned no recent criminal history.

“I’m a father. You kidnapped me in the morning and took me from my kids,” he said.

After his arrest, he was held at an ICE office in Fresno and then transferred to Bakersfield. He said he was taken back and forth while his blood pressure climbed until he eventually ended up spending about seven hours in an emergency room in Bakersfield.

“They asked me, ‘Are you afraid to go back to your country?’ And I said yes, and I figured that was going to hold everything and at least give me a chance in court,” he said.

After several days, agents transferred him to Camp East Montana on the outskirts of El Paso.

“I didn’t know where I was going,” he said.

The facility has been a focal point for lawsuits from civil rights organizations and detainees, who have complained about harsh conditions, including not getting enough to eat and insufficient medical care. In September 2025, ICE’s own internal watchdogs found dozens of violations, the Washington Post reported.

Arreguin spent five days there before he says his phone communication was cut off and he was put on the plane to southern Mexico.

“At least I am safe here, and I’m not behind the walls of a detention center where I could die,” he said.

Crowded deportation flight

Arreguin said his flight carried roughly 300 fellow deportados, all shackled and chained at the wrists and ankles. He counted 22 women and one minor.

“They shackled a 14-year-old kid,” he said.

Arreguin described agents restricting people’s access to the bathroom and water during their 36 hours of travel.

Meanwhile, officers taunted him: “Oh, look, it’s the famous Mr. Arreguin,” they said, holding up their phones with news stories about his arrest and social media videos his daughter made to draw attention to his case.

Just before they deplaned, he said, agents hurried down the aisles, removing shackles. He interpreted it as an effort to keep Mexican officials from seeing how they had been transported.

“A lot of people are afraid to even say anything about how they were treated,” he said.

ICE did not respond to CalMatters questions about the flight or the conditions Arreguin described.

Others on the flight who spoke to CalMatters on condition of anonymity corroborated the details Luis gave. ICE has a long-standing operational policy that mandates passengers in custody are shackled with handcuffs, waist chains and ankle restraints during flights, including during layovers and refueling stops.

One detail the former Central Valley resident said he’ll never forget: “Everybody on that plane had their work clothes on. Every single one of them.”

Changing Mexico deportation strategy

Since this spring, the administration has largely stopped sending Mexican nationals back across the land border. Instead, it’s flying them deeper into Mexico, where officials believe deportees dropped near the Guatemala border are less likely to try to cross back into the United States.

In Tapachula, Mexican officials fed Arreguin and gave him a debit card loaded with 2,500 pesos, about the equivalent of $130. “They didn’t have to give me that,” he said. It got him as far north as Mexico City. His adult daughter paid for the rest of the trip to Mexicali, where, as a teenager, Luis was able to cross the border freely with his Fresno church group.

The border city is receiving fewer deportees now than it has in the past decade. In 2024, U.S. authorities returned more than 43,000 Mexicans through Baja California crossings at Tijuana and Mexicali, about one in five of all repatriations nationwide, according to Mexico’s Interior Ministry.

In the first seven months of 2026, just 1,567 people came through the Mexicali crossing, less than 2% of the national total. The numbers fell as the Trump administration shifted to flying Mexican deportees farther south to Tapachula and Villahermosa, which together took 48,000 people over the same time period, nearly half of all returns.

Those figures don’t include people who were removed to Tapachula and then made their own way north again, like Arreguin.

“You know you can’t just take people away from their family,” he said.

What now?

“Don’t cry,” Luis tells his oldest daughter, holding his phone outstretched in front of him to FaceTime her in front of the Cathedral of Mexicali in Baja California.

In Fresno, Luis’ wife is packing up their house to move. The family doesn’t have the money to stay without Luis paying rent as the family’s main breadwinner. His two youngest children, 6 and 10, will have to change schools.

“I’m tired of crying,” he says. “It takes a lot out of me when I’m speaking about what I had to go through and what I’m going through and how I was treated,” he said.

But, he’s working on finding a lawyer to help fight his deportation and return to his family.

“I have to fight,” he said.

Until then, his daughter is paying for his motel and food. She is maxing out her credit cards. She is looking for a place in Mexicali big enough for the whole family to visit him for Thanksgiving.

For decades, Arreguin worked to give his children a better life in the United States. Now his daughter Elaina is trying to make him comfortable in Mexico.

You’ve supported me for years, she told him. “Now I can do that for you.”

CalMatters photojournalist Larry Valenzuela contributed to this report.

text:
A pair of California congressmembers are mounting resistance to the Trump administration after reports of a proposal to use ships — including a maritime training vessel at Mare Island — for deportation voyages.

In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday, Democratic Reps. John Garamendi, who represents Solano County, and Salud Carbajal, of Santa Barbara, said the plan “is outrageous and should be immediately discarded.”

Garamendi is a senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, and his district includes the Cal Poly Maritime Academy in Vallejo, where the 500-foot Golden Bear has served as a training ship for mariners over three decades. He told KQED that deportation journeys by ship could take many days, as opposed to hours on an airplane, and would be costly and inhumane.

“An airplane is expensive enough. A ship is several times more expensive,” he said. “Immigrants are often detained in very unsafe facilities. Immigrants have died in these facilities. And to add to this complex, dangerous program of detention, to put immigrants on a ship in the middle of the ocean with no healthcare anywhere nearby … makes absolutely no sense.”

The letter follows reporting by the New York Times earlier this month that the departments of Homeland Security and Defense are considering a plan to use ships, possibly including ferries and commercial vessels as well as the Golden Bear, to transport hundreds of people to Central and South America.

The Golden Bear served as a training vessel at Cal Poly Maritime Academy for 30 years. It is set to be transferred back to the U.S. Maritime Administration as the academy transitions in the coming months to a new training ship, according to the academy.

The Golden Bear has been an invaluable floating classroom that just returned from a three-month trip training cadets on navigation, engine mechanics and other skills essential to the maritime industry and military fields, Garamendi said.

“Any efforts to use the Golden Bear as a floating prison to hold, detain and deport migrants would be a dangerous misuse of government and taxpayer property,” the letter to Mullin said. “Mass relocations by sea would require moving hundreds of detained individuals through international waters and raises enormous operational, safety and legal challenges.”

In addition, the congressmembers said, “the plan recalls catastrophic historical examples of deportations by sea that violated human rights and resulted in deadly consequences.” They reference 19th-century expulsions of Irish refugees and Chinese immigrants, and mass deportations of Mexicans in the 20th century, all of which employed ships.

Garamendi said he’s not opposed to immigration enforcement, but he faulted Republicans for scuttling Democratic legislation to address immigration issues “humanely and sanely,” and instead turning to strategies he called cruel.

“The entire Trump immigration program to deport the worst of the worst has descended into deporting anybody they can get their hands on, and often doing it in a very, very dangerous way,” he said, adding the plan for deportation ships “makes no sense at all. Do not do it. Don’t even consider it.”

Homeland Security officials did not immediately respond to KQED’s request for comment by press time.

title: Trump's Great Persecution: ICE Raids Ignite Business Fears | U.S. | EL PAÍS English
authors: Dianne Solis, Anita Snow, Susan Ferriss
description:
A UCLA study found $3.2 million in accumulated losses in the first two weeks after the 2025 raids.
And in Chicago’s La Villita, an immigrant-dense neighborhood, business has nosedived after raids there last year.
No matter the soundtrack in the dining room, it’s Mexican rancheras and corridos in the kitchen.
Dianne Solis wrote for The Dallas Morning News and The Wall Street Journal, collectively for more than three decades.
Anita Snow spent more than 35 years with The Associated Press covering Latin America and the U.S. Southwest.
text:
This story was co-published with El Pais and Puente News Collaborative a bilingual nonprofit newsroom, convener and funder dedicated to high-quality, fact-based news and information from the U.S.-Mexico border. KTEP News is a founding member of Puente News Collaborative.

In McAllen, Texas, home builder Mario Guerrero had grown so frustrated with immigration raids on contractors’ worksites across the state’s southern reach that he traveled to Washington, D.C. earlier this year to lobby for help from federal officials.

He returned home empty-handed.

“They literally told us they are going after every ethnicity that is not an American,” said Guerrero, head of the South Texas Builders Association, recalling his meetings with officials from ICE, the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. “I said, ‘Well, what is an American?’”

Fast-forward from those futile winter meetings, and it now takes builders twice as long to finish a starter home because of a scarcity of workers, immigrant or U.S.-born, Guerrero said. The 33-year-old, who voted for Donald Trump three times, warned of greater trouble ahead for home builders and the country’s economy. Mom-and-pop builders must repay construction loans within a year, he said, and a slowdown will trigger a cascade of problems. One McAllen-area concrete company has already filed for bankruptcy, citing ICE raids.

The Trump administration’s fierce crackdown on immigrants has punched hard at the nation’s immigrant-heavy industries like home construction, restaurants, food production and health care. And there are no solutions in sight for workplace chaos unleashed by one of the largest immigration dragnets since the Great Depression. U.S. food production alone is highly vulnerable. A 2020 analysis of Census data found that 43% of frontline food workers nationwide were immigrants – and often worked in Trump-voting counties.

This impact on the U.S. economy is a headline consequence of Trump’s drive to rid the country of every undocumented person and immigrant deemed unwanted. The campaign has led to tragedy – even death. It’s also fostered a sense among Latino and other immigrants that they face unprecedented persecution in a country that had thrived on their hard work and politicians once boasted was “a nation of immigrants.”

The push against immigrants, and the pull of their vital role in the U.S. economy, has business leaders wrestling with contradictions. Many support Trump. They’ve leaned into his tax-cutting, deregulation agenda, even as they’ve warned that mass deportations would yank away valued workers, trigger bankruptcies and fuel higher consumer prices.

For decades, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce has pushed for pro-immigration solutions. It’s joined labor unions to urge Congress to create a path to legal permanent residency – and eventual citizenship – for longtime undocumented workers. The Chamber and the newer American Business Immigration Coalition also argue that there are too few immigrant visas for employers to sponsor people to enter legally and fill shortages in year-round, less-skilled but essential jobs.

But Trump rose to power vowing to deport “bad hombres,” falsely blaming immigration for depressing U.S. wages. Today, he’s supercharged deportations. And the only foreign workers he seems warm to are temporary guest workers. In fact, Trump companies have a history of hiring foreign workers, including undocumented laborers and legal, foreign guest workers.

Records show that the U.S. Department of Labor approved a request for 175 seasonal guest workers at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida. That made the winter White House the fifth-largest recipient in Florida of approvals for workers on nonimmigrant H-2B visas. When employers in 2025 protested a sudden uptick in ICE raids at worksites, Trump floated the idea of letting employers take charge of undocumented workers who might be detained. “They can pay taxes,” he said, hastening to add: “They’re not getting citizenship.”

The losses grow

It’s hard to precisely measure the impact raids have had on the U.S. economy. Inflation remains high, along with food and gas prices. A vexing war with Iran is disrupting global energy markets. A boom in the artificial intelligence business masks the gloom. But in certain industries, bosses predict that more ICE raids will be disastrous.

In Los Angeles County, where nearly half the population is Latino, about 95% of Latino entrepreneurs report financial stress a year after violent ICE raids on workplaces and homes. A UCLA study found $3.2 million in accumulated losses in the first two weeks after the 2025 raids. And in Chicago’s La Villita, an immigrant-dense neighborhood, business has nosedived after raids there last year. “Worse than Covid,” said Michelle Macias of Carnicería Aguascalientes, citing a 60% slide in revenue. Macias added a message for ICE agents:

“Go away, please go away … We have suffered enough.”

In Texas, where many immigrants’ first jobs are in restaurants, a survey by the Texas Restaurant Association found more than a third of restaurateurs said they lost employees this year to immigration enforcement. Half said they were already reeling from losses in 2025.

Nationwide, the construction industry needs to attract about 350,000 new workers this year to meet demand, according to the Associated Builders and Contractors organization. In 2027, that number is expected to jump to more than 450,000.

Labor experts warn of the myth that every immigrant worker deported means a U.S. worker can fill the job. Quite the reverse happens, said Elizabeth Cox and Chloe N. East, professors at the University of Colorado at Boulder. Their research found no evidence that bosses are increasing wages to attract U.S.-born workers.

Despite economists’ research, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News recently that real wage growth is coming and that the immigration crackdown is returning jobs to U.S. workers.

A U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson also brushed off complaints that the crackdown was selectively hurting business sectors.

“Let’s be clear, if there was any correlation between rampant illegal immigration and a good economy, Biden would have had a booming economy,” the spokesperson said.

Families, businesses wrecked

A deportation or detention can wallop a family business and shatter a family. That happened to Jason Quiroga, a U.S. citizen, when his Cuban-born wife was picked up by ICE at a scheduled check-in with immigration officials in Dallas. His construction business employed 16 people, but it floundered when he had to care for his toddler daughter and elderly father, roles his wife Niury had held.

Quiroga said he took on his detained wife’s legal case, filing pleadings himself after a bad experience with attorneys. The immigration system’s complexity astounded him. “Something has to change,” he said.

Lydia Gonzalez, a veteran caterer who runs the Latino Culinary Institute and Association, echoed the need for change. Immigrants from Mexico are the core of many restaurants’ staff, she said. No matter the soundtrack in the dining room, it’s Mexican rancheras and corridos in the kitchen.

But at a recent hearing on the ICE crackdown, co-organized by the Texas Civil Rights Project and others, Gonzalez testified in a crowded Dallas church that fear has overcome the local restaurant trade. Some employers now go out and pick up employees fearful of being stopped during work commutes. Others have cut hours because of shrinking staffs.

“It is going to continue to impact us for generations to come because we are being racially profiled and the heads of households are being deported on a regular basis,” Gonzalez said.

Pumping the brakes

This summer, Markwayne Mullin, Homeland Security’s top cop, appeared to signal that tapping the enforcement brakes was ahead in industries like agriculture. “Because this narrative that it steals American jobs is true in some industries, it’s not true for all industries,” Mullin said in a chat with Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt at a meeting of the National Governors Association.

If not enough Americans are filling jobs, “we can plug those holes,” Mullin said, implying foreign workers could fill gaps.

The blowback was swift. Greg Bovino, former commander of the Border Patrol, said in an online post that Mullin “delivered a masterclass in how to give terrible answers.”

Mullin walked back his comments, saying “No amnesty for illegal aliens. Ever.”

But while it might not please the MAGA base, Trump has gone out of his way to plug some holes, as Mullin said. The administration increased H-2B visas, permits for lesser-skilled guest workers – the kind Mar-a-Lago employs. The permits are for seasonal, nonagricultural labor, like hotel work. Congress caps the permits at around 66,000 a year. But the Trump administration used its authority to add more than 64,700 “supplemental” emergency visas for businesses claiming they’d face irreparable harm without foreign workers.

Joe Del Bosque, an organic melon and tomato farmer in California’s Central Valley, is a grower who worries about his crops. In full harvest, Del Bosque had dozens of workers from El Salvador working under Temporary Protected Status, traditionally granted to people whose home countries are deemed unsafe. With harvest winding down and after money-saving layoffs, his TPS workforce is now down to around two dozen.

After weeks of uncertainty over the future of TPS, the protection has been retained for 170,000 Salvadorans nationwide. But it’s been pulled from others. Some 350,000 Haitian workers in the U.S. lost their protection and their rights to work and stay in the country.

Why are Salvadorans treated differently? One answer might be the support – like access to a notorious maximum-security detention center – the Salvadoran government has given to Trump’s rampant deportation drive.

“Some … people have been with us for more than 20 years,” Del Bosque said. “They have families and have already sent their kids to college. They have bought homes. They have lives here.”

The H-2A seasonal farm guest worker program isn’t much of an alternative, Del Bosque said, because it requires employers to provide housing – a proposition too expensive for many farmers.

“It almost gives us fear to stand up and say we need some immigration reform because there are so many people who are adamantly against that,” Del Bosque said. “They refuse to admit that Americans won’t do this (work).”

Trump, however, has suggested that he agrees that Americans won’t do farm work, raising eyebrows with a remark that foreign migrants do grueling labor “naturally.”

The president has also tried to roll back some H-2A rules to cut farmers’ costs. With executive directives, he eliminated required wage rates and has tried to let employers deduct housing from workers’ wages. (Housing is free, by law, for H-2A workers.) A federal judge has challenged both Trump directives.

Like H-2B visas, Trump is familiar with the H-2A program. Records show that Trump Vineyard Estates in Virginia, owned by his son, Eric, received approval to bring in 36 H-2A workers in 2026. These guest worker permits do not create a path for workers to legally settle in the U.S.

A changed landscape

A few short years ago, scenes of migrants at the Rio Grande on the Texas-Mexico border were unforgettable. Some immigrants said touching U.S. soil was the best day of their lives, while people around the country were horrified by images of a Border Patrol agent on horseback, pushing back Haitian immigrants.

By mid-2024, the unauthorized immigrant population peaked at almost 16 million, up from about 11 million a decade earlier, according to the nonprofit Migration Policy Institute. Before Trump’s America First rhetoric became policy, President Joe Biden expanded humanitarian parole during his presidency, including issuing more TPS permits.

At the Dallas Federal Reserve, vice president and labor economist Pia Orrenius said the current crackdown is pushback to what many voters saw as an extreme migration surge.

“These extremes generate backlashes,” the economist said.

In Florida, businesses dependent on Haitian immigrants, like care providers for seniors, are scrambling to draw up a plan B.

Jewish Community Services of South Florida reluctantly laid off 18 Haitian homecare workers when their TPS expired. Now, with deportation flights underway, they’re at risk of being sent home to one of the Western Hemisphere’s most violent, impoverished nations. The nonprofit agency employs more than 300 homecare workers who serve hundreds of older people, including Holocaust survivors.

The service now struggles to fill vacancies in an industry already beset with worker shortages and rising overtime for remaining staff.

“We are heartbroken we had to do this,” spokeswoman Alicia Vigil Blanco said of the layoffs. “Some of them had been employed by us for years.”

Vigil Blanco said clients of Jewish Community Service, many of them homebound seniors, were saddened and confused by the sudden loss of beloved companions. Immigrant workers helped them bathe, dress and eat, and listened to their stories. They even prayed with them and took them to doctor appointments.

“A good number of our clients don’t have any family left and have no one else nearby to help them,” Vigil Blanco said.

Denise Belville, executive director of the Home Care Association of Florida, said two agencies closed after TPS ended for Haitian workers. Each company terminated at least 80 employees.

Belville said Florida’s home and health care industries have been battered by the end of TPS for 113,000 Haitians. Their clients are also devastated, with “no one now to take care of them,” she said.

Cascading problems

In Mission, Texas, Eliud Cavazos, CEO of 57 Concrete, felt the worsening sting of ICE raids. In filings to support the company’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy, he said his business was hit with a “sudden and sustained decline” in orders from residential builders that coincided with increased ICE enforcement.

Builders experienced “acute labor shortages, work stoppages, and project suspensions,” said the CEO’s court filing.

In a phone interview, Cavazos added, “They are just going to residential areas and hunting people in subdivisions.”

To adjust, he’s drummed up new business in commercial construction, which hasn’t yet faced the same enforcement scrutiny. He’s working in Brownsville, where Elon Musk is expanding SpaceX rocket operations and a liquefied natural gas storage project is underway.

Fear of more ICE interference has led to desperate theater. The South Texas Builders Association recently took to social media with a video featuring the group’s head of government relations, Benny Melendez, dressed like an ICE agent at a construction site.

Facing the camera, he takes off his balaclava and says, “Only cowards hide under a mask.” Then he strips off a heavy bulletproof vest and dons an orange construction vest and white hard hat, a hammer in hand.

“Our cities and especially our industry are being really affected by ICE operations…Sooner than later, we will all feel the negative impact on our wallets.”

Melendez then invokes Lorenzo Salgado, the Mexican construction crew boss whose July 7 killing by an ICE agent provoked demands for accountability. “What happened to Lorenzo Salgado in Houston, Texas, just crossed all the lines,” Melendez says.

A dream deferred

Across the border, in Mexico, deported workers try to build new lives.

Ivan Parras, a 33-year-old brought to the U.S. as a child from Mexico City, was a Dreamer. Like 495,000 others, he benefited from Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA. Parras held a work permit, became a member of the Teamsters union, and drew a good salary building temporary structures for trade shows in Las Vegas.

Then, a drunk driving charge mushroomed into a deportation.

He left behind a partner and a daughter.

“I always had a really good job installing booths,” said Parras, now a call-center worker in Mexico City. “I always had a good salary, cars, money. I still help provide for (my family), but making pesos isn’t the same as dollars.”

Alfredo Corchado contributed to this story, reporting from Chicago.

Dianne Solis wrote for The Dallas Morning News and The Wall Street Journal, collectively for more than three decades. She is now an independent writer and editor based in Dallas, specializing in immigration, justice and borders.

Anita Snow spent more than 35 years with The Associated Press covering Latin America and the U.S. Southwest. She is now an independent writer based in Tucson, Arizona, focused on immigration, the border and the environment.

title: Judge threatens ICE with contempt, sanctions in Minnesota re-arrest case - MPR News
description:
Saltos told MPR News his worst fear had come true.
Saltos is one of seven instant re-arrest cases confirmed by MPR News, though immigration lawyers suspect there are more cases.
Saltos told MPR News he escaped gangs in his home country of Ecuador after they attacked him and killed his brother.
In an order, Bryan wrote ICE “failed to release” Saltos “thereby violating” his release order.
He wrote ICE must release Saltos “immediately,” or the government could face sanctions.
text:
Around noon on Oct. 19, Milton Saltos Velasquez was told he was being released from immigration detention per a judge’s order. He said he didn’t manage to get a foot outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building before he was immediately re-arrested.

Saltos told MPR News his worst fear had come true. He said other immigrants being held with him in county jail had warned him ICE was instantly re-arresting people this way.

Saltos was handcuffed and processed again. Then he was loaded into a vehicle, with other men he said had also been re-arrested, to drive the roughly two hours to Kandiyohi County Jail, which contracts with ICE.

They were well on their way to the jail when Saltos said a message came over the agents’ radio telling them to turn around.

One of the men was to be released again.

Saltos is one of seven instant re-arrest cases confirmed by MPR News, though immigration lawyers suspect there are more cases. ICE officials previously told an immigration attorney that their lawyers identify good candidates for re-arrest — usually people who were arrested without warrants or probable cause in the first place.

This tactic comes as the grounds for immigrants to challenge their detentions have gotten narrower. In March, an appeals court sided with the Trump administration's novel and controversial policy of holding immigrants in detention instead of giving them bond hearings.

‘I couldn’t stop crying’

Saltos, 45, has a pending asylum application. In 2023 an asylum officer in Texas wrote that Saltos “demonstrated credible fear of persecution or torture,” according to court records. Saltos told MPR News he escaped gangs in his home country of Ecuador after they attacked him and killed his brother. He said his children and the rest of his family are still in Ecuador. He oversees the treatment of his comatose father remotely, checking on him over video calls.

Saltos was arrested by ICE agents as he arrived at work on Oct. 6 and was held in detention in Freeborn County Jail in Albert Lea.

Speaking to an MPR News reporter in Spanish, Saltos said the worst part of being in detention was not being able to help care for his family.

“Pues me desesperaba porque yo quería ver a mi padre, quería verlo, quería estar pendiente,” Saltos said.

“I was getting desperate because I wanted to see my father, I wanted to be there for him.”

Saltos’ lawyer immediately alerted the judge presiding over the case, U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan, to the re-arrest.

In an order, Bryan wrote ICE “failed to release” Saltos “thereby violating” his release order. He wrote ICE must release Saltos “immediately,” or the government could face sanctions.

The agents bringing Saltos to the Kandiyohi County Jail were forced to turn around.

Saltos said when he realized he would truly be released, he cried the rest of the evening.

“No paraba de poder llorar a la vez de emoción, a la vez alegría, a la vez tristeza,” Saltos said.

“I couldn’t stop crying from the emotion, joy and sadness at the same time.”

Bryan, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, has condemned ICE’s instant re-arrest strategy before.

When another man was instantly re-arrested on Sept. 9, Bryan ordered his release for a second time, writing that if such a re-arrest legally constitutes release, that “would render habeas relief meaningless.”

Saltos’ lawyer, Sherene Mostaghimi, said she was happy her client’s case was assigned to Bryan and she’s glad Saltos is home safe.

But she said these re-arrests are emblematic of the expensive, sometimes seemingly endless legal cycle immigrants are getting stuck in.

“It’s pretty abusive of the system,” Mostaghimi said. “It’s just wasting people's time.”

She said ICE didn’t provide a good reason for her client’s re-arrest other than claiming they had followed the release order when they first released him around noon.

“It’s just so ludicrous that to me, the government thinks they can get away with doing whatever they want,” Mostaghimi said.

When asked for comment about Bryan’s rulings against the government, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote:

“ICE complies with all lawful court orders. When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time. Instead, if ICE does not appeal the ruling, it may seek to rearrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage.”

Pending rulings

Other federal judges have been slower to take a position on the tactic, including Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud, a President Donald Trump nominee.

Tostrud is currently presiding over at least two instant re-arrest cases. Both men were re-arrested more than a month ago and are still in ICE custody.

Tostrud has ruled against the federal government in some cases involving ICE in the past year.

In February, he held the government in contempt for moving a detainee to Texas after he ordered ICE to keep him in Minnesota. This summer, Tostrud threw out the Department of Justice’s lawsuits against the state of Minnesota and local jurisdictions that sought to overturn their policies limiting cooperation with ICE.

However, it’s unclear how Tostrud will rule in the re-arrest cases.

Tostrud is presiding over the case of one of the first men MPR News spoke to when these re-arrests came to light.

“At least in Alejandro’s case, I think additional briefing and the production of evidence can make for a good decision,” his lawyer Daniel Suitor said.

Suitor said it makes sense that judges would take time to analyze the legality of these re-arrests because they don’t have appellate guidance to follow on the definition of “release” in habeas cases.

In an Oct. 1 order, Tostrud denied the other man’s request for an expedited decision and wrote “perhaps” the re-arrest had violated his order, but he needed more information to decide one way or another.

Attorney Stacey Rogers represents the detained man in that case and was taken aback by Tostrud’s “perhaps.”

“It really surprised me because I think as a judge, if you make a decision, you want that decision to be upheld and respected. So, at what point are we okay with that not being upheld or respected?” Rogers said.

Rogers said she fears these re-arrests could set a dangerous precedent for law enforcement because many of these cases hinge on warrantless arrests and due process violations. Due process means persons in the country, not just citizens, generally have the constitutional right to be told why they’re being detained and to have a hearing before a neutral decisionmaker.

“If we start to allow the Constitution to slip in one area, it's going to be very easy for the Constitution to slip in other law enforcement arrests,” Rogers said.

“The concern should be broader than just immigration.”

description:
They are also preparing in case the Trump administration dispatches immigration officers or other federal officials to election sites.
The training comes as President Donald Trump and his administration are threatening state and local election officials with criminal charges if noncitizens vote.
"They're telling us what they are going to do, and what they're going to do is challenge the election results," he told USA TODAY.
Afterward, volunteers will stay on to watch ballot counting and local election certification, in case either is contested.
Trump's challenge to the 2020 election results changed how election protection groups operate, said Anderson-Reed.
text:
Zachary Mueller led a video call in mid-October for about 200 people seeking to learn how to monitor federal activity near polling places and mobilize if the Trump administration disputes the midterm election results.

Mueller is a senior strategist at States at the Core, one of dozens of nonpartisan and partisan groups organizing tens of thousands of grassroots activists to monitor the polls until Election Day. They are also preparing in case the Trump administration dispatches immigration officers or other federal officials to election sites.

The training comes as President Donald Trump and his administration are threatening state and local election officials with criminal charges if noncitizens vote. Meanwhile, federal immigration authorities are carrying out mass arrests that have swept up U.S. citizens.

"We are in this absurd timeline in which we've got to be here on a Wednesday night in October, thinking about how we are going to protect the basic backstop of American democracy," said Mueller, who added "our widely safe and effective and consistent election process" is being "undermined by people in positions of power."

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump "has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections."

"While extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections, including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion. President Trump is making clear that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable," Bis said.

The outcome of the elections will determine how much power Trump can wield during his final two years in office, how many of his priorities he can enact and whether Congress investigates his administration's actions and tightens the purse strings. The Trump administration has not shut the door on having immigration officers or federal officials near or in polling locations on election nights.

States at the Core, which began teaching people how to document immigration enforcement activity about 18 months ago, expanded its trainings in May to include how communities can respond if federal officials appear at polling places or challenge election results. More than 50,000 people have completed the Immigration and Customs Enforcement or election trainings, Mueller said.

"They're telling us what they are going to do, and what they're going to do is challenge the election results," he told USA TODAY.

'Make sure that people's voices are heard'

The training urged community-level organizers to plan how they will respond Nov. 4 through Nov. 8, if local, state or federal officials challenge election results. In some places, that could mean protesting in the streets, presenters said, or holding news conferences to defend local counts and election officials.

To help ensure all voters can cast a ballot and have it counted, the nonpartisan Election Protection Coalition and other groups have ramped up their efforts, said Andrew Walchuk, policy director and counsel for Common Cause. The coalition – which includes Common Cause, State Voices and the NAACP – has organized thousands of trainings in 40 states for "poll guardians" as well as a nationwide hotline staffed with volunteers and legal staff.

It is still accepting volunteer poll watchers, Walchuk said.

"There is a huge community of folks ... who are fighting back and are pushing back to make sure that people's voices are heard," Walchuk said.

Local groups will likely focus on jurisdictions with past election issues and communities targeted by the administration, Walchuk said. Afterward, volunteers will stay on to watch ballot counting and local election certification, in case either is contested.

"We have faith in the people who are part of our communities and spend all year preparing to run effective elections. So, we want to have their backs. We want to be able to say, 'No, they were following the law,'" he said.

In many places, the organizers will appear alongside official observers sent by political parties, the Department of Justice and Congress.

Last month, Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said her agency would send 1,000 observers nationwide, calling it DOJ's largest election-monitoring effort.

A record number of bipartisan congressional staff will also be present in up to 45 closely contested races, said Rep. Joe Morelle, the top Democrat on the House Administration Committee.

"We want contemporaneous notes should there be a challenge or a contest for anyone," he said.

Grassroots organizing

Lili Baiman of Ohio Buen Vecino Network said her group has trained 2,500 people in recent months to document federal activity near polling places and to report it to hotlines or election officials. About 1,200 will serve as observers in Ohio's major cities. Others are focused on coordinating rides to the polls and childcare while people vote.

Baiman, a naturalized citizen, said the observers want to be an "extra layer of support" for anyone worried they might get picked up while voting legally.

"It is very challenging for someone like me to show up to a polling location. Even though I am a citizen – even though I've voted in all of these elections – I still am walking around on a day-to-day basis being like, 'I can still be detained,'" she said.

In Davidson County, Tennessee, poll observers are already stationed at 15 high-traffic early voting locations and will be at all 178 precincts on Election Day, said Jennifer Brinkman with Nashville Indivisible. Brinkman said volunteers are trained on election law and will document or report any activity they believe could intimidate voters.

"The goal is to make sure that every eligible voter that wants to vote is able to vote very safely without intimidation," she said. "We'll either have a big day of celebration, which is what I'm hoping for...or if there are some kind of weird shenanigans going on, I think we'll be prepared for that also."

Poll guardians

State Voices has seen an increase in people who want to be involved, said the organization's president, Alexis Anderson-Reed. More than 10,000 calls have already come into her group's voter hotline.

"There's a palpable feeling that, no, we are responsible individually and collectively for our democracy," said Anderson-Reed, whose nonpartisan group advocates for democracy.

Local organizers in Nevada have trained observers in all 17 counties. In Michigan, they will be at 300 polling locations, while more than 1,000 trained volunteers will be at the polls in North Carolina. Some states will also have roving poll watchers at ballot drop boxes as well.

Like States at the Core, State Voices is preparing for potential post-election challenges. The Election Sabotage Response Network has lawyers on standby, while staff and volunteers expect to stay engaged through certification and congressional review of the results in January.

Trump's challenge to the 2020 election results changed how election protection groups operate, said Anderson-Reed.

"Things really have shifted post-2020 in the way we have to staff elections, the way we have to think about elections, the way that we have to ensure that we're moving through the process of the certification," she said.

text:
Anti-immigrant protesters seeking to intimidate traders and shut down foreign-owned shops across South Africa have repeatedly invoked a misleading claim amplified by at least two government ministers in 2024.

In October 2024, the deaths of six children in Soweto, initially thought to have been caused by consuming contaminated snacks bought from a spaza shop, triggered a government crackdown in Gauteng.

On 23 October 2024, Small Business Development Minister Stella Ndabeni-Abrahams told Parliament that “for you to be able to trade, the Immigration Act, section 15 says that you must at least invest a minimum of R5-million into the economy for you to get a business visa.”

The claim, a version of which was repeated by Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni, was reported in the news media.

While the claim was correct in regard to business visas, immigration lawyers agree that there are other legal ways for foreign nationals to operate businesses in South Africa.

Operation Dudula

Still, soon after Ndabeni-Abrahams’ statement, Operation Dudula started to argue that foreign owned businesses should not be allowed to operate if they had not invested R5-million into the economy. African Transformation Movement (ATM) then leader Vuyo Zungula repeated the claim multiple times in an interview with SABC News on spaza shop regulation in November 2024.

With anti-immigrant protests sweeping South Africa in 2026, the claim is again being used to target foreign businesses. In a video clip circulated widely online, protesters in Qonce confronted a Nigeria-born car wash owner. The businessman insists that he is documented. The confrontation in the video clip escalates nonetheless.

“We are here to tell you: according to Immigration Act 2002, sections 13, 15 and 19 you are not allowed to operate any kind of business, not unless you have a minimum investment of R5-million and above,” the interviewer says.

“We are not asking you. You have to close this car wash now. It belongs to South Africa.”

The interviewer is seen holding a microphone with an eNCA logo and the clip was broadcast by eNCA in May 2026. The channel subsequently apologised for broadcasting the clip “without the requisite context or balance”. But, the apology did not clarify what context or balance was missing.

Politicians, protestors and news journalists have continued to amplify the R5-million “investment” claim.

For instance, in June, protesters reportedly forced the closure of foreign-owned shops in Lydenburg, Mpumalanga, demanding that their owners provide proof of a R5-million investment.

Also in June, Alfred Duma Municipality closed foreign-owned shops in a “compliance campaign”. The campaign included demands that foreign business owners provide proof of a R5-million investment, according to a telephonic interview with one shopkeeper. He asked not to be named due to safety concerns.

Despite a KwaZulu-Natal Division of the High Court in Pietermaritzburg order that the municipality allow the shops to open, a Newzroom Afrika journalist questioned one of the applicants involved if they had invested R5-million.

Case law supports foreigners’ right to be self-employed

Nyiko Manyusa, an attorney with Lawyers for Human Rights (LHR) specialising in immigration law, said the claim was a cynical distortion of the Immigration Act.

The R5-million investment threshold was a requirement attached to certain business visa applications, he said. It did not apply automatically to every foreign national who operated a business in South Africa.

The right of refugees and asylum seekers to operate businesses in South Africa has been upheld by case law and the courts.

In 2012 the Somali Association of South Africa took the government to court over a crackdown on spaza shops in Limpopo.

In 2014, the Supreme Court of Appeal ruled that there was “no blanket prohibition” preventing refugees and asylum seekers from engaging in self-employment. The court upheld the applicants’ ability to apply for and renew trading licences and found that Limpopo authorities’ actions in preventing them from trading on the basis of their immigration status were unlawful. Central to this judgment was affirming that the right to “seek employment” in Section 27 of the Refugees Act included self-employment.

Refugees do not have to invest R5-million

Liesl Fourie, an attorney at the Nelson Mandela University (NMU) Refugee Rights Centre in Gqeberha, agreed that lawful refugees and asylum seekers do not have to invest R5-million before they can operate businesses.

“The simple reason for that is that refugee and asylum seekers’ visas allow them to work in the country. They are allowed to operate a business, they are allowed to open a business and employ other people,” said Fourie.

The same applied to foreign nationals holding certain special dispensation permits, such as the Zimbabwean Exemption Permit (ZEP) or Lesotho Exemption Permit (LEP), which, according to a December 2023 statement on their extension, allowed holders to “work, seek employment and conduct business in the Republic of South Africa”.

Fourie added that South Africa did not operate a refugee encampment system where asylum seekers were routinely provided with accommodation and basic necessities. Their access to social assistance was also limited, leaving many dependent on employment or small businesses to support themselves.

Uncertainty over amendments to the Refugees Act

In January 2020, amendments to the Refugees Act complicated matters. These introduced additional restrictions on asylum seekers’ rights to work and study, including requirements relating to permission from the Department of Home Affairs.

Some of these amendments, which restricted access to asylum procedures based on how or when applicants entered South Africa and whether they possessed certain immigration documents, were struck down by the Constitutional Court in July. It was this judgment which precipitated violent protests in Durban and Johannesburg in October.

However, other provisions relating to asylum seekers’ “permission to work” had remained in place.

These had not been enforced, said Fourie. She said this was because they were impractical and potentially even unconstitutional – particularly given that asylum seekers had limited access to financial support while waiting for their applications to be processed.

“How are asylum seekers supposed to support themselves, waiting for a Refugee Appeals Authority (a statutory body that hears appeals against rejected asylum applications] hearing date, if they do not work?” she asked.

No response from ministers

Viewfinder submitted queries to Ndabeni-Abrahams and Ntshavheni, via their respective ministries. These asked that they clarify their 2024 statements – which implied that foreign nationals must invest R5-million before being allowed to operate businesses in South Africa.

Small Business Development Ministry communication officer Luyanda Mbalana acknowledged the query and committed to respond by Monday. No response had been received by the time of publication. The Ministry in the Presidency also did not respond. DM

text:
The Supreme Court stripped immigration judges of the ability to pause certain deportation proceedings on Tuesday, declining to block a deal slammed as “egregious collusion” between the Justice Department and the state of Texas.

The unsigned order on Tuesday halts the practice known as “administrative closure,” which allows judges to pause deportation cases. The practice affects thousands of cases a year, and has been granted 360,000 times since 1990, according to statistics by the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

The procedure clears a judge’s dockets while other circumstances surrounding the migrant are resolved, including appeals of criminal cases or if they are seeking humanitarian protections or other legal status. It can also give some people relief in difficult circumstances, such as those who were the victims of certain crimes or children who were abused or abandoned.

Data has previously shown that most immigrants whose cases return to court after administrative closure are ultimately allowed to stay in the U.S.

The first Trump administration had said that judges lacked the authority to perform the practice, but the Biden administration restored it through a rule issued in 2024.

There were no noted dissents to the Supreme Court’s decision, and the Court provided no explanation for its reasoning. The decision hands the Trump administration another tool in its mass deportation campaign as immigration officials wantonly violate court orders and pressure judges to issue more deportation orders.

The ruling upholds an extraordinary judiciary maneuver by the state of Texas and the Trump administration, as critics said.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton had originally sued the government over the Biden administration rule in 2024. The case was brought to federal court this June, where Texas officials argued that the rule was “one part of the Biden-Harris Administration’s campaign to undermine our immigration laws,” and said it exceeds the government’s authority.

Hours after Texas officials filed that case, Texas and the Trump Department of Justice — which oversees immigration judges — jointly filed in the same court asking for the Biden rule to be thrown out. The judge promptly granted that order.

Three cities challenged that order, with their lawyers saying in a filing to the Supreme Court that the Texas-DOJ deal amounted to “egregious collusion.”

“The government … announced in advance that it would not defend a disfavored regulation and then colluded with the challenger from the moment that suit was filed,” the lawyers challenging the deal said.

text:
By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) – A federal judge on Tuesday temporarily blocked US President Donald Trump’s administration from ​implementing a new rule that would ‌cut the amount of time refugees have to contest decisions to strip them of their legal status to 10 days from 30 days.

• US District ‌Judge ​Julia Kobick in Boston issued ⁠an order that ⁠through November 6 puts on hold the rule issued by US Citizenship and Immigration Services on October 14

• Refugee advocacy groups ​sought the order as part of a lawsuit filed on Monday challenging the ⁠rule and a plan ⁠for a broader review of refugees

• ​Kobick said the USCIS rule should be put ​on hold to preserve the status ‌quo until the case could be heard by a colleague

• Erez Reuveni of Democracy Forward, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said the ⁠decision “provides meaningful protection for people who were already facing termination notices”

• USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler in ⁠a statement ‌called the lawsuit a “frivolous attempt ⁠to disrupt the Trump administration’s commitment ​to ‌enforce our country’s immigration laws ​as intended ⁠by Congress”

• The US Department of Homeland Security, which oversees USCIS, had estimated the new rule would affect as many as 186,000 refugees

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston, Editing by ​Rosalba O’Brien)

text:
The U.S. Courts of Appeals for the thirteen "circuits" issue thousands of precedential decisions each year. Because relatively few of these decisions are ultimately reviewed by the Supreme Court, the U.S. Courts of Appeals are often the last word on consequential legal questions. The federal appellate courts sometimes reach different conclusions on the same issue of federal law, causing a "split" among the circuits that leads to the nonuniform application of federal law among similarly situated litigants.

This Legal Sidebar discusses circuit splits that emerged or widened following decisions from August 2026 on matters relevant to Congress. The Sidebar does not address every circuit split that developed or widened during this period. Selected cases typically involve judicial disagreement over the interpretation or validity of federal statutes and regulations, or constitutional issues relevant to Congress's lawmaking and oversight functions. The Sidebar includes only cases where an appellate court's controlling opinion recognizes a split among the circuits on a key legal issue resolved in the opinion. This Sidebar refers to each U.S. Court of Appeals by its number or descriptor (e.g., "D.C. Circuit" for "U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit").

Some cases identified in this Sidebar, or the legal questions they address, are examined in other CRS general distribution products. Members of Congress and congressional staff may click here to subscribe to the CRS Legal Update and receive regular notifications of new products and upcoming seminars by CRS attorneys.

text:
U.S. Circuit Judge Toby Heytens, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, asked Owen a hypothetical question about whether Virginia could have enacted a law that instead ordered cities and counties to exit their agreements with ICE individually, instead of the state unilaterally canceling all the agreements. Owen did not directly answer Heytens’s hypothetical question, instead insisting that the law at the center of the lawsuit was a violation of the contracts clause of the Constitution, which bars states from passing laws impairing public contracts.

The appeals court panel appeared more receptive toward Virginia officials’ defense of their state’s ban on ICE cooperation, while the same panel appeared more favorable toward the DOJ’s arguments against the state ban on face masks for federal officers. Multiple other states, including California and New York, along with some cities, such as Philadelphia, have passed laws banning federal immigration officers from wearing face masks, but federal courts have blocked all of those bans. The block on the California ban was upheld by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

Virginia Solicitor General Tillman Breckenridge faced the sharpest questions from the panel regarding the mask ban. Heytens was deeply skeptical that the Virginia law purporting to regulate federal officers passes constitutional muster.

“It strikes me that states have little, if any, ability to regulate the federal government qua the federal government,” Heytens said, appearing dubious of Virginia’s argument that it can regulate what federal officers wear.

THE ‘COME-AND-TAKE-IT’ SUPREME COURT TERM: AT-HOME PRAYER, PLANES, AND HOME DISTILLING

The panel did not indicate during the hearing how it would rule or when it would issue a ruling. The 4th Circuit panel included U.S. Circuit Judges Robert King, an appointee of former President Bill Clinton; Heytens; and DeAndrea Benjamin, also a Biden appointee.

The Trump administration has had a mixed record on immigration-related cases in lower federal courts, but its record has gotten better the higher disputes have made it in the judiciary, being especially successful at the Supreme Court. The eventual ruling by the panel could be appealed to either the en banc 4th Circuit or the Supreme Court.
