text:
A Romanian woman with diagnosed bipolar disorder is on life support at a Mesa hospital after an apparent suicide attempt at an Arizona ICE detention facility last week, her family said, citing what officials told doctors.

But the family is demanding a full investigation into what happened to Andreea Marin at ICE's Eloy Detention Center.

Marin, 38, was teaching English in France, with a master's degree in education and child development studies, before bipolar disorder "took over" her life in her mid-20s, her brother told the Arizona Daily Star.

"She loved working with children," her brother said Monday night. He asked the Star not to publish his full name, as he's still coming to terms with what's happening to his sister and his grief. "She was very academically driven. Unfortunately this condition, bipolar, took over almost everything."

Marin, who is originally from Romania, may not have been receiving her medication at Eloy, said her brother, a naturalized U.S. citizen.

"We've been pushing (ICE officials) to get her medication," he said. "They told us, 'Don’t worry, the medical staff here will take care of her and give her any medication she needs.' Like, 'Hey, just trust me.' And here we are. A broken trust."

Marin was airlifted from Eloy to Banner Desert Medical Center on Friday, Oct. 23. Doctors said the personnel who transported Marin told doctors she'd tried to hang herself in her cell, her brother said.

"At this point, it's just hearsay. That's why we're needing answers for what the hell happened in that facility," her brother said. "We want a full investigation. We’re demanding answers."

They also want to know why a vulnerable woman like Marin had to be detained in civil ICE detention in the first place, especially since she'd been diagnosed with a serious mental illness.

Marin was in the process of getting a green card and citizenship through her mother, also a naturalized U.S. citizen, her brother said.

It was only thanks to the medical staff at Banner Desert that the family was notified Sunday about Marin's hospitalization two days earlier, her brother said.

"Bless those people," he said of hospital staff. "They found us. It wasn't ICE. It wasn't Eloy."

His mother cried out and fainted after seeing Marin unconscious and "handcuffed" to the hospital bed by the wrists and ankles, her brother said.

"She was devastated," he said, his voice breaking. "I'm telling you, I don't even know the words to describe the wailing, the sound that a mother makes. … I'll never take that out of my memory.

"And I've never seen my dad cry. My dad is weeping, not crying," he said.

Missed court hearing

Marin had been detained at Eloy for less than two weeks, her brother said. In mid-October she was briefly arrested, then detained by ICE upon her release, after missing an Oct. 1 Maricopa County Superior Court hearing. She did not receive the letter notifying her about the hearing, he said.

The letter had been returned as undeliverable, her brother said he learned after calling the court.

In her 20s, Marin had a fiancé and a teaching career in France. She'd travel and visit her family in the U.S. on a 10-year tourist visa. But later she began to struggle with bipolar disorder.

"She was a very good person. She would light up the room," her brother said. "She loved her nephews, she loved her family. She loved her cat Thomas. She traveled throughout Europe and the States with Tom. She was a beautiful person."

By around 2017, she had returned to the U.S. — legally on a visa, her brother said — to be closer to family. She began the process of getting a green card and citizenship through her mother, a naturalized U.S. citizen, her brother said.

But she continued to struggle with her mental health at times. During a manic episode in October 2025 — which Marin didn't remember later, according to her brother — she was arrested. During booking, she allegedly assaulted a corrections employee.

She was charged with aggravated assault due to the incident, which happened while her parents were already in the process of getting Marin help at a Glendale treatment facility, her brother said.

At the treatment center, Marin got stabilized and returned to her job in Tempe after her release, her brother said.

But this month, Marin missed the Oct. 1 court hearing related to the 2025 felony charge of aggravated assault on a corrections employee.

Her brother said the court issued a warrant, despite Marin not having received notice of the hearing. A couple of weeks later, Marin was pulled over by police for running a stop sign. She was arrested when the police saw the warrant on her record, he said.

That same night, a judge ordered Marin released and rescheduled her missed court hearing for Oct. 27, citing the "miscommunication," her brother said.

But immigration agents detained Marin after she left the police station late that night, he said.

"They didn't give her any due process" before locking her up in ICE custody, he said. "She’s not a convicted felon. She only had a charge, and failure to appear in court, because of a clerical error with the court system itself. ... She should have never been arrested."

Her brother said he didn't see marks on Marin's neck at the hospital. As he took pictures, an immigration officer standing guard tried to make him leave the room and delete the photos. Hospital staff defended his right to stay in the hospital room, he said.

"Everybody was arguing. Everybody's policy is different," he said.

ICE, CoreCivic response

On Sunday, the Star reached out to both CoreCivic, the for-profit prison company that operates Eloy, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, after hearing from several Eloy detainees about a possible suicide attempt Friday.

ICE initially refused to comment unless the Star identified the detainee. But a CoreCivic spokesperson confirmed in a Monday email that an Eloy detainee had been hospitalized Friday, after they were found unconscious in their cell around 12 p.m. that day.

On Oct. 23, "a staff member at the Eloy Detention Center called a medical emergency after finding an unresponsive individual in their living area," CoreCivic's statement Monday said. "Responding medical staff arrived quickly, began lifesaving measures, and called for emergency medical services. EMS arrived and continued those efforts, and the individual was transported to a nearby hospital, where they continue to receive care."

ICE handles medical care at Eloy through its healthcare arm, ICE Health Services Corp.

CoreCivic said officials advised ICE about the Oct. 23 incident "immediately." Yet ICE spokeswoman Yasmeen Pitts O'Keefe responded with sarcasm on Oct. 25, after the Star inquired about the suicide attempt described by the Eloy detainees.

"Go back to your 'sources' to provide us names with A#s (alien identification number) or DoBs (date of birth) so we can properly research," Pitts O'Keefe wrote Sunday.

At the time, the Star had not yet identified Marin or reached her family.

ICE did not immediately respond to the Star's Tuesday request for comment on the family's account.

Marin's family contacted the office of U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, as they struggled to communicate with ICE about whether Marin was getting proper care for her mental health condition. They later learned she'd been hospitalized in critical condition.

Kelly's office is seeking information from ICE to help the family get answers, the office said in a statement Tuesday.

"This is horrific and unacceptable," Kelly said in the statement. "ICE has a responsibility to keep people in its custody safe and provide them with the medical care they need. Their failure to do so here may cost a woman her life and raises the question of how many others may be at risk. The family deserves answers about what happened and there must be accountability to keep it from happening again."

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Arizona, also called for a full investigation.

"Instead of exercising discretion, ICE is indiscriminately detaining vulnerable people — including pregnant women and individuals with serious mental health conditions — to fuel Trump’s mass deportation agenda," she said in a statement Tuesday. "ICE’s failure to notify Andreea’s family, and keeping her handcuffed at the hospital, show a stunning level of callousness and a basic lack of human decency. I’m calling for a full and independent investigation into Andreea’s treatment in ICE custody. Her family deserves answers, and ICE must be held accountable."

Immigrant deaths rising

As the number of detained immigrants has risen dramatically, advocates have warned of alleged negligent medical care and inhumane conditions in ICE detention facilities.

At least 60 people have died in ICE custody since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025.

For-profit prison companies, like CoreCivic and Geo Group, have seen rising revenue under the second Trump administration, which has focused on maximizing the number of people held in detention, regardless of whether they pose a public threat.

ICE detention is civil detention, not criminal, meaning no one in immigration detention is serving a sentence for a crime, regardless of whether they have a prior criminal record. About 70% of current ICE detainees have no criminal conviction on their record, and many with convictions have only traffic violations, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Among the dead is Haitian national Emmanuel Damas, a 56-year-old father who died at a Scottsdale hospital in March after collapsing at CoreCivic's Florence Correctional Center, where he was being held in ICE detention.

Doctors told Damas' family he died from septic shock, stemming from an untreated tooth infection. CoreCivic provides medical care at Florence.

The Star reported in May on the suicide attempt of Eloy detainee Alexander Hernandez, of Cuba. He told the Star he tried to hang himself after being denied medical care for excruciating back pain, an account his family confirmed. The incident happened two days after Hernandez said he'd been placed in solitary confinement as "punishment" for demanding medical care.

Hernandez survived and is still detained at Eloy.

A Star investigation into Eloy's use of solitary confinement found detainees say they risk being put into solitary confinement if they're honest about feelings of depression or thoughts of suicide, or complain about poor detention conditions.

Poor health care alleged

Detainees and immigrant-rights advocates have reported poor medical care in ICE facilities. Several detainees with diabetes have died in ICE detention.

NBC News reported last month that coroners have determined diabetes was "a contributing factor" in at least six ICE detainee deaths during Trump's second term.

In May, the Star reported on a Cuban asylum seeker who is suffering from lasting vision problems after his diabetes went untreated for eight days while detained at the Florence Staging Facility, a short-term processing facility run by ICE.

By the time Deris Perez Martinez was transferred to Florence Correctional Center, he was nearly in a diabetic coma, he told the Star. Perez Martinez shared his medical records with the Star, showing his blood sugar had soared to 499 mg/dL, almost five times the normal range.

Another Eloy detainee, Maria Valero Brinez, said Friday she's five months pregnant with a high-risk pregnancy and fears losing her baby at Eloy, the Star reported. Valero Brinez said she's been bleeding off and on and has been denied routine medical care, despite losing a previous pregnancy due to the same complication she's experiencing now.

text:
WOODLAND, Calif. —

People gathered in Woodland for a march and rally on Tuesday, demanding action after a man who was observing ICE agents in the street was struck by a federal immigration vehicle.

The protest started outside of the Yolo County District Attorney's Office and will end outside of the Yolo County courthouse.

Speakers at the rally include former Woodland Mayor Vicky Fernandez and Antonio Moreida, the man who said he was hit by the ICE vehicle.

Moreida said he was struck by a federal immigration SUV while documenting ICE activity. Footage of the incident was captured by multiple cameras and is being investigation by Woodland police.

Protestors are calling for three actions: for the Yolo County District Attorney to prosecute the ICE agent involved, for Attorney General Rob Bonta to take over the case if charges are not filed within a reasonable time, and for Woodland police to disclose all communications with ICE.

"This is not acceptable behavior, and we need our government at the local, state and federal level to support us as citizens and, as some people are not citizens, but they need to be treated with humanity and dignity," Steve Murphy with Indivisible Yolo, said.

The Department of Homeland Security initially said ICE did not hit a pedestrian and that "an agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes."

Woodland police disputed DHS' claims, saying the agency's statement was "inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed" by the department's investigators.

An ICE spokesperson then issued a statement that said, "Our officers deliberately attempted to avoid making contact with this anti-ICE protestor and drive around him, while also braking. We strongly urge individuals to not stand in the middle of active roadways while a law enforcement vehicle is approaching."

Woodland police disputed DHS' claims, saying the agency's statement was "inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed" by the department's investigators.

Woodland police said investigators determined the pedestrian did not jump or slide off the hood of the vehicle. They added the the driver applied the brakes before the collision.

Police said its investigating the collision independently and will submit a complete investigation to the district attorney's office for review.

The Yolo County District Attorney's Office said they have not yet received the report and therefore have no comment at this time.

text:
In Brief

Supreme Court denies emergency request to reinstate administrative closure

Agreement between Trump administration and Texas blocks postponing deportation cases

Federal judge Reed O’Connor approved agreement declaring Biden rule unlawful

Cities including Baltimore and Centro Legal de la Raza challenged the agreement

The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three U.S. cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure,” while litigation continues in the dispute.

The Supreme Court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump’s first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges “effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country.”

Trump’s administration and the state then jointly asked U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O’Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O’Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O’Connor’s decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump’s administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using “manufactured litigation” with “ideologically aligned” Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.

text:
Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, a 43-year-old man from Guatemala who was arrested by federal immigration authorities in Escondido and transferred to the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego on Oct. 9, died at the facility just over two weeks later on Saturday.

His death was the 30th in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody this year and the 63rd of President Donald Trump’s second term. It comes amid heightened scrutiny of ICE practices and heavy criticism of conditions inside the center by detainees, activists and elected officials.

An ICE news release said facility staff found Jimenez unresponsive in a cell and tried to wake him at 11:31 a.m. before contacting medical personnel, declaring a medical emergency and calling 911. CPR was administered at 11:38 a.m. and paramedics from California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection arrived at 11:52, about 20 minutes after he was found unresponsive.

He was pronounced dead at 12:23 p.m., less than one hour after staff first noticed his condition.

Deaths in ICE detention have increased under the Trump administration’s unprecedented mass deportation campaign from 26 in former President Joe Biden’s four years in office.

This is the first death reported at Otay Mesa in Trump’s second term.

San Diego County Supervisors Terra Lawson-Remer and Paloma Aguirre held a press conference Tuesday afternoon to insist on cooperation with inspections and a new investigation.

“My heart goes out to their family,” Aguirre said. “The men and women detained are not abstract numbers. They’re members of our community.”

The San Diego County Supervisors sued ICE and CoreCivic, the private company that operates the Otay Mesa Detention Center and other immigration facilities, to force an inspection in June.

A three-part inewsource investigation published later that month found dozens of immigrants who described deteriorating health and inadequate care at Otay Mesa Detention Center in court records, a disproportionate number of ambulance calls for seizures, and care described by a detainee who was a Type 1 diabetic that medical experts said was “potentially life threatening.”

More recently, the county found that the facility failed to promptly report confirmed tuberculosis cases to county health inspectors. The litigation over the county inspections is ongoing, and a mediation meeting between the parties in court is scheduled for Thursday.

“No one should lose their basic human rights just because they’re behind bars,” said Lawson-Remer, chair of the county board of supervisors. “We should not have to sue the federal government every time a public health officer needs to walk inside an ICE detention facility.”

Lawson-Remer and Aguirre said Tuesday they have sent a letter to ICE and CoreCivic demanding that they cooperate with a San Diego County Medical Examiners’ Office investigation, preserve records related to Jimenez’s death, and provide a written account of actions taken to correct problems found in the county’s June inspection.

A spokesperson for CoreCivic said in a statement that, “We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care,” and directed further questions to ICE.

CoreCivic said ICE is responsible for reviewing deaths in custody.

ICE said Jimenez had been deported three times. It said his death was under investigation and that an autopsy would be conducted to determine the official cause and manner of death.

ICE said he was convicted for selling liquor to a minor and had been arrested several times.

83% of people held at Otay Mesa on a typical day last fiscal year had no criminal conviction, which is about the same as the national figure, according to the most recent data posted by ICE.

By LINDSAY WHITEHURST

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court declined to intervene Tuesday in a dispute over a Biden-era immigration regulation that allowed immigration judges to pause some deportation proceedings.

The high court turned down a request from Democratic-led cities who say the rule was used to help crime victims and neglected juveniles and should be revived.

Texas and the Trump administration agreed to a court order blocking the regulation after the state sued. Texas alleged that the practice called administrative closure was dramatically expanded under former President Joe Biden and effectively allowed people to stay in the country indefinitely.

The cities of Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio and New Haven, Connecticut, along with the legal group Centro Legal de la Raza, had asked to join the case to defend the regulation. They filed an emergency appeal before the Supreme Court after a judge refused to allow them to intervene.

Represented by the group Democracy Forward, they argued that Texas and the Trump administration had worked together to allow the regulation to be permanently blocked in court, bypassing a public rulemaking process.

The Justice Department had urged the justices to deny the appeal, saying the cities had no legal standing to challenge the settlement and they had not shown they’d suffer immediate legal harm.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to unfreeze a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration judges to use their discretion to temporarily close deportation cases for immigrants.

In an unsigned order, the court rejected a request from three cities with large migrant populations — Baltimore as well as Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut — to pause an agreement between Texas and the Trump administration that threw out the policy.

There were no noted dissents.

The regulation, known as “administrative closure,” gives immigration judges discretion to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for migrants while the migrants seek humanitarian protections or other forms of legal status in the country.

The Trump administration has pushed to curtail judicial processes for unlawful migrants, and the high court’s conservative majority has been largely deferential to executive authority in the area of immigration policy.

Deportation hearings in immigration court are legal proceedings initiated by the Department of Homeland Security in which an immigration judge determines whether a migrant should be removed from the United States. Often, an immigration judge will pause or dismiss a case to allow the individual to pursue legal relief.

While dismissals were viewed as a positive outcome for migrants, immigration attorneys have said the Trump administration, as part of its immigration crackdown, began to use dismissals to detain people at immigration courts and place them into expedited removal without allowing them to fight their case.

Last year, federal agents arrested hundreds of migrants at immigration courts — in some cases after their deportation cases were dismissed.

In court filings, the cities argued that administrative closure promoted “efficiency” and protected “due process rights.” They also argued that the practice has existed in various forms for decades.

In June, the state of Texas sued the federal government, arguing that the policy granted “indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country.”

While dismissals were viewed as a positive outcome for migrants, immigration attorneys have said the Trump administration, as part of its immigration crackdown, began to use dismissals to detain people at immigration courts and place them into expedited removal without allowing them to fight their case.

Last year, federal agents arrested hundreds of migrants at immigration courts -- in some cases after their deportation cases were dismissed.

In court filings, the cities argued that administrative closure promoted "efficiency" and protected "due process rights." They also argued that the practice has existed in various forms for decades.

In June, the state of Texas sued the federal government, arguing that the policy granted "indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country."

text:
San Diego officials expressed concern Tuesday after an immigrant detainee’s death at Otay Mesa Detention Center, continuing what civil rights activists and other critics call a grim trend of increasing deaths in ICE custody.

Shortly after 11:30 a.m. Saturday, a staff member at the Department of Homeland Security facility “called a medical emergency after finding an unresponsive (detained) individual in their assigned living area,” according to a statement from CoreCivic, the private-prison company that runs the center.

“Responding medical staff arrived quickly, began lifesaving measures and called for emergency medical services … EMS arrived and continued those efforts, but the individual was pronounced deceased before being transported from the facility,” the statement said.

The company released no further information about the person or the circumstances of the death.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care,” the Tennessee-based company stated. “Our government partners at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement … were notified immediately.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

During a news conference Tuesday, county Supervisors Paloma Aguirre and Terra Lawson-Remer called on the Trump administration and CoreCivic to cooperate with county investigators and clear the way for ongoing inspections at the Otay Mesa center, near the U.S.-Mexico border.

“Earlier this year, we took ICE to federal court for blocking public health inspections amid disturbing reports of unsafe conditions at Otay Mesa,” Lawson-Remer said. “Now a man has died inside that facility. When the federal government flouts due process and shuts the door on independent health inspectors, we cannot look away. We need answers, accountability and the ability to protect the health and safety of everyone held inside.”

The lawsuit “wasn’t a political exercise – it was a necessary step to protect human lives,” Aguirre said.

“Ensuring basic human rights, medical oversight and safety within our borders is non-negotiable,” she said. “ICE and CoreCivic must be held accountable for these failures right now, before another family is forced to suffer this same unimaginable grief.”

The San Diego County Medical Examiner’s Office conducted an autopsy on the detainee Monday, according to the supervisors. A cause of death has yet to be released.

During their briefing, Aguirre and Lawson-Remer also announced that they had sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE Director David Venturella demanding that the latter agency and CoreCivic take the following steps:

Cooperate fully with the medical examiner’s investigation, including making staff available for interviews and turning over all requested records, logs and video;

Preserve all data related to the death, including medical records, any sick-call requests, housing-unit logs staff rounds and video;

Provide a timeline of care from intake to death, including any health conditions noted upon the person’s entry, requests for medical help, medical visits and welfare checks;

Where privacy law requires it, share this information with the family and, with their consent, with the county;

Provide a written accounting of corrective actions taken since the county inspection in June, including improvements to tuberculosis reporting, vaccine supply and any delays in providing prescribed medical devices;

Confirm that the appropriate consulate has been notified if the decedent was a foreign national and publish ICE’s death notice and detainee death report without delay; and

Allow ongoing inspection access under county public health authority so its team can verify that the listed measures are being taken.

After ICE denied supervisors access to the detention center, the county sued and secured a federal court order allowing an inspection in June.

That scrutiny identified failures to promptly report suspected tuberculosis cases, a lack of vaccines in stock and delays in providing necessary medical equipment, according to the supervisors.

In September, the county issued another notice of noncompliance after a suspected tuberculosis case allegedly went unreported for about three weeks.

The county’s public health officer is evaluating additional oversight measures, including follow-up inspections. Litigation over the county’s ongoing inspection authority remains unresolved, with the parties slated to meet again this Thursday.

Aguirre and Lawson-Remer requested a written response from federal officials by Nov. 10.

While exact numbers of such fatalities are elusive, the ACLU claimed last month that at least 57 people have died while in U.S. immigration detention since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term – more than double the number of deaths recorded in the previous four years combined.

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in June, the mortality rate of ICE detainees – based on 52 known deaths at the time – had reached its highest level in over a decade and more than doubled since Trump’s current term began. The rate at that time was nearly four times that of the Biden administration, and more than 2 1/2 times as high as that of the first Trump administration, the watchdog organization reported.

“Urgent action is needed to address this crisis and prevent further deaths,” the report concluded.

title: Trump's DOJ sues University of Delaware over in-state tuition policies for immigrant students - WHYY
description:
Who qualifies for in-state tuition?
“In-state resident tuition policies are a set of conditions that people can meet to get the in-state tuition rate.” These policies can account for circumstances beyond a student’s immigration status.
Baker pointed to military families as one example, explaining that in Virginia, children of active-duty service members whose parents file taxes in the state may qualify for in-state tuition.
She eventually learned about another program, “First State Promise,” which allowed her to pay the in-state tuition rate.
The outcome could have implications for students who rely on residency policies to qualify for in-state tuition.
text:
What are journalists missing from the state of Delaware? What would you most like WHYY News to cover? Let us know.

For Diana Sanroman-Espinosa, the difference between attending the University of Delaware as a student with Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals status and attending as a lawful permanent resident came down to thousands of dollars.

Her family paid over $10,000 out of pocket for her first semester at UD, she said. After she obtained permanent residency, she became eligible for financial aid and scholarships, bringing her out-of-pocket cost down to about $200 for a semester.

Now a graduate student at UD, Sanroman-Espinosa is watching as the university faces a legal challenge from the Trump administration’s U.S. Department of Justice over its tuition policies for students without lawful immigration status.

On Oct. 1, the DOJ filed a complaint against UD, arguing that the university’s student residency classification policy allows some students without lawful immigration status to qualify for in-state tuition, while denying the same benefit to U.S. citizens from other states. The department characterizes the policy as unequal treatment favoring undocumented students.

UD said it is reviewing the complaint and declined to comment further because the matter is pending.

The case comes amid a broader Trump administration effort to challenge state policies that allow certain students without lawful immigration status to pay in-state tuition rates. The dispute raises questions about how colleges determine residency for tuition purposes, who can qualify for those rates and what the financial consequences could be for students if the policies are restricted.

Who qualifies for in-state tuition?

Dominique Baker, an associate professor of education and public policy at the University of Delaware, said residency policies can apply to a broader range of students than the debate over undocumented students might suggest.

“It’s a set of policies that say ‘who are people who can qualify for the in-state tuition rate.’ It’s really important to say that, because people often think that that means that this is only talking about undocumented students. That could not be further from the truth,” Baker said. “In-state resident tuition policies are a set of conditions that people can meet to get the in-state tuition rate.”

These policies can account for circumstances beyond a student’s immigration status. Baker pointed to military families as one example, explaining that in Virginia, children of active-duty service members whose parents file taxes in the state may qualify for in-state tuition.

“If you are the child of an active-duty service member and your parent files taxes in the state of Virginia, as an example, then you can qualify for in-state resident tuition,” Baker said. “That is really popular in the state of Virginia, in part because there is such a large military presence.”

Baker said residency policies can help colleges fulfill their public mission by making higher education more affordable for the people they serve. Limiting access could lead some students to delay college, choose a different educational path or decide not to enroll at all.

A student’s experience navigating college

Sanroman-Espinosa came to the United States from Mexico at age 2 and later completed her primary education in the U.S. She attended UD for her first semester as a DACA recipient before obtaining permanent residency the following spring.

When she began applying to college, she said she didn’t realize her immigration status would complicate the process. During an application meeting with her high school guidance counselor, she encountered an error related to her Social Security number.

“I was like, ‘It is valid, I got it through DACA,’” she recalled. “And counselors were like, ‘Oh, DACA students have to apply to college differently. Well, we’ve never done that, so you’re kind of on your own.’”

Her teachers stepped in to help, taking time away from school to accompany her to UD offices. Sanroman-Espinosa had earned a 4.2 GPA and ranked among the top students in her graduating class. Still, she wasn’t sure if she could afford higher education at all.

“I was a straight-A student, I was top 20 of my class, I was an honor student,” she said. “It was just insane to them that because of my legal status, I wasn’t able to go to college when I had all these other criterias that would basically [make] me a perfect student to go to college. But because of my legal status, I wasn’t allowed to.”

After several meetings with university staff, Sanroman-Espinosa said she was initially told she would be classified as an international student. She eventually learned about another program, “First State Promise,” which allowed her to pay the in-state tuition rate. However, the program did not provide the financial aid she needed.

“That just makes tuition be the same price as being an in-state student,” she said. “Other than that, no scholarships were allowed.” She said she wasn’t able to submit a Free Application for Federal Student Aid or FAFSA as a DACA student.

Her family paid about $10,000 out of pocket for her first semester. Her parents used savings to help cover the cost, and she recalled that her mother even had sold her car.

“I sacrificed a lot of my personal time to make sure that I didn’t miss those deadlines,” she said.

During her first semester, Sanroman-Espinosa left the country for about a month to complete the process that led to her permanent residency. She described the experience as one of the most traumatic periods of her life, explaining that she traveled with her brother to a part of Mexico where neither had family nearby to support them.

After returning to Delaware, she notified university staff that her immigration status had changed. The following semester, she qualified for merit-based scholarships and submitted the FAFSA successfully. Sanroman-Espinosa remembers checking her student account and realizing that her out-of-pocket cost had dropped from thousands to hundreds.

“I stayed the same student from the fall semester to the spring semester,” she said. “The only thing that changed was my legal status and that made a huge difference in the financial aid I got.” She said it was because she “qualified for all these merit-based scholarships.”

In-state tuition does not eliminate every financial barrier

Even when students qualify for in-state tuition, the cost of higher education can remain a significant obstacle. Students without lawful immigration status generally cannot access federal student aid based on that status alone, including federal Pell Grants and federal student loans. Eligibility for state aid, university scholarships and private scholarships varies.

Baker said that these barriers remain even when a student qualifies for the lower tuition.

“There are a number of financial barriers that still remain even when an in-state resident tuition policy is in place, because it is the case that these students — particularly when we’re talking about undocumented students — they do not have access to the Pell Grant. They do not have access to federal student loans,” Baker said.

Sanroman-Espinosa’s experience illustrates the distinction: Qualifying for in-state tuition helped her avoid higher tuition rates, but it did not provide the scholarships or federal aid she later became eligible for after obtaining permanent residency.

Sanroman-Espinosa also worries that students could lose an opportunity to pursue higher education because of costs beyond their control. For her, the issue isn’t simply paying more for college, but whether some students can continue at all.

“It would just be an extreme financial strain on them,” she said. “It makes me sad, because if that were to happen, I think there would be a lot of conversations of students being like: ‘My education journey ends here.’”

What happens next?

The U.S. Justice Department’s complaint puts UD’s tuition policy under legal scrutiny. The university has said it is reviewing the complaint and will not comment further while the matter is pending.

The outcome could have implications for students who rely on residency policies to qualify for in-state tuition. Baker said limiting these policies could affect college enrollment and the educational choices available to students.

For Sanroman-Espinosa, the dispute brings back memories of how difficult it was to find help when she first applied to college. She did not learn about the tuition program until she attended multiple meetings and submitted requests for assistance. She later helped other DACA students who were also unfamiliar with the process.

Her message to students facing similar uncertainty is to keep pursuing their education and not mistake financial or legal barriers for a lack of academic ability.

“If you’re an amazing student, you’re an amazing student no matter what,” she said. “If anything, the work you put [in] for your studies is enough. Just keep fighting for your education.”

text:
FRESNO, Calif. – Congressman Jim Costa (CA-21) was joined by Congressman Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Fresno County Supervisor Luis Chavez, and Nora Zaragoza-Yáñez of Faith in the Valley in a virtual press conference today to address recent immigration enforcement operations across the San Joaquin Valley and Central Coast and demand greater transparency and accountability from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

During the press conference, Costa highlighted his efforts to lead members of California’s congressional delegation, including U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, in demanding answers from federal immigration authorities about enforcement priorities, detention practices, and the impact of recent operations on California communities.

BACKGROUND

Since January 2025, the Trump Administration has expanded federal immigration enforcement operations across the country, including in California's San Joaquin Valley and Central Coast. Recent enforcement activity beginning October 2026, has raised concerns among local families, community advocates, and elected officials about detention practices, enforcement priorities, and access to information about individuals taken into custody.

In response, Congressman Costa led a group of 12 legislators in a letter raising serious concerns about federal immigration enforcement tactics and emphasized the responsibility of federal agencies to operate with transparency, accountability, and respect for the constitutional rights and safety of California residents.

In their letter, the lawmakers requested detailed responses to the following:

Explain the purpose and duration of ICE operations across California, including increased enforcement activity in the San Joaquin Valley beginning October 5, 2026.

Clarify immigration enforcement priorities by identifying the criteria ICE agents use to question, arrest, and detain individuals, including whether operations are targeted or involve broader enforcement activities.

Provide transparency on arrests and detentions by releasing a county-by-county breakdown on individuals detained since October 5, including those prior criminal convictions, pending criminal charges, or no criminal record.

Ensure proper agent vetting and training by detailing background checks, screening requirements, and training standards, including whether any requirements have been modified, shortened, or waived.

Strengthen personnel accountability and oversight by requesting details on ICE officer deployments, professional conduct standards, agent training on constitutional rights and use of force, and procedures for investigating alleged misconduct, including any administrative review or personnel investigation initiated following the October 9 incident involving an off-duty ICE officer in Fresno.

Protect due process and access to essential services by demanding transparency on detention locations, processing and transfer procedures, access to legal counsel, notification of rights, family communication, and necessary medical care following an arrest.

Strengthen coordination with local authorities by clarifying whether state and local law enforcement agencies and elected official were notified or consulted before ICE operations began and outlining protocols to ensure public safety and address community concerns.

The lawmakers also emphasized that enforcing federal immigration law does not diminish the government's responsibility to protect public safety, uphold due process, and ensure accountability for the actions of federal officers.

The Members of Congress and Senators requested a written response from ICE and DHS no later than October 30, 2026.

The letter was signed by: Congressman Jim Costa (CA-21), Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Representatives Zoe Lofgren (CA-18), Josh Harder (CA-09), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Adam Gray (CA-13), Lou Correa (CA-46), Gil Cisneros (CA-31), Robert Garcia (CA-42), Nanette Barragán (CA-44), and Norma Torres (CA-35).

text:
SALINAS, Calif. —

Protesters gathered outside the Monterey County Jail in Salinas on Tuesday following reports of federal immigration agents near the facility.

Later Tuesday, the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office placed the jail on lockdown. The sheriff's office said it was suspending new bookings and inmate releases and closing the facility to public visitation, except for attorneys visiting clients.

The office said the temporary measures were being taken out of an abundance of caution to ensure everyone’s safety.

KSBW captured video of a person who identified themself as an ICE operative saying agents were conducting a targeted operation involving people at the jail.

A small crowd gathered outside the facility, with protesters calling for the agents to leave. Some shouted profanities.

KSBW video also captured a tense exchange between Monterey County Supervisor Wendy Root Askew and an ICE agent about the jail’s decision to pause inmate releases.

The agent questioned whether holding people who might otherwise be released violated their Fourth Amendment rights.

Askew said the county would not release anyone at a location where ICE was present and clarified that the county policy concerns staging immigration enforcement.

In September, Monterey County supervisors adopted a policy prohibiting county property from being used as a staging area, processing location or operations base for civil immigration enforcement. The policy includes exceptions for activities such as the lawful execution of a judicial warrant and criminal enforcement.

The Sheriff’s Office said Monday it had not been notified of the reported activity and could not verify the identity of those involved or the operation’s purpose. Federal agencies are not required to notify the Sheriff’s Office when conducting independent operations, the office said.

“The Monterey County Sheriff’s Office remains committed to complying with California law, including the California Values Act (SB 54) and the TRUTH Act, which establish requirements and limitations regarding local law enforcement interactions with federal immigration authorities,” the office wrote.

In response to a KSBW inquiry about ICE detentions in Monterey, Santa Cruz and San Benito counties from Oct. 13 to Oct. 27, the Department of Homeland Security said it would not discuss law enforcement operations, citing operational security and officer safety.

DHS said it enforces federal laws daily in the three counties but did not provide county-level detention numbers.

The department also listed five people it described as public safety threats arrested by ICE in California but did not say whether any were arrested in the three counties.

The department said their convictions included homicide, drug trafficking, aggravated assault, burglary, weapons offenses, child cruelty, identity theft and fraud.

text:
A US appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.

The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump's efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the November 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.

The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in. The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Tuesday in the case.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government "asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state's traditional domain, upending the state's policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike."

The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.

The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent a state from counting votes, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people on its list had actually submitted a mail ballot.

Justice Department officials said on October 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.

California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump's fellow Republicans in the midterms.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that ‌limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has long asserted that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.

All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on October 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.

The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.

California says the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data."

"At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt," lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing. "At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election."

Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizens risk wrongly flagging naturalized US citizens for removal from the rolls.

The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. text:
SAN DIEGO, Ca. — Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, a 43-year-old illegal alien from Guatemala, died Oct. 24 while in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego. Jimenez’s criminal history includes a July 2024 conviction for selling liquor to a minor, as well as prior arrests for battery against a spouse, violation of a court order, child abuse, disorderly conduct, providing false identification to a peace officer, and being under the influence of drugs.

At approximately 11:31 a.m. Oct. 24, facility staff observed Jimenez in his assigned safety cell and attempted to wake him after he was unresponsive. Facility staff contacted medical personnel, declared a medical emergency, and called 911. Medical personnel began cardiopulmonary resuscitation at approximately 11:38 a.m. Paramedics from the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection arrived at approximately 11:52 a.m. and continued lifesaving measures. A paramedic pronounced Jimenez deceased at approximately 12:23 p.m.

Jimenez’s death is under investigation. An autopsy will be conducted to determine the official cause and manner of death.

On an unknown date, Jimenez entered the United States at an unknown location without being admitted, inspected, or paroled by an immigration officer. An immigration judge ordered Jimenez removed to Mexico on Oct. 23, 2006, and ERO removed him to Mexico later that day. Jimenez was again removed to Mexico in March 2008 and April 2008, following immigration enforcement encounters and reinstatement of his removal order. In November 2016, U.S. Customs and Border Protection apprehended Jimenez at the Paso Del Norte Port of Entry in El Paso, Texas, and released him pending potential review of relief application with USCIS. He failed to appear for appointment. On Oct. 9, 2026, ERO San Diego encountered Jimenez during enforcement operations in Escondido, California, reinstated his prior final order of removal, and transferred him to the Otay Mesa Detention Center pending removal to Mexico.

Consistent with ICE policy, Enforcement and Removal Operations San Diego completed required notifications to the Department of Homeland Security, the ICE Office of Inspector General, and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility through the Joint Intake Operations Center. ERO San Diego notified Jimenez’s next of kin and the Consulate of Guatemala.

ICE makes official notifications to Congress, non-governmental organization stakeholders, and the media upon reports of in-custody deaths and posts news releases with relevant details on its public website. Information is available in the ICE Newsroom and on the Detainee Death Reporting page.

ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure, and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental, and mental-health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility; a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arriving at a facility; access to medical appointments; and 24-hour emergency care. At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.

The Supreme Court declined Tuesday to intervene in a dispute over a Biden-era immigration policy that allowed immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings, leaving in place a court order blocking the regulation.

The justices rejected an emergency appeal from Democratic-led cities and a legal advocacy group seeking to defend the policy, which they said helped crime victims and neglected juveniles.

In a statement provided to Newsweek by Democracy Forward, which represents the applicants alongside Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann LLP, the applicants and their co-counsel said they were "deeply disappointed" by the decision.

Read More on News

Texas sued to block the practice, known as "administrative closure," arguing that it had expanded dramatically under former President Joe Biden and effectively allowed some immigrants to remain in the United States indefinitely. Texas and the Trump administration later agreed to a court order blocking the regulation. Administrative closure allows immigration judges to temporarily put deportation cases on hold, including for immigrants pursuing humanitarian protections or other forms of legal status in the United States.

Baltimore, Columbus (Ohio), and New Haven (Connecticut), along with the legal group Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the policy. After a judge rejected their request, the cities and the group filed an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court.

"For decades, these procedures have allowed immigration judges to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for people pursuing lawful immigration relief, including survivors of violence, abused and neglected children, and victims and witnesses who cooperate with law enforcement," the applicants and their co-counsel said in a statement.

"Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country."

The Justice Department urged the justices to reject the appeal, arguing that the applicants lacked legal standing to challenge the settlement and had not shown they would suffer immediate legal harm.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued in a filing with the Supreme Court that the cities were using their request to intervene in the case to mount a broader challenge to the settlement.

"This Court should not allow applicants to put the cart before the horse," Sauer wrote. He also argued that the cities had "failed to establish any irreparable harm" while their appeal proceeded.

text:
A detainee died Saturday at the Otay Mesa Detention Center, marking at least the 29th reported death in ICE custody so far this year, after a record 33 deaths in 2025.

At around 11:36 a.m., a staff member at the facility found the person, later identified as 43-year-old Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, unresponsive in their assigned living area, according to a statement from CoreCivic, the private prison company that runs the detention center.

Medical staff attempted lifesaving measures and called for emergency medical services, CoreCivic said. EMS arrived and continued those efforts, but the person was pronounced dead before being transported from the facility, according to CoreCivic.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care,” CoreCivic’s statement continued, adding that ICE was notified immediately.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to request for comment, however later revealed Gutierrez's identity and criminal history.

Gutierrez’s death is under investigation, according to a statement from ICE. An autopsy will be conducted to determine the official cause and manner of death.

The San Diego County Medical Examiner’s office did not have further details as of Tuesday morning. The Mexican Consulate in San Diego said the person who died was not a Mexican national. The same ICE statement said Gutierrez was from Guatemala.

Related Stories

This marks at least the 29th death in ICE custody that the agency has reported, though earlier this year ICE shifted away from reporting deaths of newly released detainees.

The death also comes after months of complaints from people held at the Otay Mesa Detention Center of insufficient medical care, bad food, cold temperatures and more. A report earlier this year from the California Department of Justice found overcrowding, as well as limited access to water and medical care, and other conditions the state attorney general called “substandard” and “subhuman.”

Complaints from detainees also sparked multiple attempts at oversight visits by members of Congress, as well as a health inspection by San Diego County officials.

Two County supervisors were denied access for that inspection earlier this year, then sued ICE and CoreCivic in federal court, with a judge ordering the facility to allow that inspection. The county's report found conditions "generally within state standards" but identified some issues, including two cases of tuberculosis the facility did not communicate according to health protocol.

In the midst of the county’s lawsuit, the Department of Homeland Security announced ICE had purchased the Otay Mesa Detention Center from CoreCivic outright, making it federal property and raising questions about access by state and local agencies for future inspections.

“Those findings were a warning, and this family deserves to know whether anyone listened,” San Diego County Supervisor Paloma Aguirre said in a statement on the death Monday evening.

“ICE and CoreCivic need to reach this family without delay, cooperate fully with a thorough investigation, and share what they find with the family and the public,” Aguirre continued. “Our inspection raised serious concerns. ICE and CoreCivic must answer for them and fix them, so no other family has to wait for answers the way this one is waiting now.”

They argued the rule was approved by Congress, giving authority to immigration judges to halt deportation proceedings for immigrants who have pending applications and qualify for legal status.

The plaintiffs said that crime victims who are undocumented might stop cooperating with local law enforcement if they are at risk of being deported, even if they qualify for specific visas that help them stay in the country during the criminal prosecution. The cities also argued that they could lose tax revenue if their residents are deported.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court issued a one-sentence ruling denying a request from the plaintiffs to protect the procedures that had been in place during the Biden administration.

The case can go back to a lower court to decide if the cities can intervene, or the cities can ask the Supreme Court to have a hearing.

text:
By Andrew Chung

Oct 27 (Reuters) – The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant ​legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure,” while litigation continues in ‌the dispute.

The Supreme Court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day.

Baltimore and the other litigants said the ‌federal government ​improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation. In a statement, the litigants ⁠and the lawyers representing them from the ⁠liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday’s decision.

“Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country,” they said in the statement.

“This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny,” ​they added.

Representatives from the Justice Department and the Texas attorney general’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same ⁠person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition ⁠or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative ​closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS ​OF CASES

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending ‌the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump’s first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office ⁠that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges “effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country.”

Trump’s administration and ⁠the state then jointly asked US District Judge ‌Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O’Connor ⁠did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and ​the legal ‌services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend ​the rule, but ⁠O’Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O’Connor’s decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump’s administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using “manufactured litigation” with “ideologically aligned” Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in ​New York; editing by Will Dunham)

text:
A judge denied Monday a request to hold Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak in contempt of court in a lawsuit concerning immigration arrest records.

While acknowledging that Kozak and his counsel, Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss, didn’t fully comply with a court order requiring them to produce immigration arrest records, Laramie County Judge Robin Cooley wrote in her decision that there wasn’t clear evidence showing their noncompliance was willful.

A Colorado law firm requested records from the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office related to a deputy’s April immigration arrest of Mario Fabian Valenzuela-Robles, a Mexican national with three children who are U.S. citizens. The legal practice, Lichter Immigration, is representing Valenzuela-Robles in ongoing immigration proceedings, and the evidence is vital to his defense in federal court, the firm has said.

Alleging that it faced barriers to obtaining certain records, Lichter Immigration, represented by former Wyoming GOP Chair Drake Hill, sued Kozak and his office in July. Later that month, Cooley ordered Kozak to provide additional records concerning Valenzuela-Robles’ detention.

But Kozak and Voss didn’t fully comply with that order, missing the agreed-upon deadline by two days. Some documents were in a format the plaintiffs couldn’t open or read. Kozak’s office didn’t provide a log explaining why certain documents were withheld. Because of these shortcomings, Lichter Immigration requested Cooley to hold Kozak and his office in contempt of court.

But noncompliance alone, Cooley wrote in her decision, “does not establish civil contempt.”

“Plaintiffs have not proven by clear and convincing evidence that the failure to comply was willful,” Cooley wrote. Kozak also noted this point. “The law says you have to willfully, you know, withhold the evidence, and so of course we didn’t do that,” he said in a phone call to WyoFile.

That being said, Cooley continued, just because the defendants’ noncompliance wasn’t willful “does not make it acceptable.”

She noted that the defendants helped draft the terms of the order compelling production of records. Cooley also pointed out that Hill had asked Voss in an August letter to address concerns about the records.

The defendants’ failure to address those concerns “prolonged a dispute that should have been resolved without the necessity of further Court proceedings,” Cooley wrote.

While declining to hold Kozak in contempt, Cooley ordered the sheriff and Voss to provide within 10 days a log explaining why certain records were withheld, records in a readable format and written explanations addressing each of the alleged missing records the plaintiffs had identified.

Kozak said he had talked with Voss and expects to comply with the order in the next couple of days.

A federal court in Boston has temporarily blocked a new immigration policy that would limit the time refugees have to respond if their refugee status were revoked. Under the Trump administration’s new rule, refugees only have 10 days to prepare a case if U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services decides to end their status, down from the 30 days they’ve had since the early 1980s.

The ruling comes one day after the International Institute of New England and other New England-based refugee advocacy organizations filed a class action lawsuit in Boston on Monday.

Judge Julia E. Kobick has yet to rule on the other aspects of the lawsuit: The advocacy groups also sued the Trump administration over the decision to not process applications for green cards from refugees who were admitted during the Biden administration, and requiring USCIS to re-interview refugees who have already been vetted.

The Department of Homeland Security said in an email to NHPR that these policies are about strengthening accountability, alleging that there was an “alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures under the Biden Administration in order to rush processing and maximize the number of refugees admitted to the United States.”

“This lawsuit is yet another frivolous attempt to disrupt the Trump administration’s commitment to enforce our country’s immigration laws as intended by Congress,” wrote USCIS Spokesman Zach Kahler.

Over the past 15 years, more than 5,000 refugees have been resettled in New Hampshire, according to data from the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services. But Thielman said the outcome of this case could affect about 550 refugees admitted to New Hampshire during the Biden administration, about half of whom don’t have a green card.

“We want the court to tell the government to stop re-vetting refugees who arrived during the last administration. We think that's unfair just to target people who arrived during one administration. And actually, that's unconstitutional against the law,” said

text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, rejected an emergency request to restore immigration judges' authority to temporarily close certain deportation cases, leaving in place a nationwide restriction that prevents judges from using a Biden-era regulation to pause proceedings while immigrants pursue other forms of legal protection.

The justices denied an application from three cities and an immigrant legal advocacy group seeking to suspend a federal court judgment that invalidated the regulation. Their one-sentence order offered no explanation, and no justice publicly dissented.

The restriction stems from a June 22 lawsuit filed by Texas against the Trump administration. That same day, the Justice Department agreed with the state that the regulation was unlawful, and U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor entered a consent judgment vacating the rule nationwide.

The practice, known as administrative closure, allowed immigration judges to remove cases from their active calendars while immigrants awaited decisions on humanitarian protections, visa petitions or other applications that could permit them to remain in the United States. With the restriction still in effect, affected proceedings can move forward while those applications are pending.

Administrative closure has been used by crime victims cooperating with law enforcement, children seeking special immigration protections, and immigrants awaiting decisions on other applications. Cases removed from active court calendars can later be reopened. Approximately 360,000 immigrants received administrative closure between 1990 and 2026, according to government statistics.

The Biden administration formally authorized the practice under a 2024 regulation, restoring discretion restricted during President Donald Trump's first term. After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department changed its position, arguing that immigration judges lacked authority to suspend deportation proceedings indefinitely.

Texas challenged the regulation, claiming that it exceeded federal immigration law by allowing judges to postpone decisions on whether immigrants should be deported. O'Connor's June judgment also restricted the administration from adopting future regulations permitting similar administrative closures without express authorization from Congress.

Some immigration courts had already begun reopening administratively closed cases by September, according to the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, which reported that courts were interpreting the June judgment broadly. The organization also described concerns about the treatment of requests to terminate removal proceedings, a separate procedure that can end a deportation case.

Baltimore, Maryland; Columbus, Ohio; New Haven, Connecticut; and the California-based legal services organization Centro Legal de la Raza sought to intervene in the lawsuit, accusing Texas and the Trump administration of coordinating litigation to eliminate the rule while bypassing federal rulemaking requirements.

Represented by Democracy Forward, the challengers argued that the agreement circumvented the Administrative Procedure Act, which generally requires federal agencies to provide public notice and an opportunity for comment before repealing regulations.

The cities warned that eliminating administrative closure could discourage immigrant crime victims from cooperating with police and increase deportations among residents. Centro Legal said the restriction would increase demand for legal assistance as more immigration proceedings moved forward.

O'Connor rejected their request to intervene on August 21, finding that the cities' claims of lost tax revenue, reduced crime victim cooperation, and other potential harms were too speculative or indirect to establish legal standing. He also found that Centro Legal's anticipated increase in legal services costs was insufficient to justify intervention.

Federal lawyers subsequently urged the Supreme Court to deny emergency relief, arguing that the challengers lacked standing and had failed to demonstrate immediate harm. The Justice Department also maintained that the June judgment applied prospectively and did not automatically require immigration courts to reopen cases previously placed in administrative closure.

After the Fifth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to suspend the judgment, the cities and Centro Legal asked the Supreme Court to restore the regulation while their appeal proceeded.
