text:
EL PASO, Texas – An illegal alien from Mexico was sentenced in a federal court in El Paso to 110 months in prison for conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in serious bodily injury, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents, Manuel Alejandro Melendez-Cereceres aka “Monstro,” 42, was a member of an alien smuggling organization. In his role, Melendez-Cereceres recruited and coordinated drivers and vehicles to transport smuggled aliens either to harboring locations or to exchange points where the aliens would be picked up by an additional driver and transported further into the United States.

On May 15, 2025, U.S. Border Patrol agents in Tornillo interdicted a smuggling event and apprehended a foot guide. During the smuggling event led by the guide, one of the illegal aliens being smuggled fell from a fence and suffered serious bodily injuries which led to surgery for a right hip socket fracture, a right hip joint fracture, a sacral fracture and a right heel bone fracture. Through a search of the foot guide’s cell phone, agents discovered communications between the guide and Melendez-Cereceres.

Melendez-Cereceres was arrested at his residence in June 2025 and indicted for four counts related to alien smuggling. On June 11, 2026, he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in serious bodily injury. In addition to the nine-year federal prison sentence, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone also ordered a money judgement in the amount of $672,101.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations and the U.S. Border Patrol investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Mathew Engelbaum prosecuted the case.

The case is supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the Department’s lead effort in combating high-impact human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations (TCOs). A highly successful partnership between the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes human smuggling and trafficking and related immigration crimes that impact public safety and border security. JTFA’s mission is to target the leaders and organizers of Cartels and TCOs involved in human smuggling and trafficking throughout the Americas. The Attorney General has elevated and expanded JTFA to target the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking groups operating not only in Mexico and the Northern Triangle countries of Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras, but also in Canada, the Caribbean and the maritime border, and elsewhere. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by the Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, the Office of International Affairs, and the Office of Enforcement Operations, among others, JTFA has dedicated Assistant U.S. Attorney prosecutors from the Southern District of California; District of Arizona; District of New Mexico; Western and Southern Districts of Texas; Southern District of Florida; Northern District of New York; and District of Vermont. JTFA also partners with other U.S. Attorney’s Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS, including HSI and Customs and Border Protection, Border Patrol and Office of Field Operations as well as FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 483 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and/or trafficking; more than 436 U.S. convictions; and more than 371 significant jail sentences imposed, and forfeitures of substantial assets.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure,” while litigation continues in the dispute.

Advertisement

The Supreme Court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Advertisement

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump’s first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

Advertisement

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges “effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country.”

Trump’s administration and the state then jointly asked US District Judge Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O’Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Advertisement

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O’Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O’Connor’s decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump’s administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using “manufactured litigation” with “ideologically aligned” Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

Advertisement

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; editing by Will Dunham)

the arrangement.[br /][br /]"It is impossible to convey how the government's refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak," the missive remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so, but it looks like we're going to need a court order. I'm sorry that it comes to that," Ellison told CNN's Sara Sidner Tuesday morning. "Any prosecutor can tell you, you can't go forward with half a file. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.

text:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration in a dispute about whether the administration and Texas engaged in an "egregious collusion" to scrap a Biden-era immigration regulation.

The court, in a brief and unsigned opinion on Oct. 27, declined to immediately restore the regulation, which allowed immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. None of the justices publicly dissented.

Three cities with substantial immigrant populations and a group that provides legal services to immigrants said the administration is trying to get around the federal rules for repealing a regulation. Instead of proposing a change and seeking public comment, the cities said, the administration backed a legal challenge to the rule by Texas.

When the cities − Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – and Centro Legal de la Raza asked a federal judge in Texas to let them defend the policy since the federal government would not, the judge said they lacked a legal right to get involved.

In an emergency request, the challengers asked the Supreme Court to put the policy back into effect while they appeal the judge's ruling. They said the abrupt policy change could affect hundreds of thousands of immigration cases, including those involving people eligible for lawful status.

"Rather than follow the law and allow the public to be heard, the Department of Justice colluded with Texas to erase longstanding immigration procedures in a single day, putting families, survivors of violence, and entire communities at risk," said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, which is representing the challengers.

The Justice Department argued that because a federal judge ruled that the legal-services group and the cities can't defend the rule in court, they also can't ask the Supreme Court to get involved before that ruling is potentially overturned through their ongoing appeal.

"This Court should not allow applicants to put the cart before the horse," the government told the justices in a filing.

The Justice Department also said the challengers' assertions of the number of immigrants who will be affected without immediate intervention is speculative.

Under the rule adopted in 2024, immigration judges can pause deportation proceedings under certain circumstances, including when a crime victim or witness is helping law enforcement investigate or prosecute a crime.

The cities say the rule codified immigration court procedures that existed in some form for decades but that have become controversial. Critics say the procedures are a form of amnesty.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- Rep. Jim Costa and several California lawmakers have sent a letter to Acting ICE Director David Venturella seeking greater transparency about ongoing immigration enforcement operations they say have been carried out across the state.

The lawmakers said they have received little to no information about ICE operations that have been reported in communities including Fresno, Madera and Kerman.

Local leaders say the reported increase in enforcement activity has sparked fear and unrest throughout the Central Valley.

"I have never seen the level of fear in our communities, fear of going to work, fear of going to school, fear of going shopping," Costa said.

Costa, joined by Rep. Salud Carbajal and other local leaders, called for answers regarding the reported increase in ICE activity. In the letter, the lawmakers request accountability and information about the agency's operations.

"They've been very lacking in transparency and their responsibility to respond as they should to members of Congress," Costa said.

Local organizations estimate that about 100 people were detained in the Central Valley in recent weeks and say that number has since increased. They also report impacts on the region's workforce, particularly in agriculture and construction.

According to local advocates, some processing plants have experienced a 25% to 30% drop in attendance, while homebuilders have reported difficulties finding workers.

During a press briefing on Monday, advocates also criticized ICE's tactics, alleging that enforcement operations target workplaces and citing what they describe as documented examples of racial profiling.

"No one should be treated with such brutality. We, both as a community and a country, should not tolerate these violent ICE tactics, thuggish tactics," Carbajal said.

Carbajal also questioned the timing of the reported enforcement surge.

"It's not coincidental. This is happening right around the election; they are deporting individuals who are undocumented. They are detaining gobs and gobs of American citizens," he said.

Advocates further claim that some people detained in the Central Valley have been transferred to detention facilities elsewhere in California. They also allege that detainees from outside the state have been flown into the Fresno Processing Center.

"They were actually transported from Texas, from Florida, from New Mexico. Those types of tactics are just cruel," Supervisor Chavez said.

The lawmakers have asked Venturella to respond to their questions by Oct. 30. ABC30 reached out to ICE for comment and was awaiting a response at the time of reporting.

text:
The parents of Alex Pretti, a Minneapolis intensive-care nurse who was shot and killed by federal immigration agents in January, spoke publicly for the first time on Tuesday.

They accused the Department of Justice (DOJ) of denying them information about the investigation, as well as ignoring them.

"We are here begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right," Susan Pretti, Alex's mother, said.

Susan Pretti, along with her husband, Michael, said officials have failed to give them updates about the shooting. They said they decided to speak out to demand transparency, accountability, and respect, after sending the DOJ an unanswered letter in July.

"Our son was murdered," Michael said. "We all saw it and the lack of cooperation is just baffling. It's disappointing."

Michael said he will no longer stay silent. He said the deadly shooting was unjustified, as well as called out U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Dan Rosen, who is the U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota.

"Look in your heart and do what is right. Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable," Michael said of the agents who shot his son.

Pretti, 37, was killed on January 24 during President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement -- Operation Metro Surge -- in Minneapolis. The DOJ later announced a civil rights investigation into the shooting.

In the letter, according to CNN, the family said while they met with Rosen, he refused to share information with them. The family wants federal officials to identify the agents who fired their guns, confirm whether the FBI investigation remains active, and return property they says is no longer needed as evidence.

"It is impossible to convey how the government’s refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak," the letter noted, per CNN. "Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that 'I can’t tell you for all kinds of reasons,' without providing a single one."

State officials have separately said the federal government stopped providing materials needed for their own inquiry.

"We are working on this case every single day. My office is working in a collaborative way with the local county attorney. We're working together to make sure that the truth and justice prevails in Alex Pretti's case," Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a Democrat who is leading a lawsuit against the DOJ, told CNN on Tuesday.

"We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so," he added. "But it looks like we're going to need a court order. I'm sorry that it comes to that."

The DOJ has said victim-family communications may take place at later stages of a case.

No criminal charges have been announced in Pretti’s death.

"We're hoping that the federal government will stop fighting this," Steve Schleicher, an attorney who is representing Susan and Michael Pretti, said.

ALBANY — New York immigrant rights organizations have stepped into the legal fight over the state’s tuition policies, filing a friend-of-the-court brief earlier this month in support of laws that allow certain noncitizen students to qualify for in-state tuition at public colleges and universities.

The filing, known as an amicus curiae brief, allows organizations that are not direct parties to a lawsuit to share their perspectives and legal arguments with the court. The brief was filed on behalf of the New York Immigration Coalition, the Hispanic Federation, Latino Justice and Rural and Migrant Ministries to defend New York’s policies in a federal lawsuit brought by the U.S. Department of Justice in August.

The federal lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Albany, challenges the constitutionality of New York laws the Justice Department contends are providing in-state tuition and financial assistance for students in the U.S. illegally. The case lists as defendants the state of New York, Board of Trustees of the State University of New York, Board of Trustees of the City University of New York and the New York Higher Education Services Corporation.

Similar lawsuits were filed in August by the Justice Department against Connecticut and Vermont, which brought the number of federal cases challenging state laws that extend in-state tuition eligibility for certain noncitizen students to 17.

The litigation invokes a section of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which bars states from offering post-secondary education benefits based on residency to noncitizens, unless U.S. citizens are eligible for the same benefits. The Justice Department has asserted that the state laws “unconstitutionally discriminate against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rates or scholarships,” incentivize illegal immigration and grant benefits to undocumented immigrants that citizens cannot access.

New York established its in-state tuition policy for noncitizen students through legislation that was signed into law in June 2002, making it the fourth state in the country to adopt such a measure. The policy was later expanded through the José Peralta New York State DREAM Act in 2019, which opened access to state-administered financial aid eligibility for those with certain documented and undocumented statuses, including DACA status, as well as lawful permanent residents and other qualifying students.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

For that population, in-state eligibility requires at least two years of attendance at a New York high school, graduation, and application to a state college within five years of graduating. At SUNY and CUNY institutions, in-state tuition is generally at least 50% lower than out-of-state tuition.

The immigrant rights organizations argue that offering in-state tuition to noncitizens should remain under state jurisdiction pursuant to the 10th Amendment. They emphasized the law’s dual economic benefits because they contend noncitizen students contribute to state revenue through tuition payments to higher education institutions and, upon entering the workforce, further contribute to the state’s economy.

Gittel Evangelist, director of communications at Rural and Migrant Ministries, said the organization participated in the legal brief because of its work with immigrant and farmworker communities across the state.

A hallmark of the organization’s programming is an empowerment program for immigrant youth aged 14-18. Nearly all students who complete the program go on to college, Evangelist said, adding that the students tend to be high achievers and pursue a variety of fields, often drawn to where they can “make the biggest difference in their communities.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Ultimately, it hurts the economy and the social fabric of the whole state when an idea like this is floated,” Evangelist said. “An educated society is a more productive society and the students we work with certainly have the passion to contribute greatly to our state economy and to our society.”

Though the state’s public higher education systems do not track or publicly release a numerical breakdown of noncitizen student enrollment, it’s estimated that over 29,000 immigrant students are enrolled in higher education across New York. This figure includes both public and private institutions.

They are among more than half a million undocumented students enrolled in colleges and universities nationwide, according to data from the Higher Ed Immigration Portal, an initiative of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a nonpartisan coalition of nearly 600 college and university leaders.

Across the country, outcomes in these lawsuits have varied across states. Some of the cases remain pending in many jurisdictions, while lawsuits in Illinois, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas and Kentucky have led to the removal or invalidation of existing in-state tuition policies. Other states, like Florida, have preemptively removed their policies, according to data compiled by Inside Higher Ed.

Advertisement

text:
When U.S. immigration officials sent a Salvadoran man to Mexico, he relived the trauma he’d experienced when he’d fled his own country — trauma that had won him protection from deportation there.

Juan Antonio Pineda Vaquerano fled El Salvador in 2022 after police there tortured him, he said, and in 2024, a U.S. immigration judge believed his evidence that he would be tortured again if returned to his homeland.

But, in 2025, after President Donald Trump returned to office, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested him at his scheduled check-in appointment and sent him to Mexico. In the process, he said, they broke his hand and placed him in a restraint that has been called a torture device by human rights workers.

Pineda Vaquerano is among more than 300 people that the Trump administration has sent to countries where they have no ties after immigration judges granted them protection from deportation to their home countries because of legitimate fear of persecution or torture — people who fit the international definition of refugees — according to a report from Human Rights First.

“This is just a complete subversion of the global protection system,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First. “At the core it’s the most perverse part of their very deliberate attempt to send people to places where they have no connections or ties and they might and in many cases have faced immense harm. It’s really unprecedented.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main.

According to the report, the Trump administration has systematically targeted people who were granted protection from deportation as part of its third country removals program, breaking from decades of policies that allowed people with these protections to remain in the U.S. Many of those people had protection as members of the LGBTQ+ community from countries that do not allow those identities to exist freely.

U.S. immigration law offers three kinds of protection to people fleeing their countries. Asylum, the most well known, offers a path to citizenship, but it is discretionary, meaning that judges can choose not to award it. Historically, that typically happened because the person seeking protection had some kind of serious criminal history, but under both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration, the U.S. government added requirements that disqualified most people arriving at the border from obtaining asylum, meaning they had to turn to other forms of protection to stay in the country.

The other two kinds of protection are not discretionary — if someone qualifies, the judge has to grant them refuge. The first, withholding of removal, means that the person met the U.N. definition of a refugee and is more likely than not to be persecuted if returned to their home country. The second, protection under the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, offers refuge to people who can prove they will likely be tortured if returned.

Under both withholding and protection under the Convention Against Torture, the immigration judge technically issues a removal order to deport the person but then blocks their own order by granting one of these protections. Before the second Trump administration, people with this status had to check in periodically with the U.S. government and renew their work permits, but as long as they stayed on U.S. soil, they generally would not be forced to leave.

In 2019, the Trump administration restricted anyone who had passed through another country after leaving their own country and before entering the U.S. from getting asylum.

In 2023, the Biden administration reintroduced this restriction for anyone who did not use the CBP One mobile application to make an appointment to request protection at a port of entry. Many asylum seekers struggled to get appointments through the app, and many found themselves in danger in Mexico. Instead of waiting in danger, they chose to cross between ports of entry, blocking them from receiving asylum.

A federal judge has since blocked the restriction, but Human Rights First researchers identified at least 41 people who received one of the other forms of protection instead of asylum because of that restriction whom the Trump administration has now sent to third countries.

“It had nothing to do with the merits of their claim, and as we know, the wait times for CBP One were super long,” Arvey said. “There were people who didn’t know about the app, who couldn’t access it in their language, who were afraid to wait in Mexico. We just in particular have been so horrified to hear about those cases.”

Pineda Vaquerano said he crossed the U.S.-Mexico border in the summer of 2022 in Texas. A Texas judge initially denied his case, but he was one of about 6,000 people affected by an ICE data breach, and he was given a second chance at his case, this time from a Georgia detention center with notoriously low grant rates for protection.

Even without an attorney representing him, he managed to convince an immigration judge based on all of the evidence he brought with him from El Salvador, including a broken clavicle suffered at the hands of police there, that he would be tortured if returned to his country, and she granted him protection under the Convention Against Torture.

“It was a relief,” he said in Spanish. “I felt more at peace because they weren’t going to send me to my country.”

ICE released him from custody in January 2024, he said, after he won his case. He moved to Maryland where his cousin lived.

His wife and five of his children were still in El Salvador, so he said he began working two jobs — one as a cook at a restaurant and a second overnight cleaning kitchens for restaurants and hotels — to send money back to help them. He knew that because he hadn’t gotten asylum, he wouldn’t be able to sponsor them, but he hoped to save money to somehow reunite with them.

Because of his status, he still had to check in with ICE periodically. At his first appointment, in September 2025, he said officers made him sit at the ICE check-in office the entire day before informing him that they were detaining him.

He told them that he couldn’t be sent back to El Salvador, that he was worried that they would do to him what they had done to Kilmar Armando Ábrego García, a Salvadoran man who had also won protection from deportation there. ICE deported Ábrego García there anyway, and the Salvadoran government immediately imprisoned him.

But the ICE officers in Baltimore told Pineda Vaquerano that he wasn’t going to El Salvador, he said. They planned to send him to Mexico.

“It was difficult,” Pineda Vaquerano said. “I had told my family I didn’t want to go (to the appointment), but I knew I had to do things the right way.”

He spent about a month in custody before officials drove him from an Arizona detention center to the Nogales border, he said. Before that first attempt to hand him over to Mexico, he said, officials broke his hand trying to force him to sign documents, and they beat him before placing him in The WRAP, a full body restraint that deportees have complained ICE uses as a torture device.

“It’s remembering the same thing that happened in my country,” he said. “In my country, they broke my clavicle, and in the U.S., they broke my hand.”

Mexican officials refused to accept him in such a medical condition, he said, and the ICE officers drove him hours back to the detention center. It took three more tries before a Mexican official agreed to accept him, he said.

Mexican officials sent him on a bus to Tabasco, a border state with Guatemala. He begged officials not to deport him to El Salvador and showed them the documents about his case in the U.S. He said they gave him permission to remain in Mexico for 10 days.

He said he faced discrimination because of his nationality and lack of legal status in Mexico, especially when trying to get medical care for his injured hand. It healed crooked, he said.

He applied for refugee status in Mexico and recently received his residency there, he said. His family has now joined him.

But, they are still struggling. He earns roughly $10 a day at a fruit shop, and his son has a serious medical condition involving his brain. He said the hospital there hasn’t been able to help his son, and the family is trying to figure out how to move to Monterrey, where they’ve heard there are more neurology specialists.

He said the family needs about $700 for tickets to travel to Monterrey.

Pineda Vaquerano said he would give his own life if it would help his son heal and he would gladly donate an organ, but he can’t do anything to help with his son’s brain condition.

“I ask God, ‘Why so many things?’” he said. “I don’t understand.”

text:
McALLEN — A section of border wall that the federal government planned to build along a beloved South Texas wildlife refuge could end up cutting through the refuge instead.

The federal government is considering changing its plans for a border wall that it intended to build on a levee that runs adjacent to the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge. The change is an attempt to resolve a legal dispute in which government contractors are accused of trespassing on property near the refuge belonging to Hidalgo County Irrigation District No. 2.

During a hearing in federal court on Oct. 14, Assistant U.S. Attorney Lance Duke said the federal government was considering taking up the suggestion proposed by the irrigation district to relocate the border wall currently under construction.

“My client is in the process of looking into, basically, moving the wall from its current expected path — where we were originally planning to go through [the irrigation district’s] property — and instead move it through the wildlife refuge,” Duke said. “We recognize that will probably just create additional litigation from other interested parties.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. Customs and Border Protection did not confirm the agency was considering relocating the wall through the refuge but said it was aware of the lawsuit.

"CBP remains committed to enhancing border security at Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, while continuing coordination with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and other relevant federal and state partners,” the spokesperson said. “CBP is aware of the pending litigation and remains confident in its legal authorities and assessments."

In July, CBP moved forward with plans to construct 2.8 miles of border wall on a levee located adjacent to the wildlife refuge.

However, the irrigation district, a public corporation that distributes water to cities, farmers and ranchers, alleged that government contractors trespassed on their property during construction, specifically on the 60 feet of land it owns on either side of an irrigation canal.

The irrigation district sued Spencer Construction LLC and Royal Concrete Products LLC in September, seeking a restraining order against the contractors to halt construction.

A state district court in Hidalgo County issued a temporary restraining order against the contractors on July 30, which a federal judge extended after the U.S. government removed the case to federal court. A temporary restraining order is still in place.

During a hearing in August, the general manager of the irrigation district, Anthony Stambaugh, testified the contractors did not ask permission to enter onto their property.

He added that the presence of a border wall within their property would tighten the space around the canal, making it difficult for crews to conduct maintenance or repairs on the canal in a timely manner.

Lance Kirby, the attorney for the irrigation district, told the judge the issue would be resolved if the border were built 15 to 20 feet south of the current alignment.

“It’s music to my ears. It’s what we’ve been hoping for and asking for all along,” Kirby said in response to Duke’s announcement.

However, Duke had argued that Texas trespass law could not prevent the federal government from building a border wall on land it does not own. He added that a border wall at the proposed location was inevitable, even if the federal government had to move forward with condemnation.

The Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, sometimes referred to as the jewel of the national wildlife refuge system, is a 2,000-acre haven for wildlife that sits along the Rio Grande, south of the city of Alamo.

It’s a well-known and treasured destination for many who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley where school field trips to the refuge are like a rite of passage.

Its property has been a potential target for border wall construction since President Donald Trump first began pushing forward his border security agenda in 2017.

Border wall plans there activated members of the community to hold public demonstrations to spare the refuge from construction. Then in 2019, congressional lawmakers succeeded in protecting the refuge and other sensitive areas by assuring that appropriated funds could not be used to build a border wall there.

However, during Trump’s second term, CBP has been able to work around those restrictions through the One Big, Beautiful Bill, Trump’s signature funding bill which bypasses the appropriations process to fund border wall construction.

“I am concerned by reports that the federal government may reroute approximately 2.8 miles of border wall through the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge,” said U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, a Democrat from Laredo who was among the lawmakers who had secured protections for the refuge and other areas.

Cuellar added language to the Homeland Security Appropriations bill the 2027 fiscal year that would preserve those protections, but Congress is unlikely to take up the bill for a vote until the end of the year.

“I support strong border security, but there are better ways to secure our border than building through a wildlife refuge or cutting communities off from the Rio Grande,” Cuellar said, adding that the government should be investing in Border Patrol personnel, technology, intelligence, ports of entry, and infrastructure that address border security needs.

“DHS and CBP need to be transparent about any proposed change in the alignment at Santa Ana, including where the funding would come from, how the refuge would be affected, and what alternatives are being considered,” Cuellar said.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) no longer lists detained individuals with final removal orders in its online database.

According to The Associated Press, starting on Sept. 15, detainees with removal orders stopped appearing in the government’s online locator system, which was first put in place by the Obama administration.

“As we understand it, the administration changed their policy and as reported through people who didn't want to say on record, but people who were apparently with the administration,” said Frederick Carroll, the legal director at ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties.

The administration justifies this, he said, by saying that these individuals have already received due process and have final orders of removal, so there was nothing left to do.

“But that couldn't be further from the truth,” Carroll said. “In fact, due process means fundamentally the ability to challenge a judge's order. And in this case, even an order of removal from an immigration judge is not the final period on the case.”

He said the government is looking to scare people into hiding and limit their access to those who could help them, such as lawyers and families.

In a statement, ICE said it makes custody determinations based on bed space and all detainees have access to phones to contact families and lawyers.

“Illegal aliens in detention with final orders of removal are being prioritized for removal from the United States,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement. “Despite a historic number of injunctions, (Department of Homeland Security) is working rapidly and overtime to remove these aliens from detention centers to their final destination — home.”

Immigration lawyers say their recently detained clients have not appeared on the detainee locator system.

On Oct. 17, Hằng Huỳnh Đỗ was detained on her way to work at Peacock Nails in Lemon Grove. As of Monday, she still did not appear on the online detainee locator system.

“This is really consistent with the pattern of this administration of creating this climate of fear, of uncertainty,” said Ian Seruelo, an immigration attorney and chair of the San Diego Immigrant Rights Consortium. He does not represent Đỗ.

Over the past week, Seruelo has had trouble locating his detained clients.

“We didn't get any information from the detention facility. All they can say is that this person is not in the facility right now,” he said. “And I said, ‘Can you give me more information?’ They said, ‘No.’ So it's really very, you know, concerning.”

He was finally able to locate one of his clients, who is currently being held in Mississippi.

With Đỗ’s case, ICE said she violated the conditions of her visa and has a final order of removal issued in absentia last year. But without knowing where she’s being held, the ACLU said that makes it hard to file for habeas corpus relief. A habeas lawsuit must generally be filed with the court where the person is located.

ICE said detainees may not show up on the locator system for several reasons, including at the person’s request, because of a filing they’ve made, or if they are being transported.

This comes on the heels of a surge in immigration enforcement in the final stretches of the midterm election cycle. Immigrant rights activists have noted an increase in ICE activities in the county.

On Sunday, Our Lady of Guadalupe in Barrio Logan held a Eucharistic procession to the ballot box. The Rev. Scott Santarosa said it’s to support the immigrant community and send a message that voting is sacred.

“Voting is sacred because it's the way we form our society using our consciences,” he said. “So we really are trying to make that connection in a time where I think some people are doubting the integrity of our system or even maybe denigrating how sacred democracy is.”

Brenda Morales, a parishioner at the church and a member of Faith in Action, a grassroots organization that helps immigrants, said she felt a duty to join the procession to support the community.

“I know we see it on social media, the news. We hear it, she said. “And I think I just feel a big responsibility to be here for them, especially with all the families being separated, all the kids, seeing literally their parents getting taken, not understanding.”

As for the enforcement surge, Carroll said there isn’t much that activists, lawyers or community organizations can do, other than react, so it’s important that people know their rights.

“So if people know their rights in advance, that is to say, ‘No.’ That they don't have to open the door,” he said. “If someone does not provide them a legitimate judicial warrant signed by a judge, they don't have to let people into their home.”

text:
New Jersey immigration activists and a local elected official said they are disappointed in the lack of action by state officials in the wake of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency’s admission it used a warehouse site in Roxbury to process people it had detained.

“I'm really frustrated because a lot of communities are suffering, and the response just seems very lukewarm,” said Sandra Wittner, a town council member from Dover.

In September, activists with a group called PROJECT NINJA, or the No Ice in North Jersey Alliance, submitted photos, videos and detainee testimony to the state attorney general purporting to prove people were arrested by ICE in Dover and driven about five miles west to the Roxbury warehouse. The Trump administration plans to convert the facility into a 1500-person immigration detention center but has so far been blocked by a federal judge in a lawsuit brought by New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill.

The governor and her attorney general, Jennifer Davenport, pledged to hold ICE “accountable” and take legal action if they determined the Trump administration had violated that court order.

Then came a revelation from ICE officials on Oct. 13. In an email to New Jersey Rep. Analilia Mejia, the agency admitted it had brought detainees to the Roxbury site for initial processing after they were arrested in Dover on two occasions, on Sept. 4 and 8.

Two weeks after ICE’s admission, neither Sherrill or Davenport have taken additional legal action.

“We're not actually clear on why,” said PROJECT NINJA co-founder Birdie Green. “ It's very frustrating to be screaming at the top of your lungs like, ‘There's something wrong here. We need somebody to do something about it,’ and to get no response.”

In emailed statements, both said they were told by the Trump administration that ICE would no longer bring detainees to the Roxbury site. A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michael Symons, said her office is continuing to review reports that ICE detained people at the warehouse.

“We will continue to review the facts carefully, and we will take appropriate action if we learn that ICE is violating a court order,” Symons said.

But neither statement addressed why New Jersey officials haven't taken further legal action to hold ICE accountable for the activity it already acknowledged.

The Trump administration’s plans for the Roxbury warehouse has become a flashpoint in the local Congressional race, where incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. is vying against Democrat Rebecca Bennett. ICE’s use of the warehouse has faced stiff opposition from local residents and local officials. Kean has faced criticism from his own party over his lack of engagement on the issue, and Bennett has fared favorably in recent polls showing the seat could help Democrats regain the House of Representatives in next week’s midterm elections.

Wittner said the lack of action follows a pattern among state leaders. She said she’s seen little done to crack down on ICE agents who flout other New Jersey laws — specifically the state’s ban on agents wearing masks and a requirement that their automobiles be equipped with license plates on the front and back of any vehicle.

“Where is the empowerment of our law enforcement to actually uphold those laws?” she said. “ There's no point in saying it if you're not gonna actually empower anybody to do what they can to actually uphold those laws.”

Roxbury is well outside Wittner’s Dover council district, but she said she was compelled to get more fully involved in opposition to the warehouse detention facility by a message in September on a community WhatsApp group. A Dover resident had posted saying her father had been taken by ICE.

On the morning of Sept. 4, Wittner said, ICE had conducted a series of raids in the North Jersey town, adding that ICE activity has become a regular occurrence in her community where more than three-quarters of the population is Latino. A little after 8 a.m., she said WhatsApp groups set-up by a rapid response team of anti-ICE locals and activists lit up like a Christmas tree with messages: “My coworker was taken," "My cousin was taken," "My neighbor was taken," "My dad was taken."

“The message about the dad was what prompted us to really dig into this deeper,” Wittner told Gothamist.

Wittner said she spoke with the man’s daughter later that day. The woman’s father told her ICE had driven him west from Dover after his arrest.

“He thought maybe he was near Pennsylvania, and that they were in a building,” Wittner said, recounting her conversation with the man’s daughter. “She knew about Roxbury, and she's like, ‘Well, there's nowhere else he could have gone.’”

That account, along with videos taken by local residents purporting to show ICE vehicles driving from Dover to the Roxbury site, became the basis for activists’ claims that the Trump administration was violating the federal court order forbidding ICE from using the Roxbury site to detain people it arrests.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told Gothamist the agency cannot comment on ICE’s use of the facility due to the pending litigation.

ICE has said no detainees have been brought inside the warehouse. But David Broderick, an attorney for PROJECT NINJA, said the court’s order against conducting enforcement activities covers the whole site — not just the warehouse.

Green said she hopes Davenport’s office will seek a contempt of court order against ICE. Wittner said she wants state officials to fight harder to be allowed to inspect the site. Rep. Mejia has been asking to visit but thus far her request has been ignored by ICE, according to her office.

“I don't know why the state isn't demanding to get in there to,” Wittner said. “There has to be something they can do.

Broderick said he will be looking for the New Jersey attorney general to take additional action by November 16 when the White House and state officials are due to provide status reports on discussions between the parties to the judge.

“I hope that the state does want to make a point that ICE just can't willy-nilly violate court orders without some type of sanction,” he said. “They've already been sort of publicly humiliated and embarrassed. Hopefully, there'll be more to it.”

text:
A Utah couple admitted in court to using bolt cutters to remove handcuffs and help a suspected illegal alien escape from Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Utah.

Officials said Kelzie Ryann Luna, 21, and George Sanchez-Juarez, 22, pleaded guilty to theft, disposal and conversion of government property, and aiding and abetting.

On Monday, Oct. 26, they were each sentenced to four days in prison. A U.S. magistrate judge also sentenced them to pay a $600 fine and $28 in restitution and serve six months of supervised release.

“Obstructing ICE operations and any other law enforcement carries real and serious consequences, including federal charges, imprisonment, and a permanent federal criminal record,” said U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak for the District of Utah. “Those who choose to take the law into their own hands will be held accountable.”

Federal agents went to a Salt Lake City Home Depot on Oct. 8, 2025, to arrest four people who had previously been deported, according to court documents and statements made at Luna and Sanchez-Juarez’s plea and sentencing hearings.

As agents arrested one person, another man in handcuffs escaped from a vehicle and ran across the street.

Court documents said Luna, a passenger, and Sanchez-Juarez, the driver, helped the man escape in a white Volkswagen Golf. They bought bolt cutters to remove his handcuffs and later bragged about helping him get away while cursing ICE.

“These defendants knowingly and deliberately interfered with officers performing their duties and attempted to shield an individual from the law. Their actions were not harmless. They undermined public safety, obstructed justice, and showed blatant disregard for the rule of law,” said Homeland Security Investigations Denver Special Agent in Charge Charles Engle. “We will use every lawful tool available to identify, investigate, and hold accountable anyone who attempts to impede federal law enforcement or aid those seeking to evade lawful arrest.”

title: ICE arrests surge at Seattle-area Home Depot parking lots. Neighbors are on the lookout
description:
Since August, Home Depot parking lots around Seattle have become hotspots for immigration arrests.
Volunteers show up to parking lots with breakfast, get to know the workers, and watch for ICE.
They'll post up in Home Depot parking lots every day for a few hours to keep workers company.
Megargee and other community members started keeping watch at Seattle-area parking lots about a year ago.
One man who was arrested in September made his living for 30 years in these parking lots, getting hired for odd jobs.
text:
U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents have been known to target Home Depot parking lots, sometimes pretending to be hiring for a job, but more often than not, they simply swarm.

The agents don’t bother hiding their intentions. They question people. Some people, often men looking for work, get corned. Others run.

“It’s horrible,” one man said on a late September day. “There's an awful rush of adrenaline. Your heart is pounding. Everything makes you nervous, but that anxiety, that they’ll take you away, that’s what makes you run without fear.”

The man knew what it’s like to run.

KUOW is not naming him because he’s in the country without legal status.

He was standing in the corner of a parking lot near a Home Depot in the Seattle metro area.

Since August, Home Depot parking lots around Seattle have become hotspots for immigration arrests. Day laborers looking for work frequently wait outside these stores. As arrests continue to rise, community groups have been hosting neighborhood watches, connecting with workers and their families, and watching as these arrests unfold.

“You leap over whatever there is,” the man without legal status said.

He pointed to a nearby fence that stood about six feet high surrounding the parking lot. He said he’s seen people take one leap to climb over it.

Other day laborers like him have been living in the U.S., some for decades. Older men in worn gray Carhartts, canvas jeans, and Seahawks sweaters wait in the parking lot, too. Some are in their 70s.

In the past year, there have also been new faces, neighbors who are worried about them, like Chris Megargee.

“It's been pretty awesome to deliver a message of welcome and respect and love and dignity in contrast to the message of rejection and hatred… the administration's been pushing out,” Megargee said.

Megargee is one of many volunteers with an adopt-a-corner program. Volunteers show up to parking lots with breakfast, get to know the workers, and watch for ICE. It’s part of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network. They'll post up in Home Depot parking lots every day for a few hours to keep workers company.

“We have no illusions about stopping ICE from doing what they do,” Megargee said. ”But if they show up, we document what they're doing, film what they're doing, remind the guys of their rights, and support men who've been detained.”

Since President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown began, immigration arrests outside of Home Depots and other big-box stores have become increasingly common. Portland, Los Angeles, and other cities have reported major raids at these stores, where workers are frequently arrested.

Human rights researchers point to parking lots as a central part of mass deportation efforts, in which hardware and grocery store parking lots have become a place immigration enforcement regularly patrols to look for people to arrest.

They use a combination of factors including skin color, spoken language, and skills offered to build what’s called reasonable suspicion to stop someone and interrogate them about their legal status.

Megargee and other community members started keeping watch at Seattle-area parking lots about a year ago. In the past two months, they’ve documented at least 40 arrests.

ICE declined to comment on whether this was evidence of a specific operation.

As these arrests continue, the volunteer group has come up with a strategy to help keep the workers safe: hiring them.

“They're far safer in your backyard raking the leaves or building a fence or doing some drywall or painting inside than they are standing here on the corner,” Megargee said.

One man who was arrested in September made his living for 30 years in these parking lots, getting hired for odd jobs. He also spent those years building a life with his partner, who asked to remain anonymous. She’s a green card holder and afraid of immigration enforcement. Her partner proposed to her years ago, but they never got married – that’s one avenue many use to get their loved ones legal status.

The last day he went to find work, she told him not to go. They’d been seeing lots of reports online of ICE in the area. She told him it was dangerous.

She was standing in the kitchen where she warned him when she spoke to KUOW. Her walker was stored nearby; she isn’t able to work much because of a hip injury.

She and her partner have a son together. He’s in his early 20s and is a U.S. citizen.

Their son found out his father had been arrested by ICE first. He got the call from the watch group at the parking lot that morning.

“He left running,” his mother recalled. “I stayed here waiting. When my son returned, he told me they took him.”

Her son wasn’t allowed to see him after he was arrested; ICE officers wouldn’t let him.

At the detention center, his father soon opted to be voluntarily deported, and ten days later, he was in El Salvador, where he was born.

While some families decide to follow their family members to the countries they are deported to, his wife and son, like many others, will stay in the U.S. while they work to get him the legal status they both have. They may have to wait a while.

text:
Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour.

Judith Clark, 77, was the inspiration for Walter’s portrayal of prisoners in the Donmar Warehouse all-female Shakespeare trilogy, including Brutus in Julius Caesar and Prospero in The Tempest.

Clark had been invited to speak about rehabilitation and restorative justice at a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Julius Caesar in Stratford-upon-Avon next month, but her application to visit Britain was refused last week.

She had also hoped to attend the UK launch of her daughter Harriet Clark’s first novel, The Hill, on 5 November.

Kennedy said that while the Home Office had rules governing visas for people with serious criminal convictions, there was also ministerial discretion, which should be exercised in Clark’s case.

“This is a woman in her 70s who served a long sentence for political activism, which involved no violence on her part, and whose clear remorse and exceptional works within the prison system led to her early release,” she said. “She was deemed to pose no threat to US society and in my view she poses no threat whatsoever to the UK’s national security.”

Walter said immigration rules designed to protect the public should allow flexibility in exceptional cases such as Clark’s. “There is no other purpose behind the short visit she wants to make other than to reward us with her presence as a speaker in our post-show conversation and to celebrate her daughter’s first book launch,” she said.

Lloyd said Clark had become a touchstone for the creative team’s understanding of repentance, redemption and rehabilitation during the making of the Donmar trilogy.

“To say she did her time and turned her life around is an understatement,” she said. “To have her speak in the UK would be an inspiration in the realm of restorative justice.”

Clark joined the student movement against the Vietnam war in the late 1960s and became involved in the Weather Underground, a radical organisation that emerged from the American anti-war movement. She was later involved in the May 19th Communist Organization, which pursued armed revolutionary activity.

In 1983, she was convicted for her role as a getaway driver in an attempted robbery of a Brinks armoured truck in New York in 1981, during which a security guard and two police officers were killed. She was sentenced to three consecutive terms of 25 years to life.

In 2017, the then-New York governor Andrew Cuomo commuted her sentence, allowing her to seek parole. She was released in 2019, after serving 37 years.

During her incarceration at Bedford Hills correctional facility in New York, Clark helped establish an Aids education and support group, developed programmes to help mothers maintain relationships with their children, raised service dogs for veterans and first responders and helped build a college education programme.

She has since worked in criminal justice reform and support for formerly incarcerated women. In 2025, she became director of the Survivors Justice Project, which works to secure legal relief for survivors of domestic violence facing prison sentences.

Walter and Lloyd met Clark while researching their Shakespeare trilogy, which reimagined the plays as productions staged by women in prison. Walter said Clark had helped her understand Brutus, the politically conflicted character in Julius Caesar, who struggles with the moral consequences of his actions. Her story also informed Walter’s portrayal of Prospero in The Tempest.

“By the time I met Judy she had developed into one of the most exemplary and evolved human beings I have ever met or am likely to meet,” Walter said.

The RSC has invited Clark to take part in a post-show discussion entitled Can Art Save Lives?

It would also include a company member introduced to theatre after prison through the charity Clean Break.

Kennedy first met Clark more than 30 years ago at Bedford Hills while making a television documentary about women in prison. “Her remorse for her participation in criminal conduct was very evident to all who were involved with her,” she said.

In her own letter supporting her visa application, Clark said she had publicly disavowed her actions and apologised for the harm she had contributed to a decade into her sentence. She spent the remainder of her imprisonment trying to turn her remorse into work benefiting the prison community, families and those harmed by crime.

Clark hoped to visit Britain from 4 to 15 November with her wife, Cheryl Moch. Her daughter has said that The Hill draws on her own experience of visiting her mother throughout her imprisonment. Despite their separation, she wrote, Clark had found ways to mother her.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “It’s our longstanding policy not to comment on individual cases.

“All applications for entry clearance in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the Immigration Rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

title: How Unchecked Immigration Enforcement Risks Making U.S. Cities Less Safe
description:
But no amount of effective local policing can compensate for the harms of the current federal immigration enforcement agenda to public safety, including decreased public trust in law enforcement.
What, then, should cities do when federal immigration enforcement is actively threatening public safety?
Local city and state governments are proving that they are not powerless to respond when federal immigration enforcement undermines public safety.
The shooting in New York City is a stark reminder of what is at stake when immigration enforcement undermines public safety.
We cannot judge the effectiveness of an immigration enforcement system based on how many people are arrested or deported.
text:
ICE actions are harming trust between locals and police.

The growing violence associated with the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign was on display again recently in New York City, when plainclothes Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers shot and wounded 28-year-old Oscar Belgal while his terrified 5-year-old sat in the car’s backseat. The New York City shooting is the latest in a troubling pattern of violent immigration enforcement encounters across the country and points to a larger issue: What happens when the federal government’s aggressive pursuit of deportations undermines the work of keeping communities safe?

Cities across the country are increasingly being forced to confront this question. One of the fundamental responsibilities of local police is to respond to emergencies and preserve public order. But no amount of effective local policing can compensate for the harms of the current federal immigration enforcement agenda to public safety, including decreased public trust in law enforcement.

The problem goes deeper than any single confrontation between ICE officers and community members. From the start, the Trump administration has made clear that sheer arrest volume is the goal: maximizing civil immigration arrests to meet quotas while minimizing accountability for tactics that violate basic policing norms such as the use of minimum force and the use of masks and unmarked cars. While prior administrations of both political parties typically focused arrest and deportation on those with criminal convictions, under Trump, ICE treats any person in violation of civil immigration law — regardless of their ties to the U.S. and their contributions to their communities — as a serious and violent criminal.

Despite false claims of targeting the “worst of the worst,” as of July 2026, most ICE arrests were of noncitizens with no criminal record, with only 27% of people arrested by ICE having a criminal conviction at all, a record low. In the New York City area, more than three-quarters of the people arrested by ICE that month had no criminal history. Recently, ICE has gone even further: targeting noncitizens with legal status and those appearing in court following the government’s rules, sweeping in longtime residents, workers and parents with no criminal records. Federal agents have focused on low-level immigration violations at the expense of prioritizing bona fide public safety threats such as child trafficking, drug smuggling and domestic terrorism.

This indiscriminate enforcement approach is facilitated by an unprecedented infusion of funding from Congress, with more than $170 billion for immigration enforcement last year making the agency the size of a small military force. This has led to rapid expansion of the ICE workforce, including 8,000 new hires, leaving ICE at approximately 29,000 employees, approaching the size of the FBI — with plans to hire another 5,000 by the end of 2026. But this hiring surge comes with less training and vetting than ever before, and many recruited using explicit white nationalist rhetoric. This means ICE officers with little or no training on use of force, constitutional rights or de-escalation tactics. In July, a newly hired ICE officer with a documented history of domestic violence shot and killed a young father in Maine who ICE later admitted was not even the intended target of the operation — just one tragic example of the public safety consequences of a poorly trained and unprofessional ICE workforce.

The Trump administration is also using financial incentives to lure an increasing number of local police departments into agreements that deputize local police to directly enforce federal immigration laws, turning everyday police interactions like routine traffic stops into detention and deportation. Effective policing depends on trust. But years of research show that when local police serve as a force multiplier for ICE, communities become fearful of their local police departments and are less likely to report crimes. Police officers need witnesses willing to come forward, and community members need to feel safe in reporting crimes. In Tennessee, a police chief reported that a noncitizen caretaker delayed calling 911 for an unresponsive infant, reportedly out of fear of immigration enforcement. The baby later died.

There have already been several reports of declines in crime reporting among immigrant communities fearful of deportation. A study published this year in the American Economic Review found that involving local police in federal immigration enforcement made Hispanic victims less likely to report crimes, while increasing the likelihood that they would become crime victims.

All this presents a real problem for police departments. Victims of domestic violence may hesitate to seek help. Victims of violent crime now have to fear arrest and detention. Potential witnesses lose incentive to cooperate with law enforcement and provide critical information about drug trafficking, sex trafficking or other serious offenses.

What, then, should cities do when federal immigration enforcement is actively threatening public safety? New York City has long recognized the importance of keeping local policing separate from federal immigration enforcement. City laws generally prohibit the NYPD from participating in civil immigration enforcement and restrict the use of City resources to support these operations, allowing police to focus on their core public safety duties.

Cities and states across the country are already taking steps to limit federal overreach and protect their communities. More than 30 localities have adopted policies restricting the use of public property as staging grounds for immigration operations. Cities like Boston, Chicago and Los Angeles are filing public records requests to increase transparency around ICE and Department of Homeland Security actions. And states like Illinois and Minnesota have established independent commissions to investigate alleged federal misconduct and document its impact on communities. Local city and state governments are proving that they are not powerless to respond when federal immigration enforcement undermines public safety.

However, cities cannot solve this problem on their own. While local and state governments can and should take steps to protect their communities and hold federal agents accountable, they cannot fundamentally change the laws behind immigration enforcement. That responsibility lies with Congress. Lawmakers must reform the outdated laws enacted in the 1980s and 1990s that made detention and deportation the one-size-fits-all response regardless of whether someone poses a public safety threat. We need a new framework that prioritizes the safety of communities over arrest and deportation numbers. Construction workers driving to job sites or parents picking up their children at school shouldn’t be top targets for arrest, and federal law enforcement agencies should not treat entire communities as a threat.

There is a better way forward: ensuring immigration enforcement is centered on four key principles: compliance, safety, proportionality and accountability. That means giving people a viable pathway to earn permanent legal status. It means focusing enforcement resources on genuine public safety threats, instead of treating every immigration violation as justification for aggressive enforcement. It means ensuring proportional consequences for violations, rather than relying on deportation as a one-size-fits-all solution. And it means giving the federal courts and Congress more authority to hold federal agencies and agents responsible when they abuse their authority, so that accountability isn’t left only to states.

The shooting in New York City is a stark reminder of what is at stake when immigration enforcement undermines public safety. We cannot judge the effectiveness of an immigration enforcement system based on how many people are arrested or deported. The real test is whether it protects public safety, encourages compliance with the law and holds those enforcing it accountable. And by those measures, the current approach is failing miserably.

title: Report: Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment
description:
The United Kingdom is betting on artificial intelligence to ‘fix’ immigration.
The systems rely on technologies renowned for bias, disproportionately harming the most vulnerable people on the move, and therefore encoding discrimination into the infrastructure of border control.
They operate in near-total secrecy: officials routinely invoke ‘national security’ to stonewall FOI requests, redact disclosures.
Recommendations AI will not fix the immigration system.
But the deeper problem is the ideology that frames migration as a permanent emergency to be solved by algorithms, criminalising migrants and normalising an “automated Hostile Environment”.
text:
The United Kingdom is betting on artificial intelligence to ‘fix’ immigration. Driven by a techno-solutionist ideology that reduces the complex human phenomenon of migration to a technical problem awaiting a technical fix, successive governments, including the current Labour administration, have committed to embedding AI across the immigration system and at the nation’s borders.

About the report

Based on desk and literature research, expert interviews, and analysis of Home Office documents obtained through freedom of information (FOI) requests, this paper argues that this is no longer rhetoric: AI is being woven into crucial parts of the immigration machinery, and is poised to shape all of it.

We document a rapidly expanding catalogue of deployments. Within the immigration system, AI is being trialled or used to estimate the age of people seeking asylum, summarise asylum interviews and country policy information, prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (IPIC) tool, sift through irregular entrants’ mobile phones, and automatically flag potential “sham” marriages with a red or green light. At the border, live facial recognition, AI-powered drones and satellites, and foreign-built autonomous surveillance towers are marshalled to “stop the boats”, while obscure programmes such as Cerberus promise to pre-empt unknown threats, marking a decisive shift from reactive to ‘predictive’, proactive enforcement.

This automated fortress raises grave and converging concerns. The systems rely on technologies renowned for bias, disproportionately harming the most vulnerable people on the move, and therefore encoding discrimination into the infrastructure of border control. They operate in near-total secrecy: officials routinely invoke ‘national security’ to stonewall FOI requests, redact disclosures. In at least one instance, the authorities have pressured a researcher to withdraw published findings.

Much of this technological arsenal is not British but supplied by US, Israeli, and other foreign defence and security giants, producing technological dependency, and techno-political lock-in, that reality sits awkwardly with the Government’s stated ambition to be an “AI maker”, not an “AI taker”. All of this unfolds within a regulatory vacuum that ministers have shown no intention of filling, having instead promised the world’s most “unfettered” environment for AI experimentation, even as the Government seeks to “modernise” the European Convention on Human Rights in ways that threaten the right to asylum itself.

Recommendations

AI will not fix the immigration system. But the deeper problem is the ideology that frames migration as a permanent emergency to be solved by algorithms, criminalising migrants and normalising an “automated Hostile Environment”.

This paper therefore sets out five recommendations:

Reject AI techno-solutionism and put people ahead of their data-driven reduction;

Recognise and fill regulatory gaps, banning undemocratic uses such as mass live surveillance of public spaces and strictly regulating high-risk applications before deployment;

Enhance structural transparency in the public interest, with stronger FOI laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools;
