text:
The black vehicles with tinted windows converged on the bus stop just after 5:30 a.m. It was June 18, 2025, and Pedro Vasquez Perdomo and his co-workers were drinking coffee, waiting for a ride to a construction job in Pasadena, California.

Masked, armed men poured from the vehicles and charged at them. Vasquez Perdomo thought they were probably immigration agents, but he couldn’t be sure. The agents wore plain clothes with no visible badges and didn’t identify themselves. They seized the 54-year-old Vasquez Perdomo, handcuffed him, chained his feet, waist and hands, and hauled him away. No one showed him a warrant or told him why they were arresting him, he later wrote in a declaration.

“It felt like a kidnapping,” he wrote.

The agents drove Vasquez Perdomo and his coworkers to B-18, an immigration processing site in the basement of a federal building in downtown Los Angeles. Some lawyers had dubbed the facility a “black hole,” because detainees could be hard to locate or reach there. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

Eleven days earlier, about 20 miles away, another confrontation with immigration agents had ended in handcuffs.

Brayan Ramos-Brito, a 29-year-old US citizen, was protesting outside a Department of Homeland Security office in Paramount when federal authorities accused him of assaulting a Border Patrol agent. Because he was at the anti-ICE protest, Ramos-Brito wasn’t confused about who was arresting him, his lawyer said.

He was arrested on a Saturday and taken south to Santa Ana City Jail in Orange County. By Monday, he had entered the federal criminal system with a case, an assigned public defender and a judge preparing to review his detention.

Vasquez Perdomo and Ramos-Brito, both arrested by federal agents in the same metro area in the same month, entered two very different legal systems. The federal criminal system that Ramos-Brito experienced, despite its faults, is open and transparent, with the rights and protections that Americans have come to expect.

In contrast, the immigration system that swallowed Vasquez Perdomo is secretive and unpredictable, one in which people are moved between detention facilities with little to no warning, struggle to reach a lawyer or let their families know where they are, and are deported to countries they have no ties to as a result of shadowy deals with foreign governments.

In a criminal case, the process is public almost immediately. A judge oversees the proceedings, hearings are often held in open court, and defendants have access to lawyers—in fact, the government provides an attorney if someone doesn’t have a lawyer or can’t afford one. In addition, court records show what the government is alleging, where the person is being held, and where their next court appearance will be.

Immigration cases are much harder to follow, attorneys say. Officers have to clear a lower legal threshold to make an arrest, people arrested often can’t get a lawyer, and attorneys often can’t figure out where people are detained and can’t see the evidence against them.

Ramos-Brito is a US citizen, while Vasquez Perdomo is not. Their experiences weren’t a function of their status in the country, but rather the features of the systems they encountered. When immigrants face criminal charges, they have more protections than they would in ICE custody, immigration attorneys say. And in the rare instances when US citizens have gone into immigration detention, they too confront more secrecy and fewer guardrails.

That’s because the government has historically handled immigration cases as civil, administrative matters that don’t require the same safeguards as criminal cases.

“It is baked into the design of the immigration detention system that…there is very little oversight that the courts can impose, in part because of the civil nature of detention,” said César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, an Ohio State University law professor who studies the intersection of criminal and immigration law.

Since the 1890s, the Supreme Court has interpreted immigration proceedings as a civil process in which the outcome is not supposed to be punitive, but “in reality it’s experienced very differently,” García Hernández said.

The immigration system has increasingly functioned more like the criminal justice system, attorneys say, with widespread arrests and harsher and longer detentions.

Vasquez Perdomo eventually became one of the plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit, Vasquez Perdomo v. Mullin, challenging both how immigration agents were stopping and arresting people in the Los Angeles area, and the lack of access to lawyers for people inside the B-18 facility.

The differences between the immigration and criminal systems actually begin before an arrest.

Vasquez Perdomo and Ramos-Brito were caught up in the same immigration enforcement surge, dubbed “Operation at Large,” that began in June 2025. US Customs and Border Protection agents had joined ICE officers and were turning up at places like Home Depots and car washes without always looking for a particular person, said Carl Bergquist, an attorney with the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, one of several organizations that joined the lawsuit.

Agents were relying on broad clues, like where someone was, what language they spoke or the clothes they wore, to decide whom to stop, he said. The lawsuit argues those clues amounted to unconstitutional racial profiling, Bergquist said.

Vasquez Perdomo, who is Hispanic, believed his own arrest fit that pattern. “I think that I was arrested that day at the bus stop because of how I look,” he wrote in his declaration.

Both federal immigration and law enforcement officers can make arrests without warrants. Law enforcement can do so if they are in a public place and witness a crime, or have reason to believe someone committed a crime. Immigration officers can do so if they have reason to believe someone is in the country unlawfully and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

But warrantless arrests are supposed to be the exception, not the rule, said Lauren Wilfong, with the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, who’s one of the attorneys representing Vasquez Perdomo and others in the case. The default, Wilfong said, is an investigation that establishes probable cause and leads to a warrant.

But agents flipped the order of operations during the immigration enforcement surge in summer 2025, Wilfong said.

“They’ve sort of inverted that logic to say, ‘OK, well, we’ll grab them now. We’ll justify it later,’” Wilfong said. The lawsuit argued that ICE was ignoring the escape-risk requirement, and that the agency’s practices in Los Angeles violated the Fourth Amendment, which protects people from unreasonable stops and arrests.

Vasquez Perdomo’s account follows that inverted sequence. Agents had already surrounded and handcuffed him before one asked him for identification, he said.

Attorneys also said that getting an immigration warrant is easier. In a criminal case, an arresting officer typically needs a warrant signed by a judge. But immigration officers can rely on administrative warrants that the agency produces and signs itself, Bergquist said. “The level of evidence is lower” to get an administrative warrant, he added.

Ramos-Brito had also been arrested on the spot, without a warrant, but once federal authorities accused him of a crime, his lawyer could get to him quickly.

Two days after the arrest, Bo Griffith, a deputy federal public defender, had been assigned to Ramos-Brito’s case and saw him before the first hearing. Ramos-Brito was still wearing the clothes from the protest. His shirt was ripped, and Griffith could see bruises and scrapes on his body. He looked “beat up,” Griffith recalled.

Griffith also had the criminal complaint, which a federal agent had written and federal prosecutors had filed. It was only a few pages, accusing Ramos-Brito of interfering with an agent trying to arrest someone else, and of threatening to kill an officer, Griffith said.

“There was no real evidence in it,” Griffith said. “It was just kind of a synopsis of what the agents were alleging had happened.” But Griffith could compare that account with what his client told him and begin trying to disprove it. He called Ramos-Brito’s family and began gathering bystander videos from the protest.

“What the videos showed immediately was that the complaint was wrong,” Griffith said.

One clip, he said, showed an officer shove Ramos-Brito, while others revealed officers taking him to the ground and dragging him across the pavement.

Getting such a level of clarity early on about the government’s allegations is rare in the immigration system. When ICE detains someone, the agency prepares a form that shows why agents arrested the person and whether they deemed the person might escape before a warrant could be obtained. The document shows whether an arrest was lawful, Wilfong said.

But lawyers often don’t see the agents’ account of an arrest until the case is well underway, if at all. In the meantime, lawyers may have only their client’s account to work from.

The lack of information can extend to someone’s immigration history. Attorneys sometimes have to file slow-moving public records requests to get a client’s full file, all while the immigration case keeps moving forward, Bergquist said.

“There could be damaging information that only the government knows, but they’re not telling you,” he said.

At B-18, there was a more fundamental information problem: Lawyers and families sometimes didn’t even know whether their client or relative was at the facility.

B-18 was meant to be a temporary holding place where ICE could process people before releasing them or moving them to longer-term detention. It had no beds, showers or medical facilities. During the June 2025 raids, ICE was bringing people to B-18 faster than they could be processed, at times holding more than 300 people there, according to court records.

When Vasquez Perdomo arrived at B-18 after his arrest, he shared a room with 52 people, he wrote in his declaration. They had no mattresses and were forced to sleep on cement benches or on the floor. There was only one working toilet.

He was held at B-18 for a day and a half before ICE transferred him to another detention center. “I was lucky,” he wrote, “I met people who had been there for three days and counting.”

At times, staff would require lawyers to provide a detainee’s immigration ID number, known as the A-number, to allow visits, even when people hadn’t yet been assigned one, said Lindsay Toczylowski, an immigration lawyer and co-founder of the Los Angeles-based nonprofit Immigrant Defenders Law Center. Other people took days to appear in ICE’s online locator, or their information was incorrect. By the time the information was updated, ICE had already transferred some people to other facilities, Toczylowski said.

The limited access to clients became the other major constitutional fight in the Vasquez Perdomo lawsuit, which argued that ICE was denying people their due process under the Fifth Amendment.

When ICE’s online locator failed, Toczylowski said, lawyers often had no choice but to show up at the facility, hope their clients were still there and, if so, hope they’d be allowed to see them. “You had to go to B-18 and argue” to “try to find out if who you’re looking for was there,” she said.

Later that June, Martha Vasquez went to B-18 to search for a family friend.

Federal agents had arrested A.G., a 40-year-old construction worker who is identified by initials in court records, on June 23, while he was parked outside a Home Depot in Marina del Rey, in Los Angeles County.

“We had no idea where AG was taken after his arrest,” Vasquez, who’s not related to Vasquez Perdomo, wrote in a declaration.

For a day, his family searched ICE’s detainee locator in vain. Emails and calls to ICE got no response. Finally, Vasquez went downtown to B-18.

She waited in line for hours with many other people. Officers speaking through an intercom would tell her, “Hold on, we’ll let you know if you can come in or not,” and then not return with an answer. Staff also told her that because they had so many detainees, they could not tell her exactly who was there.

Vasquez finally said she had paperwork from a lawyer that needed A.G.’s signature. They let her inside, but they brought out the wrong detainee.

When A.G. finally appeared, he was still wearing the clothes he had been arrested in over 24 hours earlier. Vasquez wrote that he looked “sad, concerned, dirty, scared, and very tired.”

She saw him for about two minutes.

The trouble Vasquez had locating and then speaking with her family friend exposes another difference between the two systems.

In a criminal case, if someone can’t afford or access a lawyer, the court will appoint one. That right comes from the Sixth Amendment, which applies to criminal prosecutions.

Because immigration cases are civil, the government generally doesn’t provide a lawyer. Finding one often falls to family or friends, said García Hernández, the Ohio State law professor.

ICE’s 2025 detention standards require facilities to post a current list of pro bono legal-service providers and allow detainees to call them for free. But that doesn’t guarantee that someone will get a lawyer, García Hernández said. The organizations listed may be hours away from the detention center and have limited capacity to take new cases, he said.

Vasquez Perdomo happened to have an outside network that moved quickly. In the first hour after his arrest, community members, volunteers and staff were talking to witnesses, Wilfong said. That evening, organizers held a vigil at the bus stop and asked anyone who had seen the arrests or knew the men to come forward.

People did, helping organizers identify Vasquez Perdomo and his coworkers, find their families and connect them with attorneys, Wilfong said. “That’s how I think we were able to get around some of those incredibly challenging issues that are systemic to the way that immigration enforcement was operating,” Wilfong said.

Days after his arrest, Vasquez Perdomo’s lawyers filed a habeas petition in court challenging his detention. ICE later transferred him to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, an immigrant detention camp roughly 90 miles northeast of Los Angeles, where an immigration judge granted him bond on July 3, 2025. He was released on July 8, nearly three weeks after his arrest.

Vasquez Perdomo had lived in Pasadena for decades, working as a day laborer. About two months after his arrest, he said in an updated declaration that he still intended to return to the same bus stop for work. But he was also avoiding leaving home unless necessary because he feared being stopped again.

Ramos-Brito, by contrast, didn’t need an outside network to assemble around him.

“We knew where he was,” Griffith said. “His family could visit him…It wasn’t like he just disappeared.”

Having access to his client gave Griffith a way to challenge what was happening to Ramos-Brito while the important decisions in his case were being made. The defense could put evidence contradicting the government’s account before the court and document Ramos-Brito’s injuries. And when a magistrate judge denied bond, Griffith said, lawyers could file a written challenge with a district judge.

At the Santa Ana Jail, Griffith could walk over, show his identification and usually speak with Ramos-Brito that day. “It’s kind of useless having an attorney if you can’t talk to him,” Griffith said.

Prosecutors eventually reduced Ramos-Brito’s felony charge to a misdemeanor. After deliberating for a little more than an hour, a jury acquitted him in September 2025.

In immigration detention, not having a lawyer, or struggling to communicate with one, can leave people making decisions that shape the course of their case before they understand the consequences, attorneys say.

Even when a lawyer reaches someone in time, access to their client can disappear overnight. “I’ve met with someone and said, ‘OK, we’re going to file your petition tomorrow, and let’s just finalize your declaration,’” Wilfong said. “And then they’re transferred that night out of state, and I can’t file anymore.”

Criminal defendants generally have to remain close to where they are charged, so they can be brought back to court, said García Hernández. ICE faces no comparable geographic limit in its detention network, he added.

More than a year later, the Vasquez Perdomo lawsuit has produced court orders addressing both issues at the center of the case. In September, a federal judge’s ruling put new restrictions on ICE’s use of warrantless arrests across Los Angeles and surrounding counties, ordering agents to document why they believe someone might get away before a warrant could be obtained. The judge had not yet ruled on the lawsuit’s allegation that ICE’s stops can amount to racial profiling. A separate order requires ICE to grant people who are arrested and taken to B-18 regular, private access to lawyers. The government is appealing that order, and the broader case continues.

For all the procedural differences between them, the stakes in both the immigration and criminal systems can be enormous. Immigration detention is legally classified as civil, but it can involve the same loss of freedom as criminal incarceration, except without the oversight and openness of a criminal case, attorneys say.

“They look the same. They feel the same, and they are as harmful to the people inside them as any federal prison I’ve ever been inside of,” Toczylowski said of immigration detention centers. Under the current administration, she said, their use has become “so blatantly punitive” that “the law and the reality don’t match.”

Deportation can add layers of harm, like separating someone permanently from their family and community, or returning them to a country where they face persecution, torture or even death, Toczylowski said.

“If you look at the system side by side,” she said, “our civil immigration detention looks a lot more like criminal custody than it ever has before.”

text:
With the protracted war in Iran, a pending firing squad execution, the most expensive election cycle in US history, the unaffordability of everyday necessities, outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases, relentless ICE raids and arbitrary detainments (including of children), attacks against selective press outlets, the continued demand for justice for Epstein victims and survivors, and ongoing threats to civil liberties and civil rights, what’s happening to Haitians in the United States might not register for most Americans. But the plight of Haitians living here offers a lens into how America’s light and credibility as a beacon for human rights and civil liberties is quickly fading, shamefully growing dark at rapid speed.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

A vital part of the sweeping Immigration Act of 1990, signed into law by President George H.W. Bush, was Temporary Protected Status (TPS). This congressionally created program provided protection from deportation and extended work permits for immigrants experiencing natural disaster, armed conflict, or other extraordinary and temporary conditions in their home countries. The law did not provide permanent protection, and was specifically meant to be temporary, but with an important caveat allowing for review and extension of status. This mattered because armed conflict itself might not be temporary, as evidenced by the US wars in Vietnam and Afghanistan.

Now, however, instead of protecting foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home country, the country is vilifying them.

The contrasts between George H.W. Bush’s statement upon signing the Immigration Act and Donald Trump’s public statements cannot be more glaring—and that is shameful for the United States. Bush noted that the act’s objectives included “support for the family as the essential unit of society” because the law sought to balance family reunification and employment pathways. This falls in stark contrast to the utterly false and crass campaign slogan Donald Trump spread about Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio: “They’re eating cats and dogs.”

After Trump and the right continued to amplify this untrue rumor about Haitians, the administration moved to revoke their TPS. The Supreme Court was forced to weigh in and decided, in a 6–3 ruling, to allow the revocation to proceed. Justice Elena Kagan’s dissent in the case, Mullin v. Doe, underscores our point. As she noted, President Trump’s targeted actions against Haitians must be understood for what they are—xenophobic and racist. She offered some of Trump’s statements to prove her point. “Haitians are ‘eating the dogs…they’re eating the cats. They’re eating—they’re eating the pets of the people that live [in Springfield, Ohio].’” His crudity suggests Haitians are infected with disease: “Haitians in the United States “probably have AIDS.” That their nation is a “‘shithole country,’ which is ‘filthy, dirty, [and] disgusting.’” In his more than apparent disgust toward Haitians—very likely because they are Black—he has stated that they are “poisoning the blood” of the United States. As Justice Kagan surmised, “The references–of filth, disease, and primitiveness—are shot through with racial stereotypes and tropes.” She concludes, “It is hard to imagine the statements being made today of any White community.”

Yet the United States’ dismantling of human rights is not a matter of mere crude words. The effects are serious and proof of America’s backsliding on democracy and the rule of law. Consider the death of Pierre Damas Bel. Authorities labeled his death a suicide. On August 31, near Springfield, Ohio, Bel stopped his car on the shoulder of a highway, exited, stepped in front of an oncoming tanker truck, and was killed. It would be more accurate to say that the 20-year-old Haitian immigrant was the victim of the Trump administration’s cruel and erratic immigration policies. In this case, he was one of the innumerable immigrant victims caught in the horrific trap of an administration that views Black immigrants as both unworthy of legal protection and as a threat.

Bel had only been in the United States since 2024. He was a first-year college student. He had been an honors student in high school. Pierre was a lieutenant in the Marine Junior Reserve Officer Corps and volunteered at local charities. He dreamed of becoming a doctor.

Tragically, like so many other Haitians, he was driven to depression after the administration stripped TPS from some 330,000 Haitians Bel’s asylum claim was pending when he died. Like many of his neighbors in Springfield, he was summoned to a local ICE office and fitted with the ankle monitor. And like them, he was traumatized, shamed, and humiliated—treated like a criminal.

From a civil liberties point of view, forcing ankle monitoring on Haitians in the US is a serious problem for several reasons. First, it is a departure from standard law enforcement protocols, because he had not committed a crime and did not pose a risk of harm to anyone. According to the local government in Springfield, Ohio, Haitians are more likely to be victims of crime there than to commit offenses. Contrary to Donald Trump’s statements, non-detained immigrants have a very high compliance rate with immigration appointments. Thus, this shift is not only unnecessarily invasive but also procedurally unprecedented. Second, an ankle monitor is highly restrictive, limiting the distances one may travel, affecting employment, schooling, and caregiving. Third, ankle monitoring imposes stigmatization and can result in a severe emotional strain—as was the case for Bel, according to his family members. Fourth, for an administration that claims to be fiscally responsible, the program is a clear waste of resources: Many of the individuals being fitted with ankle monitoring devices have pending legal claims and were already cooperative.

Today, Haitians in the US are being stalked by ICE. As a headline in the French publication, Le Monde read in early October, “ICE agents are chasing Miami’s Haitians: ‘No one goes out anymore, the streets and churches are deserted, people are afraid of being arrested.’” It seems that cruelty is the point. And this is why Americans should be concerned.

The president has justified breaching constitutional norms and ignoring judicial rulings based on a theory of protecting national security. This served as the underlying justification of ICE raids and lawlessness in the Twin Cities, where Alex Pretti and Renée Nicole Goode were gunned down by government agents. That is also the community represented by Representative Ilhan Omar, whose home was raided by federal immigration agents on October 12, in an effort to “build [a] case for stripping her citizenship” according to The Wall Street Journal. It was the argument used for deploying National Guard troops in Los Angeles and Washington, DC. It has also been the justification for barring news organizations from briefings at the White House.

A healthy and functioning democracy does not pander to racial stereotypes to promote policy. Both constitutional precedent and civil rights laws make this clear. As Justice Kagan expressed, Donald Trump’s “statements fairly shout, in their racial undertones and overtones alike, that race entered into the President’s resolve to remove Haitians from this country.” Moreover, a well-functioning executive does not weaponize government against law-abiding immigrants and citizens. A nation committed to the rule of law does not brazenly kill its citizens and then blame them for their deaths.

While Americans may have moved on from the plight of immigrants among us, their experiences under this administration provide a lesson and a warning. Their case shows how the Trump administration ignores the rule of law, disregards precedent, is willing to impose psychological threats and harms against innocent individuals, and cares very little about disrupting the lives of law-abiding individuals. Americans should worry that immigrants are simply the canaries in the coal mines.

text:
Last week, Representative Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home was raided by agents from the Department of Homeland Security. Omar has not been indicted or criminally charged, but the Trump administration has now said that it was investigating whether Omar had acquired her US citizenship through fraudulent means after arriving in the country as a 12-year-old from Somalia.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

There are multiple allegations the DHS appears to be pursuing, one claiming that Omar’s father lied on her immigration paperwork to say she was 17 instead of 18, thus allowing for her to acquire citizenship through her own father’s naturalization. Another allegation apparently being investigated is one that has regularly percolated through the conservative media sphere for years: that Ilhan Omar’s ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother, and that she fraudulently sought to extend her own citizenship to him through incestuous means. The government has apparently acquired her DNA to pursue this, reportedly by having taken discarded garbage from her home (though the government has denied the account of this specific method).

The Wall Street Journal reported after the raid that the Trump administration was pursuing something that had never been attempted before against a member of Congress: denaturalization and removal from the United States. Tom Homan, Trump’s so-called “border czar,” then confirmed to Fox News that such extreme measures were on the table.

Denaturalization is in vogue right now. Deportation, detainments, visa revocations, and entry bans have all been part of the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant crusade. But there are simply not enough -citizens present in the United States, whether documented or undocumented, to fulfill the national cleansing that the government appears to be openly salivating after.

On New Year’s Eve in 2025, the DHS posted a picture of a peaceful, unnaturally spotless beach and a perfect blue sky, with the caption: “America After 100 Million Deportations. The peace of a nation no longer besieged by the third world.” There are estimated to be roughly 15 million undocumented migrants present in the United States, 13 million green-card holders, and 3 million documented noncitizens on temporary visas. In a perfect Republican world, one where every undocumented and documented noncitizen is deported, you still only get to 31 million, well below the magic number needed to supposedly ensure America’s prosperity. Thus, naturalized citizens—those who went through all of the legal hoops, learning American civics and all the little bits of this country’s history—have to be next on the chopping block. And as a high-profile political antagonist of President Trump, Omar is an inviting target. Back in May, when discussing Omar, Trump had mockingly imitated her saying, “The Constitution gives me certain rights,” before dismissing her as a “phony” and saying she should “get the hell out.”

While Omar is not the most leftist member of the Democratic Party (she is not a member of the DSA, for instance), she is something that is arguably just as bad in the Republican Party’s imagination: a Somali American, the first to be elected to Congress.

Trump has aimed his ire at many different ethnic groups over his two terms, but he has targeted the Somali community in an especially venomous way. Days before Omar’s house was raided, Trump posted that her home state of Minnesota, which has the nation’s largest Somali American community, was “being taken over by Somali Immigrants” and urged Minnesotans to “fight back,” adding that the “Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing.” In particular, Trump promised those fighting the alleged malign influence of the local Somali community that, if need be, “the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

Omar, perhaps the most prominent Somali American in the country, has been the prime target within this larger communal attack for years. Since she first ran for Congress in 2018, Omar has been accused of antisemitism, being “Somalia-first,” supporting multiple terrorist groups, secret communism, financial and tax fraud, both polygamy and adultery, and being a foreign agent. While most of these allegations have come from Republicans, many Democrats have joined the pile-on, in particular to attack Omar’s criticism of Israel. (This lack of solidarity from some Democrats continues even now; Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer has not commented on the raid despite its having happened over a week ago, and Minnesota Senator Amy Klobuchar only questioned the raid’s timing, while offering no support for Omar or larger criticism of the move.)

While the denaturalization of a serving member of Congress is unprecedented, past governments have tried to denaturalize elected officials, driven by the same anti-immigrant, partisan dynamics that are behind the anti-Omar campaign. Perhaps the most notable such target was Stanley Nowak, a Polish American union organizer who briefly served as a Democratic state senator in the Michigan legislature from 1939 to 1948. Nowak had worked in the past with communist publications and organizations in the 1920s, but never said that he himself was a member of the Communist Party. Nevertheless, in 1942, Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s government initiated proceedings to denaturalize him on the basis that he had concealed his connection to communist groups while applying for citizenship. As with Omar, the aim was to use charges of immigration fraud as a pretext to remove someone whose leftist politics the government deemed unacceptable.

The case only proceeded for a few months before FDR’s attorney general dropped the matter, but it was revived in 1952 during the Truman administration, dragging on until 1958 under the Eisenhower administration, with Nowak’s citizenship being revoked and then restored later by the Supreme Court. The ultimate failure to deport Nowak could be construed as a victory for the rule of law, but nativism and a hatred of those who criticized the United States were what governed his prosecution, and those sentiments have only built, grown, and spread to new hosts since then.

Even if all 26 million naturalized American citizens were to be deported en masse, the work of building the ideal fascist state would not be complete. After all, the Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to end birthright citizenship, thus making the millions of Americans born to immigrant parents vulnerable to removal. There are also those whose parents are American citizens but are of the same irksome race that noncitizens are, like Somalis or Haitians, or of enemy nationalities, like Palestinians and Iranians, who will almost undoubtedly come on the chopping block in the coming months and years. Then there are people who, though they may be white, Protestant, and otherwise spotless in their racial makeup, are deemed to have voided their right to Americanness by opposing the state of Israel—thus “becoming Palestinian,” as Trump once described Schumer. The idea of making someone born in the United States, to American parents, stateless is no vice to certain members of Congress, such as Randy Fine, who wrote a letter this year demanding the revocation of the passports and the barring of reentry to activists and journalists who attended the funeral of Ali Khamenei, accusing them of treason, a crime punishable by death in the United States.

The breadth of this crusade is one of the reasons it is ultimately useless to note the obvious shoddiness of the case against Omar. This is an administration that recognizes no limits and knows it is dealing in deceit, a massive, systemic fraud of its own. The point of this case is to be a stress test for wide-scale denaturalization in the remaining years of Trump’s second term. Even if the move against Omar fails, we cannot rely on one of the most right-wing Supreme Courts in American history to be so forgiving towards lesser-known individuals, not to mention that every time one of these cases makes its way through the courts, the Trump administration will take notes and fine-tune its approach. Through these proceedings, the government will be able to know better what matters it can simply ignore the decisions of courts on, and what angles the Democratic Party will simply ignore either out of lack of care or silent agreement. Omar may be the story now, but there are thousands more waiting to be written with bitter hands, out of sight.

text:
The Justice Department said Monday it has filed charges involving 48 noncitizens in connection with election crimes, illegal voting and fraudulent voter registration.

The department says the cases in California, Florida, Nevada, New York and Pennsylvania involved noncitizens voting in federal elections and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship either to register to vote or to cast a ballot.

More than half of the charges were brought in California against noncitizens from a wide variety of countries, including Belize, Mexico, Cambodia, India, Canada and the Philippines. The charges include false statements on a naturalization application, illegal voting and falsely claiming citizenship to vote. Most were lawful permanent residents, many of whom were alleged to have voted in the 2020, 2022 or 2024 elections.

Nine of the charges were brought in Pennsylvania against noncitizens from Cuba, Poland, Israel, Kenya, Russia, Greece and the Netherlands for illegal voting. Most were lawful permanent residents alleged to have voted in the 2022 or 2024 elections.

Six charges were brought against noncitizens in Florida, two of whom were Cuban nationals and two of whom were Canadian nationals. All of those charged were alleged to have illegally voted in the 2022 or 2024 elections.

Four charges were brought in New York against lawful permanent residents from Germany, Ireland, Guyana and Jamaica, and one was brought in Nevada against a lawful permanent resident from the Philippines — all for illegal voting.

The DOJ announcement comes as the Trump administration has been looking for noncitizen voters throughout the country in the months leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm election, alleging it is a major problem.

Last month, the DOJ announced that 10 foreign nationals in Minnesota and seven in Texas had been charged with illegal voting in federal elections or falsely claiming citizenship.

It also comes just days after a federal judge in California ordered the Trump administration to halt investigations in nine states into whether noncitizens are registered to vote.

Multiple organizations across the political spectrum have shown noncitizen voting is extremely rare. The nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research said most allegations of noncitizen registration or voting are the result of misunderstandings, mischaracterizations or fabrications about voter data, while the nonpartisan Brennan Center put the incidence of suspected noncitizen voting at .0001%.

text:
During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump’s administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.

The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.

Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.”

The Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.

Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government’s request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.

Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote.

The federal government is simply asking California to enforce its own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state’s refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting.

The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.

Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government’s list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.

Even if election staffers spent just three minutes checking each of the expected 2.75 million mail ballots against the government’s list, the process would take 140,000 man-hours, Waxman said — or about 16 years of working time.

Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”

If the administration disagrees with how California runs its elections, it can ask Congress to change that process, said attorney Sam Siegel, representing California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.

The federal government has provided no credible evidence to support its suspicions, said Siegel.

“It has no basis in law or in fact,” he told the panel. “We just dispute the premise that noncitizens are voting.”

But Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, said everyone has an interest in ensuring that only eligible citizens vote. He suggested that granting the administration’s request for an emergency order could provide clarity.

“Without an injunction, you will never know” if that is happening, Bumatay told Siegel.

Bennett said the panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.

___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho.

___

This story was first published Oct. 25, 2026. It was updated Oct. 26, 2026, to correct the name of the attorney who represents California’s secretary of state. He is Sam Siegel, not Siegal or Seigel.

text:
A US appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens. The decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump's efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the November 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. "In the midst of an ongoing election, the United States asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state's traditional domain, upending the state's policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike," stated the majority opinion, which was joined by two judges: Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, dissented. The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election. The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent votes from being counted by a state, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people allegedly registered to vote in California had actually submitted a mail ballot. Justice Department officials said on October 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump's fellow Republicans in the midterms. Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its so-called "sanctuary state" policies that ‌limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Trump has long asserted that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud. All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud. The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on October 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens. The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case. California says the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data." "At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt," lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing. "At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election." Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizens risk wrongly flagging naturalized US citizens for removal from the rolls. The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters' sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one. text:
A federal appeals court ruled 10-7 Friday, October 23, 2026, that ICE can detain certain immigrants throughout their deportation proceedings without granting them bond hearings, overturning an earlier decision requiring hearings within 90 days and allowing detention to continue even after prolonged confinement.

The full Fifth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that immigrants who entered the United States without lawful admission have no constitutional right to individualized hearings assessing whether they pose a danger or flight risk before being detained while their immigration cases proceed. The decision establishes binding precedent in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested the three men whose challenges led to the ruling after they had lived in the United States for years. Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, a Mexican national, had lived in the country for more than 22 years before his December 2025 arrest. Alejandro Villegas Angel, also from Mexico, had lived in the United States since 2011 and has two American-born children. Miguel Angel Gomez Alvarado, a Honduran national who entered in 2012, has a child who is a U.S. citizen.

Federal district judges ordered the men released after finding that their detention without bond hearings violated the Fifth Amendment's guarantee of due process. A three-judge Fifth Circuit panel upheld those orders in July and required immigration authorities to provide hearings within 90 days to assess whether continued detention was justified.

Writing for the majority, Judge Cory Wilson concluded that immigrants who entered without inspection are subject to mandatory detention under Section 1225 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, even if they have lived in the country for decades.

In July 2025, the federal government expanded its interpretation of that provision to cover immigrants arrested within the United States who had never been formally admitted. Previously, many such detainees were processed under Section 1226, which allows immigration judges to consider release on bond while deportation proceedings continue.

Wilson rejected the argument that the Constitution requires authorities to assess each detainee's dangerousness or flight risk before holding them under the mandatory detention provision. Addressing their claimed right to freedom from physical confinement, he wrote that immigrants could secure their release by leaving the country.

"They can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country," Wilson wrote.

Detention throughout removal proceedings can satisfy constitutional due process protections while deportation remains a viable outcome, according to the majority. The three men had been held for periods ranging from three weeks to approximately three months, and the court said their claims did not establish a separate constitutional violation based on the length of confinement.

Seven judges dissented, with Judge Leslie Southwick arguing that immigrants detained inside the United States have constitutional protections requiring an opportunity to challenge prolonged confinement. Judge Dana Douglas separately warned that the majority's reasoning gave immigration authorities sweeping detention powers without adequate judicial safeguards.

A federal judge in Texas began applying the ruling the same day it was issued. U.S. District Judge Xavier Rodriguez suspended government response deadlines in certain immigration detention cases involving claims that prolonged confinement violates constitutional protections.

On October 1, the Supreme Court agreed to hear a related dispute in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha over whether immigrants arrested inside the United States fall under Section 1225's mandatory detention requirement or Section 1226's provisions allowing bond hearings.

text:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.

McALLEN — A section of border wall that the federal government planned to build along a beloved South Texas wildlife refuge could end up cutting through the refuge instead.

The federal government is considering changing its plans for a border wall that it intended to build on a levee that runs adjacent to the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge. The change is an attempt to resolve a legal dispute in which government contractors are accused of trespassing on property near the refuge belonging to Hidalgo County Irrigation District No. 2.

During a hearing in federal court on Oct. 14, Assistant U.S. Attorney Lance Duke said the federal government was considering taking up the suggestion proposed by the irrigation district to relocate the border wall currently under construction.

“My client is in the process of looking into, basically, moving the wall from its current expected path — where we were originally planning to go through [the irrigation district’s] property — and instead move it through the wildlife refuge,” Duke said. “We recognize that will probably just create additional litigation from other interested parties.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. Customs and Border Protection did not confirm the agency was considering relocating the wall through the refuge but said it was aware of the lawsuit.

“CBP remains committed to enhancing border security at Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, while continuing coordination with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and other relevant federal and state partners,” the spokesperson said. “CBP is aware of the pending litigation and remains confident in its legal authorities and assessments.”

In July, CBP moved forward with plans to construct 2.8 miles of border wall on a levee located adjacent to the wildlife refuge.

However, the irrigation district, a public corporation that distributes water to cities, farmers and ranchers, alleged that government contractors trespassed on their property during construction, specifically on the 60 feet of land it owns on either side of an irrigation canal.

The irrigation district sued Spencer Construction LLC and Royal Concrete Products LLC in September, seeking a restraining order against the contractors to halt construction.

A state district court in Hidalgo County issued a temporary restraining order against the contractors on July 30, which a federal judge extended after the U.S. government removed the case to federal court. A temporary restraining order is still in place.

During a hearing in August, the general manager of the irrigation district, Anthony Stambaugh, testified the contractors did not ask permission to enter onto their property.

He added that the presence of a border wall within their property would tighten the space around the canal, making it difficult for crews to conduct maintenance or repairs on the canal in a timely manner.

Lance Kirby, the attorney for the irrigation district, told the judge the issue would be resolved if the border were built 15 to 20 feet south of the current alignment.

“It’s music to my ears. It’s what we’ve been hoping for and asking for all along,” Kirby said in response to Duke’s announcement.

However, Duke had argued that Texas trespass law could not prevent the federal government from building a border wall on land it does not own. He added that a border wall at the proposed location was inevitable, even if the federal government had to move forward with condemnation.

The Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, sometimes referred to as the jewel of the national wildlife refuge system, is a 2,000-acre haven for wildlife that sits along the Rio Grande, south of the city of Alamo.

It’s a well-known and treasured destination for many who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley where school field trips to the refuge are like a rite of passage.

Its property has been a potential target for border wall construction since President Donald Trump first began pushing forward his border security agenda in 2017.

Border wall plans there activated members of the community to hold public demonstrations to spare the refuge from construction. Then in 2019, congressional lawmakers succeeded in protecting the refuge and other sensitive areas by assuring that appropriated funds could not be used to build a border wall there.

However, during Trump’s second term, CBP has been able to work around those restrictions through the One Big, Beautiful Bill, Trump’s signature funding bill which bypasses the appropriations process to fund border wall construction.

“I am concerned by reports that the federal government may reroute approximately 2.8 miles of border wall through the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge,” said U.S. Rep. Henry Cuellar, a Democrat from Laredo who was among the lawmakers who had secured protections for the refuge and other areas.

Cuellar added language to the Homeland Security Appropriations bill the 2027 fiscal year that would preserve those protections, but Congress is unlikely to take up the bill for a vote until the end of the year.

“I support strong border security, but there are better ways to secure our border than building through a wildlife refuge or cutting communities off from the Rio Grande,” Cuellar said, adding that the government should be investing in Border Patrol personnel, technology, intelligence, ports of entry, and infrastructure that address border security needs.

“DHS and CBP need to be transparent about any proposed change in the alignment at Santa Ana, including where the funding would come from, how the refuge would be affected, and what alternatives are being considered,” Cuellar said.

title: The Press Shouldn't Hype Trump's Bogus Alaska Lawsuit | Washington Monthly
authors: Joshua A. Douglas, Bruno V. Manno, Jon Marcus, Michael T. Nietzel
description:
Last week, headlines blared about President Donald Trump’s lawsuit in Alaska to block the certification of the results if his favored candidate, incumbent U.S.
Trump’s Department of Justice also filed a lawsuit against California, seeking to segregate ballots cast by purported noncitizens.
These lawsuits are best understood as press releases—fanciful press releases, to be sure—but nothing more than that.
As numerous legal scholars have explained in great detail, Trump’s lawsuits in Alaska and California will surely fail.
Trump’s lawsuit to stop the certification of the result is farcical.
text:
Let’s all take a deep breath. We will need to do that a lot as Election Day nears and the results are counted.

As the election approaches, every day brings a flurry of news stories with bombastic headlines about the latest attack on the midterm election. Last week, headlines blared about President Donald Trump’s lawsuit in Alaska to block the certification of the results if his favored candidate, incumbent U.S. Senator Dan Sullivan, does not win his close race against the Democratic nominee, former U.S. Representative Mary Petola. (It was front-page news in The New York Times, with the headline “Trump’s Threat Could Thwart Vote in Alaska.” “Could” is doing a lot of work there; his lawsuit will have zero impact on the vote.) Trump’s Department of Justice also filed a lawsuit against California, seeking to segregate ballots cast by purported noncitizens. Concerns also arose about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents spotted at the polls in Florida (they were simply there to vote).

But these headlines lack proper context, leading to predictable concerns about Trump meddling in the elections. Rest assured: None of the lawsuits have merit, and courts will surely reject them.

That’s not to say, of course, that there is no cause for concern about the midterms given Trump’s past and his ongoing attempt to change normal election procedures despite having no authority to do so. We must remain vigilant when a president of the United States seeks to undermine a free and fair election. But we should not fall prey to Trump’s main goal: To sow confusion and discord among the electorate, which could cause many to stay home or doubt the results.

Filing a lawsuit does not mean the lawsuit has merit or is going anywhere. These lawsuits are best understood as press releases—fanciful press releases, to be sure—but nothing more than that.

As numerous legal scholars have explained in great detail, Trump’s lawsuits in Alaska and California will surely fail. The Alaska case suggests that voters are confused by two Dan Sullivans on the ballot, as someone with the same name as the incumbent U.S. Senator is also running. But the Alaska Supreme Court already rejected a similar claim earlier this year, before the ballots were printed. Trump’s lawsuit to stop the certification of the result is farcical. It is both too early, as there are no results yet, and too late given that he could have sued months ago. Moreover, the ballot clearly labels Senator Dan Sullivan as the incumbent. And there is no federal law that would give it the remedy it seeks, essentially to change the election result.

Derek Muller, the Notre Dame election law professor, said that “the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.” The California case is just as weak, especially given that the database the Trump DOJ is citing regarding noncitizen voters is woefully inaccurate. The federal law it uses, which makes noncitizen voting illegal, does not direct states on how to administer their elections while voting is underway. In addition, it is not clear whether the DOJ has the legal authority to bring these cases.

But these facts have not stopped people from assuming that Trump can influence the election in some way. The Constitution is clear: The president has no authority over election administration. Though lawyers should not use the courts for political reasons, saying something in a legal filing does not mean it will come true. As Professor Rick Hasen, the UCLA law professor and election law expert, wrote, “To say these are press releases masquerading as lawsuits does not convey how weak these cases legally are.”

Every news headline about these cases should have the appropriate context. Perhaps the news media should adopt a universal convention. Every headline and push notification about a Trump lawsuit over the election should begin with the phrase, “Without Any Legal Authority…” or “Without Any Evidence…” Articles about the Alaska lawsuit should say, “Without Any Legal Authority, Trump Seeks to Meddle in Alaska Election.” The California news should begin, “Without Any Evidence of Noncitizen Voting, Trump Asks Court to Separate Ballots in California.” That added context could help avoid the confusion that these lawsuits have generated. Confusion is the point. Trump wants to sow discord among the electorate so that if Republicans lose, he can claim that the election is rigged. He is weaponizing the courts for a political narrative, not a legal one. We can choose not to let that happen by how we discuss these cases.

Of course, lawyers must defend the lawsuits in court, which they are admirably doing. The point is not that we should let our guard down. We must be smart consumers of information about Trump’s electoral moves. That starts with headline writers and journalists helping the electorate understand these cases as press releases, not actual legal uncertainties.

While perhaps bumpy, the election will proceed as expected. Millions of people will cast their ballots—in fact, many already have through early or mail-in voting. Thousands of election workers will uphold democracy by counting ballots fairly and accurately. Election officials will certify the results. Close races may lead to post-election lawsuits. All of that is normal.

What is abnormal is the president meddling in election processes. It’s also unconstitutional and unprecedented. Let’s make sure the American people have that vital information in every headline, push notification, social media post, and news story. Our short attention spans value sound bites over detailed nuance. But our democracy requires the American public to understand that nuance so that what are essentially press releases under the guise of lawsuits do not undermine people’s faith in the election.

text:
A federal appeals court ruled on October 23, 2026, that President Donald Trump violated the Constitution when he took control of approximately 4,000 California National Guard members during immigration enforcement protests in Los Angeles in 2025, rejecting his administration's claim that the unrest amounted to a rebellion.

In a 2-1 decision, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit upheld an injunction against the deployment, finding that Trump exceeded the powers Congress granted the presidency. The judges also refused to let the administration withdraw its appeal of the original order, allowing the court to establish a precedent governing similar federalizations.

Trump ordered the troops into federal service on June 7, 2025, as protests spread across Los Angeles following immigration enforcement operations. The administration authorized a 60-day deployment, arguing that National Guard members were needed to protect federal personnel and property amid confrontations between demonstrators and law enforcement.

California Governor Gavin Newsom and Attorney General Rob Bonta sued, challenging Trump's authority to take command of the state's troops. U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer issued an order blocking the deployment and directing the administration to return control of the Guard to Newsom, prompting an appeal that initially resulted in the injunction being stayed.

Trump invoked 10 U.S.C. § 12406, a federal law permitting presidents to federalize National Guard units during an invasion, rebellion or danger of rebellion, or when they are unable to execute federal law using regular military forces. Judge Jennifer Sung, writing for the majority, found that the conditions in Los Angeles failed to satisfy the rebellion provision, even under the substantial deference courts ordinarily give presidential assessments of such threats.

The panel concluded that Trump's determination fell outside the range of reasonable judgments permitted by the statute. While the administration cited violent incidents and threats to federal operations, the majority found that the evidence failed to establish a rebellion or sufficient danger of one against federal authority.

The judges also rejected the government's alternative justification that the Guard was necessary to execute federal law. Relying on the Supreme Court's December 2025 ruling in Trump v. Illinois, the panel found that the administration had failed to establish its authority to use regular military forces for that purpose or demonstrate an inability to carry out the task with those forces.

Those findings led the majority to conclude that Trump's initial federalization order encroached on Congress's constitutional authority to determine when state military forces may be called into federal service. The court also found California likely to succeed on its related Tenth Amendment claim, affirming Breyer's preliminary injunctionA preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider the likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.Read more → against the deployment.

The Trump administration sought to withdraw two related appeals after the deployment ended, but the Ninth Circuit refused to dismiss the challenge involving the original June 2025 order. The judges cited the extensive litigation already completed and the possibility that California could face similar federalizations in the future.

In a separate order issued the same day, the majority warned that allowing parties to abandon fully litigated appeals could enable them to manipulate the development of legal precedent by withdrawing cases likely to produce unfavorable rulings. The court permitted the administration to dismiss its separate appeal concerning an extension of the deployment, which had received substantially less judicial review.

Judge Eric Miller, appointed by Trump, joined Sung's majority opinion and wrote separately about California's legal claims. Judge Mark Bennett, another Trump appointee, dissented, arguing that the court should have allowed the administration to withdraw its appeal and that the majority had made errors in upholding the injunction. He also questioned its reliance on the Supreme Court's intervening decision, which the parties had only briefly addressed.

Newsom welcomed the ruling as a victory for the Constitution and the rule of law, while Bonta said the decision reinforced limits on presidential authority over state National Guard forces. California officials maintained that the administration had used unrest surrounding immigration enforcement operations to justify an unlawful deployment.

text:
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.

In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.

list 2 of 3All you need to know about US midterms 2026

list 3 of 3US judge blocks federal operations seeking to identify non-citizen voters

end of list

The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.

But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.

In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.

The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.

The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.

Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.

The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.

California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.

The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.

But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.

The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.

Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.

In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.

But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.

“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”

Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.

It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.

But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.

The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.

Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.

In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.

Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.

Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.

Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.

Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.

But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.

Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.

In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.

text:
Wendy Mendez, an English for speakers of other languages (ESOL) teacher at Vel Phillips Middle School in Oshkosh, was deported last week, Wednesday, Oct. 21, according to a source who requested to remain anonymous.

According to the anonymous source, Mendez was transferred at least three-to-six times to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) detention facilities, two of them being located in Kentucky and Louisiana.

According to a Facebook post by Deb Nez, Mendez’s friend, Mendez has been in six detention centers in eight days across five different states.

“Wendy (Mendez) has been subject to different forms of torture including three days of solitary confinement, sleeping on concrete floors with blankets that are like rags, or beds covered in mold and a host of other mistreatments,” Nez wrote in a Facebook post on Oct. 22.

Story continues below advertisement

According to Nez’s Facebook posts, Mendez is a school teacher and psychologist with three master’s degrees who lived in Wisconsin for six years and currently has two kids in the U.S., one of whom is a special needs child for whom Mendez was a primary caregiver.

“He (Mendez’s kid) cannot understand why his mother is not here with him,” Nez wrote in a Facebook post on Oct. 22. “Every time that he (comes) back from school, he sees her car and starts yelling that Mommy is home.”

Nez wrote on Facebook that Mendez was placed into ICE custody for failure to appear at an immigration hearing at the immigration court in Chicago.

“They had no knowledge of that because the court sent the notice to their previous address from more (than) three years ago,” Nez wrote in the Facebook post. “USCIS (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) had their new address within days of them moving to the new house.”

According to Nez, lawyers presented the proof to the immigration court that showcases an error in the notification system, with the motion being accepted by the court, waiting for the judge’s decision.

Nez wrote in a different Facebook post Oct. 25 that Mendez is “safe and doing okay.”

“However, mentally and emotionally, she is still recovering from the horrific experience she went through with (the) U.S. immigration,” Nez wrote on Facebook. “She said ‘worse than you can imagine.’”

According to the Oshkosh Area School District’s Communications Director (OASD), Katie Nieman, the OASD cannot comment on individual employee matters due to privacy laws.

According to the OASD’s message to Vel Phillips Middle School families released Oct. 26, Mendez is not going to teach students, a decision which was not based from bad performance.

“Due to unforeseen circumstances, Mrs. Mendez is currently out of the classroom for the foreseeable future,” the OASD wrote Oct. 26. “She is an employee in good standing and has been placed on an unpaid leave of absence. At no point was this a school safety or performance-related issue. The district is working through the process of obtaining more details and will provide more information if we are able.”

According to the OASD’s statement, Mendez’s students will be informed about the situation tomorrow Oct. 28.

The OASD’s statement said the administration is making a plan to cover Mendez’s classes, adding that there are resources available to students.

“We are keeping Mrs. Mendez and her loved ones in our thoughts during this difficult time,” the OASD wrote. “If you feel your child needs additional support during the school day, please contact our Vel Phillips Middle School counseling office directly at 920.718.4268 x3403 or our main school office at 920.718.4268.”

Mendez moved to Oshkosh from Costa Rica in 2020 with her husband Richard Godrey and two sons.

“A Vigil for the Missing” will be held Oct. 30 at the Oshkosh Opera House Square from 6 to 7 p.m.

According to the ICE Online Detainee Locator System website, a detainee who is currently in ICE custody or who has been in the U.S. Customs and Border Protection custody for more than 48 hours can be located in the system with an Alien Registration Number or biographical information.

According to the Washington Post, people held in ICE detention centers who have received final orders of removal will no longer be listed in the Online Detainee Locator System, even if they are appealing the order or have another legal basis to remain in the country.

The Advance-Titan reached out to the Winnebago County Sheriff’s Office Lieutenant of Communications Jesse Jensen and is waiting for response.

text:
AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.

Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).

It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.

Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.

The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.

It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.

The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.

Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.

It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.

Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”

Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”
