Reports of a possible federal immigration enforcement surge in California in the weeks before the midterm elections appear to have reached the Central Coast, with several sightings reported over the weekend.

The first reported sighting was Saturday morning, when people began sharing reports on social media of federal agents at the Santa Cruz County Main Jail.

The Sheriff’s Office later clarified that federal agents were at the jail to take a person into custody. The office did not specify why the agents wanted to detain the person and said they left without detaining anyone.

“The Sheriff’s Office remains committed to protecting public safety, maintaining community trust and carrying out its responsibilities in accordance with California law and applicable county policies governing cooperation with federal immigration authorities,” the Sheriff’s Office said on social media.

The office also clarified that federal agents determine their own enforcement activities and schedules, and that the Sheriff’s Office does not assist with that enforcement.

The Sheriff’s Office further clarified that:

It does not notify U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement of scheduled release dates.

It does not participate in civil immigration enforcement.

It does not provide criminal history information to ICE for civil immigration enforcement purposes.

It complies with valid judicial warrants and court orders as required by law.

The Monterey County Rapid Response Network also reported that two people were detained in Seaside on Sunday morning. One person was detained near Sonoma and Yosemite streets.

The network said the enforcement appeared to be targeted. It provided no further information, but said, “The individuals were taken by ICE officers wearing vests with ‘ICE Police’ lettering on them.”

“The Network has observed an increase in activity in the Seaside area for the last few weeks. Enforcement is mainly targeted, meaning ICE agents know who they are after,” the Rapid Response Network said.

"They were in town conducting targeted investigations and made some apprehensions. Seaside PD was not involved, nor were we notified of the apprehensions until we inquired. It would be helpful to be notified if apprehensions are done proactively on their behalf because it helps us communicate facts to our community. Seaside PD wants to know when there’s any law-enforcement taking enforcement action that’s preplanned in our community. We will always respect Investigations, but our motto is to be open and honest with our community," said Seaside police chief Nick Borges.

NBC Bay Area reported that advocates with the Santa Clara County Rapid Response Network said ICE agents were in the lobby of the Main Jail on Hedding Street in San Jose on Sunday. Advocates went to the jail that morning and said agents were also just outside the building, apparently waiting for people to be released.

On Saturday, members of the same network were at Elmwood Jail in Milpitas, watching ICE agents there for a third consecutive day. Activists said they want agents to know their actions are being witnessed and documented.

Santa Clara County is a sanctuary county, but no sanctuary policy can prohibit agents from waiting in public areas of a jail, NBC Bay Area reported.

The Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office said it does not coordinate with ICE or notify the agency of release dates. The office has also been tracking ICE visits and said agents have been visiting the jail lobby for more than a year, taking 60 people into custody who were scheduled for release.

NBC Bay Area said it contacted ICE for comment on Sunday’s San Jose activity but had not received a response.

text:
A U.S. appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.

The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the Nov. 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.

The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in. The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Tuesday in the case.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government “asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike.”

The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.

The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent a state from counting votes, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people on its list had actually submitted a mail ballot.

Justice Department officials said Oct. 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.

California is the most populous state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its “sanctuary state” policies that ‌limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.

All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct. 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.

The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.

California says the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data.”

“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing Tuesday. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”

Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizens risk wrongly flagging naturalized U.S. citizens for removal from the rolls.

The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.

“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat.

title: These Midterms, ICE Is Truly on the Ballot
description:
It is worth noting that when the public supports such rhetoric in elected officials, that rhetoric becomes real—it affects lives.
Consider immigration enforcement, with 50 percent of Americans in February supporting the deportation of all immigrants lacking permanent legal status and 48 percent opposing it.
Yet, public opinion toward harsh immigration enforcement is softening as well.
Also, last year, Pennsylvania voters ousted a Republican sheriff in favor of a Democrat who ran on ending the local partnership with ICE.
With control of Congress and immigration enforcement on November’s ballot—and with those elected responding to voter preferences—how we vote signals the direction our nation will decide to go.
text:
Next week, America votes in the midterms. And as Election Day approaches, a new rhetoric of crime and illegality has emerged with familiar implications.

While the “tough-on-crime” era of the 1980s and 1990s may have passed, similar dialogue today is anchored in “tough-on-immigration” policies. For example, Republicans and allied groups spent $53 million on immigration ads across 27 states from January to June. And even old tough-on-crime era rhetoric has reemerged as campaign strategy, with “soft on crime” being a lead attack of the Republicans, and President Donald Trump invoking the notorious 1988 Willie Horton ad at a campaign rally against Democrats. The enforcement behind this rhetoric has also grown: The Department of Homeland Security says Immigration and Customs Enforcement hired 12,000 new officers and agents last year, ICE arrests have more than doubled in 15 states and D.C. this year, and many sheriffs are partnering with ICE to perform functions of federal immigration agents through the 287(g) Program.

It is worth noting that when the public supports such rhetoric in elected officials, that rhetoric becomes real—it affects lives. My new study of elected prosecutors, published in the Journal of Public Economics, provides evidence of exactly that.

District attorneys are among the most influential actors in the criminal legal system, with nearly unfettered authority over whether to charge people with crimes and which charges to file, and in the vast majority of districts they are elected. I set out to understand whether DAs were influenced by the desire to be viewed as tough on crime. My study suggests they were, finding that across nearly 40 states during the era of rising incarceration (from 1986 to 2006), the admissions rate to state prisons increased by 3 percent during election years for district attorneys. Over those two decades, this translates to 63,000 additional prison admissions, more than a sold-out Soldier Field. But this figure only measures the election year bump; it does not capture how political incentives may have affected criminal sentencing throughout the entire election cycle.

The political incentives DAs faced may have included running currently for reelection, discouraging future challengers, and positioning for future higher office. Crime and arrest rates did not go up in DA election years, suggesting the election year increases reflected DA behavior in raising the level of criminal sentencing. The increases were notably stronger in the South and in Republican counties. So it appears the criminal legal system became tougher on crime when and where the political stakes were highest.

When voters began asking less for harsher courts, however, the election year effect declined. The General Social Survey, a survey of public opinion, finds that after about 1994, Americans’ preference for harsher courts softened. This is when the election year effects fell. So it also appears elected prosecutors were listening to voters in both directions.

This holds for today’s immigration debate. Granted, the two eras bear important differences. Tough-on-crime policies held near consensus from the public and were often bipartisan in support; tough-on-immigration policies largely are not. Consider immigration enforcement, with 50 percent of Americans in February supporting the deportation of all immigrants lacking permanent legal status and 48 percent opposing it. Such support is politically polarized. This has translated to mixed signals—with protests and local opposition in blue states contrasting with $70 billion in Republican-backed congressional funding to ICE and the Border Patrol. Still, the deliberate stoking of fear of criminality today mirrors that of the past.

Yet, public opinion toward harsh immigration enforcement is softening as well. For example, 62 percent of Americans in February opposed ICE tactics, and approval of the president’s handling of immigration had fallen 10 points from a year earlier. Also, last year, Pennsylvania voters ousted a Republican sheriff in favor of a Democrat who ran on ending the local partnership with ICE.

With control of Congress and immigration enforcement on November’s ballot—and with those elected responding to voter preferences—how we vote signals the direction our nation will decide to go. On Election Day, we will all be called to make a choice both on how we view ourselves as Americans and on how we view our neighbors—whether they have permanent legal status or not. And these stakes are not abstract; they could mean more Americans killed by federal immigration agents, more children left without their parents, more human beings sent to prisons in countries that are not their own.

Both my research and our recent times point to a deeper, sobering lesson. This lesson serves as both warning and promise: What we reward when we elect is what grows.

text:
One year after a Customs and Border Protection officer shot a pastor in the face with a chemical agent at an Oakland protest, the pastor has filed suit against the federal government.

According to a lawsuit filed on October 23, in the United States District Court of Northern California, the pastor, Jorge Bautista, seeks damages for claims of assault and battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and the violation of his civil rights. According to an earlier federal tort claim that started the legal process, Bautista is seeking $5 million in damages. Bautista, an Oakland resident, serves as pastor of a United Church of Christ congregation in San Mateo.

“The force used by the United States, by and through their agents, was unreasonable

and excessive under the circumstances, including in light of the fact that Plaintiff was not committing any crime, and did not pose a threat,” the legal complaint reads.

The protest began after news reports from The Oaklandside and other outlets confirmed that a federal immigration operation was about to unfold in the East Bay with the assistance of the Coast Guard’s Alameda base. In the morning hours of October 23, dozens of protesters showed up at the Oakland entrance to Coast Guard Island, at Dennison Street and Embarcadero; Bautista arrived to join a vigil organized by the Interfaith Movement for Human Integrity. Around 7 a.m., a CBP convoy rolled in, with some officers stepping out of their vehicles at the bridge entrance and setting off stun grenades. Our reporters and photographers on the scene captured the moment when one CBP officer shot Bautista in the face with a chemical round at point blank range. The lawsuit against the government by Bautista attaches photos by Jerome Parmer and David Bacon that were published by The Oaklandside. The operation was ultimately called off.

Bautista is suing the government and an unnamed CBP agent under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which waives immunity for government officials if they act in a negligent manner, and under the No Kings Act, signed into law earlier this month by Gov. Gavin Newsom, which allows California residents to file lawsuits against federal agents for violating their constitutional rights.

Within days of the new law taking effect, several lawsuits that had previously been filed by residents against federal agents were amended to cite it. The law, Senate Bill 747, was co-authored by State Senator Scott Weiner, of San Francisco, and Aisha Wahab, who represents East Bay cities including Fremont, Pleasanton and Livermore.

The Civil Rights claim centers on the argument that the CBP officer, whose name is not known to the plaintiff, violated Bautista’s rights under the First and Fourth Amendments to the United States Constitution. The lawsuit claims Batista had the “right to be free from retaliation for exercising protected speech and conduct and the right to be free from unreasonable and excessive force.”

Bautista’s claims of physical and emotional harm center on the effects of the chemical agent, described in the suit as a noxious powder, and the projectile that held it. The complaint says that the amount of chemical agent shot into Bautista’s face caused his “eyes, nose, and throat immediately began to burn and he was quickly unable to breathe.”

“He suffered immediate and lasting pain,” the lawsuit says, and experienced “trouble breathing following the assault and he continues to experience severe trauma from the memory of the assault and his fear that he would die from asphyxia.”

In a conversation with The Oaklandside in the days after the event, Bautista told us that he was starting to recover but that he was still suffering from pain to his jaw from the projectile and was emotionally spent. He said he felt like the officers were aggressive, there to “hurt” people.

According to an analysis by Physicians for Human Rights, the pastor was shot from about three feet away by a 40-millimeter grenade launcher, which “discharges a plume of pulverized CS (tear gas compound) or OC (pepper agent) in a cloud that extends up to 30 feet in front of the shooter from the muzzle of the weapon.” The group called this a muzzle blast round and said it was used less frequently to police protests than other chemical irritants such as aerosol grenades and liquid sprays.

The submission of the lawsuit means that the U.S. government typically has 60 days to file an answer or a motion to dismiss. According to the lawsuit, the U.S. government did not respond “substantively” to Bautista’s earlier tort claim within the six months. That claim was submitted in January and the CBP acknowledged receipt on February 3. If there is no settlement, Bautista through his lawyer, the Oakland attorney EmilyRose Johns, has requested a jury trial.

“The United States is responsible for the acts and omissions of its agencies, including Customs and Border Protection, and its component agencies, and for the conduct of its employees acting within the course and scope of their employment,” the lawsuit argues.

Johns told The Oaklandside that the shooting of Bautista was a violation of “policy, the law, and human decency.”

“At a time where there is renewed concern over CBP and ICE’s violent and unlawful behavior in our community, holding these officers to account and protecting the community members who exercise their constitutional rights to protest their presence in our community could not be more important,” she said in an email.

The attack on Bautista occurred after surges of CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents occurred in other cities, including Los Angeles and Chicago. Federal officers in multiple cities have fired tear gas into protesters and have also, in some cases, shot at protesters with live ammunition, leading to the deaths or injuries of U.S. citizens, permanent residents, and immigrants. According to the New York Times, at least 23 people have been shot by federal immigration agents since the advent of the second Trump administration in January 2025, including those that have led to the deaths of Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, Silverio Villegas Gonzalez in a Chicago suburb, and Ruben Ray Martinez in South Padre Island, Texas.

text:
U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Houston-area U.S. Reps. Sylvia Garcia and Christian Menefee met with members of the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) on Monday to discuss how President Donald Trump's immigration policies are affecting Houston's workforce. Jeffries called for cutting off all funding to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Jeffries praised U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia for her work in pressing for comprehensive immigration reform, in the vehicle of the American Dream and Promise Act of 2026. The bill, of which Garcia is the lead sponsor, would provide a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants brought to the United States as children, as well as immigrants with Temporary Protected Status and Deferred Enforced Departure statuses.

"That is just the beginning of what needs to happen in terms of getting this national nightmare that the people here in Houston and all across America have been experiencing and get to a much better place here in the United States of America, which will certainly include dramatic change as it relates to immigration enforcement and our continued commitment not to give a dime to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine," Jeffries said.

Jeffries said that ICE and the Department of Homeland Security should not count on getting any funding from Democrats in Congress without structural changes to the agency, including greater accountability.

"If you’ve got rogue ICE agents who think they’ll never be held accountable," he said, "then we’re going to continue to see the type of violence that has been unleashed and brutality on law-abiding immigrant communities and on American citizens as we horrifically saw with Alex Pretti and Renée Nicole Good."

Jeffries, as the leader of the Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives, is in a strong position to become the next Speaker of the House if his party wins a majority of seats in the chamber in the midterm elections. His visit to Texas came one day before Trump’s Tuesday visit to the state — in the president’s case, to hold rallies in Lubbock and Corpus Christi.

Garcia, who introduced Jeffries, stressed that aggressive immigration enforcement measures under Trump were hurting not only immigrants but the Houston economy.

"Make no mistake, this is an affordability issue," Garcia said. "When workers are afraid to show up for work, families lose paychecks. When customers are afraid to leave their homes, restaurants, and small businesses lose money. And when construction workers are afraid to go to a job site, homes will not get built."

title: I've represented dozens of immigration cases in my career. This is the one that broke me. - MS NOW
authors: Clarissa Pharr, Jessica Falkner, Madeleine Lippey, Lisa Rubin, Julianne McShane
description:
And as yet another family milestone approaches without her, two independent physicians have warned immigration authorities that Liliana’s health is rapidly deteriorating.
Under the Trump administration, I have witnessed firsthand the devastating outcomes of shortsighted executive memos and the steady militarization of our immigration system.
Then they sent her across the country to Richwood Correctional Center, a detention facility in Monroe, Louisiana.
Under the second Trump administration, detentions have skyrocketed, with nearly 13 % of all detained immigrants nationwide held in Louisiana-based facilities.
Along with Liliana’s family, I’m alarmed by her condition and deeply worried for her.
text:
Liliana’s blood pressure is dangerously high, a complication of her poorly managed diabetes. Her doctors are urgently concerned for her health, pointing to signs of liver failure and potential symptoms of recurring cancer.

Yet she is unable to get the care she needs. That is because Liliana, who I am referring to by her middle name to protect her confidentiality, has spent more than a year in an immigration detention center in Louisiana, more than 1,000 miles from her children in Maryland and from a community where she has built her life for almost a decade.

During that time, Liliana has missed the birth of her first grandchild. Now her daughter is pregnant again. And as yet another family milestone approaches without her, two independent physicians have warned immigration authorities that Liliana’s health is rapidly deteriorating.

I have been representing Liliana for the past year as she remains in detention. She has no criminal record. She has strong ties to her community, finds joy doing painting and remodeling work and spends her free time making arts and crafts.

As an immigration attorney, I have represented dozens of immigrants seeking humanitarian relief. After a while in this line of work, you believe you have mapped the full geography of our broken system. But working on Liliana’s case dismantled that certainty, showing me the depths of injustice our immigrant neighbors face.

Under the Trump administration, I have witnessed firsthand the devastating outcomes of shortsighted executive memos and the steady militarization of our immigration system. With recent reports that Immigration and Customs Enforcement has ordered its agents to increase the number of daily nationwide arrests by 1,000, we are likely to only see more detentions like this — detentions that protect no one, but inflict incredible harm on people and communities across the country.

Liliana should never have been detained in the first place. When her daughter survived human trafficking as a minor, Liliana supported her cooperation with U.S. federal law enforcement, leading to her daughter becoming a T-visa applicant. Through this specialized status established by Congress to protect trafficking survivors, Liliana is eligible for protection through a pending derivative T-visa application. In coming forward to help the U.S. federal government, their family entered into the government’s intended framework: assist law enforcement and receive protection from detention and removal while their case is pending.

Instead, a year ago Liliana was detained during a routine ICE check-in, after explaining she could not wear an ankle monitor for medical reasons related to her diabetes. Rather than accommodating her, the ICE officers laughed, she told us. Then they sent her across the country to Richwood Correctional Center, a detention facility in Monroe, Louisiana. Longtime immigration attorneys understand that transfers to the Fifth Circuit in Louisiana are not due to a lack of capacity in local facilities. More often than not, it is an intentional tactic to move a client across state lines, limit their access to counsel and keep them in due-process limbo.

According to the ACLU of Louisiana, the state’s detention centers have become a “black hole” for systematic human rights abuses, medical neglect and inhumane living conditions. Under the second Trump administration, detentions have skyrocketed, with nearly 13 % of all detained immigrants nationwide held in Louisiana-based facilities. And now the administration is seeking to potentially increase that number.

Richwood Correctional Center officials have largely ignored the urgent warnings from the two doctors who have evaluated Liliana’s condition and warned of her dangerously high blood pressure and early liver failure.At the same time, my organization, Ayuda, has partnered with Louisiana pro bono counsel Flavia Moody, who is admitted to the Fifth Circuit and is preparing an amended petition and a temporary restraining order in an existing habeas corpus case to challenge the lawfulness of her detention. The habeas process is actively moving forward, but the process is moving at a painfully slow pace, notoriously common within the state’s Fifth Circuit.

More articles

Under ICE’s own Performance-Based National Detention Standards, individuals with severe, deteriorating medical conditions, pending humanitarian relief claims and clean records are prime candidates for release on humanitarian parole or supervision. Any single one of these reasons are grounds for her release. Liliana has all three. And yet she remains miles away from her family, in limbo and under unimaginable conditions.

Through my weekly conversations with Liliana, I have witnessed her rapid deterioration. We have limited time together, which makes it even harder to get information, assess how she’s doing and see what can be done to help. Her health is spiraling on multiple fronts, aggravated by the systematic neglect at the Richwood Correctional Center. Her unmanaged diabetes is causing hypertension so severe, Dr. Sugarman warns it could trigger a stroke. Most recently, I learned her hand is discolored due to an untreated surgical wound from a recent procedure performed in detention.

I am also concerned since she has a history of cancer and has been showing symptoms pointing to a possible recurrence. At every turn, it seems like there is no reprieve for her health. Liliana tells me no one at the facility takes her or her needs seriously, and that she’s facing harassment from staff and another detainee. Along with Liliana’s family, I’m alarmed by her condition and deeply worried for her.

As a lawyer, a daughter dedicated to keeping families whole and an American citizen, I am appalled to witness our government inflict such suffering — not in the service of the law, and certainly not in defense of public safety, but out of a hollow impulse to wound the already wounded. Liliana’s ordeal is not an accident of bad luck or an isolated bureaucratic failure. It’s the deliberate architecture of our deportation policy, working as it is currently designed to, treating congressionally enacted protections as inconveniences to sidestep rather than binding law.

Since July 23, 2025, Liliana has been unlawfully detained, separated from her family and fighting for her life. We have exhausted every legal and humanitarian path. Her prolonged detention violates binding precedent (ICWC v. Noem), squanders taxpayer funds and actively jeopardizes her health and safety.

It is Liliana herself who best captures the sheer cruelty of the system holding her hostage. From inside the Louisiana facility, she told me, “There is a lot of injustice here, how they treat us, the food they give us is for animals and they don’t give us the medication we need to live. I hope there is justice for all the mothers who are here, who have kids back at home, who are sick, who have autism, who cry for their kids. The only thing I can say is that I hope there is justice for everything that is happening to us.”

Justice begins with ICE releasing Liliana today.

title: What the Supreme Court Has Said About Third-Country Deportations - Newsweek
description:
The Supreme Court is preparing to decide a major challenge to the Trump administration’s use of “third-country” deportations, a practice that allows the government to remove some migrants to countries other than their own.
The wider case comes before the Supreme Court as the justices consider the legal limits of the administration’s broader third-country removal policy.
What the Supreme Court Said The Supreme Court first intervened in the case on June 23, 2025, when it stayed a preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy in Massachusetts.
In an unsigned July 3 opinion granting the government's request for clarification, the Supreme Court said the lower court could not use a separate remedial order to enforce the injunction after the high court had stayed it.
On September 29, the Supreme Court again intervened, putting the lower court’s final judgment on hold and agreeing to hear the case.
text:
The Supreme Court is preparing to decide a major challenge to the Trump administration’s use of “third-country” deportations, a practice that allows the government to remove some migrants to countries other than their own.

60 Minutes reported that migrants deported by the United States to Ghana were subsequently transferred to countries to which U.S. immigration judges had previously ruled they should not be returned.

The program covered Moussa Diawara, a Malian national who had lived in the United States for approximately 25 years and had been granted withholding of removal to Mali. Instead, U.S. authorities deported him to Ghana, where he said officials placed him on a flight to Mali within five days.

Read More on Politics

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrote in a post on X that Ghana had provided the United States with “diplomatic assurances for his safety” and questioned the credibility of Diawara’s fears of persecution. James Percival, the agency's top lawyer, said third-country removals can be used when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them or when an immigration judge has barred their return to that country.

The wider case comes before the Supreme Court as the justices consider the legal limits of the administration’s broader third-country removal policy. The high court has allowed the policy to remain in effect while the litigation proceeds, but it has not ruled that the policy itself is lawful.

The case, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., concerns people with final removal orders who face deportation to countries that were neither designated in their removal orders nor previously identified in writing as potential destinations.

Federal immigration law sets out a sequence for where people with final removal orders may be sent, including, depending on the circumstances, a country they designate, a country of citizenship or nationality, or a country where they previously lived. If those options are unavailable, the law provides additional destinations, including a country whose government will accept the person. Separate federal protections prohibit removal when the applicable legal standard for persecution or torture has been met.

Under DHS guidance issued in March 2025, officials first determine whether the proposed receiving country has provided assurances that people removed from the United States will not be persecuted or tortured. If the State Department considers those assurances credible, DHS guidance permits removal without further procedures.

Without such credible assurances, DHS informs the migrant of the destination. Officers do not affirmatively ask whether the person is afraid of being sent there. A migrant who independently expresses fear is referred to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for screening.

What the Appeals Court Said

The policy prompted a class-action lawsuit that ultimately reached the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

In September, the appeals court largely upheld a lower-court judgment against DHS. It concluded that existing statutes and regulations require effective notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise fear-based claims before removal to a third country.

“An individual’s right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” the court said.

The appeals court reached a similar conclusion about torture claims, saying a person’s right to avoid removal to a country where they are likely to be tortured “means little” without prior notice and a meaningful opportunity to assert that fear.

“The statute and regulations prescribe hearing-related procedures for fear-of-persecution claims with no exception for third-country removals,” the court wrote. “We reject DHS’s efforts to create such an exception from whole cloth.”

The appeals court did not decide whether the policy violated the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. It upheld parts of the judgment on statutory and regulatory grounds but overturned two rulings on the order in which DHS must consider destination countries, finding that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge that issue.

The court also questioned the use of diplomatic assurances, noting that the record did not identify which countries, if any, had provided them. It expressed doubts that a country could guarantee protection from persecution or torture for every deportee, contrasting such broad promises with federal rules that provide for individual assurances in some cases under the Convention Against Torture.

DHS has disputed the lower courts’ interpretation. The government argues that immigration law gives the executive branch discretion over third-country removals and does not establish the additional procedures the lower courts imposed. It also argues that federal law bars the claims and restricts lower courts’ ability to issue classwide relief interfering with the government’s execution of removal law.

For countries that have provided adequate assurances, the government argues that no additional constitutional process is required. For countries without those assurances, it says its notice and fear-screening procedures satisfy due-process requirements. DHS has also argued that court-imposed restrictions create operational burdens and threaten diplomatic arrangements necessary to persuade other countries to accept deportees.

What the Supreme Court Said

The Supreme Court first intervened in the case on June 23, 2025, when it stayed a preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy in Massachusetts. That injunction required DHS to provide migrants with written notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise claims that they could face torture before removing them to an undesignated third country.

The court's June order did not explain granting the stay. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented. The Supreme Court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Those same three justices also said they would have denied the government's subsequent request to stay the final judgment in September 2026.

“In matters of life and death, it is best to proceed with caution,” Sotomayor wrote on June 23. “In this case, the Government took the opposite approach.”

“Rather than allowing our lower court colleagues to manage this high-stakes litigation with the care and attention it plainly requires, this Court now intervenes to grant the Government emergency relief from an order it has repeatedly defied.”

Sotomayor called the court’s intervention “so gross an abuse of the Court’s equitable discretion.”

Sotomayor said the dispute followed a series of removals and attempted removals to countries where migrants allegedly faced danger. “It wrongfully deported one plaintiff to Guatemala, even though an Immigration Judge found he was likely to face torture there,” she wrote. “Then, in clear violation of a court order, it deported six more to South Sudan, a nation the State Department considers too unsafe for all but its most critical personnel.” She added that a district court had “only narrowly prevented a third set of unlawful removals to Libya.”

The court again considered the dispute days later. Justice Kagan wrote separately on July 3 that although she agreed the district court could no longer enforce an injunction the Supreme Court had stayed, she continued to believe the justices should not have intervened in the first place.

“I continue to believe that this Court should not have stayed the District Court's April 18 order enjoining the Government from deporting non-citizens to third countries without notice or a meaningful opportunity to be heard,” Kagan wrote.

Sotomayor, this time joined by Jackson, dissented again. She accused the majority of allowing the administration to circumvent normal judicial procedures and concluded: “Today's order clarifies only one thing: Other litigants must follow the rules, but the administration has the Supreme Court on speed dial.”

Sotomayor pointed to the attempted removal of eight migrants to South Sudan, arguing that they risked being sent there without an opportunity to raise claims that they could face torture or death. “The United States may not deport noncitizens to a country where they are likely to be tortured or killed,” she wrote in July, in a dissent joined by Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. “International and domestic law guarantee that basic human right.” She said the government sought to send the eight to South Sudan and turn them over to local authorities “without regard for the likelihood that they will face torture or death.”

The attempted removals involved a country the U.S. government itself warns Americans not to visit. The State Department currently classifies South Sudan at Level 4: Do Not Travel, citing unrest, violent crime, kidnapping, landmines and health risks. Its advisory says armed conflict is ongoing, violent crime is common, and the U.S. government has limited ability to provide emergency consular services there.

In an unsigned July 3 opinion granting the government's request for clarification, the Supreme Court said the lower court could not use a separate remedial order to enforce the injunction after the high court had stayed it. “The May 21 remedial order cannot now be used to enforce an injunction that our stay rendered unenforceable,” the court said.

Bennett Gershman, a law professor at Pace University, told Newsweek, “I don’t think we can infer anything from the Supreme Court’s emergency stay which allows the policy to continue.” He said granting a stay to allow a full review was a familiar occurrence and meant the court considered the case sufficiently important to examine its merits.

“The administration will likely argue that it has the constitutional and statutory authority to summarily deport noncitizens who have serious criminal records and who pose a threat to U.S. national security to any country that is willing to take them,” Gershman said. “The lawyers for the individuals threatened with deportation will argue that various immigration statues require the right to due process, including the right to raise claims under the Convention Against Torture that their safety will be threatened and they will face persecution and torture when they are placed in unsafe jurisdictions.”

After additional proceedings, the district court entered a final judgment in February 2026 that set aside the DHS guidance. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld that judgment on September 18, although it rejected a separate claim concerning the statutory sequence DHS must follow when choosing a removal destination.

On September 29, the Supreme Court again intervened, putting the lower court’s final judgment on hold and agreeing to hear the case. The September order did not contain a written dissent, although it noted that Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson would have denied the government’s request for a stay.

What Happens Next

The justices are set to hear arguments on December 9. They will consider whether the district court had jurisdiction, whether it could grant classwide declaratory relief and vacate the DHS guidance, and whether the policy violates federal immigration law, due process protections, or U.S. law implementing the Convention Against Torture.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

text:
An immigrant detained at an ICE facility in Folkston, Georgia, died on Friday, reigniting calls for the facility to be shut down and an investigation into the center as it faces an ongoing hunger strike protesting abusive conditions.

Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old from El Salvador, was found with a “ligature around his neck,” according to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). According to the agency, facility staff found Sandoval at 1:46 am, and began lifesaving procedures. But he was pronounced dead at 2:28 am.

Sandoval, who was being held in the D. Ray James facility near Folkston, is the 60th known person to die in ICE detention since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term. He had only been in the facility for 21 days, having been arrested by ICE and sent to the facility earlier this month.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation said that it has been requested to conduct an investigation into Sandoval’s death, per The Guardian, and ICE said that his death is “under investigation,” though it didn’t specify by whom. In a statement about his death, ICE highlighted Sandoval’s alleged criminal history.

Immigrant advocates reiterated calls to shut the facility down in response to Sandoval’s death.

Sandoval “should not have died in a cage owned by a company that gets paid to fill them. GEO Group and ICE have turned the incarceration of people into revenue streams,” said Murtaza Khwaja, the executive director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta. “This system that profits from human suffering will keep producing it. We demand a full independent investigation into Mr. Sandoval’s death, and demand that Folkston Processing Center be shut down permanently.”

The Folkston facility, owned by the notorious GEO Group, is already facing scrutiny over poor conditions. Earlier this month, roughly 500 people at the facility went on hunger strike, and organizers with the Shut Down Folkston Campaign say that 12 people are still maintaining the strike. It’s unclear if Sandoval was a participant.

Those on hunger strike say that they have faced torture, including solitary confinement and force feeding. They are protesting conditions at the facility as well as violations of asylum protocols, advocates have said.

On Monday, Georgia’s U.S. senators, Raphael Warnock (D) and Jon Ossoff (D), demanded an investigation and inspection of the Folkston center in response to the hunger strike.

“We are troubled by reports of medical neglect and retaliation by custodial officers in response to the mass hunger strike,” senators wrote in a letter to Department of Homeland Security officials.

“Reports from local advocates suggest that approximately 500 detainees are now participating in the hunger strike due to facility conditions and that at least thirteen participants have allegedly been placed in solitary confinement in response. If accurate, the use of restrictive housing to penalize individuals for reporting poor conditions would constitute retaliation and an abuse of disciplinary authority,” the lawmakers said.

text:
05:03

00:00

Court ruling fails to end wait for thousands of immigrants stuck abroad without visas

Late last year, Dustin Hoffman and his wife Gloria started the paperwork to secure a visa for her to live in the U.S.

The couple, along with their 5-year-old daughter Chaya and Hoffman's 12-year-old step son Israel, lived together in Argentina, where Hoffman had moved in 2013 after doing a deployment with the U.S. Army in Iraq.

"My daughter is growing up and she's very smart and my stepson he's very smart," Hoffman said. "But the resources in Argentina for an autistic child and the school system in Argentina … I don't know. I just feel like I needed to give my daughter the same opportunities that I had growing up."

But nearly a year later, the kids and Gloria are stuck in Argentina in bureaucratic limbo due to continuing delays in the processing of their visa.

That's because this January the Trump administration banned the processing of immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries. Many of the migrants were already in the process of getting a visa. Some already had the visa approved; they were just waiting to get the physical visa delivered to them.

Hoffman's wife is from Colombia, one of the countries on the list.

A federal judge this August ordered the ban to be lifted, but Hoffman's family still has not gotten their visa, and the State Department continues to ask them to provide additional evidence to prove they have the financial means to live in the U.S. without becoming a public charge.

Attorneys representing migrants say the Hoffman family's case is emblematic of a wider problem: They say the Trump administration is not complying with the federal court order and is instead slow-walking the processing of the visas.

"So while technically the ban doesn't exist, it doesn't matter practically if people are still not being able to get their green card interviews or have their interviews not be finished and not get their immigrant visa stamps foils and be able to come into the United States," said Alexis Axelrad, the president elect of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

A new training creates additional delays

The visa ban affected more than 280,000 immigrants who had applied for visas by the time the policy went into effect in January.

According to an analysis by the libertarian think-tank Cato Institute, the ban targeted thousands of close family members of U.S. citizens and permanent residents, including spouses and minor children. The Cato report called it "one of the most extreme legal immigration policies in U.S. history."

Now stuck in their countries unable to come to the U.S., many are rethinking what to do.

The State Department declined to comment for this story, telling NPR "the matter referenced is subject to pending litigation." On its website, the State Department acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect due to the court ruling.

The agency told NPR in August it had paused the processing of visas as it launched an in-depth "training program" for embassies and consulates on identifying immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers — a public charge.

This means even immigrants with visas approved would have to go through additional screening.

This pause is uncommon, a former State Department consular officer told NPR. She asked not to be identified because she fears it could affect her job prospects.

"I've never seen a substantial pause on visa processing … I really haven't," the former consular officer said. "The department is doing this because this is what the policy is from the president … to reduce illegal immigration, remigrate people and only accept refugees from South Africa."

But families such as the Hoffmans are stuck in limbo. He says he misses his daughter, stepson, and wife every day. He said his daughter cries "all the time" and asks for her father. His wife is overwhelmed.

"Let me put it this way: Our family is a family. We need to be there for each other," Hoffman said. "Just like any family, it's not functioning very well while we're separated."

The brightest is left behind

During his first term, President Trump said he wanted to attract the brightest immigrants to come to the U.S.

Right-wing organizations, including the America First Policy Institute, have also endorsed a "merit-based" immigration system.

"America's immigration system should prioritize immigrants with education, skills, and well-paying jobs waiting for them in the U.S. because these individuals are most likely to contribute to America's society and economy, benefitting all Americans," the organization wrote in March 2026.

But the battle over visa processing has affected many immigrants who fall into the high-performing category.

One of them is Dr. Fernando Lizcano, a Colombian national whose research focuses on major cardiovascular health challenges in the U.S., including obesity.

He applied for an EB-1A visa, which is reserved for immigrants "of extraordinary ability," including "an outstanding professor or researcher," according to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

"My intention is to continue with my academic biomedical research in the United States," Lizcano told NPR from his office in Bogotá. "(I) have been exploring opportunities also where I could combine all my experience in endocrinology with molecular biology, translational research."

Because USCIS deemed him qualified for an EB-1A, all that was left for him was to apply for the visa itself and get it stamped in his passport.

But he is still in Colombia, awaiting for the State Department's final approval.

"This is not fair," Lizcano said.

The waiting game is taking an emotional toll on many of the immigrants — and their loved ones — whose visas are now up in the air.

Hoffman, the U.S. veteran awaiting his wife's visa to be approved, is worried about his own mental health. He told NPR his doctors have increased his psychiatric medicines.

"I was OK before all this started happening," he said.

He works as an Uber driver, and with Trump's war in Iran, gas prices have skyrocketed, cutting into his income.

He's struggling to pay both his mortgage in the U.S., and rent in Argentina for his family.

"We're living on a dream and a prayer right now," Hoffman said.

Audio transcript

STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:

We have an update on part of the Trump administration's immigration policy. At the start of this year, the administration stopped giving visas to people from 75 countries. It argued that people from those countries would probably need too much government support if they came here. A federal judge struck down that policy two months ago, but immigration attorneys say the government is still purposefully slow-walking those visas, affecting hundreds of thousands of eligible immigrants. Here's NPR's Sergio Martínez-Beltrán.

SERGIO MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN, BYLINE: Dustin Hoffman now sits in a relatively empty and completely quiet home in a green leafy suburb of Houston. The Iraq War U.S. Army veteran was excited to move his wife, Gloria, and the rest of the family from Argentina here. The schools in this area are top-rated, a great opportunity for his 5-year-old daughter and his stepson.

DUSTIN HOFFMAN: So January 1, I came up here. I came to Houston. I started buying furniture, you know, bought beds, bought a table, even toys and all this stuff for the kids 'cause, you know, I'm - I came here to set up the house so that they could come home and not just come to a house.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: But nearly a year after buying the Houston home, the family continues to be in a multi-continental limbo. That's because his wife's visa has yet to be approved by the U.S. government.

HOFFMAN: I had congressional inquiries done, you know, just going back and forth, and they continuously sending the same message. Gloria's visa cannot be approved at this time because she is from one of the countries affected by the 75-country pause. We'll have to wait until things change or until the law changes. And that was the message over and over.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Gloria is from Colombia, one of the 75 countries from which the Trump administration decided in January to stop processing visas. But a federal judge in August overturned the Trump administration's ban, which could affect about 280,000 immigrants. But immigration attorneys say the Hoffman family's case is not unusual. They say visas from those 75 nations are not being processed and that the State Department is stalling its compliance with the federal order.

Alexis Axelrad is the president-elect of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

ALEXIS AXELRAD: While technically the ban doesn't exist, it doesn't matter. Practically, people are still not being able to get their green card interviews, or have their interviews not be finished and not get their immigrant visa stamps - foils and be able to come into the United States.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: The State Department's website acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect, but the agency, citing pending litigation, declined to comment to NPR on the charge they are foot-dragging. The agency told NPR it has paused the processing of visas as it launched an in-depth training program for embassies and consulates on identifying immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers, a public charge.

This means even immigrants with visas already approved would have to go under an additional screening. Here's Axelrad again.

AXELRAD: It's terrible timing for these poor people who've already been waiting, done everything the right way, as we hear people want them to do it the right way, have waited.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: According to the libertarian think tank CATO Institute, a majority of the immigrants affected are close family members of U.S. citizens or permanent residents, including spouses and minor children. But the fight for the processing of visas is also affecting those looking for an employment-based visa. Dr. Fernando Lizcano is a Colombian national whose research focuses on major cardiovascular health challenges in the U.S.

He applied for an EB-1A visa, which is for immigrants, quote, "of extraordinary ability," including outstanding professors or researchers.

FERNANDO LIZCANO: My intention is to continue with my academy at biomedical research in United States, also to develop drugs for diseases that have a high prevalence, like diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular diseases.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Because U.S. citizen and immigration services deemed him qualified, all that was left for him was to get the visa approved and then stamped in his passport, but he is still in Colombia, awaiting the State Department's final approval.

LIZCANO: This is not fair.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: The waiting is taking an emotional toll on many of the immigrants and their loved ones who wait in limbo. Hoffman, the U.S. veteran awaiting his wife's visa approval, says this has taken a toll on his own mental health.

HOFFMAN: My doctor has doubled all my psychiatric medicines, which - you know, I was OK before all this started happening.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Hoffman says he's struggling to pay for his mortgage in the U.S. as well as his family's rent in Argentina. He works as a Uber driver, and with Trump's war in Iran, gas prices have skyrocketed. Hoffman says just making ends meet now is harder than ever.

Sergio Martínez-Beltrán, NPR News.

title: HIAS & Partners Sue the Trump Admin Over Anti-Refugee Policies
description:
For decades, the government could terminate refugee status only with 30 days’ notice and an opportunity to respond.
The Trump-Vance administration’s new policies instead let the government terminate refugee status with only 10 days’ notice.
The new rules threaten thousands of refugees nationwide and undermine the commitments Congress established in the Refugee Act of 1980 to provide protection and stability to people fleeing persecution.
They are represented by Democracy Forward, the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP), and pro bono counsel.
HIAS is a 145-year-old international Jewish humanitarian organization dedicated to transforming the lives of refugees, asylum seekers, and immigrants.
text:
Silver Spring, Maryland — Today, HIAS filed a class-action lawsuit alongside five other refugee advocacy organizations and 4 individuals plaintiffs from Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Colombia, and Iraq challenging three recent Trump administration policies that strip refugees of legal protections without due process.

The lawsuit challenges actions by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) that dramatically rewrite longstanding immigration protections. For decades, the government could terminate refugee status only with 30 days’ notice and an opportunity to respond. The Trump-Vance administration’s new policies instead let the government terminate refugee status with only 10 days’ notice. Those unable to defend themselves in this shortened period are subject to removal and detention.

The lawsuit argues that the administration’s actions violate the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Administrative Procedure Act by attempting to subject lawfully admitted refugees to mass revetting and a blanket hold on adjustment of status, which Congress never authorized. The new rules threaten thousands of refugees nationwide and undermine the commitments Congress established in the Refugee Act of 1980 to provide protection and stability to people fleeing persecution.

According to DHS’s estimates, about 113,000 refugees have pending applications for permanent residency, and the new termination rule could affect as many as 186,000 refugee cases.

“In the space of mere months, this administration has broken the sacred promise of safety and a better future that our country has offered to refugees for generations,” said Smita Dazzo, deputy domestic lead at HIAS. “Not content to merely turn away the refugees we once welcomed with open arms, the Trump administration is now deliberately seeking to send people back to danger.

The case is PANA et al. v. USCIS. Plaintiffs in the case include Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans (PANA), Jewish Family Service of Western Massachusetts, International Institute of New England, African Communities Together (ACT), HIAS, Refugee Council USA, and four individuals from Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Colombia, and Iraq who fled persecution or were unlawfully detained while waiting for a decision on their green card applications. They are represented by Democracy Forward, the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP), and pro bono counsel.

For media inquires, please contact media@hias.org.

HIAS is a 145-year-old international Jewish humanitarian organization dedicated to transforming the lives of refugees, asylum seekers, and immigrants. With a sharpened focus, we deliver vital support through protection services, mental health care, economic empowerment, Jewish community engagement, and robust advocacy—defending the rights of all displaced people to rebuild their lives and creating a world of welcome, safety, and opportunity

title: McGovern Continues Demanding Answers from DHS on El Salvador TPS
description:
More than three months after the lawmakers first wrote to DHS, approximately 200,000 Salvadoran TPS holders and their families remain in limbo.
Salvadoran TPS holders should not have to live their lives wondering every day whether the government is going to rip the rug out from under them,” said McGovern.
“On July 9th, 2026, we sent the attached letter to your office urging you to extend the Temporary Protected Status designation for El Salvador.
The Department of Homeland Security has provided no further information as to whether the TPS designation for El Salvador will be cancelled or extended.
### McGovern is a leading voice on U.S. relations with El Salvador in Congress.
text:
WASHINGTON—Congressman James P. McGovern (D-MA), Ranking Member of the House Rules Committee and Co-Chair of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission, is leading 43 colleagues in again demanding answers from the Department of Homeland Security over the future of Temporary Protected Status for approximately 200,000 Salvadorans living in the United States.

In July, McGovern led 80 Members of Congress in urging DHS to extend TPS for El Salvador, warning that terminating the designation would harm the American economy and potentially return people to a country facing severe human rights and economic crises. The letter detailed deteriorating human rights conditions in El Salvador, including mass arbitrary detentions, forced disappearances, deaths in custody, and reports that people deported to the country have been incarcerated upon arrival without judicial review or due process. More than three months after the lawmakers first wrote to DHS, approximately 200,000 Salvadoran TPS holders and their families remain in limbo.

“The Department of Homeland Security has had months to answer our straightforward questions. Salvadoran TPS holders should not have to live their lives wondering every day whether the government is going to rip the rug out from under them,” said McGovern.

In their follow-up letter sent on October 22, the lawmakers note that the administration failed to respond to their July letter urging an extension of TPS for Salvadorans—even as the deadline to extend the designation has come and gone.

“On July 9th, 2026, we sent the attached letter to your office urging you to extend the Temporary Protected Status designation for El Salvador. As of October 22, 2026, we have still not received a response,” the lawmakers wrote. “Since we sent that letter, the initial expiration date of the designation has passed. The Department of Homeland Security has provided no further information as to whether the TPS designation for El Salvador will be cancelled or extended. As a result, over 200,000 Salvadorans are currently living in limbo.”

Salvadoran TPS holders have lived and worked lawfully in the United States for decades. Nine out of ten participate in the U.S. workforce, contributing billions of dollars to the economy and paying approximately $1.5 billion in federal, state, and local taxes each year. More than 150,000 U.S.-citizen children have a Salvadoran TPS-holder parent in the American workforce.

“Keeping hundreds of thousands of people in this kind of legal limbo is cruel and wrong,” McGovern added. “They deserve to know whether they can keep working, supporting their families, and living in the communities they have called home for decades. Silence is not an acceptable answer.”

The full text of the October 22 follow-up letter is available here.

The July 9 letter, signed by 80 Members of Congress, is available here.

###

McGovern is a leading voice on U.S. relations with El Salvador in Congress. Earlier this year, heled 27 Members of Congress in demanding information about Salvadorans deported by the United States and held incommunicado in El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison, citing serious concerns about due process, enforced disappearance, and documented abuses in Salvadoran detention facilities. Leading human rights organizations have documented mass arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearances, deaths in custody, and serious due process violations under the Bukele government, some of which may constitute crimes against humanity..

McGovern has also organized multiple congressional hearings into Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s suspension of civil liberties and rule of law which has been used to target journalists, human rights defenders, trade unionists, and political opponents.

text:
Para leer en español, haga clic aquí.

A Republican mental health clinician and a one-term Democratic House representative are both hoping their identities as the daughters of Mexican immigrants will appeal to voters in the Oregon House district with the highest share of Hispanic residents.

Republican Noemi Legaspi is challenging incumbent Rep. Lesly Muñoz, a Democrat and labor organizer, to represent House District 22, spanning a stretch of the Willamette Valley that includes Woodburn, Gervais, parts of Salem and rural Marion County.

It’s expected to be a tight race in a district where more than half of the 39,000 registered voters are nonaffiliated. Among the rest, one quarter are Democrats and 19% are Republicans. In her first campaign in 2024, Muñoz narrowly beat the incumbent Republican, Tracy Cramer, by less than one percentage point, or 161 votes.

More than half of the district’s population is also Hispanic, and Woodburn, where both the candidates live, has had the most federal arrests per capita in Oregon since the launch of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, according to the Deportation Data Project.

Both women’s campaigns center around their identities as the daughters of Mexican immigrants, though only Muñoz explicitly supports Oregon’s sanctuary law and is actively outspoken against federal immigration enforcement efforts in her district.

Legaspi, who has been endorsed by several law enforcement associations, said she supports better coordination between local law enforcement and federal immigration agencies to “keep families and communities safe.” As the former chair of the Woodburn School District, she abstained from a vote in March 2025 supporting a resolution expressing support for the privacy and rights of immigrant students, the Oregonian reported.

Muñoz declined an interview and Legaspi did not respond to multiple calls and emails requesting an interview. However, both candidates did respond to the Capital Chronicle’s voter guide questions.

Muñoz has made investing more in public schools, expanding access to healthcare and abolishing the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency her top priorities.

“I believe in multiracial solidarity, fully funding public education, healthcare for all, affordable housing, abolishing ICE and building communities for people, not data centers that extract our resources,” Muñoz said in her written response to the voter guide.

To improve outcomes for Oregon students, Muñoz said she’d support sending more money to public universities and community colleges and boosting technical education programs. When it comes to healthcare, she said she’d defend funding for the Oregon Health Plan and the Healthier Oregon program, which provides health insurance to people regardless of immigration status.

Muñoz’s campaign is backed by the state’s most prominent labor unions for caregivers, educators, nurses and farmworkers.

She’s also backed by the Salem chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, a local group that pushes for policies to help the working class, including efforts to prevent data center development. Hundreds of volunteers from the group have canvassed for her campaign.

Munoz, like the Democratic Socialists of America, said she supports more regulations for artificial intelligence and the data center industry.

Legaspi said she’s running to represent working families, saying the cost of living is the biggest issue she sees people in her district facing. If elected, she said she’d oppose tax and fee increases that disproportionately affect working families.

“I am tired of paying more and getting less from our government,” she wrote.

Legaspi said her top budget priorities would be education, public safety, behavioral health and addiction treatment, as well as services for seniors and people with disabilities and wildfire prevention and recovery.

“We are spending a lot of money on homelessness and housing services that have failed to deliver results,” she wrote. “We need to seriously consider reprioritizing that spending on things that will actually get people off the streets and off drugs.”

Legaspi said Oregonians should welcome the benefits that data centers bring, such as investment, jobs and tax revenue. However, she said supports stronger transparency requirements for data centers, such as clear reporting on energy and water use, jobs created, wages paid and impacts to local infrastructure.

name: Litigation
title: Federal police don't belong in churches - Reason Magazine
authors: Ryan Curtis, Jacob Sullum, Christian Britschgi, Matthew Petti, Eric Boehm
description:
Unsurprisingly, religious leaders are concerned about the sudden allowance of federal police into their sacred spaces.
In their complaint, each of the 27 faith organizations suing the DHS describes how the risk of immigration enforcement impedes their religious exercise.
The Central Conference of American Rabbis writes that immigration enforcement against a synagogue would induce fears of "the persecution of Jews by government agents before and during the Holocaust."
In August, it was revealed that federal agents had been spying on churches in Minneapolis—even before January's protests against "Operation Metro Surge."
The second argument says DHS enforcement violates the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause, which protects religious expression and association.
text:
From deportations without due process to random and discriminatory detentions and searches, the Trump administration's immigration crackdown raised many constitutional concerns. Now, in a lawsuit advancing in federal court, 27 religious organizations say the administration's immigration policies violate another constitutionally protected activity: Americans' right to the free exercise of religion.

Last week, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the religious groups' lawsuit, docketed as Mennonite Church USA v. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), could continue. The lawsuit was brought against the federal government in February 2025, after the Trump administration overturned a longstanding policy that heavily restricted immigration raids around "sensitive sites," including churches, schools, hospitals, daycares, playgrounds, rehab facilities, funerals, and weddings. This policy was most recently outlined in a 2021 memo—dubbed the "Mayorkas Memo" for Alejandro Mayorkas, the DHS secretary at the time—but U.S. immigration enforcement first established the standard in 1993.

After repealing the Mayorkas Memo, the DHS issued a one-page document instructing officers to use "a healthy dose of common sense" when deciding whether to operate at previously protected sites.

Unsurprisingly, religious leaders are concerned about the sudden allowance of federal police into their sacred spaces. In their complaint, each of the 27 faith organizations suing the DHS describes how the risk of immigration enforcement impedes their religious exercise. The Church of the Brethren says a DHS enforcement action would "destroy all sense of peace and safety in what is supposed to be a place of sanctuary for congregants."

The Central Conference of American Rabbis writes that immigration enforcement against a synagogue would induce fears of "the persecution of Jews by government agents before and during the Holocaust."

"We have congregations which have reported members no longer feel comfortable attending services, members who are concerned for their safety, congregations which have had to add costly security measures," Carey McDonald, executive vice president of the Unitarian Universalist Association—one of the 27 plaintiffs—tells Reason.

The fear of police action driving down attendance isn't just a financial problem, McDonald says; it is fundamentally an attack on Unitarian Universalists' (U.U.) beliefs. "A core part of our theology and our practice is to welcome the stranger. To force us to choose between our long-held theological commitment[s] vs. trying to keep our people physically safe…this is a violation of our constitutionally protected rights."

The DHS repealing the Mayorkas Memo isn't the only way immigration police have infringed U.U. religious expression. In August, it was revealed that federal agents had been spying on churches in Minneapolis—even before January's protests against "Operation Metro Surge."

McDonald tells Reason that First Universalist Church of Minneapolis, which had hosted an anti-ICE event led by the Sunrise Movement in December 2025, was one of the targeted churches. "This is direct evidence from the government itself that it is seeking to interfere with our rights to practice our faith. We must assume that this is not an isolated incident."

Indeed, it isn't; the DHS has conducted arrests and surveillance on plenty of other churches across the country. In January 2025, a man in Georgia was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) during a church service. By August 2025, Religion News Service recorded "at least 10 instances of apparent immigration enforcement activity conducted by ICE or other federal agents on or immediately near church grounds since [President Donald] Trump's inauguration." In February of this year, CBS News reported that two men in New Jersey were taken away while they were "just about to head inside" a Pentecostal church for their Sunday worship.

Because of these tangible harms, the D.C. Circuit ruled that the 27 plaintiffs have standing, writing, "[the plaintiffs] are directly injured by the government's already-implemented policy of enforcing immigration laws at houses of worship, they likely have met the standard for showing 'imminent' harm," as outlined by the Supreme Court.

The case is now being sent back to the D.C. District Court, which will have to decide on all three of the plaintiffs' legal claims. Two of those claims are about religious freedom: One appeals to the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), which plaintiffs say must protect the congregations from DHS activity that "substantially burdens" their exercise of religion. The second argument says DHS enforcement violates the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause, which protects religious expression and association. While judicial precedent clarifies that certain compelling state interests can override the clause, the plaintiffs argue there are less intrusive ways to achieve the state's interest in immigration enforcement. The third claim is more procedural, arguing that the department's sudden rescission of the Mayorkas Memo violated the Administrative Procedure Act by not sufficiently considering the impact on religious organizations.

The plaintiffs are first seeking an immediate injunction against all DHS activity around their houses of worship, but the proposed order submitted in 2025 would also re-implement the Mayorkas Memo while litigation is ongoing, overturning the Trump administration's rescission.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won reelection, defeating far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula won with nearly 51.8% of the ballot, a difference of more than 4 million votes. Bolsonaro quickly rejected the outcome, saying he would ask a court to annul the result. Lula’s victory marked a stunning reversal from a first round of voting three weeks ago, when he trailed Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes. President Lula spoke to supporters after polls closed Sunday evening.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva: “This victory isn’t mine alone. This victory belongs to you. … I want you to know that everything I do, I do with you in mind. All public policies are designed with you in mind. And you have given me the distinction of being the first president of the republic to be elected four times through democratic means. This is a historic achievement that I owe to the Brazilian people.”

The results of Sunday’s election were delayed slightly, after a judge on Brazil’s electoral court ordered polls to remain open for two extra hours due to bad weather in some regions and disruptions to public transit that affected some voters. Flávio Bolsonaro lost despite winning the endorsement of U.S. President Donald Trump. He had been hoping to return his family to the presidency after his father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, was convicted for leading a failed military coup attempt against Lula four years ago. After headlines, we’ll go to Brazil for more on Lula’s reelection.
