The Israeli response is disproportionate, and there is no justification for these actions. They have closed off the city of Hebron and ordered the evacuation of an entire neighborhood in a major Palestinian city. There is no justification for these measures.”

The Guardian is reporting that lawyers for jailed U.S. activist James “Fergie” Chambers say that a Spanish court secretly handed his cellphone to the FBI. Chambers is an heir to the Cox Communications fortune, and he is the first U.S. citizen the Trump administration is looking to extradite after being accused of supporting Hamas, in connection with his donations to Palestinians in Gaza and pro-Palestine advocacy. His attorney, Aitor Martínez, said, “I’ve never seen anything like this in an extradition case. Spanish judicial authorities can’t surrender control over the personal effects of a person sought in extradition just because a foreign government has asked for them.” A Spanish treaty bars the transfer of personal items before extradition is granted.

The U.S. military has granted SpaceX access to some of the Pentagon’s most sensitive and confidential satellite tracking data. That’s according to The Guardian, which reports the new agreement between U.S. Space Force and Elon Musk gives SpaceX access to restricted information used to track satellites and debris on Earth’s orbit. This follows Musk’s efforts to privatize space traffic control. Last year, the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, led by Musk, fired scores of employees at the Traffic Coordination System for Space, while the Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to gut funding to the program.

Meanwhile, officials in Ukraine report that Musk’s internet satellite services Starlink and Starshield are functioning normally again, after the service was altered to drop connections of fast-moving objects over Ukraine, disrupting military aircraft and drone flights. On Saturday, Musk acknowledged he had intentionally throttled service to Starlink, reversing his previous claim that the Trump administration was behind the move. Musk called Starlink’s use in drone attacks a violation of its terms of service.

A federal appeals court has ruled in favor of the Trump administration’s policy allowing the indefinite detention of thousands of immigrants without the right to be released on bond. The decision by the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals would mean even immigrants who’ve lived in the United States for decades and have no criminal record could be detained for months — even years — while their cases are reviewed. Other U.S. courts have overwhelmingly opposed Trump’s indefinite detention policy, saying it violates immigrants’ constitutional and due process rights. The ruling centers on Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, with advocates warning the impacts will be felt nationwide. The American Immigration Council said in a statement, “When courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences.” The Supreme Court is set to hear a case challenging the policy during this term.

This comes as deaths in ICE custody continue to skyrocket under Trump’s second term. Over the weekend, it was confirmed a 48-year-old immigrant from El Salvador has died while jailed at the D. Ray James ICE Processing Center in Folkston, Georgia. Luis Sandoval was reportedly found on Friday morning with a “ligature around his neck.” He was pronounced dead about an hour later. He’s at least the 60th immigrant to have died in ICE custody since Trump returned to office. Sandoval’s death came amid an ongoing hunger strike inside the Folkston facility denouncing inhumane conditions. Immigrants there have been reportedly threatened with force-feeding and other retaliatory actions. The ICE facility is run by the for-profit prison company GEO Group.

In more related news, a 79-year-old pastor from Uganda has been released from a for-profit ICE jail in Colorado after 13 months in custody. The Rev. Edward Nalwamba reportedly lost 35 pounds and the strength to walk after his confinement at the Aurora ICE Processing Center, which is operated by the GEO Group. He also suffered from pneumonia for three weeks and did not receive any medical treatment. On the day of his release, Nalwamba had to be carried out by three other detainees, as ICE provided no wheelchair.

Orange County Register

Government officials attempt visit to reported ICE office in Irvine(link is external)

Victoria Le

Congressman Dave Min and local officials attempted a Thursday morning visit to office space in Irvine that reports have said has been leased for Immigration and Customs Enforcement purposes. Irvine Councilmember Melinda Liu and her chief of staff and members of Min’s office joined the congressman in the visit.

After knocking on the door, Min was met at intervals by three employees, the third of whom said he was not in a position to admit Min and attempted to schedule a visit for another time.

“There have been reports from other office buildings ICE has leased that they have used those illegally, against local zoning ordinances, to temporarily detain people and that they have refurbished some of the offices into temporary holding cells,” Min said. “And that’s the first thing I want to check out.”

Min said his office has asked several times via email to tour the office but was repeatedly told “ICE will not be facilitating a visit at this time.”

“We’ve been in touch with ICE here and our staff has had a series of communications indicating that we’d like to come by, that I’d like to stop by,” Min said. “Today was mentioned as a specific date.”

“We’re going to wait to hear back and see if ICE connects with us.,” Min said of next steps. “We’ll keep following up. We’ll go back to the drawing board.”

title: Judge finds ICE violates order in whisking detainee into Washington
authors: Jaime Adame, Letters to the Editor, Lillian Schrock-Clevenger, Leo Heffron, Ethan Clevenger, Ashli Blow
description:

In the Friday court hearing, Kasubhai ordered the immediate release of a man detained by ICE officers Oct. 17 in Madras, about 120 miles southeast of Portland.
The judge found ICE violated a status quo order issued the same day.
Questioning driver In Friday’s evidentiary hearing, Reynolds and Kasubhai grilled the ICE driver for more than an hour.
text:
A federal judge Friday, Oct. 23, said the way U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement moves Oregon detainees to Washington is “incredibly troubling.”

In a court hearing, U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai cited concerns about speed of transport and a “lack of humanity” in providing for basic needs of detainees.

“Expecting they can just pull off on the side of the road and urinate in public on the side of the road is deplorable,” Kasubhai said after hearing testimony from an ICE officer who has driven detainees to Washington, where there’s a large ICE detention center in Tacoma.

The driver said he has been instructed to pull over roadside where there’s a “nonpublic view” for detainees needing to urinate if they are confined in leg chains.

ICE is “doing everything they can to beat the clock” before Oregon judicial orders take effect.

If a detainee files what’s known as a habeas petition challenging the lawfulness of detention, Oregon judges for months have almost immediately been issuing “status quo” orders.

Because there are no overnight ICE facilities in Oregon, if a detainee has not yet been transported out of state, a status quo order typically means the person is released by ICE, pending a decision by an Oregon judge on the legal challenge. That may take weeks or months.

Most people detained by ICE in Oregon do not file habeas petitions, however, according to ProPublica data on habeas petitions and Deportation Data Project information on ICE arrests.

Another Oregon federal judge, Michael McShane, in July also spoke of ICE racing detainees to the Washington border before a habeas petition can be filed and status quo order issued. Advocates for detainees have accused ICE of deliberately doing so to separate attorneys from their clients.

In the Friday court hearing, Kasubhai ordered the immediate release of a man detained by ICE officers Oct. 17 in Madras, about 120 miles southeast of Portland. The judge found ICE violated a status quo order issued the same day.

Federal attorneys argued the ICE driver crossed into Washington at 12:55 p.m., Oct. 17, after the 12:48 p.m. filing of a petition challenging the man’s detention but two minutes before the judge’s “status quo” order, according to court documents.

A court filing from federal attorneys included a screenshot from a Google Maps application they said showed the driver’s vehicle in Washington at 12:55 p.m.

Kasubhai said the screenshot lacked a date. Testimony from the ICE officer who drove the detainee from Madras to Washington was “unreliable,” Kasubhai said, criticizing the driver’s inability to remember details when asked about the trip.

“The evidence that the government offers that they crossed the border exactly two minutes before notice of my status quo order is laughable,” Kasubhai said.

No ruling has yet been made about whether ICE acted lawfully in detaining the man in Madras. He was identified in court only by the initials “VSA.”

Two minutes make a big difference

Detainees can still challenge the lawfulness of their detention if they are being held in ICE’s Tacoma detention facility, but it poses hardship, Lorena Reynolds, the attorney representing VSA, said in an interview.

“The courts in Oregon are moving quickly on these cases,” Reynolds said.

In Washington, “because they have such a huge facility with so many people being detained, it takes longer, and while those cases are moving through the system, people are being detained, and they’re having to wait for that due process,” Reynolds said.

Stephen Manning, executive director of the Portland-based Innovation Law Lab criticized ICE transports in a July statement to Lookout Eugene-Springfield.

“Rapidly moving Oregonians out of state is a deliberate tactic by ICE to take away due process rights and separate attorneys from their clients,” Manning said in July.

Asked whether speedy transport is a “deliberate tactic,” a DHS spokesperson in July told Lookout Eugene-Springfield: “Once an alien is transferred to ICE custody, the agency makes a custody determination based on bed space and ensures their presence for immigration proceedings or removal from the United States.”

In a July court hearing, McShane, another Oregon federal judge, said: “It is a race to the border to get these folks into Washington before a petition can be filed here.”

More recently, McShane also questioned contentions by ICE about when a detainee crossed the border. In a case involving a detainee identified only by the initials “NJLI,” McShane on Oct. 16 found “insufficient facts for this Court to determine Petitioner’s district of confinement” at the time a habeas petition was filed, according to online records.

Reynolds said she didn’t know if Kasubhai’s ruling might have broader repercussions.

“But I do really appreciate the judge’s comments that when you are a public servant and you are charged with … transporting or serving people, that you have to remember that these are human beings, and these are real lives that are at issue here,” Reynolds said.

Questioning driver

In Friday’s evidentiary hearing, Reynolds and Kasubhai grilled the ICE driver for more than an hour.

Identified in court only by his initials, the driver said he could not remember the time he left Madras with the detainee nor the route he took Oct. 17, stating, “I just put it in my GPS and follow the route.”

He also said he did not remember his speed — “I had it on cruise control,” he said — though he said he followed the speed limit.

The driver said he was instructed by a supervisor to take the screenshot photo when he arrived in Washington, but said he could not recall the name of the supervisor who told him to do so.

“I get so busy sometimes, I don’t even know what the next day is,” the driver said.

Under questioning, the driver said he began driving detainees to Washington about a month ago and has been employed by ICE for about 10 months. Before working for ICE he said he had worked in retail stores and also as a digital designer.

Questioned about bathroom breaks, he said he had not been trained to offer hand sanitizer, but that he did so on his own.

“There seems to be a lack of training and regard for the monumental responsibility of transporting other human beings when they allow someone like [the ICE officer who testified] to be the only one in a vehicle taking people long distances to the District of Washington,” Kasubhai said.

ICE has what it calls National Detention Standards that are published online and include a section on “Transportation by Land.”

The standards were not brought up during Friday’s hearing. They state in part: “Detainees being transported between facilities, institutions, or jurisdiction will be moved safely and humanely under the supervision of trained, experienced personnel.”

Asked to read text messages from the date he drove the man from Madras to Washington state, the ICE officer read messages he said he sent to a supervisor about being followed.

“I had a tail almost follow me home,” the text message stated, according to the driver’s testimony. “I am hiding out for a while until I get home.”

Other text messages involved attempts to identify the license plate of the vehicle from a photograph taken by the driver.

Asked in court why he sent the messages, the driver said, “I was fearing for my safety.”

The driver was named in public court documents, but Lookout Eugene-Springfield is choosing not to name him. Assistant U.S. Attorney Gabrielle Parris-Ramfjord moved in court Friday to replace the public document naming the driver with a document identifying him only by his initials, and Kasubhai said he would allow the document to be refiled without the man’s name.

During Friday’s hearing, Kasubhai at one point questioned Parris-Ramjford.

“So we don’t worry about officers endangering people’s lives by speeding on the highway? That’s a huge public safety concern,” Kasubhai said.

“I don’t believe that is supported today in the record,” Parris-Ramfjord said in response.

name: Litigation
title: Trump administration can hold immigrants in ICE custody without bond, court rules
authors: Uriel J. García, The Texas Tribune
description: The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled detained immigrants don’t have a constitutional right to a bond hearing after they enter the country illegally
text:
Immigrants who entered the country illegally don’t have a right to seek bond while they're in custody and going through deportation proceedings, even if they’ve set roots in the U.S., a federal appeals court ruled Friday.
In a 10-7 ruling, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled that current immigration laws allow the federal government to hold detained immigrants until they're deported — regardless of whether they have made a life in the U.S. and lack a criminal history.
Trump-appointed Judge Cory Wilson wrote in the court’s ruling that if undocumented immigrants have not been legally admitted to the U.S., they are only entitled to whatever rights Congress has spelled out in immigration laws. He added that if undocumented immigrants in custody want to be free from detention, “they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country.”
In a concurring opinion, Judge Andrew Oldham agreed.
“Because such aliens remain legally unadmitted, they receive exactly the same due process rights that they would have if they had come through a legal port of entry — which are whatever rights Congress chooses to give them,” Oldham wrote.
Judge Leslie Southwick, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote in his dissent that the ruling has created an “impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents.”
Rebecca Cassler, senior litigation attorney at the American Immigration Council, who argued the case before the 5th Circuit, said the court’s ruling is an attack on constitutional due process rights, which have been guaranteed to anyone living in the U.S., regardless of immigration status.
“The right to due process is a fundamental constitutional protection, and it is meant to protect every person in this country. Because of today’s decision, that right is hollow for immigrants in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi,” she said. “But the logic of the 5th Circuit’s decision threatens everyone in this country: When courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences.”
Mass deportation efforts
The case stems from the arrest of three men in Texas by state troopers between November 2025 and February 2026 during routine traffic stops. All three have lived in the country for at least 14 years, worked during that time and have children who are American citizens. The troopers turned the men over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who held them in detention without allowing them to see a judge.
Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, Miguel Angel Gomez Alvarado and Alejandro Villegas Angel were eventually released from ICE custody after federal judges found that holding them without a chance for a bond hearing violated the men’s due process rights. The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.
Friday’s ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.
“Big win in the Fifth Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens, a principle codified in 1996 legislation but ignored by the deep state for decades,” James Percival, a lawyer in the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said on social media, referring to Clinton administration immigration law that expanded the list of immigrants who can be more easily deported.
“Rejecting due process”
Gracie Willis, an attorney with the National Immigration Project, which is representing the three Texas men, said the general public should be concerned that a federal court believes the government can hold people indefinitely without justification.
“We look at this case as an affront to due process, as the 5th Circuit rejecting due process,” Willis said. “It's really a shocking extension of this attempt to criminalize immigrants and to hold immigrants in detention without any opportunity for them to be released, thereby creating an environment of fear.”
Willis said her organization is still assessing what legal action to take and has not decided if it plans to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
She said immigration lawyers are anticipating how district courts are going to react to this ruling. Many district judges have ruled that immigrants being held in detention centers have a right to bond as long as they are not a flight risk or a danger to the community.
Even though Friday’s ruling is limited to the 5th Circuit, which includes Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the Trump administration has transferred many immigrants from other states to detention centers in Texas.
A policy change by the Trump administration
Under federal immigration laws, the government can quickly deport undocumented immigrants who recently crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without giving them a chance for a bond hearing. But for those who have lived in the U.S. for months or years before being detained, the law gave them the right to challenge their detention.
In July 2025, the Trump administration announced a policy change, saying that anyone who has been arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — regardless of how long they’ve been in the country — doesn’t have a right to bond.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear a separate but similar case that directly challenges the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy.
According to ProPublica, immigrants filed more habeas corpus petitions — a legal procedure that allows a person detained by the government to challenge their imprisonment — in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration than in the past three administrations combined.
Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.
Friday's ruling doesn't prohibit other detainees from filing habeas corpus petitions if they entered the country legally.
Politico found that more than 400 federal judges — appointed by presidents of both major political parties — have ruled in favor of immigrants’ right to due process in more than 5,000 cases since the Trump administration’s policy change last year.
In comparison, 41 judges have sided with the administration’s interpretation of the law in 250 cases, according to a Politico analysis of federal government data.
The Trump administration appealed some of the cases to higher courts, leading to conflicting rulings.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congressman Chip Roy (TX-21) sent a follow-up letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin requesting updated data on deportations since President Donald Trump took office.

The letter follows Rep. Roy’s June 10, 2026, request for information on the Administration’s progress toward fulfilling President Trump’s commitment to carrying out the largest mass deportation operation in American history.

Excerpts from the letter:

“As you work to secure our nation’s borders and immigration system after four years of deliberately reckless open-border policies by the Biden-Harris-Mayorkas administration, I write to respectfully follow up on my June 10, 2026, request for an update on the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) progress in fulfilling President Trump’s commitment to effectuating the largest mass deportation operation of illegal aliens in our nation’s history, vowing to remove one million illegal aliens per year.

To that end, Congress must ensure the executive branch dutifully enforces our immigration laws to the extent it can, especially after enduring the worst border crisis our nation has endured in recent history. Additionally, with this data, Congress can better examine whether it can provide the Trump administration with more resources and legislation to remove more illegal aliens from the country.

Further, this data provides the opportunity for Congress and the Trump administration to evaluate enforcement strategies, from prioritizing the arrest and deportation of illegal aliens with serious criminal records to conducting worksite enforcement operations that could potentially apprehend hundreds of illegal aliens at once, including those with security concerns.”

title: Democrats Can Contain the Donroe Doctrine | The Nation
authors: Ricky D'Ambrose, Lee Schlenker, Marwan Bishara, Chris Lehmann, Peter Guttman, Anthony Flaccavento, The Nation, Mychal Denzel Smith, www.thenation.com

text:
As Democrats on Capitol Hill envision regaining control of one or both chambers of Congress in November, they are already gearing up to rein in the Trump administration’s imperial agenda in Latin America.

But beyond seeing the Western Hemisphere through the lens of the issues contributing to Democratic gains in polls nationwide—heavy-handed immigration enforcement, the tariff-fueled affordability crisis, high-level corruption—legislators in Washington should prioritize a robust oversight and accountability agenda that puts the brakes on the Trump administration’s reckless militarism and coercion in the region.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

From the lethal boat strikes across the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, joint military operations in Ecuador and beyond, blatant electoral interference from Honduras to Brazil, gunpoint diplomacy in Venezuela, and the military-enforced fuel blockade of Cuba, Democrats can stem the tide of Trump’s so-called Donroe Doctrine—if they are willing to use the tools at their disposal and resist the bipartisan, interventionist consensus on the region that has long plagued Washington.

In response to Trump’s foreign policy in Latin America, Democrats have, by and large, attacked the administration on largely partisan issues, many of which intersect with areas affecting their constituents, including immigration policy, affordability, foreign aid, and corruption.

Democrats have challenged the administration’s mass deportation campaign, “safe third-country” agreements and gutting of asylum and temporary protected status; questioned the basis for imposing levies on Mexico and Brazil and their impacts on the cost of living; bemoaned the impacts of aid cuts on farm communities and the impoundment of funds already appropriated by Congress; and sought answers about the pardoning of the former Honduran narco-president and the security contracts of Blackwater founder Erik Prince in Haiti.

These areas of concern are undoubtedly significant and, because of their impacts on US communities and nexuses to domestic issues, should continue to be pursued if and when Democrats take back the House and/or Senate.

But wielding these select issues for partisan purposes or electoral gain should not overshadow equally pressing foreign policy concerns that many establishment Democrats have long avoided to prevent fissures within the caucus—areas that the administration itself has prioritized and could present significant blowback to long-term US interests if left unchecked.

Atop the agenda for Democrats should be the administration’s lethal boat strikes, which experts say amount to crimes against humanity, having left 240 people dead and cost taxpayers nearly $5 billion. Lawmakers in both chambers say obtaining the secret legal memo justifying the strikes and reasserting congressional authority over them will be among their priorities next year, but much more must be done to uncover the true cost of ongoing operations, sanction those responsible for serial killings on the high seas, and hold third-country collaborators accountable for carrying them out. Congress must clearly articulate that the president cannot direct summary executions against criminal suspects without due process and withhold funds for lethal operations against presumed traffickers in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.

Additionally, Democrats will need to obtain concrete information from administration officials about expected joint ground operations across the region under the framework of the US-led Shield of Americas and Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition. These operations have already seen US special forces deployed on missions in Ecuador and potential plans to integrate operationally in Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and elsewhere. Beyond standard training, intelligence-sharing and military financing programs, lawmakers will need to press the Pentagon and State Department on the authorities under which troops are engaged in combat, the US taxpayer resources being committed, potential civilian abuses US deployments may enable, and measurable impacts on organized crime and US public safety.

Furthermore, the Trump administration’s electoral interference in the region—from issuing ultimatums to voters in Honduras and Argentina, to endorsing a candidate in Colombia, and unleashing a pressure campaign in anticipation of this week’s final vote in Brazil—must also face consequences from Democratic lawmakers. Congress should make abundantly clear that not only do overt US actions or statements that interfere in foreign countries’ elections set a worrying precedent for the future of US statecraft and complicate day-to-day diplomacy with institutional partners; they also establish a hypocritical standard for those critical of intromission into US elections and can unduly tilt the scales in razor-thin contests.

Fortunately, top Democrats are already probing the administration’s shady dealings in Venezuela, an area that should expand to potential conflicts of interest by former administration officials now cashing in on lucrative business deals with Caracas. Not only must Democrats continue to scrutinize the neocolonial arrangement through which the Trump administration has assumed control of Venezuela’s oil revenues but also commission studies linking the Energy Department’s gold deals to organized crime, push the Pentagon on its statutory authority to take equity stakes in Venezuela’s hydrocarbon reserves, demand a return of the country’s sovereignty over its domestic affairs, and lift the comprehensive sanctions still handicapping the country’s full recovery.

Lastly, the de facto fuel blockade of Cuba, the imposition of secondary sanctions on foreign firms operating on the island, increased diplomatic pressure on countries sustaining ties with Havana, and ongoing military planning for potential kinetic or covert actions should remain a top priority for legislative oversight and debate. Reports of cronyist graft and back-channel deals between administration-linked figures seeking to swoop in and control Cuba’s key assets must also be addressed as Congress seeks accountability for the administration’s role in accelerating Cuba’s humanitarian crisis.

Ad Policy

To pursue these issues and others, legislators have a number of tools at their disposal.

First and foremost, Democrats in the majority can call hearings and issue subpoenas—whether for administration officials, their family members and business associates to testify, or to review the text of official agreements—as Representative Castro (D-TX) recently requested with regard to the Venezuela oil deal. They can also use the increased resources and personnel afforded to the majority to launch special investigations, issue committee reports, and convene temporary task forces on select topics.

Congress can also use the power of the purse—particularly through the annual federal appropriations process—by wielding funding restrictions or inserting reporting requirements for certain policies that, if Democrats win both chambers, have an increased likelihood of becoming law. Democratic leadership can also continue to restrain the administration by forcing floor debates and votes on the War Powers Resolution—as it has tried and failed over the past year on the boat strike campaign, war with Venezuela, and military action in Cuba—albeit with better chances at success come January.

And the Senate can choose to block the ambassadorial nominations for particularly partisan or underqualified political appointees for the dozen-plus vacancies at US embassies across the region and/or other top foreign policy posts charged with advancing the Donroe Doctrine from Washington.

Notwithstanding these efforts, the Trump administration will likely plow forward to reassert US dominance across the hemisphere and weaponize the economic and military diplomatic tools it has to those ends. But attempts to constrain these and related actions are well worth the fight, as congressional action can spur public frustration and mobilization over the domestic and global costs of unchecked militarism.

At the same time, vocal Democratic action may accelerate GOP dissent and intraparty infighting, creating space to further expose the frustrations and disagreements some Republican lawmakers have with aspects of Trump’s approach to the hemisphere and his apparent contempt for meaningful congressional input.

For Latin American governments, including those that have become willing, if junior, partners in Donroeism, heightened legislative action may incentive hedging, a push to invest in bipartisanism, and a diversification of the bilateral agenda beyond security and defense issues.

Perhaps most importantly, more robust congressional action can redefine the terms on which US-Latin America relations are debated, expanding possibilities for less securitized solutions and more productive, multifaceted, and respectful ties with our neighbors to the south.

text:
On Sept. 28, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts issued an order requiring DHS to remediate certain adverse consequences for the class of aliens paroled into the United States after scheduling an appointment through the CBP One mobile app, and whose parole was terminated by the federal government via mass email in April 2025. Sileiri Doe v. DHS, 1:25-cv-12245-ADB (D. Mass).

Pursuant to the Sept. 28 court order, Sileiri Doe class members may file with USCIS a request to reopen or reconsider an adverse decision or action on an immigration benefit request without a fee, if the class member believes that the adverse decision or action was made as a result of the April 2025 parole termination.

Class members may request reopening or reconsideration of an adverse decision without a fee, excluding a request for employment authorization based on parole, if USCIS issued the original decision or action between April 1, 2025 and April 21, 2026. There is no deadline for Sileiri Doe class members to file a request to reopen or reconsider such adverse decisions, pursuant to the court order.

For the purposes of this process, an “adverse decision” means a decision by USCIS on a benefit request that was denied, dismissed, deemed abandoned, administratively closed, rejected, or referred to the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR).

Requests to reopen or reconsider under this process:

Must be filed on the form designated by USCIS, following the form instructions, or in any other manner instructed by USCIS, including specific instructions for Sileiri Doe class members to ensure that the request is accepted and processed appropriately;

Must explain how the April 2025 parole termination impacted the alien’s eligibility for the benefit, and why USCIS should reopen and/or reconsider its decision; and

Will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis, and may be approved only if the alien demonstrates eligibility for the benefit, without consideration of the April 2025 parole termination.

For additional information on filing a request to reopen or reconsider without a fee, please see the instructions for Sileiri Doe class members on the Form I-589 website (for asylum applications) and the Form I-290B website (for all other benefit types).

Background

Sileiri Doe class members include all individuals who:

scheduled their appointments for entry to the United States using the CBP One app;

were paroled into the United States between May 16, 2023, and Jan. 19, 2025;

had their parole terminated in April 2025 pursuant to an email stating, “It is time for you to leave the United States” or similar language; and

remain in the United States.

The April 2025 Parole Termination Emails sent to Sileiri Doe class members were vacated by the district court on March 31, 2026, and DHS was ordered to reinstate parole for all class members. Id. On April 21, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) updated government databases to reinstate class members’ parole periods following the April 2025 terminations and issued new parole termination notices.

Pursuant to the March 31, 2026 court order, the April 2025 Parole Termination Emails had no legal effect and cannot be used by DHS as a basis for denial of any applications, as grounds for decisions regarding admissibility and detention, or as the basis for accrual of unlawful presence pursuant to INA § 212(a)(9)(B) and (C)(i), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(9)(B) and (C)(i). Note that the Sept. 28, 2026 court order requiring remediation of certain adverse consequences of the April 2025 parole terminations does not impact the new parole termination notices issued to class members on April 21, 2026.

Appeals

The process for Sileiri Doe class members to request reopening or reconsideration without a fee does not include appeals. For any benefit types that permit an appeal to be filed on Form I-290B, Notice of Appeal or Motion, or any other form, normal appeal procedures and requirements apply.

Aliens in Removal Proceedings

If you are a Sileiri Doe class member who is currently in removal proceedings before an Immigration Judge, you must have your removal proceedings terminated or dismissed by the Immigration Judge before you ask USCIS to reopen or reconsider your application for asylum and, in some cases, adjustment of status. There are limited exceptions. If you file a request to reopen or reconsider with USCIS, and USCIS no longer has jurisdiction over your case because you are in removal proceedings, USCIS will reject or deny your request. Please see the websites linked above for additional information.

description: Federal agents searched the D.C.-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday, taking the extraordinary step of executing a criminal search warrant against a sitting member of Congress just
text:
Ward 9 Council Member Jason Chavez is raising concerns about…

Public access television and grass-roots storytelling contin…



Rep. Ilhan Omar

Federal agents searched the D.C.-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday, taking the extraordinary step of executing a criminal search warrant against a sitting member of Congress just 22 days before Election Day, as the Trump administration investigates allegations involving her family’s immigration records.

The search immediately drew accusations of political intimidation from Omar’s supporters, who pointed to President Donald Trump’s repeated attacks on the Minnesota congresswoman and questioned the timing of an investigation targeting one of his most outspoken critics.

“Representative Omar is a dedicated public servant and a true ally for working families, and Donald Trump has done nothing but use racist tropes and stereotypes to attack her,” said Joel Payne, MoveOn ’s chief communications officer. “Now, he’s abusing his power to physically intimidate and harass her.”

A Justice Department spokeswoman acknowledged that Homeland Security Investigations agents, part of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, searched a District residence as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.

The spokeswoman declined to provide additional information or publicly identify the person under investigation.

According to published reports, the warrant identified possible violations involving false statements, immigration document fraud and conspiracy. Federal investigators have also examined questions concerning Omar’s finances, campaign funds and interactions with foreign citizens.

No criminal charges against the congresswoman were identified, but Monday’s search occurred less than four weeks before voters decided whether to return Omar to Congress.

The investigation follows months of public accusations from senior Trump administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance, who previously claimed that Omar committed immigration fraud.

In an interview with conservative commentator Benny Johnson, Vance asserted, without publicly presenting evidence, that the administration believed Omar had broken immigration laws. He also said he and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller had discussed how to pursue the allegations.

“What are the legal remedies now that we know that she’s committed immigration fraud?” Vance asked during the interview. “How do you go after her? How do you investigate her?”

Omar has repeatedly rejected the accusations, including claims that she married her brother to facilitate immigration fraud. Her office dismissed Vance’s allegations in March as fabricated and defamatory.

Questions about the investigation intensified in August when Immigration and Customs Enforcement refused to release records sought under the Freedom of Information Act concerning allegations surrounding Omar’s 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

The agency cited an exemption allowing law enforcement authorities to withhold records when disclosure could interfere with enforcement proceedings. The refusal did not establish that Omar committed fraud or, at the time, confirmed that she was personally under investigation.

Omar, who came to the United States as a refugee from Somalia, was elected to Congress in 2018 and became one of the first two Muslim women to serve in the House. She represents Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, which includes Minneapolis, and has frequently challenged Trump over immigration enforcement, civil rights, and his administration’s treatment of immigrant communities.

Her confrontations with the administration have made her a recurring target of the president’s political attacks. The criminal investigation also follows a frightening incident earlier this year in which Omar was physically attacked during a public appearance.

On Jan. 27, a man attacked Omar during a town hall meeting at the National Urban League’s Twin Cities headquarters in Minneapolis. The incident prompted condemnation from the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation and its Black Women’s Roundtable, which demanded accountability and warned against political violence.

“We are shocked and extremely disturbed by the attack on Rep. Ilhan Omar yesterday while she attempted to address the critical issues and chaos swirling around in Minneapolis,” Melanie L. Campbell, president and CEO of the coalition and national convener of the Black Women’s Roundtable, said in a Jan. 28 statement.

Campbell praised Omar for continuing to speak out despite threats against her.

“We believe that NO public official should be threatened or physically attacked, especially when they are serving in the best interests of their constituents,” Campbell said. “Political violence and intimidation have no place in our democracy.”

MoveOn, the progressive advocacy organization, accused Trump of using federal law enforcement to intimidate a political opponent and urged voters to respond at the ballot box.

“On Nov. 3rd, we get our chance to fight back and hold him and his corrupt administration accountable,” Payne said.

Based on reporting by Washington Informer .

title: ICE brought War on Terror detention and war tech home, new report finds
description:
The report shows that the immigration crackdown dominating the US midterm elections was not invented by the current administration.
It was built over two decades of the War on Terror, by both parties, and handed over ready to use.
A Senate oversight report released on 9 October found that around 850 men had passed through the immigration operation there.
CAGE International is an independent advocacy organisation that has documented the War on Terror since 2003, when it began campaigning for the men held at Guantánamo Bay.
Its staff include former Guantánamo prisoners, and it works to challenge state policies developed under the War on Terror and to empower communities affected by them.
text:
Without the War on Terror there would be no ICE: CAGE report traces Trump’s deportation machine back to 9/11, as migrants are once again held at Guantánamo Bay

London — Today the 26th of October 2026, CAGE International publishes The Spiralling War of Terror: How Trump Inherited the National Security Machine He Now Wields. The report shows that the immigration crackdown dominating the US midterm elections was not invented by the current administration. It was built over two decades of the War on Terror, by both parties, and handed over ready to use.

ICE was created by the post-9/11 Homeland Security Act. Its first head, Michael J. Garcia, was a career terrorism prosecutor appointed to break up the old immigration service and fold its enforcement arm into the new Department of Homeland Security [1]. The methods ICE relies on today were first used against Muslims after 9/11. More than 1,000 Arab and South Asian Muslim men were rounded up in the weeks after the attacks, many of them cut off from their families and lawyers. Today migrants are moved between detention sites with no record, and their relatives cannot find them [2]. Weeks after 9/11, the Justice Department also expanded the “automatic stay”, a rule that lets the government override a judge’s order to release someone from detention. It was used to keep Muslim men in custody who had no connection to the attacks [3]. ICE now uses the same rule to keep migrants locked up after judges order them freed.

ICE was created under President Bush and expanded under President Obama, whose nationwide rollout of the Secure Communities programme earned him the name “deporter-in-chief”. By 2019, daily immigration detention had risen from 19,000 before 9/11 to 50,000. Under the current administration, ICE has become the highest-funded law enforcement agency in the United States.

The surveillance follows the same pattern. For eleven years, the New York Police Department spied on Muslim communities across the city and beyond, sending informants into mosques and mapping where Muslims ate, shopped and prayed, without producing a single lead [4]. That approach treated whole communities as suspects rather than individuals, and it is now ICE’s model. ICE draws on fusion centres, the state and regional intelligence hubs created after 9/11 so that local police and federal agencies could pool information, which were long used to monitor Muslim communities. It uses battlefield surveillance tools from Iraq and Afghanistan on American streets. And at the US-Mexico border it deploys surveillance towers from the Israeli arms company Elbit Systems, whose sensors line the border of Gaza and whose smart fences cut through the occupied West Bank, technology built to keep Palestinians in an open air prison [5].

No company embodies this better than Palantir. Seeded by the CIA’s venture capital arm and built to hunt targets in Iraq and Afghanistan, Palantir has turned the War on Terror into a business model and brought it home. In April 2025, ICE handed it a $30 million no-bid contract to build “ImmigrationOS”, a system to track and target immigrants for deportation. Palantir also built ELITE, an app ICE uses to choose which neighbourhoods to raid. ELITE draws on Medicaid data to build dossiers on people, and gives each target a “confidence score” for their home address. Palantir’s software was behind some of the most brutal workplace raids of Trump’s first term, and its staff were on site for a mass raid in the Bronx where most of those detained were not even non-citizens. Its sole-source contract to run ICE’s case management system has grown to more than $145 million. Palantir is not a neutral supplier. It is the War on Terror’s targeting machine, now pointed at migrants, and it profits from every raid [6].

​

The same national security logic has been turned on Palestinian voices for decades. Professor Sami Al-Arian, a Palestinian academic, was arrested in February 2003 and prosecuted on terrorism charges. More than twenty years later, in March 2025, ICE arrested Mahmoud Khalil, a Palestinian graduate of Columbia University, and sought to deport him for his advocacy on Gaza. The report traces a direct line between the two.

Nowhere is the connection clearer than at Guantánamo Bay, where migrants are once again being detained. A Senate oversight report released on 9 October found that around 850 men had passed through the immigration operation there. Staff could not say whose detention rules applied, and the facilities fell short of federal standards. Last month, eight Somali men were deported after being held in Camp 6, a block built to hold the Muslim men detained without charge in the War on Terror. Among them was Adam Abdullah, a St Paul mechanic with a work permit and no criminal record, who had been told the flight to Cuba was only a refuelling stop.

The report also documents how the same laws are now turned on dissent. In the Prairieland case in Texas, protesters outside an ICE facility received multi-decade sentences after prosecutors presented their use of Signal, their black clothing and their reading material as evidence of a conspiracy. These tactics were honed over twenty years of prosecutions against Muslim defendants.

Asim Qureshi, Research Director at CAGE International, said:

“Whoever wins on 3 November will inherit this machine. These powers cannot be reformed, only abolished. The movement against ICE and the movement against Guantánamo are fighting the same system, and this report is an invitation for them to stand together.”

The report calls for an end to treating “national security” as grounds for suspending fundamental rights. It urges communities and campaigners to reject the divide between “good” and “bad” Muslims and immigrants that the security state depends on.

[ENDS]

NOTES TO EDITORS

The full report is available here.

Moazzam Begg, Asim Qureshi our Research Director, David Chmielewski a researcher at CAGE and author of the report, are available for interview.

CAGE International is an independent advocacy organisation that has documented the War on Terror since 2003, when it began campaigning for the men held at Guantánamo Bay. Its staff include former Guantánamo prisoners, and it works to challenge state policies developed under the War on Terror and to empower communities affected by them.

Reg. 54909 (31 October 2001), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2001-10-31/html/01-27447.htm; Jorjani R (2010), Ignoring the Court’s Order: The Automatic Stay in Immigration Detention Cases, Intercultural Human Rights Law Review, Vol 5

text:
The US midterm campaign is heating up as President Donald Trump and former President Barack Obama take their political battle to the campaign trail. With control of Congress at stake, both are rallying supporters and making their case to voters ahead of the November 3 election. Obama campaigned in Ohio and Michigan, backing Democratic candidates including Sherrod Brown, Amy Acton and Abdul El-Sayed. He criticised the Trump administration over its record, economic pressures and foreign policy. Meanwhile, Trump campaigned for Republicans in Georgia, defending his administration and urging voters to support GOP candidates. The competing rallies highlighted the sharp divide between the two parties over the economy, leadership, immigration and America's role in the world. text:
ICE violated 210 court orders during Operation Metro Surge. The DOJ went after the judges who said so.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In a letter released today, a bipartisan group of 174 former federal and state judges urged Eighth Circuit Chief Judge Colloton to immediately dismiss the Department of Justice’s misconduct complaint against Minnesota federal judges. The former judges argue that DOJ’s complaint is baseless because the Minnesota judges’ public remarks about ICE’s defiance of court orders merely reiterated findings their court had already made public.

During last winter’s Operation Metro Surge, ICE violated 210 court orders in Minnesota. Officials moved detainees out of state against judges’ orders and kept people locked up after judges ordered them freed. Some detainees did not get their passports, phones, or work permits back even after courts ordered them returned. In response, Judge Schiltz issued an order warning that “ICE is not a law unto itself.”

On Sept. 30, the DOJ filed an unprecedented judicial misconduct complaint against seven Minnesota federal judges, including Schiltz and Judge John R. Tunheim, over their public comments about the Trump administration’s immigration operations, including the widespread federal noncompliance with court orders and the severe strain Operation Metro Surge placed on the federal courts. The complaint asks for an investigation and seeks to bar the judges who spoke to The New York Times from any cases involving DHS. The retired judges say both requests should be denied.

“The noncompliance Judge Schiltz described was not a matter of private opinion; it was the subject of findings in the public orders of his court,” the former judges wrote in their petition to the Eighth Circuit. The letter continues, “He described what his court had already found, in a published opinion justifying its orders and what the consequences of noncompliance were for the court’s operation. A judge who reports what has already been adjudicated in public is not litigating his case in the newspaper.”

“Instead of dealing with the government’s defiance of judicial orders, the government filed disciplinary charges against the Minnesota judges who lawfully called out their misconduct,” said Nancy Gertner, former United States district judge for the District of Massachusetts. “174 retired judges have signed this letter making it clear that there is no basis for those charges.”

text:
Transcript

STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:

We have an update on part of the Trump administration's immigration policy. At the start of this year, the administration stopped giving visas to people from 75 countries. It argued that people from those countries would probably need too much government support if they came here. A federal judge struck down that policy two months ago, but immigration attorneys say the government is still purposefully slow-walking those visas, affecting hundreds of thousands of eligible immigrants. Here's NPR's Sergio Martínez-Beltrán.

SERGIO MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN, BYLINE: Dustin Hoffman now sits in a relatively empty and completely quiet home in a green leafy suburb of Houston. The Iraq War U.S. Army veteran was excited to move his wife, Gloria, and the rest of the family from Argentina here. The schools in this area are top-rated, a great opportunity for his 5-year-old daughter and his stepson.

DUSTIN HOFFMAN: So January 1, I came up here. I came to Houston. I started buying furniture, you know, bought beds, bought a table, even toys and all this stuff for the kids 'cause, you know, I'm - I came here to set up the house so that they could come home and not just come to a house.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: But nearly a year after buying the Houston home, the family continues to be in a multi-continental limbo. That's because his wife's visa has yet to be approved by the U.S. government.

HOFFMAN: I had congressional inquiries done, you know, just going back and forth, and they continuously sending the same message. Gloria's visa cannot be approved at this time because she is from one of the countries affected by the 75-country pause. We'll have to wait until things change or until the law changes. And that was the message over and over.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Gloria is from Colombia, one of the 75 countries from which the Trump administration decided in January to stop processing visas. But a federal judge in August overturned the Trump administration's ban, which could affect about 280,000 immigrants. But immigration attorneys say the Hoffman family's case is not unusual. They say visas from those 75 nations are not being processed and that the State Department is stalling its compliance with the federal order.

Alexis Axelrad is the president-elect of the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

ALEXIS AXELRAD: While technically the ban doesn't exist, it doesn't matter. Practically, people are still not being able to get their green card interviews, or have their interviews not be finished and not get their immigrant visa stamps - foils and be able to come into the United States.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: The State Department's website acknowledges the visa ban is no longer in effect, but the agency, citing pending litigation, declined to comment to NPR on the charge they are foot-dragging. The agency told NPR it has paused the processing of visas as it launched an in-depth training program for embassies and consulates on identifying immigrants who could become a burden on taxpayers, a public charge.

This means even immigrants with visas already approved would have to go under an additional screening. Here's Axelrad again.

AXELRAD: It's terrible timing for these poor people who've already been waiting, done everything the right way, as we hear people want them to do it the right way, have waited.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: According to the libertarian think tank CATO Institute, a majority of the immigrants affected are close family members of U.S. citizens or permanent residents, including spouses and minor children. But the fight for the processing of visas is also affecting those looking for an employment-based visa. Dr. Fernando Lizcano is a Colombian national whose research focuses on major cardiovascular health challenges in the U.S.

He applied for an EB-1A visa, which is for immigrants, quote, "of extraordinary ability," including outstanding professors or researchers.

FERNANDO LIZCANO: My intention is to continue with my academy at biomedical research in United States, also to develop drugs for diseases that have a high prevalence, like diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular diseases.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Because U.S. citizen and immigration services deemed him qualified, all that was left for him was to get the visa approved and then stamped in his passport, but he is still in Colombia, awaiting the State Department's final approval.

LIZCANO: This is not fair.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: The waiting is taking an emotional toll on many of the immigrants and their loved ones who wait in limbo. Hoffman, the U.S. veteran awaiting his wife's visa approval, says this has taken a toll on his own mental health.

HOFFMAN: My doctor has doubled all my psychiatric medicines, which - you know, I was OK before all this started happening.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Hoffman says he's struggling to pay for his mortgage in the U.S. as well as his family's rent in Argentina. He works as a Uber driver, and with Trump's war in Iran, gas prices have skyrocketed. Hoffman says just making ends meet now is harder than ever.

Sergio Martínez-Beltrán, NPR News.

text:
Short Reads

|

Americans’ Views of ICE Grow More Negative

A majority of Americans (56%) now say they have an unfavorable opinion of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency at the center of many of the Trump administration’s increased deportation efforts. A considerably smaller share – 35% – view the agency favorably, while 9% say they are not sure.

ICE is the least favorably viewed of the 12 federal agencies and departments asked about in a Pew Research Center survey of 5,062 adults conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4.

Republicans’ ratings of ICE are far more positive than those of Democrats. But in both partisan groups, views of the agency have grown more negative over the last year:

Two-thirds of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents currently view ICE favorably, down from 72% a year ago.

An overwhelming majority of Democrats and Democratic leaners now have an unfavorable opinion of ICE (84%), up from 78% last year.

For views of other federal agencies included in the survey, visit “How Americans View Federal Agencies.”

About this research

We conducted this survey to understand Americans’ attitudes about key federal government agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. We have tracked attitudes about federal agencies and departments for many years. For views of other agencies, refer to this fact sheet.

Why did we do this?

Pew Research Center does research to help the public, media and decision-makers understand important topics.

Learn more about Pew Research Center and our politics research.

How did we do this?

We surveyed 5,062 U.S. adults from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, 2026. Everyone who took part in this survey is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel. The survey represents the views of the full U.S. adult population.

Here are the survey questions used for this analysis, the detailed responses and the survey methodology.

Views of ICE by race and ethnicity

Majorities of Black (69%), Hispanic (67%) and Asian adults (66%) have a negative opinion of ICE. In each group, views are substantially more negative than they were a year ago.

White adults are less likely than other racial and ethnic groups to view the agency negatively, though more now express a negative opinion than a positive one.

Nearly half of White adults (49%) have an unfavorable view of ICE, up from 45% in 2025. About four-in-ten (42%) have a positive opinion, down from 48% a year ago.

Views of ICE by party, race and ethnicity

Among Republicans

White Republicans (71%) are much more likely than Hispanic Republicans to view ICE favorably (53%).

Among Democrats

Across racial and ethnic groups, large majorities of Democrats view ICE unfavorably. However, White Democrats’ views are particularly negative.

Roughly nine-in-ten White Democrats (89%) express a negative opinion, compared with smaller majorities of Asian (82%), Hispanic (79%) and Black Democrats (75%).

title: 2026 midterm elections: How can results affect international students? - Kansan.com
description: With midterm elections around the corner, international students could see potential change in immigration enforcement. Two University of Kansas seniors share their experiences navigating changing immigration legislation.
text:
Ana Pineda (left) is a University of Kansas senior international student from Honduras studying chemical engineering. Despite legal status, she became afraid after the Trump administration increased immigration enforcement measures last year. “Just expecting something that you don't think you deserve, but might happen to you. It's just it's kind of like a psychological torture that bleeds into other things in my life.”
Julia Hanson/The Kansan
Ana Pineda spent nine months in Germany taking language classes and preparing to begin college in a new country. She dreamed of a career as a cosmetic chemist and knew there were limited opportunities back home in Tegucigalpa, Honduras.
Then, Pineda found herself in Lawrence, Kansas, for her sister’s University of Kansas  graduation. She visited David Booth Memorial Stadium and Allen Fieldhouse. Pineda was drawn to the community, she said.
“You see it in movies and you think it's not real, but it kind of is,” Pineda said.
Nearly four years later, Pineda is a senior studying chemical engineering. She’s a student ambassador with many friends and a boyfriend. Her college experience was great, she said, until last year.
The
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
enacted on July 1, 2025, was a turning point in immigration enforcement funding. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
funding
increased from $10 billion to $85 billion. It also raised visa fees and made it harder for international students to work in the U.S. after graduation.
The Trump administration began
revoking international students’ visas
last year for reasons from driving infractions to protesting.
“It's just kind of like a constant anxiety now,” Pineda said. “Like, I'm scared I’m going to wake up one day, and I'm going to have an email from Homeland Security and they're gonna be like, ‘Hey, you're deported for breathing.’”
International students learn to navigate Curricular Practice Training (
CPT
), Optional Practice Training (
OPT
), obtaining a driver’s license and internship approval.
Several of these face proposed changes by the Trump administration, but the midterm elections just a few weeks away could mean change.
Pineda can’t vote, but she’s watching closely.
What can Congress do?
While ICE is under the U.S. executive branch, Congress has
plenary power
over immigration law. This means Congress makes immigration laws and has broad power over who can enter and stay in the U.S.
David Treviño is an immigration attorney in Lawrence who offers guidance to KU international students. If Kansas Republicans remain in Congress, expect no change, Treviño said.
“I just don't see any movement from the Republican side to make any radical changes or really any substantive changes to what they're currently doing,” Treviño said. “If the Democrats win, then Congress has the power of the purse.”
On Oct. 6, the Cook Political Report changed the
Kansas Senate race prediction
from Republican leaning to a toss-up. Adam Hamilton could be Kansas’ first Democratic senator in 94 years. Kansas’ District One House race
prediction
remains solid Republican.
If Democrats win the congressional races, they could pressure the executive branch for changes in DHS operations from ICE to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Treviño said. If the president doesn’t comply, Congress can restrict funding.
What's at stake?
On Oct. 7, DHS
proposed a new $70,000 charge
to universities for each F-1 international student that applies for Optional Practice Training (OPT). OPT grants students the ability to legally work in the U.S. for one year post graduation. The proposed rule would then charge $30,000 for additional OPT after the year.
According to the
DHS press release
, the rule would curb abuse of current systems by encouraging universities to be more selective when recommending students for OPT.
On July 16, DHS announced its final rule to
eliminate “duration of status.
” Typically, F-1 international students stay in the U.S. until they finish their degree -- an indefinite period of time. Once finished, they have 60 days to change their visa status or leave the U.S. According to the DHS press release, duration of status acts as a loophole for immigrants to remain in the U.S. without government oversight.
Under the new rule, students would have the duration of their study, often four years, and 30 days before and after.
The rule was intended to take effect on Sept. 15, but a federal district court in Massachusetts paused the implementation while it’s under litigation.
“If this administration does anything to interfere with that or to make it more burdensome, it really impacts the ability for the U.S. to draw or benefit from those international students that may be extremely intelligent and brilliant and can use that knowledge base to make improvements in various industries,” Treviño said.
Miguel Castro is a KU senior from Medellín, Colombia studying architecture. When applying for jobs as an international student, you’re already at a disadvantage, he said.
“Even if you have the opportunity, and there's so much paperwork, and so much stuff companies need to do to hire you that most of them just don't even consider you,” Castro said.
Miguel Castro is a University of Kansas senior international student from Colombia studying architecture. He has experienced several challenges as an international student from freshman year loneliness to finding an internship. “I’m just, I'm a minority of the minority of the minority. There are not a lot of international students at KU,” Castro said.
Julia Hanson/The Kansan
While DHS has the authority to make these rules, Congress can override them or limit funding to implement these policies.
Governors do not have the same direct authority as Congress, but they can initiate federal lawsuits and provide financial support or guidance to universities.
State Sen. Cindy Holscher is the Democratic candidate for governor against Republican state Sen. Ty Masterson. When asked how she would protect international students from federal changes to OPT, Holscher said she has no problem pushing back against the Trump administration.
“If it's not good for Kansas, it's not good for our people,  I will absolutely push back,” Holscher said in an Oct. 8 interview.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Cindy Holscher speaks Oct. 8 at her Lawrence rally. “I have no problem pushing back against the Trump administration,” Holscher said when asked how she would protect international students from OPT fees.
Julia Hanson/The Kansan
Student Perspectives
Last spring, among the changes in immigration policy, Pineda’s grades began to drop.
“I'm focusing on like a million things at once and my professors can only do so much about me not focusing enough to study for an exam,” Pineda said.
She drove to the Honduras consulate in Houston for a new passport, but it wasn’t ready when she arrived. When she was hired for an internship, she had to get KU’s approval, pay $1,700 for an extra summer class and apply for CPT.
Pineda is grateful for the support and constant information on changing legislation from KU International Student Support Services, she said.
Castro and Pineda said they always carry their official document showing legal status, just in case they are approached by officials.
“I shouldn't be worried about it, but again and again, you see that they don't care,” Castro said. “They don't care. They just racially profile people.”'
In this election season, Pineda thinks beyond her own situation.
“I think a blue wave would be awesome for all of us. I have citizen friends that are affected by it. I have friends that are birthright citizens. I have friends from the LGBTQ plus community. I have disabled friends. I'm also thinking about them because it's hard not to, you know?” Pineda said.

title: The 2025 Supreme Court Term: Significant Regulatory and Administrative Law Decisions
description:
In a 5-4 decision, the Court held that a President’s executive order cannot overturn a right established by the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution.
The court held that the President has, and indeed must have, the Constitutional authority to remove a member of the FTC, a body that also exerts broad executive powers.
The Court held that the SEC may use as an enforcement tool, ”disgorgement” in civil enforcement cases, requiring the malefactor to return any funds obtained through unlawful conduct.
The Court, in a unanimous decision, held that Enbridge’s failure to observe the deadlines set by federal law to remove a state-law based complaint to federal court was fatal.
The Court held that under the Immigration and Naturalization Act (INA), an alien standing in Mexico cannot trigger the asylum procedures in the United States.
text:
The Court has begun its 2026 Term with a bang (i.e., the Suncor climate change case), but the 2025 Term (October 5, 2025, through October 4, 2026) resulted in decisions in 68 cases, many of which were quite significant. At least 20 cases from the 2026 Term stand out.

Monsanto Co. v. Durnell (decided on June 25, 2026). In an opinion written by Justice Kavanaugh, the Court reversed a decision of a Missouri state appeals court that the plaintiff’s personal injury case could proceed to trial despite the defense that the state law failure-to-warn complaint was preempted by the Federal Insecticide & Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) and EPA’s FIFRA-based pesticide labeling rules, a point of law endorsed by the Court. At issue was the use of Monsanto’s “Roundup” pesticide, which has been challenged in many lawsuits.

Cisco Systems, Inc. v Doe (June 23, 2026). In a narrow 5-to-4 decision, the Court held that federal courts may not create new causes of action under the federal Alien Tort statute, which is essentially concerned with the Law of Nations and is accordingly strictly construed.

Flowers Foods, Inc. v. Brock (June 23, 2026). In a unanimous ruling, the Court held that Brock, a Denver-based distributor, was engaged in interstate commerce for purposes of the Federal Arbitration Act although he never left the confines of Colorado. This ruling, albeit fairly obscure now, could become more significant in the future.

Trump v. Barbara, et al. (June 30, 2026). This is the “Birthright citizenship” case. In a 5-4 decision, the Court held that a President’s executive order cannot overturn a right established by the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution. The Court’s research disclosed that there were many historical antecedents to the 1866 actions of the Congress.

Trump v. Cook, (June 29, 2026). In an opinion written by the Chief Justice, the Court held that the President’s attempt to remove a Governor of the Federal Reserve board was not “for cause” as required by the Federal Reserve Act. The Federal Reserve occupies a unique place as a federal agency which distinguishes it from other federal regulatory agencies.

Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026). The Court overturned its 1935 decision in Humphrey’s Executor which made it very difficult for a President to remove a Federal Trade Commission (FTC) commissioner. The court held that the President has, and indeed must have, the Constitutional authority to remove a member of the FTC, a body that also exerts broad executive powers.

National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Elections Commission (June 30, 2026). In a 6-3 ruling, the Court held that FEC rules limiting the ability of a political party’s ability to coordinate spending with the candidate in a political campaign, violate the First Amendment.

Chatrie v. United States (June 29, 2026). The Court held that the federal government’s collection of Google locator history in solving a credit union robbery implicates the Fourth Amendment, and requires a federal warrant to proceed. A “geofence” warrant is insufficient.

Sripetch v. SEC (June 4, 2026). The Court held that the SEC may use as an enforcement tool, ”disgorgement” in civil enforcement cases, requiring the malefactor to return any funds obtained through unlawful conduct.

Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (February 20, 2026). The Court held in a 6-3 decision that the Industrial Energy Economic Power Act (IEEPA) does not give the President independent power to impose tariffs.

S. Postal Service v. Konen (February 24, 2026). In an opinion written by Justice Thomas, the Court held that the United States enjoys “sovereign immunity” over plaintiff’s claims that a local Postal Service deliberately failed to deliver his mail. This is the “postal exemption” to the Federal Tort Claims Act.

Federal Communications Commission v. AT&T, Inc. (June 4, 2026). In an opinion written by the Chief Justice, the Court held that the FCC’s administrative forfeiture procedures are constitutional, AT&T does not have the right to request a jury trial before the administrative forfeiture proceedings take hold, and AT&T does not have a right to a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment. The FCC’s procedures differ from those employed by the SEC in the Sarkesy case that was recently decided by the Court.

Exxon Mobil Corporation v. Corporation Cimex, S. A. (Cuba) (June 23, 2026). The Court held that Exxon may proceed under the provisions of the Helms-Burton Act of 1996 to seek monetary reimbursement for its Cuban properties confiscated in the early days of the Cuban Revolution in the 1960s.

Florida v. California and Washington (May 26, 2026). In a rare Original Action filed in the Court, the Court denied Florida’s motion for leave to file a complaint against California and Washington for their failure to require applicants for commercial motor vehicle licenses to read and speak English. The filing falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

Enbridge Energy LP v. Nessel (April 22, 2026). The Court, in a unanimous decision, held that Enbridge’s failure to observe the deadlines set by federal law to remove a state-law based complaint to federal court was fatal. Moreover, the controlling statute does not recognize the concept of “equitable tolling” to affect these deadlines.

Louisiana v. Callais, et al. (April 29, 2026). In a voting rights case, the Court held that Louisiana’s revised Congressional redistricting map, which created a second Black majority district, was itself an unconstitutional gerrymander as it permits a state to discriminate on the basis of race.

West Virginia V. BPJ (June 30, 2026). The Court held that West Virginia laws mandating separate facilities for men and women athletes complies with Title IX of the Civil Rights Act. The Court agreed that the policies embraced in these state laws were substantially related to important state interests.

Mullin v. Doe (June 25, 2026). In an immigration law enforcement matter, the Court rejected a challenge to the Temporary Protected Status provided under the IN Act.

Mullin v. Al Orthro Lado (June 25, 2020). The Court held that under the Immigration and Naturalization Act (INA), an alien standing in Mexico cannot trigger the asylum procedures in the United States. Only when an alien crosses the border and presents himself to the agency are these processes triggered.

Chevron, USA, Inc. v. Plaquemines Parish (April 17, 2026). The Court held in a unanimous decision that the federal officer removal statute can be employed to remove state law-based lawsuits asserting damage claims against oil and gas companies operating in these parishes. In 2013, 42 lawsuits were filed in state courts, but the evidence showed that many of these defendants were acting at the behest of the federal government in the early days of World War II to produce more energy and oil and gas products. This fact triggered the “federal officer removal” statute. The Court holds that the defendants plausibly alleged a close relationship between the energy companies and the federal government.

text:
In the US state of Massachusetts, human rights organizations and four refugees have filed a class-action lawsuit against the administration of President Donald Trump. The plaintiffs are challenging three measures which, they say, prevent refugees from obtaining permanent resident status and speed up the procedure for terminating their lawful status.

As The Hill reports, the lawsuit accuses the US Department of Homeland Security and US Citizenship and Immigration Services of violating federal immigration law. The plaintiffs argue that the combined effect of these actions leaves refugees in “legal uncertainty.”

Repeated reviews and suspended applications

In November, the Trump administration ordered immigration officers to re-examine all refugees admitted to the United States under the administration of Joe Biden. As a result, consideration of all applications for permanent resident status was suspended indefinitely.
