text:
A rare Sunday federal appeals court hearing for the Justice Department's voting lawsuit against California closed without a ruling.

The department requested that the court issue one by Tuesday prior to the scheduled 1 p.m. PDT hearing before the district court.

The arguments followed a surprise appeal by the Trump administration, which claims a district judge did not act quickly enough to address the administration's allegations of roughly 20,000 potential noncitizen voters on the state's voter rolls.

A three-judge panel that includes two appointees of President Donald Trump and one appointee of former President Joe Biden heard arguments on DOJ's efforts to segregate ballots from the alleged noncitizens.

California officials have countered that the list is unverified and includes the names of lawful voters, despite recent charges announced by DOJ of roughly 28 individuals from the list accused of voting and immigration-related crimes.

Earlier the DOJ sent letters last week to every county in California asking local elections officials to help identify potential voters who may be in the U.S. illegally, according to a letter described to ABC News.

"Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not," according to a letter sent by Justice Department officials to every county in California and described to ABC News. "The Department strongly urges you and your agency to work with the Department of Justice to ensure the integrity of California's federal elections before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure."

Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next month's midterm election.

In court papers filed earlier this week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.

Of those 200 individuals, officials said, nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history," according to a filing.

The Justice Department's rushed efforts to have an appeals court quickly rule on its lawsuit faced considerable skepticism from the three-judge panel in Sunday's emergency hearing.

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, repeatedly questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction to step in at this stage in the litigation, and expressed considerable constitutional concerns over the lawsuit itself.

"I don't see how we have jurisdiction," Bennett said to DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly after pressing him over the timeline of the government's decision to seeking emergency appeal when a hearing before the district judge is already set for this Tuesday.

Donnelly claimed that the DOJ's decision to seek relief from the appeals court came after disclosures by the state of the numbers of mail-in ballots already being processed in advance of the election -- which number in the hundreds of thousands.

But Bennett's most significant concerns appeared to be the nature of the lawsuit and it appearing to directly contradict the Constitution's Elections Clause -- which mandates that states have jurisdictions over the manner their elections are run.

"How can it preempt something that is expressly authorized by a provision of the Constitution?" Bennett asked. "How can the legislature making laws with regard to the manner of holding elections be preempted by a criminal statute passed by the Congress, especially when both the Congress and the California Legislature have made it illegal for non-citizens to vote?"

Donnelly repeatedly pointed to DOJ's position that the way California is administering its elections -- and not acting on the hard drive of potential 20,000 likely non-citizens -- infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal statute barring voting by illegal immigrants.

That explanation didn't appear to sit well with Bennett, however, who pointed out that the Constitution specifically tasks Congress with jurisdiction over how states administer their elections and not the Judiciary.

"How can we, a federal court, do what is reserved to Congress, which Congress, in my view, hasn't done?" Bennett asked.

"Your Honor, I would just simply -- unfortunately -- disagree with you that 18 USC 611 is not an election law that fits in the power of Congress," Donnelly replied.

The judges also appeared to express concern about last-minute intervention to force California to segregate certain mail-in ballots given the state has provided a declaration saying if such an order was implemented it could have a "catastrophic" impact on tabulating the upcoming election.

Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, repeatedly pressed California's attorney Samuel Siegel over why an injunction wouldn't be appropriate to ensure non-citizens votes are being actively cast in the ongoing election.

"Without an injunction, you will never know, correct?" Bumatay asked. "Because if -- if the ballots are cast and separated, then they're going to be tabulated, and there's no way of knowing."

"Your Honor, we would respectfully disagree with that because of the number of steps that people have to take to attest to their citizenship, to declare consistent with what is required by both federal and state law that they are citizens when they register to vote," Siegel responded.

Even as Bumatay's questioning suggested he had more sympathy to granting the government some kind of relief, both Bennett and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, appeared unified that the extraordinary relief being sought by DOJ was not appropriate at this juncture.

"That's why I have a problem with the relief that's being sought here because I just don't see -- Congress and the California legislature have said non-citizens can't vote, and this lawsuit is about 'we don't like the way you're sorting citizens from non-citizens, and I just don't see 611 as telling California how to do the sorting," Bennett said.

"That's absolutely right, Your Honor, and to reiterate my earlier point, if the federal government, if the Executive Branch wants that authority in the first instance, they need to go ask Congress for it, they haven't done that," Siegel said. "They ask this court to short circuit the democratic process and issue an order, not just on the eve of an election, but as an election is underway."

In closing remarks, Bennett said the panel "will try to decide this case as quickly as possible."

A pro-ICE conservative blogger has been detained by the agency he ardently supports.

MAGA personality Samuel Sey, who describes himself as a "blogger, a teacher, a pro-life advocate, and a public speaker," was taken by ICE agents and is currently being held in an Ohio jail. The jail's website states he was booked on Oct. 21 and is still being held in custody for ICE.

A donation page made on behalf of Sey confirmed he was detained by ICE while traveling.

"He is a husband, father, school teacher, married to Annie with three beautiful children, and has been living here as a legal resident of the United States from Canada," the page stated.

The page also stated that his wife is working to get him released on bail "so he can fix any clerical issues that need to be addressed for his legal residence."

Sey previously announced on social media in 2022 that he had obtained a marriage license to wed his wife, Annie.

A DHS spokesperson told the Daily Beast, "On October 21, ICE arrested Samuel Sey, an illegal alien from Ghana, at the Columbus International Airport. Sey entered the United States legally in 2022 but overstayed his length of admission by over four years, in violation of our nation's laws. Sey has no pending applications and accepted voluntary departure. He will remain in ICE custody until removed from the United States.

"We do not pick and choose which laws to enforce or where to enforce them.

"We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return."

Sey, 39, is the author of the blog SlowToWrite. He has been vocal about his support for ICE agents, writing in one social media post, "If you love America, you should support ICE."

He's even gone as far as to say that God would actually be against people who protest ICE agents.

"God isn't just against anti-ICE protestors who persecute Christians while they are worshipping at church. He is also against the idealogy [sic] of anti-ICE protestors," he wrote in one post. "Christians who condemn the "protestors" but refuse to condemn their ideology should know that."

In another post, he proclaimed that " anti-ICE protestors are influenced by Satan."

After Minnesota mother Renee Good was shot and killed in her car in January, he echoed popular talking points on the right claiming that she was attempting to ram agents with her car, despite video evidence suggesting otherwise.

"The woman would still be alive if she didn't try to run the ICE agent over. You can be saddened by her death and admit that it was self-defense," he wrote.

While he has been largely pro-ICE, Sey is oftentimes critical of President Donald Trump, especially on the president's ever-changing views on abortion.

One post from 2024 reads: "It's a sobering sign of God's judgment on America that although thousands of babies could die because of Trump—he is a significantly better option than Kamala Harris."

text:
OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Community activists are calling on Eastmont Mall owners to stop allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to stage operations on the property, alleging the site has been used to transfer detainees for more than a year.

Dozens of advocates gathered Sunday in Parking Lot 'C' at Eastmont Mall in Oakland, staging a symbolic "die-in" to honor people who have died while in ICE custody. Organizers say the demonstration was intended to draw attention to what they describe as ongoing ICE activity at the shopping center.

"We are here today because we want ICE out of Eastmont Mall and all health care facilities," said Gabriela Galicia, executive director of the Street Level Health Project.

Galicia said legal observers have documented ICE agents using the parking lot since December 2025.

"In June 2026, a community member was picked up at their house and taken to this parking lot, where they were transferred to another ICE vehicle," Galicia said.

MORE: Investigation underway after pedestrian allegedly struck by ICE vehicle in Northern California

Advocates say the alleged enforcement activity is particularly concerning because the parking lot is adjacent to an Alameda County community health clinic. They argue the presence of federal immigration agents has created fear among immigrant families seeking medical care.

"People are afraid to come here. You become afraid to go to the clinic, you get sick and others get sick around you," said Francisco Herrera of the Nuevo Sol Day Labor and Domestic Worker Center.

A county sign posted in a portion of the lot under Alameda County control states that the area may not be used for immigration enforcement activities.

Activists are also directing their concerns toward Tidewater Capital, the private owner of the Eastmont Mall property.

"We want the owners of the property to put safety first and say to ICE, 'Do not come here,'" Herrera said.

MORE: Video of masked ICE arrest in San Francisco's SoMa neighborhood sparks outrage

The issue has drawn attention from Alameda County leaders. Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas attended Sunday's event and pledged to continue monitoring ICE activity in the area.

"I'm going to remain vigilant in protecting our communities against ICE," Bas said.

The controversy follows a recent incident involving ICE agents and a detainee who was taken to Highland Hospital for treatment. Advocates allege the man suffered fractured ribs after being tackled by an agent.

In response to questions about activity at Eastmont Mall, the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement: "ICE's presence in public parking lots is fully authorized under federal law and is a standard practice for law enforcement agencies nationwide."

MORE: ICE agents accused of breaking man's arm in dramatic arrest caught on video in Long Beach

Activists dispute that characterization, noting that Eastmont Mall is privately owned.

"This is not a public parking lot. It's a private parking lot," Herrera said.

ABC7 Eyewitness News reached out to Eastmont Mall property owners for comment but had not received a response as of Sunday evening.

Organizers say they plan to send an open letter to Oakland city leaders and mall ownership this week, asking that all ICE-related activity be barred from the property.

text:
When footage of a man being hit by federal immigration officers' SUV in Northern California became public, the Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle's hood.

Local police raised doubts about federal officials' account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning's incident involving the pedestrian, 37-year-old Antonio Moreida, citing video footage that contradicted DHS' statement.

Footage from a nearby surveillance camera, a bystander's cellphone recording and Moreida's GoPro, which had already been made public at the time of the agency's statement, told a different story of what happened on a residential street in Woodland, an agricultural city just outside of Sacramento. The incident is the latest in which DHS' account has been contradicted by officials and video evidence amid the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Police contradict ICE account

In a statement Wednesday morning, DHS said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers didn't hit a pedestrian.

"An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement in response to CNN's request for information. "The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation," apparently accusing the man of faking his injuries.

After the incident on Tuesday, Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement he found footage of the incident troubling. Investigators were working to gather evidence and statements and to review available audio and video related to the incident, including video taken from multiple perspectives, police said in a Facebook post. Woodland Police didn't take part in the ICE operation the agents were involved in that morning, police said.

The following day, Woodland Police called DHS' account "inconsistent."

"Certain claims made in the DHS statement are inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed by Woodland Police investigators," Kinnan said in an update Wednesday. The update said investigators had established, based on video evidence, the pedestrian had been hit by the vehicle driven by ICE agents and that he had not jumped onto the vehicle.

The local police department is conducting a criminal investigation into the events leading up to the collision and the actions of those involved, Kinnan said Wednesday.

By Thursday, in response to follow-up questions about the video footage, federal officials no longer said the person jumped on the hood.

"This individual chose to directly impede a law enforcement action and stand in the middle of an active road," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. "Our officers deliberately attempted to avoid making contact with this anti-ice protestor and drive around him, while also braking. We strongly urge individuals to not stand in the middle of active roadways while a law enforcement vehicle is approaching."

What footage shows

Footage reviewed by CNN shows Moreida, a Woodland resident, in the middle of the street at around 9:40 a.m. Tuesday. Moreida said he had responded to a call that morning by NorCal Resist, a group which monitors immigration operations, about ICE activity in Woodland, he told CNN on Tuesday, hours after the incident.

unknown content item

-

He said he was trying to record agents' unmarked vehicles. He had been recording one vehicle, standing on the car's driver's side, when it turned left and drove off, which he said pushed him into the middle of the street.

Video from Moreida's GoPro shows him following a black Dodge Durango with tinted windows as it drives down the street.

Then, he said he heard a loud engine before seeing the agents' black Chevy Tahoe drive toward him, which is shown in his GoPro footage, though the video has no audio.

unknown content item

-

Down the street, the bystander's cellphone video shows the Durango pass the Tahoe, which has tinted windows, on a residential street. In the video's background, people can be heard blowing whistles, presumably to alert people nearby of ICE's presence in the neighborhood.

The ICE agent driving the Tahoe moves toward Moreida and between the cars with its brake lights on, footage shows. In the bystander's video, Moreida isn't yet visible.

The SUV's wheels begin to turn to the left only a few feet from Moreida, a wider angle of surveillance footage from a home shows.

unknown content item

-

"The individual was standing in the street long enough that a reasonable person should be able to see them and recognize that they were there," said Ryan Schwank, a former ICE attorney and training instructor who reviewed the videos provided by CNN.

Schwank also took issue with ICE's characterization that Moreida was standing in the middle of an active road and impeding law enforcement's actions.

"When we're looking at Antonio's actions, he's not impeding. He's not standing blocking the vehicle from moving," he said. "He's standing and filming, and that's well within his bounds to do. He's well within his rights to do what he was doing."

Moreida's GoPro appears to show when he's struck by the front-right side of the vehicle before he drops his camera.

"Before I knew it, it just drove straight into me," he said. "I took the hood of the car straight to the chest. It initially took the wind out of me and I couldn't breathe."

The surveillance footage shows Moreida take a step back when he appears to make contact with the car. He is then seen falling toward the ground, off the front-right side of the car, the footage shows.

In the bystander's footage from behind, a screeching noise is heard before the Tahoe jolts forward. The SUV veers left before straightening out, the video shows.

The bystander's angle shows the Tahoe brake lights turn off. Moreida is then visible in the bystander's video, falling to the ground and rolling, first on his back with his legs swinging above him. He then appears seated upright in the nearby surveillance footage, this time facing the sidewalk.

The SUV's brake lights turn back on briefly before it drives farther down the street, the surveillance footage shows.

The driver, an ICE agent, stayed near the scene and called local dispatch, Woodland Police said. The agent cooperated with police during the initial investigation, the local agency said.

Moreida said an off-duty EMT provided him aid at the scene before Woodland Police officers arrived. Federal agents didn't approach him after he was hit by the SUV, he said.

Moreida said he was eventually transported to the hospital. He said he had X-rays taken of his swollen knees, where he said he had the most damage. In addition, he said he has bruises and cuts from the road.

ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February.

On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers.

"ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program," an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. "As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely."

Local officials call for investigations

Soon after it became public, local officials expressed dismay over the incident, which occurred in a rural Northern California community that's about half Latino. More than a fifth of the population is foreign-born, according to US Census estimates.

"The lack of truth in the Department of Homeland Security's statement is evidenced by video taken at the scene," Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said in a statement issued Wednesday. "All of us can be assured that the Police Department's investigation into this disturbing incident will continue to be speedy, fair, and impartial."

US Rep. Mike Thompson, a Democrat whose district includes Woodland, said ICE's statements about the facts surrounding the incident were disappointing but not surprising.

"ICE has a history of trying to hide the facts and mislead the public," he told CNN. "And this is another example of that happening."

On the day of the operation, Thompson called on Acting ICE Director David Venturella to investigate the collision, including by preserving evidence and cooperating with local authorities. As of Friday, the congressman had yet to receive a response to his letter, his office told CNN.

CNN's Taylor Galgano contributed to this report.

name: Human Rights
title: Ten days that could shake the world: democratic norms at stake in four pivotal elections
description:
Four elections on four continents within 10 days could profoundly reshape global politics, propelling the world further along its current authoritarian trajectory or marking a limited comeback for democratic norms.
In all four contests, basic democratic norms are at stake at a time when autocracy is advancing worldwide at an alarming rate.
On Sunday, Brazil will hold runoff presidential elections with a candidate from the far right in the lead.
Serbia Democracy Index rating 112 Over his 12 years as president, Aleksandar Vučić has steadily corroded the pillars of Serbia’s democracy.
Israel Democracy Index rating 48 Israeli democracy has always been partial.
text:
Four elections on four continents within 10 days could profoundly reshape global politics, propelling the world further along its current authoritarian trajectory or marking a limited comeback for democratic norms.

In all four contests, basic democratic norms are at stake at a time when autocracy is advancing worldwide at an alarming rate. According to the Sweden-based V-Dem Institute, which uses multivariable assessment tools, the democratic freedoms enjoyed by the average global citizen are down to levels last seen in 1978 – long before the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism in Europe.

The cluster of four pivotal elections could either halt that trend or reinforce it. In each contest, pro-democracy parties are in close races with current or aspiring autocrats. The outcomes in each case are likely to have spillover effects in their regions and beyond.

On Sunday, Brazil will hold runoff presidential elections with a candidate from the far right in the lead. If he wins, Flávio Bolsonaro is threatening to “change the constitution”, pardon his father for plotting a coup, and ease environmental restrictions, a critical issue for the Amazon rainforest.

On the same day, the semi-autocracy run by Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia for the past 12 years will face its stiffest challenge in the form of an unconventional student-led protest movement, fielding a slate of little-known academics and technocrats running on the simple slogan “Serbia or Mafia?”.

On Tuesday, it will be the turn of Benjamin Netanyahu to face his challengers at the polls. Israel’s leader for 19 of the past 30 years has overseen a prolonged period of democratic backsliding and spiralling human rights abuses. He is wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and risk heightened legal jeopardy from an ongoing corruption trial at home if he loses. His far-right coalition is currently trailing an opposition block.

On 3 November, at the tail end of this potentially historic 10 days, Donald Trump’s imperial-style presidency is facing a rebuke from US voters in midterm elections, with at least one chamber of Congress, and possibly two, likely to fall to the Democrats. They will then however face an uphill task in seeking to rein in Trump’s excesses which have seen the US plummet down the V-Dem Institute’s Liberal Democracy Index.

By the time the US counts its votes on Tuesday, the world could look a markedly different place. Not only are the four looming contests bunched together, they are also interwoven. Trump’s Maga movement has given overt political support to Netanyahu, Vučić, and Bolsonaro. Israeli-built Pegasus spyware has been found in the phones of student and pro-democracy activists in Serbia. Bolsonaro is strongly pro-Israel and is promising to follow the US lead and move the Brazilian embassy to Jerusalem. The US has provided much of the ordnance for Netanyahu’s wars. Serbia is committed to spending $2bn on Israeli defence systems and in September, the two countries opened a joint plant making surveillance and attack factory.

Victory for the authoritarian right in one country will bolster counterparts in others, and conversely win for pro-democratic campaigners in each contest will give hope and encouragement to their allies around the world.

The four elections may be closely interlinked, but the struggle between authoritarianism and democracy takes on very different forms in each country. The odds are different in each case, as are the stakes, but they are all close races.

Brazil

Democracy index ranking 28

Brazil has enjoyed a democratic resurgence since Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva took office on the first day of 2023, defeating an attempt by his far right populist predecessor to overturn the October election result. According to V-Dem’s measures, it now has better democratic credentials than the UK, and far better than the US.

The loser in those elections four years ago, Jair Bolsonaro, an ex-soldier who served under Brazil’s 21-year military dictatorship and still admires it, was sentenced to 27 years in jail for trying to stage a coup to hold on to power. Now his son, Flávio, is seeking to follow in his footsteps, and goes into the second round of the election on Sunday with a small but significant lead over Lula.

The younger Bolsonaro has not only pledged to free his father, but also to punish members of the judiciary involved in his prosecution. If he wins, he will have a supportive rightwing majority in Congress to work with and has vowed to change the constitution and “re-democratise the country”. The term harks back to the transition from military rule in 1985, and for the Brazilian left, it has a chilling Orwellian ring coming from the mouth of an avowed admirer of prominent members of the junta.

Bolsonaro has campaign on hard-line law and order policies addressing the chronic issue of high crime. He argues for lowering the age of criminal responsibility to below 18, sending more teenagers to jail, and calling for judicial reforms, which his critics suggest he intends to mount an attack on the independence of the courts.

Serbia

Democracy Index rating 112

Over his 12 years as president, Aleksandar Vučić has steadily corroded the pillars of Serbia’s democracy. He and his allies have taken over almost all the country’s broadcast channels, with the result that he is the overwhelming presence on the nation’s television screens over the course of the current election campaign. The future of the last two independent news channels is now in doubt, as they were bought during the campaign by a Portuguese investor with links to the ousted Hungarian regime of Viktor Orbán.

The ruling Serbian Progressive party (SNS) has turned ministries and other state institutions into political tools to the extent that, in the words of Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability, “the line between the state and the parties is almost deleted”.

Until now, the opposition parties seeking to curb Vučić have been weak and divided, but Serbian politics was transformed two years ago by the collapse of a concrete canopy on a crowd of people at a railway station in Novi Sad, killing 16 people. The tragedy crystallised a deep reservoir of disillusion across the country, and produced a student-led mass movement which has survived state intimidation since then, and is now fielding a full list of candidates against the SNS.

The candidates, like the students who nominated them, disagree among themselves on key political issues but they demonstrate a purist adherence to direct democracy. Decisions are taken by large plenum meetings, and no one has been allowed to emerge as an identifiable leader.

To win on Sunday, the students will have to break the mould of Serbian politics, and in particular, Vučić’s hold on his loyal base in the countryside. If they come close, there is a risk of unrest and violence. The SNS has a record of paying bands of thugs to disrupt opposition rallies, and those gangs may appear at polling sites if Vučić feels threatened. The students too have vowed to take to the streets to defend the victory they expect on Sunday.

Israel

Democracy Index rating 48

Israeli democracy has always been partial. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote or many other rights, while Israeli settlers next door to them are treated as full citizens and provide vital backing for Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition government. That government however will be fighting for its survival in Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.

Palestinians with Israeli citizenship are about a fifth of the population but are consistently under-represented in the Knesset. They turn out to vote in smaller numbers than Israeli Jews, with many viewing participation as pointless in a system which systematically excludes them. The main opposition bloc challenging Netanyahu is ruling out a coalition with Arab parties, even if it means the difference between a clearcut victory and an uncertain deadlock, once Knesset seats have been assigned.

Netanyahu has been Israel’s leader on and off for most of the past three decades, but in the nearly four years of his current term, in coalition with extreme settler-backed parties, he has mounted an offensive on Israeli democratic norms, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary in the name of “reform”, putting pressure on the independent press, and politicising the police, army and internal security service, Shin Bet.

The opposition bloc, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, shares much of Netanyahu’s outlook when it comes to Palestine, largely supporting the war in Gaza and refusing to countenance a two-state solution. But it is determined to expunge the corruption of his government and its autocratic excesses. It is expected to win more seats than the government coalition in Tuesday’s election, but fall short of a clear majority. For that they may have to forge an understanding with Israel’s long ignored Palestinian minority.

The US

Democracy Index rating 51

No western country in modern times has “undemocratised” itself as rapidly as the US in less than two years of Donald Trump’s second term in office. With a Congress dominated by loyal Republicans and a mostly acquiescent supreme court, he has forged an imperial presidency, frequently governing by executive order decrees, and turning state institutions into political tools – including organs of internal security, such as the justice department and the FBI – which have been weaponised against political opponents, independent prosecutors and journalists.

Administration policy, domestic and foreign, has been used to generate self-enrichment opportunities for Trump’s family and friends.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been vastly expanded with lightly trained but heavily armed recruits, and deployed across the country, trampling the civil rights of anyone, predominantly Latinos, suspected of being an illegal immigrant.

With the president’s approval ratings at record lows, the Democrats have a good chance of winning a majority in the House of Representatives and the slimmer possibility of winning the Senate too.

Even if they gain control of both chambers, however, there are limits on how far they can go to rein the authoritarian excesses of the Trump presidency. He can be expected to use his veto freely, and Democrats will not have the votes required to overturn it, or to defeat a Republican filibuster in the Senate.

In theory, Congress has the power of the purse and could try to make funding for government departments and agencies conditional on reforms. A Democratic majority would also use its control over committees to open several investigations into corruption and other wrongdoing, issuing subpoenas to government officials.

title: U.S. appeals court appears skeptical of Trump DOJ's lawsuit over California voter rolls

The Department ‌of Justice’s lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump’s administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
Trump’s Justice Department has warned ​election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls.
It has distributed to California officials a list of 20,000 people it says are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.

text:
A federal appeals court appeared skeptical on Sunday of a lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump’s administration that seeks to force California officials to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the administration says were sent to noncitizens ahead of midterm elections.

During a rare weekend oral argument, two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals sharply questioned a Justice Department lawyer about the lawsuit, a high-profile effort by the Trump administration to boost the federal government’s role in elections ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

The Department ‌of Justice’s lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump’s administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.

At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible.

Trump’s Justice Department has warned ​election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. It has distributed to California officials a list of 20,000 people it says are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.

California has said the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and, in a court filing, stated that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on suspect data.

All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit Oct. 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.

The department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.

Bennett, a Trump-appointed judge, said during Sunday’s oral argument that the lawsuit could not be reconciled with a provision of the Constitution known as the Elections Clause, which gives states the authority to set election processes.

“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California Legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”

The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.

California is the most populous U.S. state and a Democratic stronghold, with 52 seats in the House of Representatives — more than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through so-called sanctuary state policies that ‌limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has also long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, said Sunday that he was confused by the question of why the appeals court should have jurisdiction to rule at this juncture, noting that the lower court judge assigned to the case had already set a hearing for Tuesday.

title: ICE said a man jumped on the hood of their vehicle. Video — and police — say otherwise
description:
A 37-year-old man was struck by a federal immigration vehicle Tuesday morning while documenting ICE activity, an incident captured on multiple videos and under investigation by Woodland, California, police.
Videos show different angles of the incident Video shared by the advocacy group NorCal Resist shows two unmarked SUVs passing each other.
An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes.
“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days.
“As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy.
text:
A 37-year-old man was struck by a federal immigration vehicle Tuesday morning while documenting ICE activity, an incident captured on multiple videos and under investigation by Woodland, California, police.

The Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle’s hood. But local police raised doubts about federal officials’ account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning’s incident involving the pedestrian

The man, identified as Antonio Moreida, sustained minor injuries. He was evaluated at the scene by medical personnel before being taken to the hospital.

Woodland police said the vehicle that struck him was a Chevrolet Tahoe operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who were conducting an operation in the area.

The ICE driver immediately notified Woodland police dispatch of the collision and cooperated with investigators, police said.

“I heard the engine because it was smashing down the street, and that’s how I turned my focus from that to the vehicle, and just like that, they closed in on me,” Moreida told sister station KCRA 3.

The Department of Homeland Security said “ICE did not hit a pedestrian” and accused Moreida of “flopping for the camera.”

The Woodland Police Department disputed DHS’s claims, saying they’re “inconsistent” with video evidence reviewed by its investigators.

Videos show different angles of the incident

Video shared by the advocacy group NorCal Resist shows two unmarked SUVs passing each other. The camera follows one SUV as it drives away, showing its brake lights before it swerves to the left. The footage captures the moment Moreida, who is in the roadway, falls to the ground and rolls onto his back as the SUV continues driving.

Another angle from a home surveillance camera shows Moreida walking alongside and touching one of the SUVs before it drives out of frame. He then continues walking in the middle of the street, holding a GoPro camera. Moments later, another SUV enters the frame, its engine revving before it swerves and strikes Moreida with its right front side. The vehicle then drives away.

Moreida and a witness speak out

Moreida said he was at the scene to document the activity of ICE agents when the collision occurred.

“Definitely seemed to swerve into me rather than try to avoid me based off of where I was in the street,” he said.

Steve Hanes, a Woodland resident who witnessed the incident, described what he saw.

“He went right up to the car and was taking pictures on his phone. I guess they didn’t really like that because they said to step away, so he stepped away, he went down there, and then I heard a car accident, like skid marks, and some car hit the guy who was taking pictures here,” Hanes said.

Moreida explained that his GoPro camera served to document ICE activity and to record what happened in case something went wrong.

“Getting hit by a moving vehicle isn’t something you just brush off, so definitely feel sore and got my knees scraped up, my hands scraped up, you know that hit I took it to the chest, so once I fell, I rolled, the wind was knocked out of me,” he said.

Moreida later spoke at a Woodland City Council meeting on Tuesday evening and drew community support.

Woodland police said Tuesday evening that investigators worked throughout the day to gather evidence, take statements and review relevant audio and video.

“As part of that work, investigators obtained and reviewed additional video footage showing multiple perspectives of the incident, including the interaction between the pedestrian and federal personnel in the minutes before the collision,” Woodland police said. “This footage is being reviewed alongside other evidence to help establish the full sequence of events, including the actions of both the pedestrian and the driver.”

Woodland police said they did not participate in the federal operation and will investigate the collision independently and submit a complete investigation to the district attorney’s office for review.

“I’ve seen the video myself, and I find it very troubling. I understand why people in our community are upset and worried,” Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement. “Our responsibility is to conduct a thorough and impartial investigation to establish the facts. We recognize the concerns surrounding federal law enforcement activity in Woodland, and the safety and well-being of our community members remain a priority.”

DHS says ‘ICE did not hit a pedestrian’

KCRA 3 reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for comment multiple times on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, DHS shared this statement: “This is false. ICE did NOT hit a pedestrian. An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes. The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation.”

Woodland police said Wednesday claims made in the DHS statement are “inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed” by the department’s investigators.

Police said investigators established the following based on video evidence:

The pedestrian was struck by a vehicle driven by an ICE agent

The pedestrian did not jump onto the hood of the vehicle

The pedestrian did not slide off the hood of the vehicle

The driver applied the brakes before the collision

The driver remained near the scene, contacted Woodland police and cooperated with officers during the initial investigation

Defense attorney says the federal government could take over the case

The Yolo County District Attorney’s Office said it could not comment at this time as the matter is under active investigation by Woodland police.

Sacramento defense attorney Mark Reichel said from watching the videos he thought this could be a case of assault with a deadly weapon, and federal agents could be charged by the state.

But even if the district attorney decided to file charges, the case may not go before a judge because the federal government could take over the prosecution, he said.

“If the DA in Yolo County files a criminal charge, and the U.S. attorney here in Sacramento can come in federally, take the case to federal court, and then prosecute it themselves. And if the Trump administration is saying do not prosecute, we know they’re not going to,” Reichel said.

Reichel also said identifying the agent who was driving could be difficult. He noted that if the federal government does not release the agent’s identity, there would be no one to prosecute.

Local, state, federal officials speak out

U.S. House Rep. Mike Thompson, who represents the Woodland area, issued the following statement.

“ICE cannot continue to terrorize our communities. I am in communication with local law enforcement, who have informed me that ICE was operating the vehicle in question and that an investigation is underway. No one is above the law. ICE’s actions have contributed to growing distrust and fear within our communities, making transparency and accountability all the more critical. Members of our community need to feel safe.”

Assemblywoman Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said on social media, “Our community deserves answers and accountability.”

Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard joined Thompson, Aguiar-Curry, Moreida and others at a news conference Wednesday to speak about the situation.

“It’s a very sad occasion that brings us together,” Stallard said. “I can only let you know I’m beyond anger. I’m at the point of outrage, to the point where I couldn’t even sleep last night thinking about this, realizing the people in our community are living in fear because of this effort by ICE to do whatever objective they’re trying to do, but doing it in the most hateful, mean, incomprehensible method.”

Angel Barajas, who represents District 5 for the Yolo County Board of Supervisors, said a request was made to ask the Woodland Police Department and the Yolo County District Attorney’s Office whether charges should be filed in connection with the incident.

ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February.

On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers.

“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. “As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely.”

description:

Advocates responded to the jail in the morning.

text:
Advocates with the Santa Clara County Rapid Response Network said ICE agents were present in the lobby of the Main Jail on Hedding Street in San Jose on Sunday.

Advocates responded to the jail in the morning. They said agents were just outside the building as well, apparently waiting for people to be released.

On Saturday, members of the same network were at the Elmwood Jail in Milpitas, watching ICE agents there for a third day in a row.

Activists want to make it very clear to the agents that their actions are being witnessed and documented.

Santa Clara County is a sanctuary county, but no sanctuary policy can prohibit agents from waiting in public areas of the jail.

The sheriff’s office says that it does not coordinate with ICE or notify the agency of release dates. They have been tracking ICE visits as well and say agents have been visiting the lobby for more than a year, and taken 60 people into custody who were set for release.

NBC Bay Area reached out to ICE for comment on Sunday's activity but has not heard back.

text:
From thousands of miles away, a Texas dad, hiding in a country he doesn't know, reminded his son to vacuum the carpet each week.

Moussa Diawara is from Mali, but spent nearly half his life living in the United States, where he married, had two U.S. citizen children, worked and paid taxes. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported him to Ghana over the summer. Diawara has no connection to Ghana, but a judge had issued an order that he couldn't be deported to Mali, because it was likely he'd be persecuted there. Diawara said that within days of his arrival in Ghana, local officials forced him onto a flight to Mali.

"I still say to myself, 'This isn't real,'" Diawara said.

Third-country deportations are a reality for many as President Trump's administration seeks to carry out the largest deportation in U.S. history. When the U.S. government decides an immigrant can't stay in the U.S., and can't be sent to their home country, it can send them to a third country. A 60 Minutes investigation found that some of the third countries accepting deportees from the U.S. are routinely sending them back to the very countries they fled — locations where U.S. immigration judges ruled they would likely be persecuted or tortured.

What happened to Moussa Diawara

Diawara, 57, came to the U.S. on a tourist visa when he was 32. He overstayed that visa, and later applied for refugee protection, arguing he would be persecuted if he were to return to Mali. Diawara had converted to Christianity, and Mali's a Muslim-majority nation with an Islamist insurgency. He has no criminal record.

In 2012, a U.S. immigration judge ruled that Diawara could not be deported to Mali, but the U.S. could find a safe alternative if it ever wanted to remove him from the country. As a result of the ruling, Diawara was able to get a U.S. work permit. He worked as an Uber driver and was finishing a night shift on July 11 of this year when he found ICE agents waiting for him at the suburban Houston home where he lived with his wife and children, who are U.S. citizens.

Diawara spent three weeks in ICE detention in Texas, unable to speak to his lawyer or a judge. He was loaded onto a plane and deported to Ghana, a country he never visited or had any ties to, on July 31. In Ghana, Diawara said he and others were detained in a hotel by armed guards and were not allowed to make phone calls.

"I cannot call my wife, I can't contact my lawyer. I can't talk to no one," Diawara said. "I tell them, 'This is kidnapping. You guys kidnapped us.'"

60 Minutes first got in touch with Diawara in August. At the time, he was homeless and hiding in Mali, fearing for his safety after Ghanaian officials dropped him there with no money or identification.

He was able to escape to another country with the help of some local truckers after several weeks in Mali. Diawara asked for the country to not be disclosed out of concern for his safety.

Diawara acknowledged that the U.S. had a right to deport him, but not to Mali. And he believes the U.S. knew Ghana would send him there. U.S. officials gave him a medical document on the flight to Ghana with the destination listed as "SHRC Mali" — SHRC stands for Special High Risk Charter, referring to the kind of flight Diawara was on.

"So they know 100% I'm going to Mali," Diawara said.

Both of his bag tags, issued by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), also list the destination as Mali.

"Well, he wasn't flown to Mali," said James Percival, DHS's top lawyer. "He was flown to Ghana, but I can't speak to why that piece of paper says that."

A DHS spokesperson later followed up with a statement, saying the bag tags were "produced by contractors" who "are not part of the process that determines...the destination." The medication form, the statement said, was a "clerical error." Ghana's government declined to comment.

DHS says Ghana had provided the U.S. with "diplomatic assurances" for Diawara's safety. The agency also questioned the credibility of Diawara's arguments for fearing persecution in Mali.

Democrats and immigration attorney critique third-country deportations

Past administrations rarely deported people in Diawara's situation. But as part of the Trump administration's mass deportation operation, ICE has deported 25,000 people to dozens of third countries that, in return, receive millions of dollars in aid or other benefits from the U.S. government.

A judge's ruling that someone can be deported, but not to their home country, is called "withholding of removal." Diawara had this protection, and so did dozens of others on his deportation flight, 60 Minutes found.

There were 63 people on Diawara's third-country deportation flight, which left Texas on July 30, and stopped in Sierra Leone and the Central African Republic before landing in Ghana. Seventeen of the 19 people 60 Minutes reached who were deported to Ghana said they were subsequently sent, against their will, to countries U.S. immigration judges had ruled they should not be returned to, including Niger, Mali, Nigeria, Gambia and Guinea.

Immigration attorney Meredyth Yoon said she believes there's no way U.S. officials don't know what Ghana is doing to the people the U.S. deports there. She said the U.S. government was warned about Ghana's conduct in a lawsuit last year. Despite this, the U.S. sent 10 more third-country deportation flights to Ghana. Yoon believes it's a violation of international law.

A 30-page report from Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democrats, commissioned by ranking member Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), slammed the administration's third-country deportation program, critiquing it as costly and saying it undermined U.S. interests.

"Through its third country deportation deals, the Trump administration is putting millions of taxpayer dollars into the hands of foreign governments, while turning a blind eye to the human costs and potentially undermining our diplomatic relationships," Shaheen said in a February press release.

Homeland Security lawyer says third-country deportations are widely misunderstood

Percival, DHS's top lawyer, said he's not aware of any cases of Ghana sending people on to other countries against their will. He argued that third-country deportations are widely misunderstood.

Asked whether he thinks people sent to third countries are then voluntarily going back to the places they fled, Percival said, "Either they would choose to go home, and they might not always be truthful about the fact that they consented, so that's one possibility. The other possibility is that the foreign government applied their own procedures and, consistent with international law, determined that it was acceptable to return them home."

Video footage released last year shows Ghanaian officials dragging Rabbiatu Kuyateh, a nurse who lived in the U.S. for 30 years, to a flight back to her native Sierra Leone. She, like Diawara, had a withholding of removal order from the U.S. stating she couldn't be deported to her home country because she would likely be persecuted there.

Ghana isn't the only country accused of sending deportees to countries that U.S. immigration judges ruled they should not be deported to. When deportees arrive in Sierra Leone, they often get a pamphlet that says, "Sierra Leone is serving as a temporary transit location while arrangements are made to return you to your country of origin."

Percival said there is a public safety threat associated with "this population of aliens" and added that "every administration before President Trump absolutely abdicated their responsibility to the American people by letting criminals back on the street and doing no diplomatic efforts to get these people out of our country."

He says third countries like Eswatini and South Sudan have agreed to accept deportees with criminal records for first-degree murder, sexual assault, kidnapping, and armed robbery when their home countries refused to take them back.

Percival said he did not know what percentage of people who had been detained and deported were violent offenders.

Of the 63 people on Diawara's flight, 19% of the passengers had been charged with or convicted of crimes, including theft, assault, drugs or weapons possession. A 60 Minutes review found the other deportees either had a traffic violation (19%), or no criminal record at all (62%).

"This administration is following the law that Congress has passed. There are a lot of people in this population that we talk about who committed very serious crimes," Percival said. "And people should be very happy with President Trump for getting these serious criminals out of the country."

Last month, a federal appeals court upheld a ruling in a class action lawsuit that found the Trump administration's third-country policy was unlawful because it denied deportees due process. But the Supreme Court has allowed these deportations to continue until it hears the case in December.

Diawara fighting to get back to his family in the U.S.

Moussa Diawara's attorney, Reuben S. Kerben, has asked a federal judge in Washington, D.C., to order that he be returned to the U.S.

Meanwhile in Texas, Diawara's wife Barbara, a registered nurse, is waiting for him, along with their two children. Their son Corey is 16, and their daughter Chloe is 12.

"It feels really empty without him," Corey said.

He worries about his mom now.

"I'm trying, you know, not to cry in front of them, to be strong for them," Barbara said, "because they need me."

text:
Democratic congressional nominee Rebecca Bennett wrapped up her six-county tour in politically competitive Mount Olive by pledging to block a proposed immigration detention center in neighboring Roxbury, calling for stronger gun safety laws, and sharply attacking President Donald Trump and Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-Westfield) over the war in Iran.

The final stop on Bennett’s Deckplate Leadership Tour brought her to a Morris County township that could help determine the outcome of her race against Kean. Trump carried Mount Olive by three percentage points in 2024, four years after Joe Biden won it by five points. Gov. Mikie Sherrill carried the township by five points in last year’s gubernatorial election.

One of the most immediate local issues was a Department of Homeland Security proposal to establish an immigration detention facility in Roxbury, which borders Mount Olive.

“We absolutely need to make sure that detention facility is not going into Roxbury,” Bennett said. “As your member of Congress, I will do everything in my power to keep that from happening.”

Bennett, a 15-year U.S. Navy veteran and mother of two, also sought to balance protecting Second Amendment rights with additional safeguards against gun violence.

“It is our constitutional right to keep and bear arms. I deployed with weapons of war,” Bennett said. “I’ve trained people how to use weapons of war, and also, I’m a mom. I worry every day about sending them off to school because I know that they may not come home.”

She argued that gun ownership rights and measures to prevent gun violence need not be mutually exclusive.

“We can make sure we have the ability to safely bear arms and also that we are putting in smart gun safety policies,” she said. “Like background checks, like red flag laws.”

Foreign policy also emerged as an issue when Bennett was asked about escalating tensions with Cuba and the Trump administration’s increasingly confrontational approach toward the communist island.

At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Trump suggested that American warships returning from the war in Iran could make a stop near Cuba, raising the possibility of U.S. military intervention.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said, describing a scenario in which an American warship would stop about 50 yards off the Cuban coast before Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be sent to negotiate an agreement, according to the Associated Press.

Rubio subsequently urged Cubans seeking political change to pursue what he described as a discreet partnership with the CIA.

Rather than focus specifically on Cuba, Bennett used the question to deliver a broader indictment of the administration’s foreign policy, particularly the war in Iran, which she said has claimed American lives and driven up gasoline prices.

“Donald Trump and Tom Kean Jr. dragged us into a needless war in Iran that has cost the lives of American service members and sent gas prices soaring here at home,” Bennett stated. “I spent fifteen years serving our country in uniform, so I know how important it is that we have serious leaders who don’t drag us into never-ending foreign conflicts. What we need to prioritize right now is ending the war in Iran and investing in our communities here at home.”

Kean spent Sunday crisscrossing the 7th district, including stops in Bridgewater and New Providence.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said, describing a scenario in which an American warship would stop about 50 yards off the Cuban coast before Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be sent to negotiate an agreement, according to the Associated Press.

Rubio subsequently urged Cubans seeking political change to pursue what he described as a discreet partnership with the CIA.

Rather than focus specifically on Cuba, Bennett used the question to deliver a broader indictment of the administration’s foreign policy, particularly the war in Iran, which she said has claimed American lives and driven up gasoline prices.

“Donald Trump and Tom Kean Jr. dragged us into a needless war in Iran that has cost the lives of American service members and sent gas prices soaring here at home,” Bennett stated. “I spent fifteen years serving our country in uniform, so I know how important it is that we have serious leaders who don’t drag us into never-ending foreign conflicts. What we need to prioritize right now is ending the war in Iran and investing in our communities here at home.”

Kean spent Sunday crisscrossing the 7th district, including stops in Bridgewater and New Providence.

text:
By Jan Wolfe

Oct 25 (Reuters) - A federal appeals court appeared skeptical on Sunday of a lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump's administration that seeks to force California officials to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the administration says were sent to noncitizens ahead ‌of midterm elections.

During a rare weekend oral argument, two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals sharply ‌questioned a Justice Department lawyer about the lawsuit, a high-profile effort by the Trump administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms.

The Department of ​Justice's lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump's administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.

At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible.

Trump's Justice Department has warned election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. It has distributed to ‌California officials a list of 20,000 people it says ⁠are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.

California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and, in a court filing, stated that the Justice Department's assertions relied on suspect data.

All available evidence indicates ⁠that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on October 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit ​asked ​a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on ​the administration's list from the rest of the ballots, and ‌not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.

The department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.

Bennett, a Trump-appointed judge, said during Sunday's oral argument that the lawsuit could not be reconciled with a provision of the US Constitution known as the Elections Clause, which gives states the authority to set election processes.

"It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause," Bennett told Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly. "How can we ‌do that?"

The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states ​for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the ​vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the ​moves as federal overreach.

California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold, with 52 seats in the House ‌of Representatives — more than any other state. Democrats are seeking to ​regain control of the House from Trump's ​fellow Republicans in the midterms.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through so-called sanctuary state policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has also long asserted that California's immigration ​policies have facilitated voter fraud.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an ‌appointee of former President Joe Biden, said on Sunday that he was confused by the question of why the appeals court ​should have jurisdiction to rule at this juncture, noting that the lower court judge assigned to the case had already set a ​hearing for Tuesday.

(Reporting by Jan Wolfe; Editing by Edmund Klamann and Noeleen Walder)

“It’s something very painful to see your parents in that position,” Villanueva said. “And knowing you can’t do anything, you feel helpless.”

The rally followed recent ICE activity across southeastern Massachusetts. Advocates said more than two dozen people were detained in New Bedford, Dartmouth and Fall River last month, though the exact number has varied among organizations reporting the arrests.

LUCE describes itself as a coalition of immigrant-led grassroots organizations that provides organizing, information-sharing and mutual-aid support throughout Massachusetts.

Andrea James, an independent candidate for Massachusetts governor, told the crowd she supports abolishing ICE.

“We don’t need ICE in Massachusetts,” James said. “We need the diversity, the workforce, the love of immigrant families.”
