text:
This article is a partnership between ProPublica and The New York Times Magazine.

This story is exempt from our Creative Commons license until Nov. 25.

The new patrol officer parked his black Dodge Charger outside a house off Main Street and approached on foot. A Mexican ballad was playing. Someone had called in a noise complaint, claiming it sounded as if people were fighting.

But as the officer, Jaron Alexander, got closer, he found nothing of the sort. A middle-aged woman greeted him as her daughter, Joanna Martinez, petite and visibly pregnant, looked on. “What kind of party are you all having?” she remembers him asking. Behind her were three generations of an extended family. They were celebrating a 3-month-old’s baptism over pozole verde, horchata and beers.

Alexander ran some IDs and found no issues. The music wasn’t even that loud, he thought. He told them to have a good night, and then he left.

That encounter, in early October last year, was the first of many that Alexander and Martinez would have in tiny Ingram, a 1.5-square-mile town of 1,900 people beside the Guadalupe River. But it was the only one before Ingram signed an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that would roil the town and tear Martinez’s family apart.

“Her and I, at the beginning, I felt like we were running into each other all the time,” Alexander told us, in one of eight conversations over four months that offer a rare window into the thoughts of one of the local police officers on the front lines of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In a town as small as Ingram, drivable in five minutes end to end, more run-ins were probably inevitable. Later that October, Alexander pulled over a work truck for rolling through a stop sign, and soon there Martinez was, demanding that he let her friends go rather than let immigration take them. He didn’t. He pulled over another driver in November who turned out to be her cousin, the father of the baby they celebrated at the baptism party. Alexander handed him over to immigration agents as well.

He pulled over Martinez herself a few weeks before she was due to give birth, she says, surprising her when he knew her name and the type of car she typically drove. He warned her that the car’s window tint was illegal and let her go. After that, he says, he caught a glimpse of her and her husband and their newborn daughter in the toy aisle at Walmart. Martinez told us she doesn’t think it was even her that day — her baby girl was then just days old, and she couldn’t imagine running errands with her so soon. But in Alexander’s memory, she was shopping for Christmas presents, just like him.

Alexander, who is in his mid-30s, with dirty blond hair already turning gray, says he didn’t come back to Ingram to help deport his neighbors. In his telling, he just ended up making it part of his job. The town was where he started his law-enforcement career years earlier, before he took a better-paying position with the county, as a sheriff’s deputy. But things recently started to fall apart, first in his marriage, next at the sheriff’s office: A 185-page internal investigation found that he had an affair before his divorce was final and used a county vehicle to carry it out, then lied about it all. He says the investigator called him an “embarrassment to the profession.” The sheriff’s office fired him. (Alexander said at the time, and again to us, that he did not have the affair.)

Ingram’s Police Department took him back just when its new chief — its eighth in five years — was under pressure from the City Council to do more: more traffic stops, more citations, more arrests, more numbers. Alexander says he told the chief that the sheriff’s office had a deal with ICE and that Ingram should look into it; maybe it could help the department grow. “Blame me,” he eventually told people. “It’s my fault in a way.”

Donald Trump had retaken the presidency with a promise to carry out “the largest deportation in the history of our country.” America was still figuring out what that meant. Finding and expelling up to 4% of the U.S. population — the 14 million residents who are estimated to be undocumented — wasn’t something a few thousand ICE agents could do on their own.

Underway in Chicago that fall, and soon in Minneapolis, was one version of how the administration could try to do it: masked agents from across the federal government surging into a liberal city to round up immigrants, beating back — even killing — the citizens who tried to stand in their path.

But a quieter kind of surge was spreading across the country at the same time. In September 2025, ICE announced new incentives for a partnership program known as 287(g). The program’s most aggressive form, the so-called task force model, which Ingram opted in to, enlists local police officers as deputy immigration agents, and the new incentives included a $100,000 vehicle stipend, a $7,500 equipment stipend for every participating officer, quarterly performance bonuses and funding to help cover officer salaries and overtime. “By joining forces with ICE,” the announcement read, “you’re not just gaining access to these unprecedented reimbursement opportunities — you’re becoming part of a national effort to ensure the safety of every American family.”

Alexander completed an online course with ICE a few weeks after the baptism party, qualifying him for time-and-a-half pay whenever he helped the agency pick up immigrants. Here in the Texas Hill Country, he soon became the local face of the national crackdown.

Ingram was just starting to recover from its worst natural disaster in a century, the flood that summer that killed at least 139 people up and down the Guadalupe River, including 25 girls at Camp Mystic. In the riverbed, towering bald cypress trees now stood at a lean, their branches swept back by a 30-foot surge of water and mud, their trunks still plastered with debris. As construction workers rebuilding the community traveled to their jobsites via Junction Highway, Ingram’s five-lane main thoroughfare, a black Charger began stopping them before they could get there.

Within three months of the baptism party, Alexander and Ingram’s other patrol officer had delivered at least 70 people to immigration agents, picking off what the police chief called a “dumbfounding” number of undocumented drivers. Within a year, they would hand over the equivalent of 10% of Ingram to ICE.

The weight of what Alexander was doing started to settle on him after Christmas. He says he was out patrolling as one of his new ICE handlers, a man in a ball cap and dark glasses, hovered nearby in an unmarked SUV. Around lunchtime, Alexander followed two Latino men in a 2008 GMC truck for several blocks before stopping them, they recall him saying, for failing to signal a turn.

A young man sat in the passenger seat. Alexander checked his papers along with the driver’s and determined that both were undocumented. The agent in the unmarked SUV rolled up behind them. Alexander realized who the man in the passenger seat was only after Martinez arrived in tears. It was her husband, Ulices Macias, the father of her newborn daughter.

“I don’t normally do this,” Martinez recalls Alexander telling her, “but I’m going to open up the car. I’m going to take the handcuffs off him.” He let the family have a moment together. In a video taken by Martinez’s younger sister, Alexander stood by, expressionless, as Martinez embraced Macias by the rear door of the Charger. He watched Macias cradle his 2-week-old baby girl, swaddled in a white blanket, and hug Martinez’s 4-year-old son, his stepson.

Then the ICE agent put the handcuffs back on Martinez’s husband, wrapped a chain around his waist and led him away. Alexander says Martinez threw herself to the ground and sobbed.

Images of the family he broke up shortly after Christmas would intrude on Alexander’s thoughts for months, he told us. But it didn’t keep him from doing his job. His next shift came a few days after he handed over Macias, and he was back in the Charger, back to stopping cars on Junction Highway.

“Mini Guanajuato”

Alexander says he didn’t always want to be a police officer. He describes himself as “kind of a chameleon.” He grew up in nearby Harper, tried a few different colleges without graduating and spent his 20s cycling through jobs in freight logistics, pest control and insurance.

Still seeking his calling, he arranged a ride-along with a police officer outside Austin. What sold him on policing was the suburban officer’s power to enforce the law as he saw fit. That day, they pulled over a woman who had a warrant out for her arrest. She was coming back from the store with children and groceries in the back seat.

“You can use your discretion,” Alexander recalls the officer telling him. Wouldn’t they be doing more harm if they took her? What would the kids do without their mother? And wouldn’t it all create more paperwork? The officer let her go. Alexander imagined himself making the same kinds of judgment calls. In 2021, he enrolled in the police academy.

Even before the floods, tensions were rising in Ingram. Hundreds of Mexican immigrants and their families had settled there in recent decades as an increasingly militarized border made it harder for seasonal ranch hands and other workers to cross back and forth. Latinos would come to make up 45% of its population, and some residents began affectionately calling Ingram “mini Guanajuato,” after the central Mexican state where many have roots. Yet when Alexander returned, Ingram’s City Council still consisted of six white men.

A council faction led by Claud Jordan, now the town’s mayor, and Rocky Hawkins, now the mayor pro tem, came to power in November 2020, in a revolt against a new sewer project. They abolished Ingram’s city administrator position and took direct control of the Police Department, cycling through chief after chief. Five former city employees say Hawkins regularly used racist slurs for Mexicans. Four say that he pressured the city to go after Latinos through code enforcement or targeted patrols, and two say that Jordan did, too. One of the employees recalls Hawkins complaining that Mexicans were “taking over Ingram.” (Hawkins and Jordan each declined to speak on the record or address detailed questions we sent them by email. In a brief text-message exchange, Hawkins said that none of it was right but declined to offer any specific concerns.)

These were the men the new chief, Dustin Breshears, had to answer to as ICE revived the task force program, which had been shut down for a dozen years until the day Trump returned to office in January 2025. ICE, under President Barack Obama, had phased out the program after some of the first sheriffs to participate in it, including Joe Arpaio of Maricopa County, Arizona, used it to disproportionately target Latinos in their communities. Investigations by the Department of Justice found that deputies in the task force program pulled over Latino drivers at up to nine times the rate of other drivers and that some retaliated violently against people who accused them of racial profiling. But now, under Trump, any law-enforcement agency, no matter how troubled or small, was encouraged to sign up.

Breshears began appearing at City Council meetings armed with statistics: number of arrests since the last meeting, number of traffic stops, number of cleared cases from the backlog of hundreds he inherited — and number of what he called “deportations.” (He later explained this was his imprecise shorthand for “immigration-related enforcement activities.”) At the council’s October 2025 meeting, held a couple of weeks after Alexander showed up at the Martinez family’s baptism party, Breshears reported a remarkable 162 traffic stops by Ingram’s two patrol officers — Alexander and Christian Perez, who was 25 — in just 20 days. (Perez declined to comment.) The officers made more stops in two months than the department had made in the entire previous year. The City Council gave Breshears an $18,000 raise.

Before Breshears arrived and Alexander returned in August 2025, the weekly blotter in The West Kerr Current, the local newspaper, documented the humdrum of community policing: loose dogs, neighborhood disputes, code violations. Then, suddenly, it was filled with drivers stopped for defective brake lights, damaged license plates, cracked windshields, illegal window tints or other unspecified “equipment violations.”

Breshears and Alexander strongly deny targeting Latinos. “It’s honestly not what’s happening,” Breshears says, noting that his half brother, wife and daughters have Mexican heritage. Ingram’s traffic stops were simply up across the board, he says, so more Latinos were getting stopped. He shared statistics showing that stops of Latinos were proportional to their share of the population.

Alexander, who on top of his roughly $70,000 base salary was now logging dozens of hours per month for ICE, told us the same. “I don’t care who’s in the car,” he says. “I really don’t.”

“El Charger negro”

As the ICE program took hold in Ingram, warnings about Alexander and his black Charger — the department has several — spread through the Hill Country and far beyond. Groups on Facebook and WhatsApp seemed to track his every move. The Charger was outside Rita’s taco shop. The Charger was near Dollar General. The Charger was parked by the church. A member of one particularly active Facebook group texted him screenshots, and he scrolled through blurry photos of himself looming behind work trucks or leaning over car windows.

Many Latino motorists trying to reach worksites up the Guadalupe began driving an extra 90 minutes each day to avoid the section of Junction Highway that Alexander patrolled. Ranch hands began sleeping at their employers’ properties in nearby Hunt, coming to town only when they knew — or hoped — that Ingram’s officers would be off duty. Residents were rattled the day a Customs and Border Protection helicopter hovered above town and the elementary school went into lockdown as the police hunted for a Mexican man who had run from one of Alexander’s traffic stops.

Workers driving between Kerrville and Hunt add an extra 90 minutes to their daily commute to avoid traffic stops in Ingram

One family notarized guardianship papers, in case the parents were detained and the children left behind. One woman swore Alexander showed up outside a memorial service and asked people for IDs. Another woman said he detained her and her husband when they returned home from church. Parties dwindled. Invite lists shrank. People began to move away, to Kerrville and San Antonio, and Alexander’s reputation reached as far as La Ceja, a village in the mountains of central Mexico, where an elderly resident said he and his neighbors were familiar with the Texas town’s police. “El Charger negro,” he said, with a knowing nod. He estimated that some 20 or 30 people in the village were recent deportees from Ingram.

Alexander’s fortunes seemed to rise as the Martinez family’s fell. With her husband gone, Joanna Martinez couldn’t afford payments on the trailer they shared. She and their infant and her 4-year-old son moved back into her childhood bedroom in her mother’s crowded home, where several relatives and their children also lived. She tried to stay connected with her husband, Macias, via WhatsApp calls while working as much as she could as a house cleaner to keep afloat. “I can’t lock myself up in my room and just cry,” Martinez says.

Winter for Martinez and her family brought a string of dark incidents. The January arrest of her cousin near the carwash as she drove to pick up her children from school. A canceled baby shower for her older sister, Jazmin, over a rumor that the Charger planned to show up. Another cousin, himself the father of a newborn, stopped and taken right in front of her mother’s house as Martinez watched.

A half dozen of the attendees from the October baptism party would soon be gone from Ingram, after being detained and deported or leaving to join relatives who had been. Some people had gotten wind that Alexander was making money off his enforcement. When a Spanish-language Facebook page shared a photo of him questioning the passenger of a beige Ford pickup, someone posted an animated image in the comments: a stack of green dollar bills growing taller and taller in an endless loop.

Alexander received his first ICE payments in early December. In January, as the country’s attention turned to the violent immigration crackdown in Minneapolis, he was often spending three or four hours a day and sometimes entire shifts working on behalf of the federal agency. By the time federal authorities announced a drawdown in Minneapolis on Feb. 12, Alexander had already made $3,264.46 from his task force hours, according to his pay stubs.

Ingram was by then one of more than 750 task force model partners around the country, up from not quite 500 when it signed up in October. At least 43 million U.S. residents, according to an analysis of ICE records by the legal data firm Titus Consulting, already lived in a county with an active task force agreement. Alexander was one of thousands of deputized officers in Texas alone.

Agencies with 287(g) task force model agreements

In interviews, Alexander described the immigration system he was enforcing as “skewed” and “weird,” but he saw himself as largely separate from these concerns. “If you’re taking federal money to do a job,” he says, “I think you should do the job.”

Still, he seemed to struggle with the contradictions of his role. He told us he sometimes shared his lunch with the people he detained and that he let them hold on to their phones to call loved ones from the rear seat of the Charger. He handcuffed them with their hands in the front rather than the back so they could use their hands.

Martinez told us about a moment when she watched him detain one of her cousins. He allowed the man’s wife and children to hug him goodbye and waited until his 7-year-old daughter wasn’t looking to handcuff him. To Martinez, it seemed as if Alexander was trying to prove to her that he wasn’t a bad person. “But I’m not going to fall for it,” she says.

There was a protest in Ingram the following day against Trump’s mass deportations. Martinez decided to go. As she stood among a few dozen protesters waving a handmade sign with the name “J. Alexander” circled and crossed out, she saw him drive by again and again.

A few weeks later, Katie Winer, the leader of the group that staged the protest, was following the Charger after Alexander detained another immigrant in a traffic stop. He approached her car and threatened to arrest her if she followed him in the future, on charges of interfering with public duties. But he also seemed to want to talk, and she recorded him as they discussed what was going on in Ingram. “I think you guys are making a bigger deal of it than they are,” he said of the people he handed over to ICE. The only outliers were “loudmouths” like Martinez and “her little crew.”

Winer interjected that Martinez’s husband was the family’s breadwinner, and it was Alexander’s actions that tore them apart.

“My actions did not,” Alexander said. “His actions did. I made a traffic stop. He was here illegally. That’s not my fault.”

Still, Alexander’s uncertainty seemed to be growing. In March, another of Martinez’s cousins confronted him outside the taco shop, pressing him about Macias as she filmed with her phone.

“If I’m being 100% honest,” he said, “I don’t enjoy when families are separated, like with the Joanna situation. That kind of fucked me up.”

“I voted to get the bad guys out”

A month later, as Ingram’s handoffs to ICE surpassed 100 people, another video of Alexander circulated among a small group of community members. It showed an evening traffic stop, at least the fifth stop Alexander made that day. He had followed a silver Ford F-250 from the highway until it pulled into the gravel driveway of a mobile home. There, the man in the passenger seat, a landscaper named Victor Ramirez Hernandez, tried to hurry inside. Alexander grabbed him before he could get there.

The truck’s driver pulled out his phone and began filming. “Why are you arresting him?” he asked.

“I’m not,” Alexander answered, struggling to place handcuffs on Ramirez as he squirmed. “I’m detaining him.” Then he wrapped his hands around the laborer’s chest, lifted him off the ground and slammed him down on the driveway. “I played nice with you, and now I’m done,” he said. He straddled Ramirez and cuffed his hands behind his back.

“He’s bleeding because you hit him,” the driver said evenly. They argued back and forth.

“You’re an idiot,” Alexander said, his face reddening. “Shut up. The more you talk it’s just making you look stupider.” (Alexander declined to comment on this incident. Breshears, who reviewed body-camera footage, says Alexander’s use of force was justified to control a potentially dangerous situation.)

Acrimony pulsed through Ingram that spring. In the Latino community, family members and neighbors accused one another of snitching, which Alexander says did happen. Young women accused one another of having affairs with him, which he denies, insisting that people just misinterpreted his attempts to be kind. “I’m friendly with the people that I meet,” he says, “especially when they’re friendly to me.”

One subject of these rumors was Martinez. She and her older sister scoffed at them. “He’s taken our whole family at this point,” Jazmin says. “And she’s going to sleep with him? It’s really annoying.” But some in the community, even cousins, stopped speaking with her. “It’s like ‘Hunger Games,’” Martinez says.

As Latinos fled and avoided Ingram, the daily takeout orders at one Mexican restaurant on the edge of town dropped to 50 from 200. A corner store catering to immigrants lost around half its revenue and most of its Latino regulars. Landlords in a mobile-home park just outside town struggled to find tenants.

But it wasn’t just Ingram’s Latino community that was reeling. For Ingram’s non-Hispanic business owners, including many Republicans in a county that voted 77% for Trump in the 2024 election, the immigration crackdown was becoming an outrage. It was taking people they worked with and knew well. It was interfering with flood reconstruction. It was hurting the local economy.

The owner of a heavily damaged strip mall on the western edge of town, Steve Edelstein, lamented the loss of two workers who were helping him rebuild. “Technically local law enforcement is doing their job,” he told a reporter for The West Kerr Current, emphasizing that he supported Trump. “But it isn’t helping the community.” A manager overseeing the rebuilding of Ingram’s Little League field, which was washed away in the flood, made an angry call to the city after two of his workers were picked up, Breshears says. A contractor helping rebuild Hunt’s destroyed post office had his crew reduced to eight workers from 30 — causing what should have been a four-day job to stretch to two weeks.

Among the people who called Jordan, the mayor, to complain was his onetime high school classmate Neal Secor, who describes himself as “one of the most conservative guys you’ll ever meet.” His family business, a cluster of rental cabins called Waltonia on the River, was nearly destroyed by the flood. He was struggling to rebuild. He says that in the spring, in two separate stops, the Ingram police detained four of his workers and handed them over to ICE — the second set as they returned from a job repairing the docks at a nearby youth camp, a favor Secor was trying to do for a neighbor.

Secor says Jordan’s defense was simple: You voted for this. They’d all voted for this.

“Let me tell you something,” Secor says he told Jordan. “I didn’t vote for this. I voted to get the bad guys out.” The two employees detained coming back from the youth camp were like family, his friends and co-workers for over a decade. “There’s still a lot of bad guys here,” he continued. “These guys aren’t them.”

Secor recalls Jordan saying that Ingram’s officers were just following the law. But, Secor wondered, why was it that he could drive 85 every day on the 75-mile-an-hour interstate and police officers just let him pass? He told Jordan he’d put 175,000 miles on his truck and never been pulled over. “It’s a matter of what laws you want to pick and choose,” he recalls telling the mayor. “We all break laws every day if you really want to get down to it.”

“God wanted me to meet you”

On an unpaved side street in the Ingram hills in April, Alexander again faced a decision over whether to separate a young family. This time he had more of a choice; ICE had yet to arrive. A woman named Norma Luján took his hand and said she was praying for him.

Luján, 61, runs a successful housecleaning company based in Ingram. She had heard of Alexander long before she confronted him. She had seen him in the Charger, too: on the side of Junction Highway as she made her way to jobs at vacation homes or youth camps up in Hunt. On the side of the highway on the way back. In her rearview mirror for four excruciating minutes one afternoon as her “girls,” as she called her crew, held their breath and sank into their seats, protected by the tint of her car’s windows and the fact that a license-plate reader would show it was registered to her, a Texas-born U.S. citizen.

In January, at the carwash, Alexander had helped a sheriff’s deputy take one of Luján’s best employees into custody. The woman, Cinthya Carranza, was a single mother and asylum seeker from Guanajuato — and Joanna Martinez’s cousin. Carranza was on her way to get her children from school after she and Luján spent the day cleaning houses. Later that day, Luján saw a Facebook post showing a familiar face in a mug shot: Carranza’s. Luján broke into tears. To her, the arrest was a signal event. The Charger had mostly stopped men up to that point. This was the moment she understood that no one was safe.

Luján started losing workers in droves after Carranza was taken — some to traffic stops, most for fear of having to drive through Ingram. Her crew of 30 people dropped to fewer than 10. She worried for her business, but she worried more, she said, for her workers, the lives they had made in Ingram and the relationships she had built with them. They invited her to parties and baptisms, surprised her with presents on her birthday. She often led them in prayer. “I love them,” she says. She promised she would try to protect them.

When Luján’s employee Maria called that April afternoon to say the officer in the Charger was outside her house, detaining her husband as he returned from work, Luján jumped into action. Maria (who asked to be identified by her middle name because she is undocumented) was eight months pregnant and already terrified that she would have to give birth alone. Alexander had taken her brother a week earlier. Now Maria was hiding behind the curtains of her home, sneaking peeks outside, hoping Alexander would let her husband go.

“Cálmate” — calm down — Luján told herself as she approached the Charger. “Cálmate.” She took a deep breath. She says Alexander was sitting in the driver’s seat with the door propped open, staring at a tablet computer.

“Look, his wife has had a complicated pregnancy,” she told him. (This was true.) “She’s in the hospital.” (For that lie, Luján says, she later prayed for forgiveness.)

Then Luján reached out and grabbed Alexander’s hand. “I pray for your being, for your soul,” she recalls telling him as she cried. “I want you to think about what you’re doing. Feel it. Feel it, please.” She squeezed his hand. “I need you to look inside your heart,” she continued, “and let him go.”

Alexander didn’t react at first, in Luján’s telling. “God wanted me to meet you,” she said. He met her gaze.

“I’m that guy that everyone talks about on Facebook,” she recalls him finally saying. “If you think I don’t lose any sleep, you’re wrong.”

Luján pushed through the lump in her throat to speak. “I’m going to pray for you every night,” she promised him. She says Alexander squeezed her hand back, then pulled away. He walked off to make a call. She couldn’t make out much of what he said. It was quiet, save for the sound of Luján’s sobs and the pebbles from the unpaved road crunching beneath the officer’s feet.

Then he returned to the Charger. “Get him out of the car,” Luján recalls him saying. “Hurry up.”

“God bless you,” Luján said. “God will repay you for this.”

Alexander says he doesn’t remember the details of his interaction with Luján, but he confirms that he let Maria’s husband go, calling it a matter of “human decency.” He knew how hard it was to raise children. “A woman needs rest,” he says. “She needs help.” Maria’s husband “needs to be there helping out.”

At first, nothing seemed to change. Over the next two months, as the Hill Country prepared to welcome summer tourists and campers back after the devastation of the floods, Alexander worked around 100 task force hours, earning close to $5,000 from ICE.

But the next time he ran into Joanna Martinez, he seemed to be having misgivings. It was early June, and he was eight months into the ICE program. He had pulled over another of her family friends on Junction Highway, a person she had known since childhood. Martinez got a phone call and rushed to the scene, as she had so many times before. “I don’t feel good about this,” she recalls him saying when she arrived. “I signed up to be a cop, not an ICE agent.” (Alexander says he remembers that they talked and that he could have said something like that.)

Later that month, he pulled over a young man from Honduras who was on his way to a soccer game with his cousin, a 12-year-old with developmental disabilities. The boy’s father says he and his wife hid across the street watching it all happen, too terrified to step out and claim their son. The parents sent a friend from church, but she was not a legal guardian. Alexander says he had no choice but to hand the boy over to ICE, adding though that if he was one of the parents, he would see it differently. “If I’m in that position, there’s no way I’m letting my kid go,” he told us. “I’m probably fighting someone.”

Within a couple of weeks, Alexander’s task force hours dropped by about 40%, according to his pay stubs. It remains unclear if he tried to step back from immigration work or whether the number of undocumented drivers in Ingram had simply dwindled because of all he had already done.

According to Chief Breshears, Ingram had logged 194 “immigration-related incidents” as of this August. Whether every handover led to a deportation, Breshears couldn’t say. Alexander says he doesn’t know how many of the 194 are people he stopped. But he says he has now let at least 10 people go — many, though not all of them, mothers of young children.

Alexander sees this, and his relationship to the Martinez family, as evidence of his humanity, despite what people say about him. “For context, I’ve deported like six of their family members, and they’re still friendly to me,” he says. “So I’m not the monster they make me out to be.”

On July 16, the skies over Ingram opened again, dropping nearly 19 inches of rain in a single day, and the Guadalupe again overtopped its banks, again destroying businesses and homes. In the predawn darkness in the early hours of the emergency, Alexander began racing toward Ingram in his black Charger to help. He had barely left his house when surging floodwaters consumed the vehicle, destroying the Charger’s engine block. A driver in a pickup truck took him back home, and that’s where he stayed until the storm receded.

“One free pass”

Alexander remains only one cog in a deportation machine for which the federal government has now earmarked $240 billion. Today more than 1,900 agencies in at least 30 states have signed up for ICE’s task force model, with more than 29,000 deputized officers. With their help, ICE recently hit a record of immigration arrests, totaling more than 50,000 in August.

On Sept. 11, Alexander met one of us at a taco spot on Junction Highway. Ingram had changed in the year since his return. Whole neighborhoods had emptied out, and residents noticed fewer drivers on the streets. In part because of the money from ICE, the Police Department had hired two additional officers. As a Mexican ballad played over the speakers, Alexander warned against making too much of the leniency he showed to families like Maria’s. “It’s like one free pass, I guess,” he said: If he encountered her husband again during a traffic stop, he would probably hand him over to ICE. He just thought letting the father-to-be go was the right call at the time. “I mean, don’t you?” he asked.

He said he hadn’t made all that much money working with ICE. But city records show that his earnings from the agency already totaled $18,793.25 in nine months, more than a quarter of his base salary. “I think it’s skewed a little bit,” he said, looking at the pay stubs we had gathered.

Alexander said it was hard for him to be out in public anymore. He can’t escape being recognized in Ingram and Kerrville. Sometimes he catches Latinos staring at him, then walking away, visibly uncomfortable. So he tries to do his shopping and errands in another town 30 minutes away.

He blamed the Facebook groups. They had created a climate of “unreasonable fear” in Ingram. “What do they think I’m going to do right now?” he asked, seated at his table in the taco shop. A steady stream of customers, many of them white, approached a counter staffed by two young Mexican sisters. He said their father used to hide out in Hunt to avoid being pulled over in town. Some of their co-workers had quit months before, too uncomfortable to serve Alexander when he came in for breakfast. But when the taco shop owner sees him, he said, she hugs him.

“I know the status of everybody in this room,” he said. He suggested everyone who worked there was undocumented. Whether they disappeared or were allowed to stay was up to him. And today, at least, he was just there for breakfast.

“They’re fine, right?”

Lucas Waldron, Audrey Dutton and Rob Davis contributed data analysis.

text:
GENESEE COUNTY, Mich. (WJRT) - A Genesee County employee was detained by ICE agents Thursday night while her asylum application is being processed, according to county officials.

Benazir Noorzad is a Human Resources Representative in the county's Benefits Division. She is lawfully in the country, per her department head Anita Galajda, Director of Genesee County Human Resources and Labor Relations.

"Benazir is one of the kindest human beings I've ever met in my life. She's very humble. She's very sweet. She is so caring. She's just a joy to be around. She's been in our office for about a year and quickly became fast friends with everybody in the office. We are all hoping that she comes back to us very soon,” Galajda said.

Noorzad came to the U.S. several years ago on a Fulbright Scholarship at Oklahoma State University. War broke out in Afghanistan during that time and Noorzad ultimately applied for asylum to avoid returning, according to county officials.

According to ICE's online detainee locator system, Noorzad was still in ICE custody at Calhoun County Correctional Center as of Sunday afternoon.

ABC12 reached out to ICE for a statement for more details on the detention, but has not received a response.

text:
REGISTER NOW

A longstanding critique of the U.S. immigration enforcement apparatus is that it is not designed to stop with immigrants, that it will, by design and by inertia, target citizens directly or indirectly, as well. During this administration, we routinely hear stories of lawful immigrants and citizens detained by ICE and Border Patrol — but building a defensible archive of these cases is difficult given the scattered and hard-to-validate circumstances of every detention. Yet documenting these cases is crucial both in terms of understanding the scale of the problem and for informing future efforts to hold immigration agencies and their officers accountable.

That’s why ProPublica’s rigorously validated database of over 500 U.S. citizens who were detained by immigration agents between January 2025 and September 2026 is so important. According to ProPublica, more than a hundred of them were held after agents questioned their citizenship, at least 70 were children or teenagers, and about 20 of those kids were handcuffed or zip-tied even though DHS says ICE does not zip-tie or restrain children. Readers of this newsletter may remember that in April 2025, a U.S. citizen was held in a Florida jail for no other reason than that ICE asked the county to hold him, and I wrote about this idea that citizenship alone will not save us. ProPublica’s database is that warning 506 times over and reinforces the concern that the administration is not drawing the line at U.S. citizens.

ProPublica’s use of what I refer to as constructed datasets, or datasets that are created from source material that was not originally intended as structured data, is a powerful tool for documenting state violence. OG groups like Forensic Architecture began by documenting state violence in Israel-Palestine, then expanded to Forensic Oceanography to document the strategic negligence surrounding maritime migration in the Mediterranean. Bellingcat expanded these methodologies and combined them with more traditional journalism, popularizing what we now call open source intelligence (OSINT), which has been mobilized in Russia’s war on Ukraine and in documenting police brutality in response to Black Lives Matter protests. Even the New York Times now has a Visual Investigations unit that uses similar methods.

Projects like these take an enormous amount of labor and attention to detail, along with a documented methodology that you might miss if you only read the alarming headline. I’ve looked through the ProPublica database and already spoken with the reporters behind the project to understand the mechanics. And that’s what we’ll get into on Tuesday, not just what they found but how they found it, what technologies make the research possible, problems they ran into along the way, and where they see the project evolving next. This is not the kind of in-depth conversation you’ll hear elsewhere, so please join us and consider powering this work with a paid subscription.

Joining me will be Nicole Foy, a reporter at ProPublica who has covered citizens detained by immigration agents since the start of this administration. Ruth Talbot is a news applications developer at ProPublica who maintains its Nursing Home Inspect database and builds interactive stories and databases. Cengiz Yar is a visuals editor at ProPublica and a longtime photographer whose work covers the Midwest, the Southwest and Texas. The project’s other credited reporters are Liliana Michelena, Bianca Fortis, Mariam Elba and Kahlie Wray.

Your browser does not support HTML5 video.

Trump’s Immigration Policy Is Driven Solely By Hate

A pro-ICE conservative blogger has been detained by the agency he ardently supports.

MAGA personality Samuel Sey, who describes himself as a “blogger, a teacher, a pro-life advocate, and a public speaker,” was taken by ICE agents and is currently being held in an Ohio jail. The jail’s website states he was booked on Oct. 21 and is still being held in custody for ICE.

A donation page made on behalf of Sey confirmed he was detained by ICE while traveling.

“He is a husband, father, school teacher, married to Annie with three beautiful children, and has been living here as a legal resident of the United States from Canada,” the page stated.

The page also stated that his wife is working to get him released on bail “so he can fix any clerical issues that need to be addressed for his legal residence.”

Sey previously announced on social media in 2022 that he had obtained a marriage license to wed his wife, Annie.

The Daily Beast has reached out to DHS for comment.

Sey, 39, is the author of the blog SlowToWrite. He has been vocal about his support for ICE agents, writing in one social media post, “If you love America, you should support ICE.”

He’s even gone as far as to say that God would actually be against people who protest ICE agents.

“God isn’t just against anti-ICE protestors who persecute Christians while they are worshipping at church. He is also against the idealogy [sic] of anti-ICE protestors,” he wrote in one post. “Christians who condemn the “protestors” but refuse to condemn their ideology should know that.”

In another post, he proclaimed that “ anti-ICE protestors are influenced by Satan.”

After Minnesota mother Renee Good was shot and killed in her car in January, he echoed popular talking points on the right claiming that she was attempting to ram agents with her car, despite video evidence suggesting otherwise.

“The woman would still be alive if she didn’t try to run the ICE agent over. You can be saddened by her death and admit that it was self-defense,” he wrote.

While he has been largely pro-ICE, Sey is oftentimes critical of President Donald Trump, especially on the president’s ever-changing views on abortion.

One post from 2024 reads: “It’s a sobering sign of God’s judgment on America that although thousands of babies could die because of Trump—he is a significantly better option than Kamala Harris.”

title: Inside a New Orleans ICE operation as immigration arrests surge: 'One at a time adds up'
authors: James Finn, Staff, Sophia Germer, The Times-Picayune
description: A recent New Orleans immigration enforcement operation that relied on days of surveillance and culminated in a confrontation over in moments was a snapshot of how the Trump administration’s strategy to ramp up immigration arrests across the country has changed. It’s quieter, more targeted — and resulting in even more apprehensions.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrest Jose Portillo-Gifaro on Frenchmen Street in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

From SUVs with blacked-out windows, the federal agents watched a gaggle of men outside the Mardi Gras Truck Stop, waiting to make their move.

As the man they were tracking walked toward his silver Honda, the parking lot exploded into sudden action. Tires screeched. Agents in tactical gear descended.

“Can you take him?” an agent asked on his static-riddled radio.

Still on foot, the man took off — darting through honking traffic on Elysian Fields Avenue, hopping a fence and disappearing into a grassy maze of 7th Ward backyards.

The chase ended minutes later with the sweat-streaked man, a 57-year-old undocumented immigrant from Honduras, handcuffed and shackled in an abandoned lot, surrounded by a half-dozen U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

Later, at an ICE processing center in St. Charles Parish, he said he’d found the agents’ tactics puzzling. “They were only focused on me,” the man, Jose Portillo-Gifaro, said in Spanish in an interview with The Times-Picayune | The Advocate. “I'm not sure why.”

Jose Portillo-Gifaro, of Honduras, runs as he realizes he is watched by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers outside the Mardi Gras Truck Stop in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

The operation, which relied on days of surveillance and culminated in a confrontation over in moments, was a snapshot of how the Trump administration’s strategy to ramp up immigration arrests across the country has changed. It’s quieter, more targeted — and resulting in even more apprehensions.

Nearly a year ago, U.S. Border Patrol-led enforcement sweeps entered cities nationwide in highly visible shows of force that drew furious protests. Agents rounded people up en masse in home improvement store parking lots, construction sites and other public spaces. U.S. citizens and green card holders, including in New Orleans , were detained.

But those tactics wound down after federal agents killed two protesters in Minnesota, and Trump’s new Homeland Security Secretary, Markwayne Mullin, promised a less-visible strategy with bigger results.

Now, without as much public attention, agents are arresting more people one by one in traffic stops — occasionally with deadly outcomes — and often before dawn. Hundreds have also been arrested at airports . Immigration judges have issued scores of deportation orders after calling last-minute hearings.

"There is more time and more resources, and a lot of officers involved in (these operations)," said Brian Acuna , a senior official in ICE's New Orleans Field Office who leads arrest operations across five southern states . "One at a time adds up."

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers handcuff Jose Portillo-Gifaro on Frenchmen Street in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

Stoked by a hiring surge, an influx of federal tax dollars and hundreds of local officers newly deputized as immigration agents, ICE has channeled the tactics into record-breaking arrest figures . Nationwide, federal agents netted a record 49,000 immigrant arrests in July alone , the last month for which complete data was available, according to ICE records obtained by the Deportation Data Project and reviewed by The Times-Picayune | The Advocate. That’s by far the highest figure of Trump’s second term. Monthly arrests under former President Joe Biden typically numbered around 10,000 , according to the Deportation Data Project.

In Louisiana, agents made a record-high 690 arrests in June and another 800 the next month. (Last December, when Border Patrol agents flooded the state, there were 643 statewide arrests.)

Increasingly, immigration attorneys say, ICE is using a growing web of license plate readers and cameras installed by local police to track targets.

“Arrest numbers are going up because cities and states are getting bullied into cooperating with ICE," said Jeremy Jong, a New Orleans-based immigration lawyer. "If ICE has access to license plate readers, they can figure out where undocumented people are and go and arrest them easier. If they have access to cameras, they can go find those people."

The recent operation was one in a flurry across the state in recent weeks. Agents detained several dozen people last week in a Border Patrol-led raid outside Baton Rouge, several officials familiar with the operation said.

Portillo-Gifaro's arrest stood apart due to his criminal record, which includes arrests for assault in California and Louisiana, though records do not show he was ever convicted. A few months ago, sheriff’s deputies in New Orleans arrested and jailed him on a count of aggravated battery with a weapon. Records from the incident are sparse, but a court filing shows prosecutors declined to charge him after they could not find the victim. Portillo-Gifaro was released in July.

Records suggest a majority of those arrested by ICE during the summer and fall surge had no criminal backgrounds.

After the agents cornered him on Frenchmen Street, Portillo-Gifaro's arrest briefly turned public as unmarked ICE vehicles screeched down the residential block and agents swarmed the backyard through which he had tried to escape.

Neighbors watched from porches as agents bundled him into an SUV.

“Let’s move,” a supervisor said.

“We’ve been out here too long.”

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrest Jose Portillo-Gifaro on Frenchmen Street in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

The operation began at 5 a.m. in the parking lot of a downtown New Orleans high-rise where the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has offices. Agents had spent days surveilling Portillo-Gifaro and knew his movements. Now they sipped coffee from portable, metal mugs as a team leader explained the plan.

Two cars loaded with agents would set up a block from Portillo-Gifaro’s workplace in an industrial patch of the St. Claude neighborhood, while another watched his Mid-City house. Agents posted at the house planned to follow from a distance as he left for work sometime between 5:50 and 6:15 a.m. They would move to arrest Portillo-Gifaro when he stepped out of his car at work.

"He's quick," the team leader said. "He'll step out and run off fast."

It was still dark when the agents fanned out across the city.

Acuna, who joined the agents staking out Portillo-Gifaro’s workplace, had reason to spotlight this operation.

Brian Acuna, Acting Field Office Director of ICE/ERO in New Orleans, holds up information on Jose Portillo-Gifaro, of Honduras, as he waits for Portillo-Gifaro to arrive to work, in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

ICE has long been critical of the Orleans Parish Sheriff’s Office, which runs the jail, for refusing to honor immigration detainers — requests from federal law enforcement for local agencies to hold people wanted for immigration violations until federal agents can detain them. Acuna said the Sheriff's Office had declined to honor a detainer ICE issued in their bid to arrest Portillo-Gifaro.

Asked about Portillo-Gifaro's case, the Sheriff's Office referred to court documents from its litigation with Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill's office. Murrill has sued the Sheriff's Office over its detainer practice, which stems from a years-old federal consent decree, saying it’s violating a ban on "sanctuary cities" adopted by the state Legislature two years ago. The litigation hinges on whether the consent decree demands override the state law.

As the sun inched upward, a few residents peered into the bulky SUVs’ windows as they walked their dogs. A cat slunk under the fence around a nearby linens business as white trucks rolled out of the parking lot to start the day's deliveries.

The clock kept ticking: 7 a.m. came and went, then 8. Still no sign of Portillo-Gifaro.

Brian Acuna, Acting Field Office Director of ICE/ERO in New Orleans, drives down Elysian Fields Ave. as law enforcement get ready to arrest Jose Portillo-Gifaro, of Honduras, in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

Agents discussed their backup plan over portable radios. If he didn't leave the house, they would knock on his front door and try arresting him on his stoop. If that failed, they would ask a federal judge for a warrant to arrest him for illegally reentering the U.S., a felony charge . Such a warrant would allow them to enter the house to arrest him.

The sun was high in the sky by the time Portillo-Gifaro emerged. He lit a cigarette on the porch. At 9:03 a.m., he placed a cooler in his Civic and started driving. Agents tailing him from the house watched him stop into a sandwich shop on Bienville Street. He hopped back into his car and headed east on I-10.

"He's still headed this way," Acuna, parked at the worksite, said into his radio.

A few unexpected turns later, Portillo-Gifaro pulled into the Mardi Gras Truck Stop, a popular hangout for day laborers. He parked against a wrought-iron fence separating the truck stop from a Lowe’s parking lot that had been a locus of arrests when Border Patrol agents swept the city last year.

Portillo-Gifaro walked toward the truck stop store, a battered blue-and-green building that sells fried chicken, drinks and snacks. ICE agents surveilling him had watched him visit here in days prior. Now, they wondered whether he'd made a pit stop on the way to a later-than-usual shift.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers wear cameras in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

"He may either be waiting for somebody, or looking for work here," an agent radioed.

By 9:36 a.m., Portillo-Gifaro hadn't left the truck stop, and the agents staking out the St. Claude workplace began driving that way. Their plan had been upended. More agents were called to the truck stop to prepare to confront the "large number of individuals" in the lot.

"This whole place is hot," one agent said over the radio.

The agents' cars spread out to avoid detection as they arrived in the truck stop's vicinity. Some parked behind an adjoining casino while others took positions in the Lowe's lot. A trucker came out of the casino, hands on hips, peering into one of the cars. Glimpsing Acuna's tactical gear, he saluted and walked back inside.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrest Jose Portillo-Gifaro on Frenchmen Street in New Orleans, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

Later, Portillo-Gifaro said the men outside the truck stop realized what was afoot. They were no strangers to dark-windowed vehicles lurking near day-laborer gathering spots. Another 15 minutes passed. Then one by one, the men began walking to their cars.

The agents sprang out of their SUVs. Portillo-Gifaro turned a shoulder and started running. He sprinted west through moving cars on a stretch of Elysian Fields that approaches a highway on-ramp. Sirens blared as the ICE fleet surged perpendicular to traffic. Portillo-Gifaro hoisted himself over a fence bearing a campaign sign for a local judge and ran into an overgrown lot. One agent followed him over the chain link.

Federal agents engulfed the block. Several chased on foot while others pulled the cars around.

In the grassy lot, the agents and Portillo-Gifaro heaved for air as they cuffed him and led him to a waiting SUV. One agent fist-bumped a man on a porch and thanked him for his patience with the swarm of feds who had flooded his yard.

Portillo-Gifaro had spent the better part of three decades in the United States, punctuated by an earlier deportation. An hour after his arrest at the ICE processing center in St. Rose, he reflected in a white-walled room on how it had come to an end.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building photographed in St. Rose, La., Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

Portillo-Gifaro first entered the U.S. illegally at age 17 after his mother died in Honduras, he recalled. He lived in San Antonio until 1995, when he was deported a first time. After the COVID pandemic, he returned to the U.S. looking for work to support his four children and wife, who were trying to build a house in the Honduran city of Villanueva. He found jobs blasting and painting boats.

The work paid better than anything at home, he said. Still, the past few years were turbulent. He was arrested for assault. Immigration agents seemed to be everywhere.

"You have to hide from ICE anytime you leave your house," Portillo-Gifaro said.

That was a contrast to when he first entered the U.S., when "you could just walk across the border, no one bothering you," he said.

Jose Portillo-Gifaro, of Honduras, is brought to an officer for intake at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in St. Rose, La., Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

That morning, Portillo-Gifaro said he had been waiting for painting work at the truck stop when the agents arrived. He said he had planned to return to Honduras in January, when he expected to have saved enough money to finish the family house.

He added that he bore the ICE agents no ill will. "They're doing their job," he said.

ICE records showed Portillo-Gifaro was held over the weekend in the Adams County Correctional Center in Natchez, Mississippi, an ICE-contracted facility . By Thursday, he no longer appeared in the agency's detention database, suggesting he had been deported.

Portillo-Gifaro’s battered silver Civic remained in the Mardi Gras Truck Stop parking lot this week. Someone appeared to be sleeping in it. A shattered window had been covered with cardboard, and the Louisiana license plate was gone.

The car driven by Jose Portillo-Gifaro, of Honduras, sits in the parking with someone sleeping inside after Portillo-Gifaro was taken by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, at the Mardi Gras Truck Stop next to Lowe's in New Orleans, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

Jose Portillo-Gifaro, of Honduras, agrees to a photo after an interview with a reporter at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in St. Rose, La., Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. STAFF PHOTO BY SOPHIA GERMER

Staff writer Justin O'Connor contributed to this report.

James Finn covers federal law enforcement and courts for The Times-Picayune | The Advocate. Email him at jfinn@theadvocate.com or contact him on Signal at jamesfinn.82.

text:
Residents of Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood and community advocates are demanding the immediate release of Roberto Lamour, a Haitian father who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from his home earlier this month and transferred to Mississippi, more than 1,000 miles away from his wife and young daughter.

Lamour was taken from his apartment at 75 Lenox Road on the morning of Oct. 3, according to his family and neighbors. The circumstances of his arrest have drawn outrage from residents, who allege that the federal agents identified themselves as New York City police officers to gain access to the building and Lamour’s apartment.

On Oct. 22, community members and elected officials gathered in Flatbush for a news conference organized by local advocates to demand Lamour’s release and his return to his wife, Darchnee, and their daughter, who is not yet 3 years old.

Rita Joseph, the New York City Council member representing the neighborhood, District 40, and chair of the Council Committee on Higher Education, joined Hands Off NYC and other community partners at the news conference. Joseph said her office was in contact with Lamour’s family and would continue advocating for his release.

“Roberto is our neighbor. He is a husband and a father whose young daughter deserves to have her father home,” Joseph said in a statement posted to Instagram.

Residents say agents posed as NYPD officers

Residents interviewed by amNewYork said several federal agents entered the apartment building by identifying themselves as NYPD officers. They said the agents repeated that claim at Lamour’s apartment door and demanded entry.

One resident, who identified herself as Angelina, told amNewYork that the occupants initially tried to cooperate with the people they believed were police officers. Once the door opened, she said, the agents entered the apartment, requested Lamour’s identification and took him into custody.

Lamour’s wife initially believed her husband had been arrested by the NYPD, according to the report. She went to a local police precinct seeking his release, only to learn that he was not there.

The NYPD subsequently told amNewYork that it had no knowledge of or involvement in the incident.

Lamour was initially taken to Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, before being transferred to a detention center in Mississippi, according to amNewYork. The transfer has left him far from his family, his neighborhood and his lawyer.

Friends have said Lamour has no criminal record.

Family separation fuels community outrage

For Lamour’s family, the detention has meant more than the loss of his presence at home. His young daughter has struggled to understand why her father is gone.

In a statement reported by amNewYork, Darchnee Lamour described how their daughter reacts whenever someone rings the doorbell.

“She cries for him repeatedly, and whenever the doorbell rings, she runs to the door, believing that her father may have returned home,” she said.

“Seeing our young daughter search for her father and cry for him is heartbreaking,” Darchnee Lamour added. “At her young age, she cannot understand why he is no longer at home with us.”

The family’s separation has become a rallying point for neighbors and immigrant rights advocates, who say Lamour’s detention reflects the fear that immigration enforcement operations have created in immigrant communities.

The 75 Lenox Road Tenant Association joined the effort to bring Lamour home, alongside Hands Off NYC, the New York Immigration Coalition and Haitian Women for Haitian Refugees, among other community partners.

At the Oct. 22 gathering, residents and elected officials called for Lamour’s immediate release and criticized the circumstances of his arrest. Public Advocate Jumaane Williams also attended the rally, according to amNewYork.

For neighbors, the allegation that federal agents misrepresented themselves to enter the building has raised particular concern about the safety and security of residents in their own homes.

Joseph pledges continued advocacy

Joseph said her office was working with Lamour’s family and would continue coordinating with local, state and federal officials to press for his release.

“As a Haitian American and the Council Member representing this community, I stand firmly with Darchnee, the 75 Lenox Road Tenant Association, and all our neighbors who refuse to let Roberto be forgotten or isolated from the people who love him,” Joseph said.

She also condemned the separation of families through immigration enforcement, arguing that the detention has brought fear and uncertainty to the household.

“No family should have to live with the fear and uncertainty of a loved one being taken away from them,” Joseph said.

The council member pledged to use available resources to advocate for Lamour and called for immigration enforcement agents to stay out of New Yorkers’ homes and neighborhoods.

“We demand the immediate release of Roberto Lamour and his return home to his family in New York,” Joseph said.

As the campaign for Lamour’s release continues, his family and neighbors are calling on federal authorities to return him to Brooklyn, where his wife and young daughter are waiting for him.

text:
The Trump administration scored a major full-panel victory at the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals Friday, which ruled that detained illegal immigrants who were never formally admitted into the U. S. are not constitutionally entitled to bond hearings while awaiting deportation.

The ruling comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha this term, a closely related fight over whether the federal mandatory-detention statute applies at all to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country — setting up the possibility that the justices could either undercut Friday's ruling or strengthen the government's hand.

The Fifth Circuit answered the constitutional question in Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez v. Sylvester M. Ortega, finding that three immigrant men detained under the mandatory-detention statute are not entitled to bond hearings under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The court held that their years or even decades of residence in the United States, along with ties to the country and their communities, do not create a constitutional right to a bond hearing.

"The Constitution does not entitle them to a bond hearing," the court wrote.

Federal Appeals Court Compares Trump Migrant Detention Policy To Japanese American Internment

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court will consider Rhoney, a case out of the Second Circuit, to determine whether the mandatory-detention law applies to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country in the first place.

Read On The Fox News App

At the center of the issue is a 9-2 circuit split over which federal detention law applies to immigrants who entered the country illegally, were never formally admitted and were later arrested by immigration authorities after living in the U.S. for years — sometimes decades after crossing the border.

The Fifth and Eighth Circuits have held that those immigrants remain "applicants for admission" under Section 1225 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, subjecting them to mandatory detention without an ordinary bond hearing while their removal proceedings play out. Nine other federal appeals courts have ruled that Section 1226 applies instead, which provides a path for them to seek release on bond.

The Supreme Court will essentially decide whether immigrants who entered illegally and have lived in the U.S. for years can be subjected to the same mandatory-detention provision that applies to certain immigrants seeking admission into the country.

If the Supreme Court sides with the Second Circuit, Barbosa da Cunha — a Brazilian national who entered the country illegally roughly two decades ago and was detained in 2025 — would have a path to seek release on bond. Such a ruling would likely apply to the three longtime immigrants at the center of Rodriguez as well, substantially undercutting the significance of Friday's ruling by eliminating the need to answer the constitutional question of whether due process requires a bond hearing.

Supreme Court Takes Up Fight Over Trump's Third-country Illegal Alien Deportation Policy

Judge Leslie Southwick pointed directly to the looming Supreme Court fight in her dissent.

Should the Supreme Court eventually determine that this court was wrong as to the statute, then the constitutional issue we address here will have far less significance. It certainly has significance at the moment," Southwick wrote.

But conservative legal experts say Rodriguez could also strengthen the administration's hand in Rhoney by undercutting one argument against the government's interpretation of Section 1225: that applying the mandatory-detention provision to longtime residents would raise serious constitutional concerns.

Michael Morley, a constitutional law professor at Florida State University, said Friday's ruling could influence how the justices approach that question because courts often consider whether a particular reading of federal law would create constitutional problems.

Federal Appeals Court Deals Blow To Trump Deportation Agenda

"The Fifth Circuit's en banc ruling in Rodriguez today takes the next step by holding that such detention would not violate the U.S. Constitution's Due Process Clause," Morley said. "This holding may impact the Supreme Court's reasoning, because an important consideration in disputes over federal laws is whether a particular interpretation would be unconstitutional."

"If the Court agrees with the Fifth Circuit's analysis that the Due Process Clause allows such detention, it may be more likely to conclude that federal law permits it, as well, Morley continued.

Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, argued that the decision could bolster the administration as the justices prepare to resolve the circuit split.

"I actually think this ruling will help the government in the Rhoney case," von Spakovsky said, pointing to the Fifth Circuit's position that the applicable immigration statute does not require bond hearings for immigrants who were never admitted to the United States.

"There was already a split in the circuit courts on this issue but the Fifth Circuit has consistently held that the applicable immigration statute does not require bond hearings for aliens who were never admitted to the United States," he said. "I will be surprised if a majority of the Supreme Court disagrees when they ultimately issue a decision in the Rhoney case."

The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled oral arguments in Rhoney, which it agreed to hear earlier this month.

text:
A federal appeals court has scheduled a rare hearing for Sunday in the Justice Department's voting lawsuit against California.

The arguments, set for 1 p.m. PDT on Sunday, follow a surprise appeal by the Trump administration, which claims a district judge did not act quickly enough to address the administration's allegations of roughly 20,000 potential noncitizen voters on the state's voter rolls.

A three-judge panel that includes two appointees of President Donald Trump and one appointee of former President Joe Biden will hear arguments on DOJ's efforts to segregate ballots from the alleged noncitizens.

California officials have countered that the list is unverified and includes the names of lawful voters, despite recent charges announced by DOJ of roughly 28 individuals from the list accused of voting and immigration-related crimes.

Earlier the DOJ sent letters last week to every county in California asking local elections officials to help identify potential voters who may be in the U.S. illegally, according to a letter described to ABC News.

"Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not," according to a letter sent by Justice Department officials to every county in California and described to ABC News. "The Department strongly urges you and your agency to work with the Department of Justice to ensure the integrity of California’s federal elections before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure."

Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next month's midterm election.

In court papers filed earlier this week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.

Of those 200 individuals, officials said, nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history," according to a filing.

text:
Federal immigration agents arrived at the Santa Cruz Main Jail Saturday morning in an attempt to take a person into custody but left without detaining anyone, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office said.

During the incident, community members, including volunteers from Your Allied Rapid Response (YARR), were present in the jail parking lot and documented the activity.

“I’m proud of our Sheriff’s Office for its professionalism and commitment to public safety, California law, and community trust,” said Tony Nuñez, who was elected in June to the 4th District seat on the Santa Cruz County Board of Supervisors. “The department has reaffirmed that it does not participate in civil immigration enforcement or coordinate ICE’s operations.”

Nuñez also praised YARR volunteers.

“They mobilized quickly, organized effectively, and maintained a calm, measured presence during a tense situation. Their preparation and dedication to looking out for our neighbors deserve our thanks.”

YARR posted on social media that the organization had received reports of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at the jail and sent trained volunteers to observe. Volunteers reported seeing several agents and two vehicles.

“Earlier in the day ICE agents left the area initially, then returned,” YARR posted on Facebook.

As of 3:21 p.m. Saturday, YARR reported that the agents were no longer present.

“The Sheriff’s Office recognizes that incidents involving federal immigration enforcement can create concern and uncertainty for individuals, families, and members of the broader community,” the agency said in a statement.

The Sheriff’s Office said it does not notify ICE of scheduled release dates, participate in civil immigration enforcement or provide criminal history information to ICE for civil immigration enforcement purposes.

The agency does, however, comply with valid judicial warrants and court orders as required by law.

It was not clear Sunday whom the agents were seeking, why that person was in custody or whether the person was scheduled for release.

It was also unclear why the agents left the jail without anyone in custody.

Sheriff’s Office spokeswoman Ashley Keehn did not respond to a request for comment.

Federal agencies determine their own enforcement activities and operational schedules, the Sheriff’s Office said.

People seeking information about their rights during interactions with immigration authorities can visit susderechos.info.
